In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah Yusuf, peace be upon him. It is entirely Meccan. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: except for four verses of it. It is narrated that the Jews asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the story of Yusuf, and so the surah was revealed, and it will come. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas said: The Qur'an was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he recited it to them for a while. They said: "If only you would relate to us." So it was revealed: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾ [Yusuf: 3]. He recited it to them for a while, and they said: "If only you would tell us a narrative." So He revealed: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of discourse﴾ [al-Zumar: 23] [See vol. 15, p. 248.]. The scholars said: Allah mentioned the stories of the prophets in the Qur'an and repeated them with one meaning in various forms, with differing wordings at the levels of eloquence. He mentioned the story of Yusuf and did not repeat it, so no opponent has been able to produce a counterpart to what was repeated, nor to what was not repeated. The inimitability (i'jaz) is for whoever reflects.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Alif. Lam. Ra. These are the verses of the Clear Book. (1)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra﴾ [See vol. 1, p. 154 onward.] Its discussion has already passed. The estimate here is: "These are the verses of the Book," as a subject and predicate. It was said: "Alif-Lam-Ra" is the name of the surah, meaning this surah named "Alif-Lam-Ra." (These are the verses of the Clear Book) meaning by "the Clear Book" the Clear Qur'an, i.e., one that makes clear its lawful and unlawful, its limits and rulings, its guidance and its blessing. It was also said: meaning these are those verses which you were promised in the Torah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 2:

The Most High's saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾. It is permissible that the meaning is: "Indeed, We have sent down the Qur'an in Arabic." "Qur'anan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning "gathered together" (majmū'an). "'Arabiyyan" is an adjective (na't) for "Qur'anan." It is also permissible that it is a preparatory qualifier (tawṭi'a) for the state, as you say: "I passed by Zayd, a righteous man," and "'Arabiyyan" is then a circumstantial state, meaning: it is recited in your language, O assembly of the Arabs. I'rab (i'rāb) means "to make clear," and from it comes the saying: "The previously married woman expresses herself clearly (tu'ribu 'an nafsihā)."

﴿So that you may understand﴾: that is, so that you may know its meanings and comprehend what is in it. Some of the Arabs use "an" with "la'alla" in imitation of "'asā" (perhaps). The lam in "la'alla" is an emphatic addition (zā'ida li-l-ta'kīd), as the poet said [[A verse in rajaz meter by al-Ajjaj; its first half is: "Tuqūlu bintī qad anā anākā"]]:

"O father, perhaps you or maybe you..."

It has also been said: "la'allakum ta'qilūn" means: that you may be hopeful of reflecting upon it, so the sense of doubt returns to them, not to the Book, nor to Allah the Mighty and Majestic. It has also been said: the meaning of "anzalnāhu" is: We have sent down the account of Yusuf. Al-Nahhas said: this is closer to the meaning, because it is reported that the Jews said: "Ask him why the family of Ya'qub moved from Syria to Egypt, and about the account of Yusuf." So Allah the Mighty and Majestic sent this down in Makkah, agreeing with what is in the Torah, and including additional details not found with them. Thus this was for the Prophet (ﷺ), when he informed them, although he did not read any book [ever] and was not in a place of books, like the revival of the dead by 'Isa (peace be upon him), as will come in its place.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 12, verse 3:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾ is a mubtada' (subject, nominal sentence opener), and its khabar (predicate) follows.

(*Ahsana al-qasas*, "the best of stories") is in the sense of the verbal noun (masdar), and the implied construction is: "We relate the best of stories." The root meaning of *al-qasas* is tracing or following something. From this comes the verse ﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him up"﴾ [al-Qasas: 11], meaning "Trace his track." The storyteller (*al-qass*) traces traces and reports them. The adjective *al-husn* ("best") refers to *al-qasas* (the act of relating), not to *al-qissa* (the story itself). One says: "So-and-so is good at relating (*husn al-iqtisas*) the narrative," meaning he is skilled in its telling. It has also been said that *al-qasas* is not a verbal noun but has the sense of a noun, as one says: "Allah is our hope," meaning "our object of hope." On this reading the meaning is: "We inform you of the best of reports."

(*Bi-ma awhayna ilayka*) meaning: by Our revelation. The *ma* together with the verb functions as a verbal noun.

(*Hadha al-Qur'an*): *al-Qur'an* is in the accusative case as a *na't* (descriptive adjective) of *hadha*, or as a *badal* (substitute) of it, or as an *atf al-bayan* (explicative apposition). Al-Farra' permitted the genitive (*khafd*), saying it is by repetition (*al-takrir*). According to the Basrans, it is a *badal* of *ma*.

Abu Ishaq permitted the nominative (*raf'*) by assuming an implied subject, as if a questioner had asked him about the revelation and it was said to him: "It is [this] the Qur'an."

(*Wa in kunta min qablihi lamina al-ghafilin*) meaning: you were among those unaware of what We made known to you.

**Question:** The scholars differed on why this surah was named *Ahsan al-Qasas* ("the Best of Stories") among all the narratives. It was said: because no story in the Qur'an contains as many lessons and wisdoms as this one. Its explanation is found in His saying at its end: ﴿Certainly there was in their stories a lesson for people of understanding﴾ [Yusuf: 111]. It was also said: it was named so for the excellence of Yusuf's forbearance toward his brothers, his patience under their harm, and his pardoning them after the reunion, without mentioning what they had done, and his generosity in forgiving them, to the point that he said: ﴿No reproach against you today﴾ [Yusuf: 92]. It was also said: because it mentions prophets, righteous people, angels, devils, jinn and humans, animals and birds, the histories of kings and kingdoms, merchants, scholars and ignorant people, men and women, and their stratagems and deceptions. It also contains matters of monotheism (*tawhid*), jurisprudence (*fiqh*), biographies, the interpretation of dreams, politics, social conduct, the management of livelihood, and a collection of benefits suitable for both religion and worldly life. It was also said: because it mentions the beloved and the one loved, and their histories. It was also said: "*Ahsan*" here means "more wondrous" (*a'jab*). Some scholars of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said: it is the best of stories because everyone mentioned in it ended in happiness. Consider Yusuf, his father, his brothers, and the wife of the al-'Aziz. It is said that the king too embraced Islam through Yusuf and his Islam was good; the one who interpreted the dream, the cupbearer, was also saved; and the witness, as it is said, [ended well]. Thus the outcome of all of them was nothing but good.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 4:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When Joseph said﴾. "Idh" (when) is in the accusative position as an adverb of time, meaning: mention to them the time when Joseph said. The reading of the majority is with a ḍamma on the sīn. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif read "yūsif" with a hamza and a kasra on the sīn. Abū Zayd related "yūsaf" with a hamza and a fatḥa on the sīn. It is not declined (diptotic) because it is non-Arabic (a'jamī), though it has been said that it is Arabic. Abū al-Ḥasan al-Aqṭa'—and he was a sage—was asked about "Yūsuf" and said: "al-asaf" in the language means grief, and "al-asīf" means the servant (or one who is sorrowful); both of these meanings came together in Joseph, and for that reason he was named Joseph.

(To his father, "O my father") with a kasra on the tā' is the reading of Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, Nāfiʿ, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī. According to the Basrans, it is the feminine marker, added to "ab" (father) specifically in the vocative, in place of the yā' of possession. The feminine marker may also be attached to a masculine noun, as in "rajulun nukhatah" and "huzaʾah." Al-Naḥḥās said: when you say "yā abatī" with a kasra on the tā', the tā' according to Sībawayh is a replacement for the yā' of possession, and on his view it is not permissible to pause except with a hāʾ. For his view there are proofs: among them, that your saying "yā abah" conveys the meaning of "yā abī"; that "yā abatī" is not said except in the definite (vocative); "jāʾanī abat" is not said; and the Arabs use this only in the vocative. "Yā abatī" is not said, because the tā' is a replacement for the yā', so the two are not combined. Al-Farrāʾ claimed that when one says "yā abatī" with a kasra, it indicates only the yā', since the yā' is intended. Abū Isḥāq claimed that this is an error, and the truth is what he (Sībawayh) said: how can the yā' be intended when "yā abatī" is not said?

Abū Jaʿfar, al-Aʿraj and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir read "yā abata" with a fatḥa on the tā'. The Basrans said: they intended "yā abatī" with the yā', then the yā' was replaced by an alif, becoming "yā abatā," then the alif was deleted and the fatḥa remained on the tā'. It has also been said: the original is the kasra, then a fatḥa was substituted for the kasra, just as an alif is substituted for the yā' in saying "yā ghulāman aqbil." Al-Farrāʾ permitted "yā abatu" with a ḍamma on the tā'.

(Indeed I saw eleven stars) There is no disagreement among the grammarians that one says "jāʾanī aḥada ʿashar" (eleven came to me), "raʾaytu" and "marartu bi-aḥada ʿashar" (I saw / I passed by eleven). Likewise thalāthata ʿashar and tisʿata ʿashar and what lies between them: they made the two words one noun and declined them with the lightest of the vowels. Al-Suhaylī said: the names of these stars have been transmitted with a chain of narration. Al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Usāmah related that Bustāna—a man from the People of the Book—came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him about the eleven stars which Joseph saw. He said: "Al-Ḥarthān, Jariyān, al-Ṭāriq, al-Dhayyāl, Qābis, al-Muṣbiḥ, al-Ḍarūḥ, Dhū al-Kanafāt, Dhū al-Qaraʿ, al-Falīq, Wathhāb and al-ʿAmūdān, which Joseph (peace be upon him) saw prostrating to him." [Note in the margin of al-Jamal: Jiryān—with a fatḥa on the jīm, a kasra on the rāʾ and a shadda on the yāʾ—is transferred from the name of a collar of a shirt. Qābis: one who kindles fire. ʿAmūdān: the dual of ʿamūd. Al-Falīq: a single star. Al-Muṣbiḥ: what rises before dawn. Al-Faraʿ, with fāʾ, rāʾ unpointed and sākin, and ʿayn: a star near the Bucket. Wathhāb, with the mīm stressed, quick in motion. Dhū al-Kitfayn: the dual of kitf, a large star. These are unobserved stars.]

Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah said: the stars are his brothers, the sun is his mother, and the moon is his father. Qatādah also said: the sun is his maternal aunt, because his mother had died, and his aunt was under his father.

(I saw them) is for emphasis. He said: "I saw them prostrating to me," and so it came in the masculine. According to al-Khalīl and Sībawayh, the explanation is that when these things were described with the act of prostration, which is a characteristic of rational beings, they were described as rational beings would be. This meaning has already been discussed in His saying: "And you see them looking at you" (see vol. 7, p. 344). The Arabs treat non-rational things with the plural of rational beings when they place them in that position, even though this departs from the original usage.

In it are eleven issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so that they plot a stratagem against you﴾, meaning they will scheme to bring about your destruction, because its interpretation is apparent. Perhaps Satan will then move them to intend you harm. The lam in "laka" (against you) is for emphasis, as in His saying: ﴿if you can interpret dreams﴾.

**The second issue:** The dream (ru'ya) is a noble state and an elevated station. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Nothing remains after me of the bearers of good tidings except the good, true dream, which a righteous man sees or which is seen for him." He also said: "The most truthful of you in dreams is the most truthful of you in speech." He (ﷺ) ruled that it is a part of forty-six parts of prophethood. It is also narrated as "a part of seventy parts of prophethood." It is narrated from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, as "a part of forty parts of prophethood." From the hadith of Ibn Umar: "a part of forty-nine parts." From the hadith of al-Abbas: "a part of fifty parts of prophethood." From the hadith of Anas: "of twenty-six." And from Ubadah ibn al-Samit: "of forty-four parts of prophethood." The soundest of these is the hadith of forty-six, and after it in soundness is the hadith of seventy. Muslim did not include in his Sahih any of these two hadiths other than these two; as for the rest, they are from the hadiths of the shuyukh (teachers). This was said by Ibn Battal. Abu Abd Allah al-Mazari said: "The majority and the most authentic version according to the people of hadith is 'of forty-six.'" Al-Tabari said: "The correct view is to say that most of these hadiths, or most of them, are sound, and each hadith has a reasonable explanation. As for his saying, 'It is a part of seventy parts of prophethood,' this is a general statement about every good, true dream, and it applies to every Muslim who sees it in his sleep, whatever his condition. As for his saying, 'of forty or forty-six,' he means by it the one whose condition was that which I mentioned about al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he was in it: whoever was one who perfected ablution in the severe cold (al-sabarat, the plural of sabrah, with a sukun on the ba: the severe cold), and was patient for Allah's sake in disliked matters, and awaited prayer after prayer, his good dream, if Allah wills, is a part of forty parts of prophethood. Whoever's condition in himself is between these, his true dream is between two parts, from forty up to sixty, not less than seventy and not more than forty."

Abu Umar Ibn Abd al-Barr pointed to this meaning and said: "The variation of reports on this subject, concerning the number of parts of the dream, is not, in my view, a contradictory or conflicting variation, and Allah knows best. It may be that the good dream of some who see it is according to the truthfulness of their speech, their fulfilment of trust, their firm religion, and their good certainty. So according to the difference among people in what we have described, their dreams are of differing numbers of parts. Whoever's intention in the worship of his Lord is sincere, and whose certainty and speech are true, his dream is more truthful and closer to prophethood, just as the prophets differ in rank. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have preferred some of the prophets over others﴾."

I say: This interpretation brings together the scattered hadiths. It is better than explaining some of them and discarding others. Abu Sa'id al-Asfaqusi (in the originals it reads "al-Asfaqusi," and the correct form is "al-Safaqusi") related it from some of the scholars, who said: The meaning of his saying, "a part of forty-six parts of prophethood," is that Allah, exalted is He, revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) during his prophethood for twenty-three years, as narrated by Ikrimah and Amr ibn Dinar from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. So when we subtract six months from twenty-three years, we find that this is a part of forty-six parts. This view was pointed to by al-Mazari in his book al-Mu'allim, and was chosen by al-Qunawi (in one copy: al-Ghaznawi) in his tafsir of Surah Yunus, at His saying: ﴿For them is good news in the life of this world﴾ (Yunus 10:64).

This view is invalid for two reasons. First: what Abu Salamah narrated from Ibn Abbas and Aisha, that the period of revelation was twenty years, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent at the age of forty, and he remained in Makkah for ten years. This is also the view of Urwah, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Shihab, al-Hasan, Ata, al-Khurasani, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, with a difference of report from him, and it is the narration of Rabi'ah and Abu Ghalib from Anas. When this report is established, that interpretation is void. Second: all the other hadiths concerning the differing numbers of parts would remain without meaning.

**The third issue:** The dream is only a part of prophethood because it contains things that are beyond ability and impossible, such as flying, the transformation of physical objects, and gaining knowledge of some of the unseen. As he (peace be upon him) said: "Indeed, nothing remains of the bearers of good tidings of prophethood except the true dream in sleep," and the hadith goes on. In sum, the true dream is from Allah, and it is part of prophethood. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The dream is from Allah and the nightmare is from Satan." Belief in it is true, and it has good interpretation. Some dreams need no interpretation at all. There is in it some of Allah's wonderful subtlety and gentleness that increases the believer in faith. There is no dispute about this among the people of religion and the people of truth, among the people of opinion (ra'y) and the people of transmitted reports (athar). Only the people of atheism and the most wicked of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) deny dreams.

**The fourth issue:** If it is said: if the true dream is a part of prophethood, how can an unbeliever, a liar, or a mixed-up person be among those who have it? True and correct dreams have occurred to some unbelievers and others whose religion is not approved, such as the dream of the king who saw seven cows, the dream of the two young men in prison, the dream of Nebuchadnezzar, which Daniel interpreted concerning the loss of his kingdom, the dream of Chosroes concerning the emergence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the dream of Atikah, the aunt of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), concerning his affair, while she was an unbeliever. Al-Bukhari also titled a chapter "The Chapter on the Dreams of the People of Prison."

The answer is that the unbeliever, the sinner, the corrupt, and the liar, even if their dreams are sometimes true, are not from revelation and not from prophethood. For not everyone who speaks truthfully about the unseen has his news counted as prophethood. It has already been mentioned in "al-An'am" (see vol. 7, p. 3 onward) that the soothsayer and others may speak a word of truth and it proves right, but that happens rarely and infrequently. Likewise are the dreams of these people.

Al-Muhallab said: Al-Bukhari only titled it this way because it is possible that the dreams of the people of polytheism are true, just as the dream of the two young men was true, except that it is not permissible to attribute them to prophethood in the way that the dream of a believer is attributed to it, for not everything that can be correctly interpreted as a dream is truly a part of prophethood.

**The fifth issue:** The dream attributed to Allah, exalted is He, is that which is free of confused dreams (adghath al-ahlam) and illusions, and whose interpretation agrees with what is in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz). The dreams that are of the category of confused dreams are the nightmares, and these are attributed to Satan. They are called "confused" (dighth) because they contain contradictory things. This was said by al-Muhallab.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) divided dreams into categories that make unnecessary every statement of any speaker. Awf ibn Malik narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Dreams are of three kinds: some are the terrors of Satan to grieve the son of Adam; some are what a man worries about in his waking life and then sees in his sleep; and some are a part of forty-six parts of prophethood." He said: I said, "Did you hear this from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?" He said: "Yes! I heard it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

**The sixth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "My son, do not relate your dream to your brothers﴾, and the rest of the verse. The word ru'ya is a verbal noun of "ra'a" in sleep, in the form fu'la like suqya and bushra, and its alif is for the feminine, which is why it is not declined. The scholars have differed about the reality of the dream. It was said: it is a perception in parts that have not been affected by any defect, such as deep sleep and other states. For this reason dreams most often occur at the end of the night, because the domination of sleep is then less. So Allah, exalted is He, creates for the dreamer a knowledge that arises, and creates for him what he sees, as he sees it, so that the perception is valid.

Ibn al-Arabi said: One sees in a dream only what can be perceived when awake. For this reason one does not see in a dream a person standing or sitting in some state; one sees only what is permissible and customary.

It was also said that Allah has an angel who presents the things seen to the perceiving faculty of the sleeper, so it presents to him physical images. Sometimes those images are examples corresponding to what happens in existence, and sometimes they are for intelligible meanings that are not perceptible to the senses. In both cases they are either bearers of good tidings or warners.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said in Sahih Muslim and elsewhere: "I saw a black woman with disheveled hair going out of Medina to Mahai'ah (al-Mahai'ah: it is al-Juhfah, the ritual boundary for the people of Syria). I interpreted her as fever." (In it, "black woman" means a woman who is black, as in the version of al-Nasa'i.)

The dream of the sword whose blade was broken, and the slaughtered cows: "I saw my sword with its blade broken and cows being slaughtered," and he interpreted it as "a man of my household will be killed, and the cows are a group of my companions who will be killed." Likewise: "I saw that I put my hands into a strong coat of mail," and he interpreted it as "Medina." And: "I saw two bracelets on my hands," and he interpreted them as "two liars who will emerge after me." There are many other examples of this kind, of which dream-symbols are coined. Some of them have a meaning that becomes apparent at once [[from ع and و ى: "fa-awwala" (he interpreted it) is written differently in the manuscripts]], and some of them have a meaning that is not apparent except after reflection. A sleeper in the time of Yusuf (peace be upon him) saw cows, and Yusuf interpreted them as years. He also saw eleven stars, and he interpreted them as his brothers and his parents.

The seventh point: If it is said that Yusuf (peace be upon him) was young at the time of his dream, and a young child has no judgment in his actions, how can he have a dream that carries a ruling, to the extent that his father said to him, "Do not relate your vision to your brothers"? The answer: a dream is the perception of a reality, as we have already explained. Therefore it can come from a young child just as the genuine perception that occurs while awake can come from him. When he reports what he has seen, he speaks truly, and likewise when he reports what he sees in sleep. Allah (glorified is He) has informed us of Yusuf's dream and that it came to pass as he saw it, so there is no objection. It is related that Yusuf (peace be upon him) was twelve years old.

The eighth point: This verse is a basis for not relating a dream to anyone who is not a sincere well-wisher and does not know how to interpret it. Abu Razin al-Uqayli related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A dream is one part in forty parts of prophethood." And: "A dream hangs on the leg of a bird as long as its owner has not related it. When he relates it, it falls. So do not relate it except to one who understands, one who loves you, or one who gives sincere advice." It was recorded by al-Tirmidhi, who said of it: "A good, sound hadith." Abu Razin's name was Luqayt ibn 'Amir. Malik was asked, "Can anyone interpret a dream?" He said, "Is prophethood a matter for play?" Malik also said: "No one should interpret a dream except one who is skilled at it. If he sees something good, he may report it, and if he sees something disliked, let him say something good or remain silent." It was asked: "Should he interpret it as good, when he sees it as disliked, in accordance with the view of one who says that it occurs as he interpreted it?" He said: "No!" Then he said: "A dream is part of prophethood, so prophethood should not be treated lightly."

The ninth point: This verse is evidence that it is permissible for a Muslim to warn his Muslim brother against someone whom he fears for him, and that this does not fall under backbiting (al-ghība), since Ya'qub (peace be upon him) warned Yusuf not to relate his dream to his brothers lest they plot against him. It also indicates that it is permissible to refrain from displaying a blessing before those whose harm is feared because of envy and scheming. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Seek help in achieving your needs by keeping them secret, for every possessor of a blessing is envied." The verse is also clear evidence that Ya'qub (peace be upon him) knew how to interpret dreams, for he knew from its interpretation that Yusuf would be exalted over them, and he was not troubled by this on his own account, for a man wishes his son to be better than himself, whereas a brother does not wish this for his brother. It also indicates that Ya'qub (peace be upon him) perceived from his sons envy of Yusuf and hatred toward him, so he forbade him to relate the dream to them, fearing that their hearts would be filled with rancor and that they would devise a stratagem to destroy him. From this, and from their action toward Yusuf, it follows that they were not prophets at that time. It is reported in the book of al-Tabari, on the authority of Ibn Zayd, that they were prophets, but this is refuted by the certainty of the infallibility of the prophets against worldly envy, against disobedience to fathers, against exposing a believer to destruction, and against conspiring to kill him. There is no regard for the view of those who say they were prophets. It is not impossible by reason for a prophet to commit a lapse, but this lapse combined several major sins, and the Muslims have agreed that prophets are protected from them. They differed only regarding minor sins, as has been mentioned earlier and will come later.

The tenth point: Al-Bukhari related on the authority of Abu Hurayra, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Nothing remains of prophethood except the glad tidings." They said: "And what are the glad tidings?" He said: "The true dream." This hadith, on its apparent meaning, indicates that a dream is glad tidings in every case, and that is not so, for a true dream may be a warning from Allah (exalted is He) that does not gladden the one who sees it. Allah shows it to the believer out of kindness and mercy, so that he may prepare for the descent of the trial before it occurs. If he understands its interpretation himself, well and good; otherwise he asks about it one who is qualified for that. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him), while he was in Egypt, saw a dream concerning Ahmad ibn Hanbal indicating his ordeal (mihna), so he wrote to him about it so that he might prepare for it. It has been mentioned earlier, in Surah Yunus, in the explanation of His saying (exalted is He): ﴿For them is good news in the life of this world﴾ [Yunus: 64], that it refers to the true dream. This hadith of al-Bukhari is, for the most part, of this type, and Allah knows best.

The eleventh point: Al-Bukhari related on the authority of Abu Salama, who said: "I used to see dreams that made me ill, until I heard Abu Qatada say: 'I too used to see dreams that made me ill, until I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "A good dream is from Allah. So when one of you sees what he loves, let him not relate it except to one who loves him. And when he sees what he dislikes, let him seek refuge in Allah from its evil and spit three times, and let him not relate it to anyone, for it will not harm him."'" Our scholars said: Allah made seeking refuge from it a means of removing its harm. Do you not see Abu Qatada's statement: "I used to see a dream that weighed on me more heavily than a mountain, but when I heard this hadith I no longer regarded it as anything." Muslim added, from the narration of Jabir on the authority of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "If one of you sees a dream that he dislikes, let him spit to his left three times, seek refuge in Allah from Satan three times, and turn over from the side on which he was lying." In the hadith of Abu Hurayra from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "If one of you sees what he dislikes, let him rise and pray." Our scholars said: All of this is not contradictory. The command to turn over is one thing, and prayer is an addition. The seer should do all of it. Rising to pray encompasses all of these matters, for when he prays, his act of prayer includes all of those actions: when he rises for prayer he turns over from his side, and when he rinses his mouth he spits, and when he stands for prayer he seeks refuge, supplicates, and humbly entreats Allah (exalted is He) that He suffice him against its evil at a time that is among the most likely for a response, and that is the last part of the night.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus will your Lord choose you﴾. The kaf (ka) is in the accusative position, because it is an adjective (na't) of a deleted verbal noun (masdar), and likewise the kaf in His saying, "as He completed it upon your two fathers before, [Ibrahim and Ishaq]", and "ma" is a kaffah (a particle that removes the government of the word it is attached to). It was also said: "wa-kadhalika" means: just as He honoured you with the dream, so He will choose you and show you favour by making the dream come true. Muqatil said: "by prostration to you." al-Hasan said: "by prophethood."

Al-ijtiba' (choosing, selection) is the selection of the most exalted matters for the one chosen, and its root is from jaba'tu al-shay', meaning I gathered the thing together, and from it comes jaba'tu al-ma' fi al-hawd (I collected the water in the basin), said al-Nahhas. This is a praise from Allah exalted is He upon Yusuf, peace be upon him, and an enumeration, among what He enumerated for him, of the blessings that Allah granted him: the establishment in the land, and the teaching of the interpretation of the ahadith (the interpretation of events, dreams and matters). They agreed that this refers to the interpretation of dreams. 'Abdullah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Had said: "The interpretation of Yusuf's dream (ﷺ) came after forty years, and that was the final point of the dream." By "al-ahadith" is meant what people see in dreams, and it is a miracle for him, for no error ever reached him in them. Yusuf, peace be upon him, was the most knowledgeable of people in its interpretation, and our Prophet (ﷺ) was similar to that, and al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) was among the most skilled of people in it. Ibn Sirin attained great eminence, natural talent and excellence in it, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, as they have mentioned, was similar to him or close to him.

It has been said regarding the interpretation of His saying, "and teach you of the interpretation of ahadith" (ta'wil al-ahadith): it means the stories of the nations and the scriptures, and the proofs of monotheism. This is an allusion to prophethood, and it is what is meant by His saying, "and complete His favour upon you", that is, with prophethood. It was also said: by bringing your brothers to you; and it was said: by saving you from every hardship.

﴿As He completed it upon your two fathers before, Ibrahim﴾ with friendship (khullah), and saving him from the fire.

﴿and Ishaq﴾ with prophethood. It was also said: from the sacrifice [[It has previously been stated that the one sacrificed was Isma'il, which is the truth, and it will also come in "al-Saffat". In another manuscript: "and the ransom from the sacrifice".]], said by 'Ikrimah, "with what will be given to you." Allah, exalted is He, informed him by His saying, "and upon the family of Ya'qub", that He would give all the sons of Ya'qub prophethood, as said by a group of the exegetes.

﴿Indeed your Lord is All-Knowing﴾ of what He gives you.

﴿All-Wise﴾ in His action concerning you.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 12, verses 7–9:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Certainly there were in Joseph and his brothers signs for those who ask.﴾ That is, for whoever asks about their story. The people of Makkah recited *"āyatun"* (singular, "a sign") in the singular, while Abu 'Ubayd chose *"āyātun"* (plural, "signs") and said: "Because it signifies much good." An-Nahhas said: "*Āyatun* here is a good reading. That is, there was a sign in the story of Joseph for those who asked about it, for they asked the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was in Makkah, saying: 'Tell us about a man of the prophets who lived in Syria, whose son was taken to Egypt, and who wept for him until he went blind.' No one in Makkah was from the People of the Book, nor anyone who knew the story of the prophets. Rather, the Jews had sent people to him from Madinah to ask him about this. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed the whole Surah of Joseph at once, containing everything in the Torah of the story and more. This was a sign for the Prophet (ﷺ), like the raising of the dead by 'Isa son of Maryam (peace be upon him)." *"Āyātun"* (signs) [in one manuscript it reads *"āyatun"*, the singular, which is the reading that matches the tafsir] are admonitions. It was also said: they are lessons (*'ibrah*). It is narrated that in some *maṣāḥif* (copies of the Qur'an) it reads *"'ibrah"*. It was also said: they are insight (*baṣīrah*). And it was said: they are wonders; one says, "So-and-so is a sign in knowledge and beauty," meaning a wonder.

Al-Tha'labi said in his tafsir: When the dream reached Joseph's brothers, they envied him. Ibn Zayd said: "They were prophets." And they said: "Does he not consent that his brothers should prostrate to him, unless his parents also prostrate to him!" So they harboured enmity toward him. The rejection of this view has already been mentioned. Allah says: ﴿in Joseph and his brothers﴾. Their names were: Ruben, who was the eldest; Shim'un, Levi, Yahudha, Zabulun, and Yashjar. Their mother was Lya (Leah), daughter of Layan, who was the daughter of Yaqub's maternal uncle. He had four sons from two concubines: Dan, Naftali, Jad, and Asher. Then Lya died, and Yaqub married her sister Rahil (Rachel), and she bore him Joseph and Benjamin. Thus the sons of Yaqub were twelve men. As-Suhayli said: The mother of Yaqub was named Rifqa, Rahil died in childbirth with Benjamin, and Layan ibn Nahir ibn Azar was the maternal uncle of Yaqub. It was also said: the names of the two maidservants were Lya and Talta; one belonged to Rahil and the other to her sister Lya, and they had been given to Yaqub. Yaqub had combined the two sisters in marriage, and it was not lawful for anyone after him, based on the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿and that you should combine two sisters, except what has already passed﴾ [an-Nisa': 23]. The response to what Ibn Zayd said has already been given, and all praise is due to Allah.

His saying, Exalted: ﴿When they said: Joseph﴾. *"Layūsufu"* (Joseph, with the emphatic lam) is in the nominative, as the subject of a nominal sentence, and the lam is for emphasis; it is the lam that introduces an oath. That is: "By Allah, Joseph [is dearer]."

(And his brother) is conjoined to it (*'aṭf*, coordination).

(is dearer to our father than we are) is the predicate. It is not made dual or plural, because it has the meaning of a verb. They only said this because news of the dream had reached them, so they conspired against him.

(while we are a band) that is, a group, and they were ten. *"'Uṣbah"* (a band) is from one up to ten; it was also said up to fifteen, and it was also said from forty down to ten. It has no singular form from its own root, like *nafar* (a group) and *rahṭ* (a company).

(Indeed our father is in clear error) They did not mean error in religion, for had they meant that they would have been disbelievers. Rather, they meant that he was going astray in the management of affairs, by preferring two over ten while they were equal in their descent from him. It was also said: "He is in manifest error by preferring Joseph and his brother over us."

His saying, Exalted: ﴿Kill Joseph﴾. There is an ellipsis in the speech: that is, one of them said, "Kill Joseph," so that this would be the most decisive way to end the matter.

(or cast him out to some land) That is, into some land, so the preposition was dropped and *al-arḍ* (the land) was put in the accusative. Sibawayh cited as evidence for the omission of *fī* (in) the following line:

*"A supple spear, when the hand shakes it, its shaft undulates within it as a fox moves along the path"* [[This line is by Sa'idah ibn Juwayyah, describing a spear that is supple when shaken. He likened its agitation, either in itself or in the state of its shaking, to the loping gait of a fox on its path. *'Usalan* is a swift movement with agitation. *Ladn* means soft and pliant. It is also transmitted as *ladhdh*, meaning delightful to the shaking because of its suppleness. (Sibawayh's evidences.)]]

An-Nahhas said: "However, in the verse this is very common, because the verb transitively takes two objects, one of which is with a preposition; when you drop the preposition, the verb reaches it directly." It was said the speaker was Shim'un, as Wahb ibn Munabbih said. Ka'b al-Ahbar said it was Dan. Muqatil said it was Ruben, and Allah knows best. The meaning is "a land far from his father," and this implicit element is necessary, because he was with his father in a land.

(so that the face of your father will be turned to you) means that he will attend to you with his whole self, with nothing else distracting him.

(and after him you will be a righteous people) That is, after the sin. It was also said: after Joseph.

(a righteous people) That is, repentant, meaning you will repent after that, and Allah will accept it from you. In this there is evidence that the repentance of a killer is accepted, because Allah, Exalted, did not condemn this statement of theirs. It was also said: "righteous" means your affair will be set right in your father's eyes without favouritism or preference.

**Question 1:** In it there are thirteen issues. The first concerns the words of the Exalted: ﴿One of them said﴾. The speaker was Yahudha (Judah), the eldest son of Ya'qub (Jacob), as Ibn 'Abbas said. It was also said that he was Ruwbil (Reuben), the son of Yusuf's maternal aunt, and he is the one who said: ﴿I will not leave this land﴾ [Yusuf: 80] [the verse]. It was also said that he was Shim'un (Simeon).

(﴿And throw him into the depths of the well﴾) The people of Makkah, the people of Basra and the people of Kufa read "fi ghayabati al-jubb" (in the depths of the well, singular). The people of Madinah read "fi ghayabati al-jubb" (plural, "ghayabat"). Abu 'Ubayd preferred the singular, because it refers to one place into which they threw him. Al-Jumah rejected this. Al-Nahhas said: This is a narrowing of the language, for "ghayabat" in the plural is permissible on two grounds. [The first is from the addition of al-Nahhas.] Sibawayh reported: "sir 'alayhi 'ashiyyanat wa-asila'nat," meaning "'ashiyyah" and "asil," so he made each time of them an "'ashiyyah" and an "asil." Likewise, he made each place that hides something a "ghayabah." [The second is that there are several "ghayabat" (depths) in the well.] It is said: "ghaba yaghibu" (he hid), "ghaybān," "ghaybah" and "ghiyāban," as the poet said:

*Ala fa-albathā shahrayni aw niṣfa thālithin*
*Ana dhākumā qad ghayyabatnī ghiyābiyā*

Al-Harawi said: The "ghayabah" is like a recess (laj)[[al-laj: the side of a pool or well that is eroded by water, becoming like a cave]] or a niche in the well above the water, where a thing disappears from sight. Ibn 'Aziz said: Anything that hides something from you is a "ghayabah." I say: From this comes the saying that the grave is a "ghayabah." The poet said:

*Fa-in ana yawman ghayyabatnī ghayabatī*
*Fa-sirū bi-sayrī fī al-'ashīrati wa-al-ahl*

The "jubb" is a well that has not been lined with stone; once it is lined, it becomes a "bi'r." Al-A'sha said:

*La-in kunta fī jubbin thamānīna qāmatan*
*Wa-ruqqīta asbāba al-samā'i bi-sullam*[[After it, as in the Diwan:
*Li-yastadrijannaka al-qawlu ḥattā tahirrahu*
*Wa-ta'lama annī 'anka lasta bi-mujrim*
*Wa-tashraqa bi-al-qawli al-ladhī qad adhaʿtahu*
*Kamā shariqat ṣadru al-qanāti mina al-dam*]]

It was called "jubb" because it was cut into the earth by cutting. The plural of "jubb" is "jibabah," "jibāb" and "ajbāb." He combined "ghayabah" and "jubb" because he meant: throw him into a dark place inside the well, so that the eyes of onlookers cannot reach him. It is said: it is the well of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It was also said: it is in al-Urdunn (Jordan). Wahb ibn Munabbih said, and Muqatil said: it was three farsakh (leagues) from the dwelling of Ya'qub.

**Question 2:** The words of the Exalted: ﴿some caravan travellers will pick him up﴾. It is in the jussive mood as an answer to the imperative. Mujahid, Abu Raja', al-Hasan and Qatadah read "taltaqit-hu" with a *ta'* (feminine verb form). This is interpreted according to meaning, because "ba'ḍ al-sayyarah" (some of the caravan) is a caravan. Sibawayh said: "saqatat ba'ḍu aṣābi'ihi" (some of his fingers fell), and he recited:

*Wa-tashraqa bi-al-qawli al-ladhī qad adhaʿtahu*
*Kamā shariqat ṣadru al-qanāti mina al-dam*

Another said:

*Ara marra al-sinīna akhadhna minnī*
*Kamā akhadha al-sarāru mina al-hilāl*[[Sarar al-shahr (with the letter sīn pointed or with a kasra) and its sarar: the last night of the month.]]

Ibn al-Arabi and others hold that the Qur'an's wording, "a company of travellers" (sayyara), indicates... [translation of this passage follows]

Actually, to be precise, here is the translation:

He did not say "it was swallowed" or "it was taken." The *sayyara* is the company that travels along the road for a journey. The speaker said this so that they would not need to carry him to a distant place, and the aim would still be achieved, since whoever picked him up from the caravan would carry him to a distant place. This was a plan in their arrangement, so that they would not need to go themselves, for perhaps their father would not give them permission, and perhaps he would discover their intention.

The third issue: this indicates that the brothers of Joseph were not prophets, either before or after, because prophets do not plot to kill a Muslim. Rather, they were Muslims who committed a sin and then repented. It was also said: they were prophets, and a prophet's lapse is not impossible in reason. So this was a lapse on their part. This is refuted by the fact that prophets are protected from major sins, as we have mentioned before. It was also said: they were not prophets at that time, and then God made them prophets. This is the more likely view, and God knows best.

The fourth issue: Ibn Wahb reported that Malik said: "Joseph was cast into the well when he was a boy." Ibn al-Qasim also narrated this from him, meaning that he was young. The evidence for this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Do not kill Joseph, but cast him into the depths of the well; some of the travellers will pick him up﴾. He said: "Only a young child is picked up." And [their] saying: ﴿and I fear the wolf will devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], and that matter belongs only to small children, and their saying: ﴿Send him with us tomorrow; he will enjoy himself and play, and we will surely guard him﴾ [Yusuf: 12].

The fifth issue: *iltiqat* (picking up) is taking hold of something from the road, and from it come *laqit* (foundling) and *luqta* (lost property). We will mention from its rulings what the Qur'an and the Sunnah indicate, and what the scholars and linguists have said about it. Ibn Arafa said: *iltiqat* is finding a thing without seeking it, and from this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿some of the travellers will pick him up﴾, that is, will find him without expecting him.

The scholars differed concerning the foundling. It was said: its origin is freedom, because free people predominate over slaves. It is narrated from al-Hasan ibn Ali that he ruled that the foundling is free, and he recited: ﴿they sold him for a paltry price, a few counted dirhams﴾ [Yusuf: 20]. This was the view of Ashhab, the companion of Malik, and it is the saying of Umar ibn al-Khattab, and it is similarly narrated from Ali and a group [of others]. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: if he intends his enslavement, he is a slave; if he intends the reward [of God] (*hisba*), he is free. Malik said in his Muwatta': "The matter with us concerning the abandoned child is that he is free, and his *wala'* (patronage) belongs to the community of the Muslims; they inherit from him and pay blood-money (*'aql*) on his behalf." Al-Shafi'i also said this, and he argued with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Patronage belongs only to the one who frees." He said: so he negated patronage from anyone other than the one who frees. Malik, al-Shafi'i and their companions agreed that the foundling does not attach patronage to anyone, and no one inherits from him by patronage. Abu Hanifa, his companions and most of the Kufans said: the foundling may attach his patronage to whomever he wishes; whoever he attaches to inherits from him and pays blood-money on his behalf. According to Abu Hanifa, he may transfer his patronage wherever he wishes, as long as the one to whom he attached has not paid blood-money on his behalf; if that person has paid blood-money for him for an offence, he may never transfer his patronage from him.

Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba reported from Ali, may God be pleased with him: "The abandoned child is free. If he wishes to attach to the one who picked him up, he attaches to him, and if he wishes to attach to another, he attaches to him." Similar was narrated from Ata', and it is the saying of Ibn Shihab and a group of the people of Medina, and he is free.

Ibn al-Arabi said: The origin of the foundling is freedom, because free people predominate over slaves, so the ruling follows the predominant case, just as he is ruled to be Muslim by following the predominant case. If he is found in a village in which there are Christians and Muslims, Ibn al-Qasim said: the ruling follows the majority. If he is found wearing the dress of the Jews, he is a Jew; if he is found wearing the dress of the Christians, he is a Christian; otherwise he is a Muslim, unless most of the village's people are non-Muslim. Others said: if there is only one Muslim in it, the foundling is judged to be Muslim, giving precedence to the ruling of Islam, which is superior and not surpassed. This is what Ashhab's view implies. Ashhab said: he is a Muslim forever, because I consider him Muslim in every case, just as I consider him free in every case.

The jurists differed concerning the abandoned child whom the evidence (*bayyina*) shows to be a slave. A group of the people of Medina said: his testimony is not accepted in this matter. Ashhab held this view, based on the saying of Umar: "He is free," and whoever is ruled to be free, evidence that he is a slave is not accepted. Ibn al-Qasim said: evidence is accepted in this, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i and the Kufans.

The sixth issue: Malik said concerning the foundling: if the one who picked him up has spent on him, and then a man produces evidence that he is his son, then the one who picked him up may claim reimbursement from the father if the father had abandoned him deliberately; but if he did not abandon him and he was merely lost from him, then the father owes nothing, and the one who picked him up was a volunteer in spending. Abu Hanifa said: if he spends on the foundling, he is a volunteer, unless the judge orders him [to do so]. Al-Awza'i said: everyone who spends on someone for whom he is not obliged to provide maintenance is reimbursed for what he spent. Al-Shafi'i said: if the foundling has no property, his maintenance is owed from the public treasury (*bayt al-mal*); if there is none, then there are two opinions: the first is that he borrows on his behalf against his own liability; the second is that it is distributed among the Muslims without return.

The seventh issue: As for *luqta* and *dawall* (strayed animals), the scholars differed about their ruling. A group of the people of knowledge said: *luqta* and *dawall* are the same in meaning, and the ruling concerning them is the same. This was the view of Abu Ja'far al-Tahawi [in one manuscript: al-Tabari], who rejected the view of Abu Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Salam that *dawall* occurs only with animals and *luqta* with non-animals, and said that this is an error. He argued with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of the slander, to the Muslims: "Your mother's necklace has been lost," and he applied this to a necklace.

The eighth issue: The scholars agreed that *luqta* is anything that is not trivial or small, or anything that cannot last; it is announced for a full year. They agreed that if its owner comes, he has more right to it than the one who picked it up, once his ownership is established. They agreed that if the one who picked it up consumes it after the year and its owner wants to hold him liable, that is his right; and if he gives it in charity, the owner has the choice between requiring compensation and accepting the reward of it. Whichever option he chooses, it is his by consensus. The hand of the one who picked it up is not free to dispose of it by charity, nor to deal with it, before the year. They agreed that the stray sheep, when it is at risk, may be consumed by the finder.

The ninth issue: The jurists differed about which is better, leaving it or taking it. Among the evidence is that the hadith indicates the permissibility of picking up *luqta* and taking a stray, unless it is a camel. He said about the sheep: "For you, or for your brother, or for the wolf," urging him to take it. He did not say about anything "leave it until it is lost or its owner comes to it." If leaving the *luqta* were better, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would have ordered it, as he said about the stray camel. And God knows best. The sum of the doctrine of the companions of Malik is that one has latitude: if one wishes, one takes it, and if one wishes, one leaves it. This is the saying of Isma'il ibn Ishaq, may God have mercy on him. Al-Muzani reported from al-Shafi'i: "I do not like for anyone to leave *luqta* if he finds it, when he is trustworthy with it." He said: "Whether the *luqta* is little or much is the same."

The tenth issue: Malik and others among the imams narrated from Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani that he said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him about *luqta*, and he said: 'Learn its container (*ifas*) and its tie (*wika*), then announce it for a year. If its owner comes, [well and good]; otherwise, it is yours to dispose of.'" He said: "What about the sheep, Messenger of God?" He said: "For you, or for your brother, or for the wolf." He said: "What about the camel?" He said: "What have you to do with it? It has its water-skin and its sandals; it comes to the water and eats the trees until its owner finds it." [Note: *ifas* is the container in which the expense is kept, whether leather or otherwise; *wika* is the cord with which the container is tied. Sandals (*hidha'*) are its hooves, by which it is strong enough to walk and reach water and trees.] In the hadith of Ubayy, he said: "Remember its number, its container and its tie; if its owner comes [well and good]; otherwise, benefit from it." In this hadith there is an addition of the number, related by Muslim and others. The scholars agreed that the container and tie of the *luqta* are among its signs and indicators. When the owner of the *luqta* comes with all its descriptions, it is handed over to him. Ibn al-Qasim said: he is compelled to hand it over. If a claimant comes who has a right to it, with evidence that it belonged to him, the one who picked it up is not liable for anything. Does he swear an oath along with the descriptions or not? There are two opinions: the first is that of Ashhab, the second is that of Ibn al-Qasim. Evidence is not required of him according to Malik, his companions, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others. Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said: it is not handed over to him unless he produces evidence that it is his. This is contrary to the explicit text of the hadith. If evidence were a condition for handing it over, then mentioning the container, the tie and the number would have no meaning, for he would be entitled to it by evidence in every case. And since the Prophet's (ﷺ) silence on this would be a delay of explanation beyond the time of need, [that is impermissible]. And God knows best.

The eleventh issue: The hadith mentioned the camel and the sheep and explained their rulings, and was silent about other animals. Our scholars differed about whether the cow is to be assimilated to the camel or to the sheep: there are two opinions. Likewise our imams differed about picking up horses, mules and donkeys. The apparent view of Ibn al-Qasim is that they may be picked up. Ashhab and Ibn Kinana said: they may not be picked up. The view of Ibn al-Qasim is more sound, because of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Guard your believing brother's stray."

The twelfth issue: The scholars differed concerning expenditure on strays. Malik, as reported from him by Ibn al-Qasim, said: if the one who picked it up spends on the animals, the camels or others, he may claim reimbursement from its owner, whether he spent on them by order of the ruler or without his order. He said: he may hold back the animal, by the expense he incurred on it, and he has priority over it like a pledge. Al-Shafi'i said: if the one who took it spends on strays, he is a volunteer; this was related from him by al-Rabi'. Al-Muzani reported from him: if the judge orders him to spend, it becomes a debt, and what he claims is accepted from him if it is a typical amount. Abu Hanifa said: if he spends on the *luqta* and the camel without the order of the judge, he is a volunteer; if he spends by the judge's order, that is a debt on its owner when he comes, and he may hold it back if its owner is present. The expenditure on it is for about three days or so, until the judge orders the sale of the sheep or the like and rules the expenditure to be paid.

The thirteenth issue: In the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying about the *luqta* after announcement: "Then benefit from it" or "Then it is yours to dispose of" or "It is yours" or "Then spend it" or "Then eat it" or "Then it is God's property, which He gives to whom He wills," as in the authentic collection of Muslim and others, there is nothing that indicates ownership, or the removal of liability from the one who picked it up when its owner comes. For in the hadith of Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani from the Prophet (ﷺ): "If [its owner] is not known..."

(if you do not know its owner): that is, you do not know who its owner is.]] "So spend it [for charity], and let it be a deposit with you. If its owner ever comes [to claim it], then return it to him." "In another narration": "Then eat it. If its owner comes, then return it to him." Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

The scholars have agreed that the owner has the better right to it whenever he comes, except for the view of Dawud (al-Zahiri) that the finder comes to own the lost property after announcing it (ta'rif), based on those apparent texts. No attention is paid to his opinion, because it opposes the consensus of the people and because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Return it to him."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 12, verses 11–12:

God's statement: ﴿They said, "O our father, what is wrong with you that you do not trust us with Joseph?"﴾ It was said to al-Hasan (al-Basri): "Does a believer envy?" He said: "How could you forget the sons of Ya'qub!" For this reason it has been said: "The father is a fetcher (jallab), and the brother is a plunderer (sallab)." At that, they agreed to separate him from his son by some kind of scheming. They said to Ya'qub, "O our father, what is wrong with you that you do not trust us with Joseph?" It was also said: when they had consulted together and parted ways according to the opinion of the second speaker, they returned to Ya'qub, peace be upon him, and said this statement. In this there is evidence that they had asked him before that to let Joseph go out with them, and he refused, as will come.

Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa', Amr ibn Ubayd and al-Zuhri read *lā ta'manna* with idgham (assimilation of the two nuns), and without ishmam (the rounding of the lips), which is the regular form, because the rule for what is assimilated is that it be sakin (vowelless). Talha ibn Musarrif read *lā ta'mannunā* with two clearly pronounced nuns, according to the original form. Yahya ibn Wathhab and Abu Razin, and it is narrated from al-A'mash, read *wa-lā timannā* with a kasra on the ta', which is the dialect of Tamim, who say *anta tiḍribu* (you strike). This has already been mentioned. All other people read with idgham and ishmam, to indicate the state of the letter before its assimilation.

﴿And indeed we are truly his well-wishers﴾, meaning in guarding him [and watching over him [[from ʿ and ī. In Ū: and his heedlessness.]]] until we return him to you. Muqatil said: there is inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in the speech. The sons of Joseph said to their father, "Send him with us tomorrow," and so on, and then their father said, ﴿Indeed, it grieves me that you should take him away﴾ [Yusuf: 13]. Then they answered with this statement, "What is wrong with you that you do not trust us with Joseph," and so on.

﴿Send him with us tomorrow﴾ to the open country.

﴿He will enjoy himself and play﴾. *Ghadan* is an adverb of time. According to Sibawayh, its original form is *ghadwun*, and it has been pronounced in its original form. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: what lies between dawn and the morning prayer is called *ghadwa*, and likewise *bukra*. *Narta'* with the nun and a sukun on the ayn is the reading of the people of Basra. The well-known reading of the people of Mecca is *narta'i* with the nun and a kasra on the ayn. The reading of the people of Kufa is *yartaʿ* with the ya' and a sukun on the ayn. The reading of the people of Medina is with the ya' and a kasra on the ayn. The first reading comes from the Arab saying *rataʿa al-insan wa-l-baʿir* when both eat as they wish, and the meaning is: they expand in plenty, and every one in abundance is *rati*. He said:

*Fa-rʿī Fazara, lā hanāka al-marta'* (So graze, O Fazara; may the pasture not bring you ease).

Another said [[The verse is by al-Khansa', lamenting her brother Sakhr. The meaning of *tartaʿu* is grazes. She describes a she-camel or cow that has lost its young; whenever she is distracted from it she grazes, and when she remembers it she yearns, advancing and retreating. So she is struck as an example of her loss of her brother Sakhr.]]:

*Tartaʿu mā ghafalat, ḥattā idhā ddakarat... fa-innamā hiya iqbālun wa-idbār* (She grazes whenever she is distracted, until when she remembers... then it is only advancing and retreating).

Another said [[He is al-Qatami.]]:

*A-kufran baʿda radd al-mawt ʿannī... wa-baʿda ʿaṭāʾika al-mi'ata al-ritāʿā* (Is it ingratitude after the death was turned back from me... and after your gift of the hundred grazing camels?).

That is, the grazing (ratiʿa) because of the abundance of pasture. Maʿmar narrated from Qatadah that *tartaʿu* means *tasʿā* (runs about). Al-Nahhas said: he took it from the statement, ﴿We went off racing (nastabiq)﴾, because the meaning is: we race running towards a specific goal. Likewise *yartaʿ* with a sukun on the ayn, except that it is for Joseph alone, ﷺ. And *yartaʿi* with a kasra on the ayn is from *raʿy al-ghanam* (tending sheep), meaning that he may train himself in this and become manly, sometimes grazing and sometimes playing because of his youth. Al-Qutabi said: *narta'* means we keep watch and guard, and we watch over one another, from your saying *raʿāka Allāh*, meaning may God protect you. *Wa-nalʿabu* is from play. It was said to Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ: how did they say "and we play" when they were prophets? He said: they were not prophets on that day. It has also been said: what is meant by play is permissible relaxation, not forbidden play which is opposed to truth. For this reason Ya'qub did not object to their saying "and we play." From this is the statement of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Why not a virgin, you play with her and she plays with you?" [[The address is to Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah. Mulla ʿAli cited al-Qurtubi as saying that *mulaʿaba* is an expression for complete intimacy, since a thayyib (previously married woman) may have her heart attached to her first husband, so her love is not complete, unlike a virgin. It is also narrated as: *tudaʿibuha wa-tudaʿibuka*. The *duʿaba* is mingling.]]

Mujahid and Qatadah read *yartaʿ* [[(yartaʿ). What is in the tafsirs of Ibn ʿAtiyya, al-Alusi and Abu Hayyan from Mujahid and Qatadah is (with the nun), and *(nalʿab)* with a jazm. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "The reading of Mujahid and Qatadah is *narta'* with a damma on the nun and a kasra on the ta', *wa-nal'ab* with the nun and a jazm."]], meaning *yurtiʿu maṭiyyatahu* (he makes his mount graze), so the object is omitted. *Wa-yalʿabu* with a raf' is an independent resumption (isti'naf), and the meaning is: he is one who plays.

﴿And indeed we are truly his guardians﴾ from everything you fear for him. Then it is possible that they went out riding, and it is possible that they went on foot. It has been reported that they carried Joseph on their shoulders as long as Ya'qub could see them, and then when they were out of his sight, they threw him down so that he would run with them, to harm him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 13–14:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Indeed, it grieves me that you take him away"﴾. It is in the place of a nominative (raf'), meaning your taking him away. He informed of his grief at his absence.

(﴿And I fear that the wolf will eat him﴾) This is because he had seen in his dream that a wolf attacked Yusuf, so he feared for him on that account. This was said by al-Kalbi. It was also said: he saw in his dream as if he were on the summit of a mountain, and as if Yusuf were in the bottom of a valley, and behold, ten wolves had surrounded him, wanting to eat him. One of them drove them off from him, then the earth split open and Yusuf vanished into it for three days. The ten were his brothers, when they conspired to kill him; the one who defended him was his eldest brother Yahudha (Judah), and his hiding in the earth was his stay in the well for three days. It was also said: he only said that because of his fear of them for him, and he meant them by the wolf; his fear was only of their killing him, so he referred to them by the wolf in concealment of them. Ibn 'Abbas said: he named them wolves. It was also said: he did not fear them for him, for if he had feared them he would not have sent him with them; he only feared the wolf, because it is the most common thing feared in the open lands. The word "dhi'b" (wolf) is derived from "taadhabat" (of the wind), meaning the wind when it comes from every direction.[[In ʿ: "al-baraari" (the deserts). It is recorded in Ruh al-Ma'ani that this derivation is attributed to al-Zamakhshari, while al-Asma'i said: "taadhabat" is derived from "dhi'b," because the wolf does it in its running; this was challenged on the grounds that deriving a verb from non-derived nouns is rare and contrary to analogy.]] So said Ahmad ibn Yahya, who said: and the word "dhi'b" is hamzated, because it comes from every direction. Warsh related from Nafi' "al-Dhib" without a hamza, since the hamza was sukun and preceded by a kasra, so he eased it and it became a ya'.

(﴿And you are heedless of him﴾) meaning, occupied with pasturing.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "If the wolf eats him while we are a band"﴾, meaning a group, "we who see the wolf and then do not turn it away from him."

(﴿Indeed, then we would be losers﴾) meaning, in guarding our flocks; that is, if we cannot repel the wolf from our brother, then we are even more incapable of repelling it from our flocks. It was also said: "losers" means ignorant of his rights. It was also said: powerless.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 13–14:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Indeed, it grieves me that you take him away"﴾. It is in the place of a nominative (raf'), meaning your taking him away. He informed of his grief at his absence.

(﴿And I fear that the wolf will eat him﴾) This is because he had seen in his dream that a wolf attacked Yusuf, so he feared for him on that account. This was said by al-Kalbi. It was also said: he saw in his dream as if he were on the summit of a mountain, and as if Yusuf were in the bottom of a valley, and behold, ten wolves had surrounded him, wanting to eat him. One of them drove them off from him, then the earth split open and Yusuf vanished into it for three days. The ten were his brothers, when they conspired to kill him; the one who defended him was his eldest brother Yahudha (Judah), and his hiding in the earth was his stay in the well for three days. It was also said: he only said that because of his fear of them for him, and he meant them by the wolf; his fear was only of their killing him, so he referred to them by the wolf in concealment of them. Ibn 'Abbas said: he named them wolves. It was also said: he did not fear them for him, for if he had feared them he would not have sent him with them; he only feared the wolf, because it is the most common thing feared in the open lands. The word "dhi'b" (wolf) is derived from "taadhabat" (of the wind), meaning the wind when it comes from every direction.[[In ʿ: "al-baraari" (the deserts). It is recorded in Ruh al-Ma'ani that this derivation is attributed to al-Zamakhshari, while al-Asma'i said: "taadhabat" is derived from "dhi'b," because the wolf does it in its running; this was challenged on the grounds that deriving a verb from non-derived nouns is rare and contrary to analogy.]] So said Ahmad ibn Yahya, who said: and the word "dhi'b" is hamzated, because it comes from every direction. Warsh related from Nafi' "al-Dhib" without a hamza, since the hamza was sukun and preceded by a kasra, so he eased it and it became a ya'.

(﴿And you are heedless of him﴾) meaning, occupied with pasturing.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "If the wolf eats him while we are a band"﴾, meaning a group, "we who see the wolf and then do not turn it away from him."

(﴿Indeed, then we would be losers﴾) meaning, in guarding our flocks; that is, if we cannot repel the wolf from our brother, then we are even more incapable of repelling it from our flocks. It was also said: "losers" means ignorant of his rights. It was also said: powerless.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 15:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when they took him away and agreed to put him into the depths of the well﴾. "An" (that) is in the accusative position, meaning: "in agreement that they would put him into the depths of the well." It is said in the story that when Ya'qub, peace be upon him, sent him with them, he took a binding covenant from them that they would guard him. He entrusted him to Ruwbil and said: "O Ruwbil! He is young, and you know, my son, my compassion for him. If he gets hungry, feed him; if he gets thirsty, give him to drink; and if he becomes exhausted [[a'ya al-rajul fi al-mashy: kalla (a man became exhausted while walking).]], then carry him. Then hurry to return him to me." He said: They began carrying him on their shoulders, so that whenever one set him down, another would lift him. Ya'qub accompanied them for a mile and then turned back. When their father's sight of them was cut off, the one who had been carrying him threw him to the ground until he nearly broke. He then sought refuge with another, but found with each of them more anger and harshness than with the other. So he appealed to Ruwbil and said: "You are the eldest of my brothers, the successor to my father over me, and the nearest of the brothers to me. So have mercy on me and have mercy on my weakness." Ruwbil slapped him a severe slap and said: "There is no kinship between me and you. Call upon the eleven stars, so that they may save you from us." He realized that their resentment was on account of his dream. So he clung to his brother Yahudha and said: "O my brother! Have mercy on my weakness, my helplessness and my youth, and have mercy on the heart of your father Ya'qub. How quickly you have forgotten his counsel and broken his covenant!" Yahudha's heart softened and he said: "By God, they will never reach you as long as I am alive." Then he said: "O my brothers! Killing a soul that God has forbidden is among the greatest of sins. So return this boy to his father, and we will pledge to him that he will never tell his father anything of what happened." His brothers said to him: "By God, you want nothing except that you should have status with Ya'qub. By God, if you do not leave him, we will surely kill you along with him." He said: "If you insist on that, then here is this desolate, lonely well, which is a refuge for snakes and vermin. Throw him into it. If he is harmed by any of that, then that is what is intended, and you will have rid yourselves of his blood. And if he escapes into the hands of a caravan that takes him to some land, then that too is what is intended." They agreed on this course. This is the saying of God, may He be exalted: (So when they took him away and agreed to put him into the depths of the well). The answer to "fa-lamma" (so when) is omitted, meaning: "So when they took him away and agreed to cast him into the well, their trial became great."

It has also been said that the answer to "fa-lamma" is their saying: ﴿They said: O our father! We went off racing one another﴾ [Yusuf: 17].

It has also been said that the implied meaning is: "So when they took him away from their father and agreed to put him into the depths of the well, they did put him into it." This is according to the view of the Basrans [[The Basran school of Arabic grammarians.]]. As for the view of the Kufans [[The Kufan school of Arabic grammarians.]], the answer is: ﴿and We revealed to him﴾, and the "wa" (and) is superfluous. The Kufans hold that "wa" may be added with "lamma" and "hatta" (until). God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿until, when they reached it and its gates were opened﴾ [Az-Zumar: 73], meaning: "its gates were opened." And His saying: ﴿until, when Our command came and the oven boiled over﴾ [Hud: 40], meaning: "boiled over." Imru' al-Qays said:

*So when we passed the courtyard of the tribe and he inclined [[The complete line: "with us through the belly of Khabt, the hill of many sand-dunes."]]*

meaning: "he inclined." From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when they both submitted and he laid him down upon his forehead, and We called out to him﴾ [As-Saffat: 103–104], meaning: "We called out to him." [[The correct view is that the "wa" in this verse is not superfluous, but is for the circumstantial clause with the implied "qad" (indeed). This serves to indicate that God prepared for the people of Paradise what increases their joy, in contrast to the people of the Fire, for whom it is opened upon their arrival as an increase in their regret. See vol. 15, pp. 284 and 104.]]

In His saying: (And We revealed to him) there is evidence of his prophethood at that time. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Qatadah said: God gave him prophethood while he was in the well, on a rock raised above the water. Al-Kalbi said: He was thrown into the well when he was eighteen years old, so he was not a child. And whoever says he was a child, it is not far-fetched in reason that a child may be granted prophethood and receive revelation. It has also been said that it was an inspiration of inner conviction, like His saying: "And your Lord revealed to the bee" [[See vol. 10, p. 133.]]. It has also been said that it was a dream. The first view is more apparent, and God knows best, and that Jibril came to him with the revelation.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs﴾. There are two views concerning this. The first: He was revealed to that he would meet them and rebuke them for what they had done. According to this, the revelation after he was thrown into the well is a strengthening of his heart and a good tiding to him of safety. The second: He was revealed to about what they were going to do to him, so according to this the revelation before he was thrown into the well is a warning to him.

(And they do not perceive) that you are Yusuf. This is because God, may He be exalted, commanded him, when the matter came to him in Egypt, not to inform his father and brothers of his place. It has also been said: by God's revelation of prophethood, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. It has also been said: the pronoun refers to Ya'qub, meaning God revealed to him what they had done to Yusuf, and that He would inform them of his affair, while they did not perceive what God had revealed to him. God knows best.

Among what is mentioned of his story when he was thrown into the well, as reported by al-Suddi and others: when his brothers began lowering him into the well, he clung to the edge of the well, so they tied his hands and stripped off his shirt. He said: "O my brothers! Return my shirt to me, so that I may cover myself with it in this well. If I die, it will be my shroud, and if I live, I will cover my nakedness with it." [[In 'A: "I will cover myself with it and conceal my nakedness."]] They said: "Call upon the sun, the moon and the eleven stars, so that they may keep you company and clothe you." He said: "I have seen nothing." So they lowered him into the well until he reached halfway down, then they let him drop, intending that he would fall and die. There was water in the well, so he fell into it. Then he took refuge on a rock and stood upon it. It has also been said that Shim'un was the one who cut the rope, intending that he would be shattered upon the rock. Jibril was beneath the leg of the Throne, so God revealed to him: "Reach My servant." Jibril said: "I hastened and descended until I met him between the falling and the striking, and I set him down on the rock, unharmed." That well was a refuge for vermin. He stood upon the rock and began to weep. They called out to him, and he thought it was mercy from them that had reached them, so he answered them. They wanted to crush him with the rock, but Yahudha prevented them. Yahudha used to bring him food. When he fell naked, Jibril descended to him. When Ibrahim was thrown into the fire naked, Jibril brought him a shirt of silk from Paradise and dressed him in it. That shirt remained with Ibrahim, then Ishaq inherited it, then Ya'qub inherited it. When Yusuf grew up, Ya'qub placed that shirt in an amulet and hung it around his neck, and it never left him. When he was thrown into the well naked, Jibril brought out that shirt and dressed him in it.

Wahb said: When he stood upon the rock, he said: "O my brothers! Every dying person has a last testament, so listen to my testament." They said: "And what is it?" He said: "When you all gather and some of you become familiar with one another, remember my loneliness. When you eat, remember my hunger. When you drink, remember my thirst. When you see a stranger, remember my strangeness. And when you see a young man, remember my youth." Jibril said to him: "O Yusuf, stop this and occupy yourself with supplication, for supplication has a station with God." Then he taught him, saying: "Say: O God, O Companion of every stranger, O Friend of every lonely one, O Refuge of every frightened one, O Reliever of every distress, O Knower of every secret conversation, O Ultimate End of every complaint, O Present in every assembly, O Living, O Self-Subsisting! I ask You to cast Your hope into my heart, so that I have no concern or preoccupation other than You, and that You make for me from my affair relief and a way out, for You are capable of all things." The angels said: "Our God! We hear a voice and a supplication. The voice is the voice of a child, and the supplication is the supplication of a prophet."

Al-Dahhak said: Jibril, peace be upon him, descended to Yusuf while he was in the well and said to him: "Shall I not teach you words which, if you say them, God will hasten your release from this well?" He said: "Yes." He said to him: "Say: O Creator of every created thing, O Mender of every broken thing, O Witness of every secret conversation, O Present in every assembly, O Reliever of every distress, O Companion of every stranger, O Friend of every lonely one, bring me relief and hope, and cast Your hope into my heart, so that I hope for no one other than You." Yusuf repeated it that night many times, and God brought him out of the well in the morning of that same day.

**On this verse there are two issues (masʾalatān, questions of law or interpretation).**

**The first:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they came to their father at ʿishāʾ﴾, meaning at night. It is an adverb of time (ẓarf) that occupies the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl). They came at night so that they would be better able to make their excuse in the darkness. For this reason it has been said: "Do not seek your need at night, for shame is in the eyes. And do not make an excuse by day for a sin, lest you stammer in your excuse." It is related that when Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) heard their weeping, he said: "What is the matter with you? Has something happened to the flock?" They said: "No." He said: "Where is Yusuf?" They said: "We went off to race one another, and the wolf ate him." He wept and cried out and said: "Where is his shirt?" – as its explanation will come, if Allah wills. Al-Suddi and Ibn Ḥibbān said: when they said "The wolf has eaten him," he fell unconscious. They poured water over him, but he did not move, and they called to him, but he did not answer. Wahb said: Yahudha placed his hand over the outlets of Yaʿqub's breath, but he could detect no breath, and no pulse stirred in him. So Yahudha said to them: "Woe to us from the Judge of the Day of Religion! We have lost our brother and we have killed our father!"
