Yaʿqub did not come round until the cool of the pre-dawn, and he awoke with his head in the lap of Ruwbil. He said: "O Ruwbil! Did I not entrust you with my son? Did I not make a covenant with you?" He said: "O father, stop your weeping and I will tell you." So Yaʿqub stopped his weeping, and he said: "O father, ﴿we went off to race one another, and we left Yusuf by our belongings, and the wolf ate him﴾."

**The second:** Our scholars said: this verse is evidence that a person's weeping does not indicate the truth of his speech, since it may be feigned. Some people are able to do that, and some are not. It has been said: "Feigned tears are not hidden," as a wise man said:

*When tears mingle upon cheeks,*
*it becomes clear who wept from who only pretended to weep.*

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 17:**

In this verse there are seven issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He, "nastabiq" (نَسْتَبِقُ), is on the pattern *nafta'il*, from *al-musabaqah* (مُسَابَقَة, racing one another). It has been said that it means *nantadil* (نَنْتَضِلُ), that is, we shoot at targets, and likewise in the reading of ʿAbd Allah: "Indeed we went off to shoot at targets" (إِنَّا ذَهَبْنَا نَنْتَضِلُ). This is a type of racing, as said by al-Zajjaj. Al-Azhari said: *al-nidal* (النِّضَال) is shooting arrows, *al-rihan* (الرِّهَان) is racing horses, and *al-musabaqah* includes both. Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: "nastabiq" means in archery, or on horseback, or on foot. The purpose of racing on foot is to train the self to run, for it is the means of fighting the enemy and of repelling the wolf from the flocks. Al-Suddi and Ibn Hibban said: "nastabiq" means we run swiftly, so that we may see which of us is faster. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: racing is a legislated practice in the Sharia, a commendable quality, and an aid in war. The Prophet (ﷺ) himself did it, with his horses, and he raced ʿAʾisha (رضي الله عنها) on foot and she outran him. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) grew heavier, he raced her again and she outran him, and he said to her: "This is for that." I say: Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ also raced a man when they returned from Dhi Qarad (ذِي قَرَد) to Madinah, and Salamah outran him. Muslim recorded it.

[[Dhi Qarad: a place near Madinah where raiders plundered the camels (liqah) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he fought them.]]

**The second issue:** Malik narrated from Nafiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) held races between horses that had been trained (*udmirat*, أُضْمِرَتْ) [[Tadmir of horses: that they are fed fodder abundantly until they become fat, then they are given only a small amount of feed so that they become light. It has also been said that their saddles are tightened on them and they are covered with blankets until they sweat beneath them, so that their flab disappears and their flesh becomes firm. This is done for a raid or for a race.]] from al-Hafya (مِنَ الْحَفْيَاءِ) [[The addition is from (Muwatta' Malik). Al-Hafya (with the vowel on the first letter or shortened): a place in Madinah, between it and Thaniyat al-Wada' there are six or seven miles.]], and their finishing point was Thaniyat al-Wada' (ثَنِيَّةَ الْوَدَاعِ) [[The thaniyah (ثنية) on a mountain is like a pass in it. It has been said: it is the high road across it, and it has been said: the highest point of the watercourse at its head. Thaniyat al-Wada' overlooks Madinah and was named so because whoever travels to Makkah bids farewell there. From it to the Mosque of Banu Zurayq is one mile.]], and he held races between horses that had not been trained, from the thaniyah to the Mosque of Banu Zurayq. And ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar was among those who raced with them. This hadith, despite its soundness on this subject, includes three conditions, and a race is not permitted without them. They are:

First: the distance must be known.

Second: the horses must be equal in condition.

Third: a trained horse should not race against an untrained horse over the same distance and to the same finishing point.

The horses which must be trained and raced, and for which this practice is established, are the horses prepared for striving against the enemy, not for fighting Muslims in civil strife.

**The third issue:** As for racing with arrows and camels, Muslim recorded from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, who said: We travelled with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and we alighted at a stopping place. Some of us were repairing their tents, and some of us were shooting at targets, and he mentioned the hadith. al-Nasaʾi recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no prize (*sabaq*, سَبَق) except in an arrow, a camel's hoof, or a horse's hoof." [[*Lasabq* (لأسبق): it is with a fatha on the *ba'* (سَبَق), meaning the wealth given to the winner for his victory; with a sukun, it is the verbal noun. Al-Khattabi said: the correct reading is with the fatha, meaning that it is not lawful to take wealth through a race except in these three cases.]] The mention of "arrow" (*nasl*, نَصْل) is established from the hadith of Ibn Abi Dhi'b from Nafiʿ ibn Abi Nafiʿ from Abu Hurayrah, mentioned by al-Nasaʾi, and the jurists of the Hijaz and Iraq hold this view. al-Bukhari narrated from Anas, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) had a she-camel called al-ʿAdbaʾ (الْعَضْبَاء) which could not be outrun. — Humayd said: or it was hardly ever outrun — then a Bedouin came on a young camel and outran it. This grieved the Muslims until he recognised it, and he said: "It is the right of Allah that nothing rises in this world except that He lowers it."

**The fourth issue:** The Muslims (in another version: the scholars) agreed that a prize on the basis of a wager is not permitted except in the hoof, the horse's hoof, and the arrow. al-Shafiʿi said: Apart from these three, the prize in them is gambling (*qimar*, قِمَار). Abu al-Bakhtari, the judge, added to the hadith of the hoof, the horse's hoof and the arrow, "or a wing" (أَوْ جَنَاحٍ), a phrase which he fabricated for al-Rashid, so the scholars abandoned his hadith because of that and because of his other fabrications, and scholars do not write his hadith under any circumstances. It has been narrated from Malik that he said: There is no prize except in horses and archery, because it is strength against the people of war. He said: The prize in horses is more beloved to us than the prize in archery. The apparent meaning of the hadith equates the prize in racing camels with the prize in racing horses. Some scholars prohibited wagering on anything except horses, because horses were what the Arabs customarily wagered on. It has been narrated from ʿAtaʾ that wagering on anything is permissible, but his statement has been interpreted, because taking it in its general sense ("on anything") leads to permitting gambling, which is forbidden by consensus.

**The fifth issue:** It is not permitted to offer a prize in horses and camels except with a known finishing point and a known distance, as we have mentioned. Likewise, in archery, a prize is not permitted except with a known target, a known number of shots, and a type of hitting, either conditioned on piercing (*khasq*, خَسْقًا) [[*Khasaqa* and *kharaqa* the arrow means it hit the target and penetrated it.]] or hitting without a condition.

There are three types of prize:

The first: a prize given by the ruler, or by a man other than the ruler from his own wealth, voluntarily, who sets for the winner something specified. Whoever wins takes it.

The second: a prize put up by one of the two racers without the other. If the other outruns him, he takes it; if he outruns the other, he takes it. It is good for him to let it stand in the direction in which he put it up, and he does not reclaim it from his wealth. There is no disagreement about this.

The third prize is disputed. It is that each of them puts up something like what the other puts up. Whichever of them wins claims his prize and the prize of his companion. This form is not permitted unless they both bring in between them an intermediary (*muhallil*, مُحَلِّل) whom neither of them is sure will not outrun them. If the intermediary wins, he takes both prizes alone. If one of the two racers wins, he takes his own prize and takes the prize of his companion, and the intermediary has nothing in it and nothing is owed by him. If the second of the two outruns the third, it is as if neither of them had outrun.

Abu ʿAli ibn Khayran, one of al-Shafiʿi's companions, said: The rule for the intermediary horse is that its speed should be unknown. It was called *muhallil* because it makes the prize lawful for the two racers or for itself. The scholars agreed that if there is no intermediary between them, and each of the two racers stipulates that if he wins he takes his prize and his companion's prize, that is gambling and is not permitted.

In Sunan Abi Dawud, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever enters a horse between two horses while he is not sure that it will not outrun them, it is not gambling; and whoever enters it while he is sure that it will outrun them, it is gambling."

In the Muwatta' from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, who said: There is no harm in wagering on horses if an intermediary enters between them. If it wins, it takes the prize, and if it is outrun, nothing is owed by it. This is the view of al-Shafiʿi and the majority of the people of knowledge. Malik's view on this varied: once he said that the intermediary is not obligatory in horse racing, and we do not follow Saʿid's view on it; then he said: It is not permitted except with an intermediary, and this is the better of his two views.

**The sixth issue:** Only a person who has reached puberty (*muhtalim*, مُحْتَلِم) may be mounted on horses and camels in a race. If their owners ride them, that is better. It has been narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (رضي الله عنه) that he said: No one rides horses in a race except their owners. al-Shafiʿi said: The least that constitutes a prize is that the horse wins by its neck (*al-hadi*, الْهَادِي) [[*Al-hadi*: the neck, because it leads forward; the plural is *hawadi*.]] or part of it, or by its rump (*al-kafal*, الْكَفَل) or part of it. A prize among archers in this manner is, according to him, the same. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan's view on this subject is similar to al-Shafiʿi's view.

**The seventh issue:** It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he raced Abu Bakr and ʿUmar (رضي الله عنهما), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) won, and Abu Bakr came close, and ʿUmar came third. The meaning of "Abu Bakr came close" (*wa-salla Abu Bakr*) is that the head of his horse was beside the flank (*sala*, صَلَا) of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) horse, and *al-salawan* (الصَّلَوَان) is the place of the rump.

**His saying, exalted is He:** ﴿And we left Yusuf by our belongings﴾, that is, beside our clothes and our goods, guarding them.

**(So the wolf ate him):** That is because they did not hear their father say: "And I fear that the wolf may eat him," so they took that from his mouth and used it as a pretext, because it was the most evident of the dangers to him.

**(And you will not believe us):** that is, you will not accept what we say as true.

**(Even if we are truthful):** that is, even if we are, said by al-Mubarrad and Ibn Ishaq.

**(In what we say):** Yaʿqub did not accept their word, because of the strong suspicion that became apparent to him concerning them and the many indications contrary to what they said, as will be explained. It has been said: "Even if we are truthful" means: even if we were, in your sight, people of trust and truthfulness, you would not believe us or suspect us in this matter, because of the intensity of your love for Yusuf. This was said by al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj and others.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 18:

His words, may He be exalted: (They came upon his shirt with false blood). In this there are three issues.

The first: His words, may He be exalted: ﴿with false blood﴾. Mujahid said: "It was the blood of a young goat (sakhlah) or a kid (jady) that they had slaughtered." [[In manuscript ʿ: "or something similar."]] Qatadah said: "It was the blood of a gazelle." That is, they came upon his shirt with blood that was falsely claimed to be his, so he described the blood with the verbal noun (masdar, "falsehood"). Its implied meaning is "blood of something having falsehood (dhu kadhib)," like the verse ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], and the doer and the object may both be named by a verbal noun. It is said: "This is the striking of the ruler" (i.e., the one struck by the ruler), "water that is poured" (i.e., water that has been poured), "water that is sunken" (ghawr, i.e., ghair, sunk away), and "a man who is just" (adl, i.e., one who is just).

Al-Hasan and ʿAisha recited "bi-damin kadhib" with a non-dotted dal (kadib), meaning fresh blood; fresh blood is called kadib. It is also reported that it means blood that has changed (in colour), as said by al-Shaʿbi. Kadib also means the white spot that appears on the nails of young people, so it is possible that the blood on the shirt was likened to that white spot because of the difference in the two colours.

The second: Our scholars, may God have mercy upon them, said: When they wanted to make the blood a sign of their truthfulness, God attached to this sign a sign that contradicts it, namely the shirt's being undamaged by tearing [[In manuscript ʿ: "takhriq" (tearing)]]. For it is not possible that a wolf would devour Yusuf while he was wearing the shirt and the shirt would remain unripped. When Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) examined the shirt and found no tear or mark in it, he deduced from this that they were lying, and he said to them: "When has this wolf been so wise that it devours Yusuf and does not tear the shirt!" This was said by Ibn Abbas and others. Israʾil narrated from Simak ibn Harb, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The blood was the blood of a young goat." Sufyan narrated from Simak, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When he looked at it he said, 'You have lied! If the wolf had eaten him, it would have torn the shirt.'"

Al-Mawardi reported that there were three signs in the shirt: when they came upon it with false blood; when its back was torn; and when it was thrown over his father's face and he regained his sight.

I say: This is rejected, for the shirt on which they came with the blood is not the shirt that was torn, nor the shirt that the bearer of good news brought. It has been said that the torn shirt is the one that was brought, and he regained his sight by it, as will be explained at the end of the surah, God willing, the Exalted.

It is also related that they said to him: "Rather, robbers killed him." Their statements then contradicted one another, so he accused them. Yaʿqub said to them: "You claim that the wolf ate him, but if it had eaten him, it would have torn his shirt before reaching his skin, and I see no tear in the shirt. You claim that robbers killed him, but if they had killed him, they would have taken his shirt. Do they want anything but his clothes?!" At that they said: ﴿You will not believe us even if we are truthful﴾ [Yusuf: 17]. This is reported from al-Hasan and others, meaning: even if we were described as truthful, you would not believe us because of the accusation.

The third: Jurists have used this verse as evidence for acting upon indicators (amarat, circumstantial signs) in several matters of fiqh, such as the qasamah (the procedure of oaths in homicide cases) and others. They agreed that Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) used the soundness of the shirt as evidence of their lying. Likewise, the one who examines must take note of indicators and signs when they conflict; what is stronger among them decides in favour of the side of preponderance, namely the strength of the accusation. There is no disagreement about judging by them. This was said by Ibn al-ʿArabi.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: Rather, your own souls have made a matter attractive to you; so patience is beautiful﴾. In this there are three issues.

The first: It is related that when his sons said to him, "The wolf has eaten him," he said to them: "Did the wolf not leave any part of him, so that you could bring it to me that I might find comfort in it? Did it not leave me a garment in which I could smell his scent?" They said: "Yes! This is his shirt smeared with his blood." That is the meaning of His words: ﴿They came upon his shirt with false blood﴾. Then Yaʿqub wept at that and said to his sons: "Show me his shirt." They showed it to him, and he smelled it and kissed it. Then he began to turn it over and saw in it no rip or tear. He said: "By God, besides whom there is no god, I have never seen a wolf more wise than this one! It ate my son and took him out of his shirt without tearing it." He knew that the matter was not as they had said and that the wolf had not eaten him. So he turned away from them, as one who is angry, weeping and grieving, and said: "O company of my sons! Show me where my son is. If he is alive, I will return him to me; and if he is dead, I will shroud him and bury him."

It is said that at that point they said: "Do you not see how our father calls us liars in our statement? Come, let us take him out of the well, cut him into limbs, and bring our father one of his limbs; he will then believe us in our statement and his despair will be cut off." Yahudha said: "By God, if you do that, I will be an enemy to you as long as I live, and I will certainly inform your father of your evil deed." They said: "Since you prevent us from this, come, let us hunt a wolf for him." He said: "Then hunt a wolf, smear it with blood, bind it with ropes, and then bring it to Yaʿqub and say: 'O our father! This is the wolf that comes to our sheep and preys upon them, and perhaps it is the one that grieved us over our brother. We have no doubt about it, and this is its blood upon it.'" Yaʿqub said: "Release it." They released it, and the wolf wagged its tail to him (tabasbasa), and it came near him while Yaʿqub was saying to it: "Come closer, come closer," until it pressed its cheek against his cheek [[In manuscripts ʿ, k, w: "against his thigh."]]. Yaʿqub said to it: "O wolf! Why did you cause me to lose my son and leave me with long grief?" Then he said: "O God, make it speak!" God the Exalted made it speak, and it said: "By He who chose you as a prophet, I did not eat his flesh, nor tear his skin, nor pluck a single hair from his hairs. By God, I have no covenant with your son. I am only a stranger wolf who came from the regions of Egypt seeking a brother of mine who was lost, and I do not know whether he is alive or dead. Your sons hunted me and bound me. Indeed, the flesh of the prophets is forbidden to us and to all the beasts. By God! I will not stay in a land where the sons of the prophets lie to the beasts." So Yaʿqub released it and said: "By God, you have brought the proof against yourselves. This is a wolf of the beasts who came out seeking the protection of its brother, while you have neglected your brother. And you know that the wolf is innocent of what you have brought."

(Rather, He made attractive to you) means: adorned for you.

(to you your souls made a matter) means: other than what you describe and mention. Then, as a preparation for himself, he said: (so patience is beautiful). The second issue: Al-Zajjaj said: "That is, my affair and what I believe is beautiful patience." Qutrub said: "That is, my patience is beautiful patience." It is also said: "That is, beautiful patience is more fitting for me," so it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted.

It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about beautiful patience and said: "It is that in which there is no complaint." More will come about this at the end of the surah, God willing. Abu Hatim said: Ibn ʿUmar Isa reportedly recited (according to what Sahl ibn Yusuf claimed) "fa-sabran jamilan" (with the accusative). He said: Likewise al-Ashhab al-ʿUqayli recited it, and he said it is likewise in the codices of Anas and Abu Salih. Al-Mubarrad said: "Fa-sabrun jamilun" with the nominative is better than the accusative, because the meaning is: "He said: My Lord, with me is beautiful patience." He said: The accusative is only as a verbal noun, meaning "I will surely be patient with beautiful patience," as in the verse:

My camel complained to me of the length of the journey... patience, beautiful, so we are both tested.

[[Another reading in the verse is "fa-sabrun jamilun," and it may be explained by supplying a subject or predicate. Another reading is "sabran jamilan," as a call to the camel.]]

Beautiful patience is that in which there is no impatience and no complaint. It is said: The meaning is: I will not live with you in a gloomy face and a frowning brow, but I will live with you as I was with you before; and in this there is an indication that he pardoned them for their wrongdoing. It is related from Habib ibn Abi Thabit that Yaʿqub's eyebrows had fallen over his eyes, so he used to lift them with a piece of cloth. He was asked: "What is this?" He said: "The length of time and the abundance of sorrows." So God revealed to him: "Do you complain about Me, O Yaʿqub?" He said: "O Lord! It is a sin I committed, so forgive me."

(And God is the One whose help is sought): a beginning and a predicate.

(Against what you describe) means: upon bearing what you describe of lying.

The third issue: Ibn Abi Rifaʿa said: It is fitting for people of opinion (ahl al-ra'y) to suspect their own opinions when considering the thought of Yaʿqub (peace be upon him), who was a prophet, when his sons said to him: ﴿We went racing and left Yusuf with our belongings, and the wolf ate him﴾. He said: ﴿Rather, your own souls have made a matter attractive to you; so patience is beautiful﴾, and he was right in this. Then they said to him: ﴿Your son stole, and we testify only to what we know, and we were not guardians of the unseen﴾ [[See p. 244 of this part.]]. He said: ﴿Rather, your own souls have made a matter attractive to you﴾, and in this he was not right.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 19:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And a caravan came﴾, that is, a passing company travelling from al-Sham (Greater Syria) to Egypt. They lost their way and wandered until they stopped near the well (al-jubb). The well was in a remote desert far from inhabited land, used only by shepherds and passing travellers. Its water was brackish, but it became sweet when Yusuf was thrown into it.

(﴿Then they sent their water-drawer﴾): he is referred to in the masculine according to the sense. Had he said "then she sent her water-drawer (warida)," it would have followed the wording, as in "wa-jaʾat." The *warid* is the one who comes to the water to draw it for the people. According to what the exegetes mention, his name was Malik ibn Du'r (Du'r: it is with an unpointed dal, and with a dhal it is a scribal error, as in the Qamus), from the Arab al-ʿAribah.

(﴿So he let down his bucket﴾): that is, he sent it down. It is said: *adlā dalwahu* when one lets down one's bucket in order to fill it, and *dallāhā* means he drew it up. This is related from al-Asmaʿi and others. *Dalā* (from the root with waw) means *yadlū dalwan*, that is, he pulled and drew up; likewise *adlā* means he sent down. When the form became heavy, they changed it back to the ya', because it is lighter than the waw, as the Kufans say. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: when the verb exceeds three letters, it returns to the ya', following the imperfect. The plural of *dalw* in the smallest number is *adlun*; when the number is larger, you say *duliyy* and *dilliyy*, with the waw changed to ya'. However, the plural is generally characterised by change, and the singular and plural should be distinguished. There is also *dilāʾ*.

Yusuf then caught hold of the rope, and when he came out he was a youth like the moon on the night of the full moon, the most beautiful of youths. The Prophet (ﷺ) said in the hadith of the Night Journey, from Sahih Muslim: "Then behold, Yusuf, and he had been given half of beauty." Kaʿb al-Ahbar said: Yusuf had a handsome face, curly hair, large eyes, a well-proportioned physique, fair complexion, thick forearms and upper arms, a slender belly, and a small navel. When he smiled, you saw light from his laughter, and when he spoke, you saw the rays of the sun in his speech from his front teeth. No one could describe him, and his beauty was like daylight at night. He resembled Adam (peace be upon him) on the day Allah created him and breathed into him of His spirit, before he committed the disobedience. It is said that he inherited that beauty from his grandmother Sarah, who had been given a sixth of beauty. When Malik ibn Du'r saw him, he said: "Oh good news! This is a boy!" This is the reading of the people of Madinah and the people of Basrah, except that Ibn Abi Ishaq read "Ya bushrā hādhā ghulām," changing the alif to ya', because this ya' causes what precedes it to take a kasra; since it is not permissible to put a kasra on the alif, its conversion was a substitute. The people of Kufah read "Yā bushrā" without idafah (construct). Its meaning has two views: first, it is the name of the boy; second, its meaning is: "O (you) good news, this is your time and your moment."

Qatadah and al-Suddi said: when the one who let down the bucket did so, Yusuf caught hold of it and said: "Oh good news! This is a boy." Qatadah said: he gave good news to his companions that he had found a slave. Al-Suddi said: he called out to a man whose name was Bushra. Al-Nahhas said: Qatadah's view is more preferable, because the naming of any person in the Qur'an occurs only rarely; rather, it comes by way of allusion, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And the day the wrongdoer bites his hands﴾ [al-Furqan: 27], and he was ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿit; and after it: ﴿Woe to me! Would that I had not taken so-and-so as a friend﴾ [al-Furqan: 28], and he was Umayyah ibn Khalaf, said al-Nahhas. The meaning in calling out "bushrā" is to announce good news to those present, and it is more emphatic than your saying "I have been given good news (tabashshartu)," just as you say: "O wonder!", meaning "O wonder, this is from your days and from your signs, so be present!" This is the view of Sibawayh, and al-Suhayli said the same. It is also said that it is like your saying "Woe, my joy!" and that *bushrā* is a verbal noun from *istibshār* (rejoicing). This is more sound, because if it were a proper name it would not be in construct with a first-person pronoun. On this view, "bushrā" is in the accusative position, since it is a construct vocative, and the meaning of the calling here is alerting: "Pay attention to my joy and happiness." On al-Suddi's view it is in the nominative position, as you say: "O Zayd, this is a boy." It is also permissible that its position be accusative, as in your saying: "O man!" and His saying: ﴿Alas for the servants﴾ [Yasin: 30]. However, "Bushrā" is not given tanwin, because it is a diptote (lā yanṣarif).

(﴿And they concealed him as merchandise﴾): the pronoun (hāʾ) refers to Yusuf (peace be upon him), while the waw refers to his brothers. It is also said that it refers to the merchants who bought him, and it is also said that it refers to the warid and his companions. "Biḍāʿatan" (as merchandise) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). Mujahid said: Malik ibn Du'r and his companions concealed him from the merchants who were with them in the caravan, and they said to them: "He is merchandise which some people of al-Sham, or the people of this water, entrusted to us to take to Egypt." They said this only out of fear of sharing (in the sale). Ibn ʿAbbas said: Yusuf's brothers concealed him as merchandise when he was drawn out of the well. That is because they came and said: "What a wicked thing you have done! This is a runaway slave of ours," and they said to Yusuf in Hebrew: "Either you acknowledge to us that you are a slave, and we will sell you to these people, or we will take you and kill you." He said: "I acknowledge to you that I am a slave," so he acknowledged it to them, and they sold him to them. It is also said that Yahudha advised his brother Yusuf in their language: "Acknowledge to your brothers that you are a slave, for I fear that if you do not do so they will kill you, so perhaps Allah will make a way out for you and you will be saved from death." So Yusuf concealed his affair for fear that his brothers would kill him. Malik said: "By Allah, these are not the marks of slaves!" They said: "He was raised in our laps, took on our manners, and was disciplined in our ways." He said: "What do you say, boy?" He said: "They have spoken the truth! I was raised in their laps and took on their manners." Malik said: "If you sell him to me, I will buy him from you," so they sold him to him. That is [the meaning of]:

**First issue:** The Almighty's words, (*wa-shaarawhu*), "and they sold him." It is said that *sharaytu* means *ishtaraytu* (I bought), and *sharaytu* also means *baatu* (I sold), and both are dialectal usages. The poet said:

*"And I sold a cloak, I wish I had been (buried) after the cloak, I would have been its (grave-)head."*

That is, *bi'tu* (I sold). Another poet said:

*"So when he bought her, tears flowed in his eye, and in his chest was a burning from blame, a scorching pain."* [[The verse is by al-Shammakh, said about a man who sold his bow to another man. *Hamiz* means "burning," and it is said it means "scorching, burning." Another version reads "from grief" (*min al-wajd*). Source: *Lisan al-Arab*.]]

**(bi-thamanin bakhsin):** *Bakhs* means "deficient," and here it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) used in place of an adjective, meaning they sold him for a price that was *mabkhus*, that is, diminished. Joseph's brothers did not intend to gain from his price; their aim was to gain from the removal of their father's attention from him. It is also said that Yahudha (Judah) saw Joseph being drawn out of the well from a distance, so he informed his brothers, and they came and sold him to the caravan that had arrived. It is also said that no, rather they returned after three days to the well to find out the news, and they saw the trace of the caravan (*sayyarah*), so they followed them and said: "This is our slave who ran away from us," and they sold him to them. Qatadah said: "*bakhs*" means "wrongful." Al-Dahhak, Muqatil, al-Suddi and Ibn Ata' said: "*bakhs*" means "forbidden." Ibn al-Arabi said: "There is no basis for this. The implication is only that his price was not paid in full according to its value. For if his brothers sold him, their aim was not to gain from his price, but rather to gain from their father's attention being removed from him. And if those who sold him were the caravan (*waridah*), then they concealed him as a stolen item, or they said to their companions: 'Send with us merchandise,' and they saw that they had received no price for him, and that whatever they took for him was entirely profit."

I (al-Qurtubi) say: His statement, "The implication is only that his price was not paid in full according to its value," indicates that if they had taken the full value for him, it would have been permissible, and this is not so. This confirms the correctness of what al-Suddi and others said, for they concluded a sale on a person who may not be sold, and therefore the price for him was not lawful to them.

Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi said: "*bakhs*" means "little." Ibn Hayyan said: "*bakhs*" means "counterfeit." It is reported from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud that they sold him for twenty dirhams, each of his brothers taking two dirhams, and they were ten. Qatadah and al-Suddi also said this. Abu al-'Aliyah and Muqatil said: twenty-two dirhams, and they were eleven, each taking two dirhams. Mujahid also said this. Ikrimah said: forty dirhams. What is reported from the Companions (*sahabah*) is more worthy of being preferred. And "*bakhs*" is an adjective (*na't*) of "*bi-thaman*" (a price).

**(darahima):** This is in apposition (*badal*) to the price, and it is an explanation of it. It is also said *darahim* (plural of *dirham*), and it is said *darahim* is a plural of *dirham* with the form *darahiim*; according to Sibawayh it may be a collective noun (*ism jam'*), and according to him it may also be that the vowel *kasrah* was lengthened so it became a *ya'*. This is not like lengthening a short vowel of a *maqsur* word, because lengthening a *maqsur* word is not permitted according to the Basrans, neither in poetry nor otherwise. The grammarians recited:

*"Her two hands throw off pebbles in every noonday heat, like the throwing of dirhams, the money-changers' coins being handled."* [[The verse is by al-Farazdaq, describing a swift she-camel in the midday heat. He likened the pebbles thrown off from beneath her hooves to dirhams flying up from the fingers when they are being counted.]]

**(ma'dudatin):** This is an adjective, and this indicates that their currency was exchanged by counting, not by weighing. It is also said that it is an expression for the small amount of the price, because they were dirhams that did not reach the point of being weighed due to their small quantity, for they did not weigh anything below the *uqiyyah* (ounce), which is forty dirhams.

**The second issue:** Al-Qadi Ibn al-Arabi said: The origin of the two currencies (gold and silver) is weighing. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not sell gold for gold, nor silver for silver, except weight for weight; whoever adds or asks for more has committed usury (*riba*)." The weight has no benefit except the quantity; as for its form, there is no benefit in it. But counting was adopted for it as a relief to people because of the frequency of transactions, for weighing would be burdensome. Thus, if coins (*mathaqil* or dirhams) were minted, it would be permissible to exchange some of them for others by counting, provided there was no deficiency or excess in them. If they were deficient, the matter returns to weighing. For this reason, clipping or filing them is among the corruption on earth, as has already been explained.

**The third issue:** The scholars differed about whether dirhams and dinars are specified (*tata'ayyan*) or not. The transmission from Malik differs on this. Ashhab held that they are not specified, which is the apparent view of Malik's position, and this is also the view of Abu Hanifah. Ibn al-Qasim held that they are specified; this is related from al-Karkhi, and al-Shafi'i also held it. The benefit of the disagreement is this: if we say they are not specified, then when someone says, "I have sold you these dinars for these dirhams," the dinars become a debt upon the one who owes them, and the dirhams upon the one who owes them. But if they were specified and then destroyed, nothing would attach to the liability of either of them, and the contract would be void, like the sale of specific goods (*a'yan*) of merchandise and other things.

**The fourth issue:** It is reported from al-Hasan ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he ruled concerning a foundling (*luqit*) that he is free, and he recited: "And they sold him for a deficient price, dirhams counted." The discussion of this has already passed.

**The fifth issue:** The Almighty's words: ﴿And they were among those who had no desire for him﴾. It is said: the intended meaning is his brothers. It is said: the caravan. It is said: the caravan that had arrived (*al-waridah*). In any case, he was not desirable to them: not to the brothers, because their aim was to remove him from his father, not to gain his wealth; nor to the caravan, because of the brothers' statement that he was a slave who had run away from them; and nor to the arriving caravan, because they feared their companions sharing with them, and they saw that a small price for him, taken alone, was better. (*Zuhd* means "little desire.")

**The sixth issue:** In this verse there is clear evidence for the permissibility of buying a valuable thing for a small price, and the sale is binding. For this reason Malik said: if someone sold a pearl of great value for one dirham, then said, "I did not know that it was a pearl, and I thought it was a *makhshalabah*" (a white bead resembling a pearl), the sale is binding on him, and his statement is not considered.

It is said: "And they were among those who had no desire for him" means: for his beauty, because Allah, though He gave Joseph half of beauty, turned away from him the inclinations of the people's souls toward him, as an honor to him. It is also said: "And they were among those who had no desire for him" means: they did not know his station with Allah, the Almighty.

Sibawayh and al-Kisa'i related: *zahidtu* and *zahidtu*, with the *ha'* vowelled with *kasrah* and with *fathah*.

﴿And the one who bought him from Egypt said to his wife, "Honor his residence"﴾. It is said: the word *ishtira* (bought) here means *istibdal* (exchange), since it was not a contract, as in His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ [[See vol. 1, p. 21.]] [Al-Baqarah: 16]. It is also said: they assumed that it was a purchase in its outward appearance, so this expression followed the apparent assumption. Al-Dahhak said: this one who bought him was the king of Egypt, whose title was al-Aziz. Al-Suhayli said: his name was Qitfir. Ibn Ishaq said: Itfir son of Ruwayhib bought him for his wife Ra'il, as mentioned by al-Mawardi. It is also said: her name was Zulaykha. Allah had placed love for Joseph in the heart of al-Aziz, so he instructed his household concerning him, as mentioned by al-Qushayri. Al-Tha'labi and others mentioned both opinions regarding her name. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was Qitfir, the minister of the king of Egypt, who bought him, and he is al-Rayyan son of al-Walid. It is also said: al-Walid son of al-Rayyan, a man from the Amalekites. It is also said: he was the Pharaoh of Moses, based on Moses' saying: ﴿And Joseph had certainly come to you before with clear proofs﴾ [Ghafir: 34], and that he lived four hundred years. It is also said: the Pharaoh of Moses was one of the descendants of the Pharaoh of Joseph, as its explanation will come in *Ghafir* [[See vol. 15, p. 312.]]. This al-Aziz who bought Joseph was over the treasuries of the king. He bought Joseph from Malik ibn Du'r for twenty dinars, and he added to the price a garment and a pair of sandals. It is also said: he bought him from the caravan people. It is also said: they bid against one another for his price until it reached many times his weight in musk, ambergris, silk, silver, gold, pearls, and jewels whose value none knows but Allah, and Qitfir bought him from Malik for this price. This was stated by Wahb ibn Munabbih. Wahb and others also said: when Malik ibn Du'r bought Joseph from his brothers, he wrote between them and himself a document: "This is what Malik ibn Du'r bought from the sons of Ya'qub, namely so-and-so and so-and-so, a slave belonging to them, for twenty dirhams. They stipulated for him that he is a runaway, and that he will not be returned except shackled and chained, and he gave them the covenant of Allah concerning this." He said: Joseph then bade them farewell and began to say: "May Allah protect you, even if you neglect me; may Allah help you, even if you forsake me; may Allah have mercy on you, even if you do not show mercy to me." They said: the sheep then cast forth what was in their bellies as fresh blood, due to the intensity of this farewell [al-dam al-'abit means fresh blood]. They carried him on a saddle with no covering and no padding, shackled, bound, and chained. They passed by the cemetery of the family of Canaan, and he saw the grave of his mother. An black man had been assigned to guard him, and the black man became heedless. Joseph threw himself upon his mother's grave, rolling himself in it, embracing the grave, and writhing, and saying: "O mother! Raise your head and see your son shackled, bound, chained, and fettered. They have separated me from my father. So ask Allah to gather us together in the abode of His mercy, for He is the Most Merciful of the merciful." The black man then searched for him on the camel and did not find him, so he followed his trail, and there he saw a whiteness on a grave. He looked closely and it was indeed Joseph, so he kicked him with his foot into the dust, rolled him over, and struck him a painful blow. Joseph said to him: "Do not do that! By Allah, I did not flee and I did not run away; I merely passed by my mother's grave, so I wished to bid her farewell, and I will not return to what you dislike." The black man said: "By Allah, you are indeed a wicked slave! You call on your father one time and your mother another! Why did this not happen in front of your masters?" Joseph raised his hands to the sky and said: "O Allah, if I have a sin with You that has disfigured my face, then I ask You, by the right of my forefathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, to forgive me and have mercy on me." The angels then cried out in the sky, and Gabriel descended and said to him: "O Joseph! Lower your voice, for you have made the angels of heaven weep! Do you want me to overturn the earth and make its top its bottom?" He said: "Be patient, O Gabriel, for Allah is forbearing and does not hasten." So he struck the earth with his wing, and it became dark, the dust rose, the sun was eclipsed, and the caravan remained unable to recognize one another. The leader of the caravan said: "Which of you has committed a wrong? For I have been traveling since such-and-such a time, and nothing like this has ever befallen me." The black man said: "I slapped that Hebrew boy." Joseph raised his hand to the sky and spoke with words I do not understand, and I have no doubt that he invoked a curse upon us. The leader said to him: "You wanted nothing but our destruction! Bring him to us." So he brought him, and the leader said to him: "O boy! He has slapped you, and this has come upon us as you have seen. If you wish to retaliate, retaliate against whomever you wish; and if you wish to pardon, that is what we expect of you." He said: "I have pardoned, hoping that Allah will pardon me." Then the dust cleared, the sun appeared, and the eastern and western regions of the earth were illuminated. The merchant kept visiting him morning and evening and honoring him, until he reached Egypt, where he bathed in its Nile, and Allah removed from him the sorrow of the journey and restored his beauty. He entered the city by day, and his light shone upon the walls. They put him up for sale, and Qitfir, the minister of the king, bought him, as Ibn 'Abbas said, according to what has preceded. It is also said: this king did not die until he believed and followed Joseph in his religion. Then the king died while Joseph was over the treasuries of the land. Qabus then ruled after him, and he was a disbeliever, so Joseph invited him to Islam, but he refused.

(Honor his residence) means his dwelling and his station, with good food and fine clothing. It is derived from *thawa bi-l-makan*, meaning he stayed in the place. This was discussed earlier in *Al 'Imran* [[See vol. 4, p. 233.]] and elsewhere.

(Perhaps he will benefit us) means he will suffice us in some important matters when he grows up.

(Or we may adopt him as a son) Ibn 'Abbas said: he was a *hasur*, one who could not father children. Similarly Ibn Ishaq said: Qitfir did not approach women and had no children. If it is asked: how could he say "or we may adopt him as a son" when he was his property, and being a son and being a slave are contradictory? It is answered: he would free him and then adopt him as a son through *tabanni* (adoption, taking someone as a son), and adoption was known among the nations, and it was also practiced at the beginning of Islam, as its explanation will come in *al-Ahzab* [[See vol. 14, p. 118 onwards and p. 188 onwards.]], if Allah the Exalted wills. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: the people with the best discernment (*firasa*, insight or physiognomic perception) are three: al-Aziz, when he discerned in Joseph and said: "Perhaps he will benefit us or we may adopt him as a son"; the daughter of Shu'ayb, when she said to her father concerning Moses: ﴿Hire him; indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy﴾ [Al-Qasas: 26] [[Vol. 10, p. 42 onwards.]]; and Abu Bakr, when he appointed 'Umar as his successor. Ibn al-'Arabi said: how strange of the exegetes that they agree in citing this report! Firasa is a rare science, as its explanation will come in *Surat al-Hijr* [[See vol. 13, p. 271.]], and this is not the case in what they have transmitted, because al-Siddiq appointed 'Umar on the basis of his experience in affairs, his constant companionship and its length, and his awareness of what he witnessed from him of knowledge and strength; this is not by way of firasa. As for the daughter of Shu'ayb, she had a clear sign, as its explanation will come in *al-Qasas* [[See vol. 13, p. 271.]]. As for the matter of al-Aziz, it may be considered firasa, since he had no apparent sign. And Allah knows best.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land﴾. The *kaf* (the "thus") is in the accusative position, meaning: just as We rescued him from his brothers and from the well, so likewise We established him, that is, We inclined toward him the heart of the king who bought him, until he became firmly established in commanding and forbidding in the city over which the king had authority.

(And that We may teach him the interpretation of events) meaning: We did that in confirmation of Ya'qub's saying: "And He will teach you the interpretation of events." It is also said: the meaning is that We established him so that We might reveal to him through a word from Us, and teach him its *ta'wil* (interpretation or ultimate meaning) and its *tafsir* (explanation), and the interpretation of dreams. Here the speech ends.

(And Allah is predominant over His affair) The pronoun refers to Allah the Exalted, meaning: nothing overcomes Allah, rather He is dominant over His own affair in what He wills, when He says to it: "Be," and it is. It is also said: it refers to Joseph, meaning Allah is dominant over Joseph's affair, managing it, guarding it, and not leaving it to anyone else, so that no plotter's scheme can reach him.

(But most of the people do not know) meaning they do not come to know His unseen. It is also said: "most" here means all, because no one knows the unseen. It is also said: it is to be taken in its apparent sense, since Allah may let whomever He wills know some of His unseen. It is also said: the meaning of "But most of the people do not know" is that Allah is dominant over His affair, and they are the polytheists and those who do not believe in *qadar* (divine decree). The wise men said concerning this verse: "And Allah is predominant over His affair": when Ya'qub commanded him not to relate his dream to his brothers, the decree of Allah prevailed until he related it. Then his brothers wanted to kill him, but the decree of Allah prevailed until he became a king and they prostrated before him. Then the brothers wanted their father's face to be clear for them, but the decree of Allah prevailed until their father's heart was constricted, and he remembered Joseph after seventy or eighty years, and said: ﴿O my sorrow over Joseph!﴾ [Yusuf: 84]. Then they planned to become righteous people after him, meaning penitent, but the decree of Allah prevailed until they forgot the sin and persisted in it, until they confessed before Joseph at the end of the matter after seventy years, and said to their father: ﴿Indeed, we were sinners﴾ [Yusuf: 97]. Then they wanted to deceive their father with weeping and the shirt [but the decree of Allah prevailed], so he was not deceived and said: ﴿Rather, your souls have enticed you to something﴾ [Yusuf: 18]. Then they schemed to make his love leave their father's heart, but the decree of Allah prevailed and the love and longing in his heart increased. Then the wife of al-Aziz plotted that if she spoke to him first she would overcome him, but the decree of Allah prevailed until al-Aziz said: ﴿Ask forgiveness for your sin; indeed, you were among the sinners﴾ [Yusuf: 29]. Then Joseph planned to be freed from prison by mentioning the cupbearer, but the decree of Allah prevailed and the cupbearer forgot. And Joseph remained in prison for several years.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 22:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When he reached his full strength﴾. Regarding "ashuddahu" (أَشُدَّهُ), according to Sibawayh it is a plural whose singular is *shiddah* (شِدَّةٌ). Al-Kisa'i said: its singular is *shadd* (شَدٌّ), as the poet said [[This is ʿAntarah al-ʿAbsi. *Shadd al-nahar* means its *ashudd*, that is, its height. *Al-labban* is the chest; it is also said to be its middle, and also said to be what lies between the two breasts. It is narrated as "*al-banan*". *Al-ʿaẓlam* is the sap of a tree or plant used for dyeing, or *al-wasmah*, a tree whose leaves are used as a dye.]]:

*My memory of him is at the height of the day, as if his chest and his head had been dyed with ʿaẓlam.*

Abu ʿUbayd claimed that among the Arabs there is no singular for it from its own form, and its meaning is the completion of strength, after which decline follows. Mujahid and Qatadah said: *al-ashudd* is thirty-three years. Rabiʿah, Zayd ibn Aslam and Malik ibn Anas said: *al-ashudd* is the attainment of *hulum* (puberty). What the scholars have said on this has already passed in *al-Nisa'* [[See vol. 5, p. 34 onward.]] and *al-An'am* [[See vol. 7, p. 134 onward.]], where it is fully discussed.

(﴿We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾). It is said: We made him the one in charge of judgment, so he would judge within the king's authority; that is, We gave him knowledge of judgment. Mujahid said: intellect, understanding and prophethood. It is also said: *judgment* is prophethood, and *knowledge* is the knowledge of religion. It is also said: it is the knowledge of interpreting dreams. Whoever said that he was given prophethood as a child says: ﴿When he reached his full strength﴾ means We increased him in understanding and knowledge.

(﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾), meaning the believers. It is also said: those who are patient in calamities, as Yusuf was patient; this was said by al-Dahhak. Al-Tabari said: although its apparent scope applies to every good-doer, what is intended is Muhammad (ﷺ). God, may He be exalted, says: just as I did this for Yusuf after he endured what he endured, and then gave him what I gave him, so I will deliver you from the polytheists of your people who aim at you with enmity, and I will establish you in the land.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 23–24 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him⁠—⁠from himself⁠—⁠﴾. She was the wife of al-'Aziz, and she asked him to lie with her. The root of al-muraawadah (seeking to seduce) is the desire and request made gently and softly. Al-rawd and al-riyad mean seeking pasture, and it has been said: it derives from ruwayd, as one says, "So-and-so walks ruwaydan," meaning gently. So al-muraawadah is gentleness in pursuit. It is said of a man, "He sought her from herself," and of a woman, "She sought him from himself." Al-rawd also means deliberation; one says, "arwadani," meaning "give me time."

(﴿And they closed the doors﴾) Ghallaqa is used for the many (doors), and one does not say ghalaqa al-bab; aghlaqa is used for both the many and the few, as al-Farazdaq said about Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala':

I kept closing doors and opening them
until I came to Abu 'Amr ibn 'Ammar.

It is said that there were seven doors; she closed them and then invited him to herself.

(﴿And she said, "Hayta laka"﴾) That is, come, approach, and come hither. It has no verbal noun (masdar) and no inflection. Al-Nahhas said: there are seven readings of it. Among the most excellent of them and the most sound in its chain is what al-A'mash related from Abu Wa'il, who said: I heard 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud reading "Hayta laka." I said: "Some people read it 'Hiyta laka.'" He said: "I read as I was taught." Abu Ja'far said: Some narrate it from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud from the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is not far-fetched, because his saying "I read as I was taught" indicates that it is marfu' (traced to the Prophet). This reading with a fathah on the ta' and the ha' is the sound reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Mujahid and 'Ikrimah, and with it read Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', 'Asim, al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: Do not stop in the Qur'an, for it is only like the saying of one of you: "Halumma" and "Ta'al." Ibn Abi Ishaq al-Nahwi read "Qalat hayti laka," with a fathah on the ha' and a kasrah on the ta'. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Ibn Kathir read "Hayta laka," with a fathah on the ha' and a dammah on the ta'. Tarafah said:

It is not that my people are the most distant when
a caller from the clan says "Hayta"

These are three readings in which the ha' is fathah. Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and Nafi' read "Wa qalat Hiyta laka," with a kasrah on the ha' and a fathah on the ta'. Yahya ibn Wathhab read "Wa qalat Hiyta laka," with a kasrah on the ha', after it a silent ya', and the ta' with a dammah. It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ikrimah: "Wa qalat Hiyta, laka," with a kasrah on the ha', after it a silent hamzah, and the ta' with a dammah. From Ibn 'Amir and the people of Syria: "Wa qalat Hiyta," with a kasrah on the ha', with the hamzah, and a fathah on the ta'. Abu Ja'far said: "Hayta laka," with a fathah on the ta', is because of the meeting of two silent letters, since it is a sound like mah and sah, which ought not to be inflected; and the fathah is light, because before the ta' there is a ya' like "ayna" and "kayfa." As for one who reads the ta' with a kasrah, he reads it so because the original is the kasrah, since a silent letter when moved is moved to the kasrah. As for one who reads with a dammah, it is because it carries the sense of an end-point, meaning: she said, "My call is for you." When the annexation is removed, it is built on the dammah, like "haythu" and "ba'du." As for the reading of the people of Madinah, there are two views: one is that the fathah is due to the meeting of two silent letters, as has passed. The other is that it is a verb from hay'a, yahay'u, like ja'a yaj'u, so that the meaning in "hi'ta" is: your state has become good. And "laka" is from a different statement, as you say: "laka a'ni" (for you, I mean). Whoever reads with a hamzah and a dammah on the ta' it is a verb meaning "I have prepared myself for you," and likewise whoever reads "Hiyta laka." Abu 'Amr rejected this reading. Abu 'Ubaydah Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna said: Abu 'Amr was asked about the reading of one who reads with a kasrah on the ha' and a dammah on the ta', hamzated, and he said: "Baatil! He made it from tahayya'tu! Go and survey the Arabs until you reach Yemen; do you know anyone who says this?!" Al-Kisa'i also said: "Hi'ta" was not related from the Arabs. 'Ikrimah said: "Hayta laka" means: I have prepared myself for you, and adorned myself, and beautified myself; and it is a reading not approved, because it was not heard in Arabic. Al-Nahhas said: it is good according to the Basrans, because it is said: "ha'a al-rajulu yuha'u wa yahay'u hay'atan," so "ha'a yahay'u" is like "ja'a yaj'u," and "hiyta" is like "ji'ta." The kasrah on the ha' in "Hayta" is a dialect of a people who prefer the kasrah on the ha' to its fathah. Al-Zajjaj said: The best of the readings is "Hayta" with a fathah on the ha' and the ta'. Tarafah said:

It is not that my people are the most distant when
a caller from the clan says "Hayta"

with a fathah on the ha' and the ta'. And a poet said about 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him:

Convey to the Commander of the Faithful, the brother of Iraq, when you come to him,
that Iraq and its people are at peace with you, so "Hayta, Hayta!"

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: "Hayta" is a word in Syriac, calling him to herself. Al-Suddi said: its meaning in Coptic [in the Nabataean ('ayn) dialect] is "Come, for you." Abu 'Ubayd said: al-Kisa'i used to say: it is a dialect of the people of Hawran that reached the people of the Hijaz, and its meaning is "Come hither." Abu 'Ubayd said: I asked a learned elder from Hawran, who mentioned that it is their language, and 'Ikrimah also said so. Mujahid and others said: it is an Arabic dialect by which she invites him to herself, and it is a word of urging and inviting toward things. Al-Jawhari said: it is said "hawwata bihi" and "hayyata bihi" when one shouts at him and calls him. He said:

Indeed the cooing dove has silenced me, so I doubted;
had it been addressed by it, it would have called out.

That is, it shouted. Another said:

Every youth drives them with "hayyat" calls.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Ma'adha Allah"﴾ That is, I seek refuge in Allah and I ask Him for protection from what you call me to. It is a verbal noun, meaning: I seek refuge in Allah with refuge; the object is omitted and the verbal noun is put in the accusative by the omitted verb, and the verbal noun is annexed to the name of Allah, as the verbal noun is annexed to the object, as you say: "I passed by Zayd, the passing of 'Amr," that is, like my passing by 'Amr.

(﴿Indeed, he is my lord﴾) meaning her husband: he is my master who has honored me, so I will not betray him. This was said by Mujahid, Ibn Ishaq and al-Suddi. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, indeed Allah is my Lord, who has taken care of me with His kindness, so I will not commit what He has forbidden.

(﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers do not succeed﴾) In the report: she said to him, "O Yusuf! How beautiful is the form of your face!" He said, "My Lord fashioned me in the womb." She said, "O Yusuf! How beautiful is your hair!" He said, "It is the first thing that will decay of me in my grave." She said, "O Yusuf! How beautiful are your eyes!" He said, "With them I look to my Lord." She said, "O Yusuf! Raise your gaze and look at my face." He said, "I fear blindness in my Hereafter." She said, "O Yusuf! Shall I draw near to you while you distance yourself from me?!" He said, "I want by that nearness to my Lord." She said, "O Yusuf! I have spread out for you the qaytun [[al-qaytun: the small private chamber; a non-Arabic word, and it was said to be in the language of the people of Egypt and the Berbers.]] so enter with me." He said, "The qaytun will not shield me from my Lord." She said, "O Yusuf! I have spread out for you a silk bed; get up and fulfil my need." He said, "Then my share of Paradise would be lost," and other such words of hers, while he kept answering her, until she resolved to him. Some have mentioned that women kept inclining toward Yusuf with a desire of lust until Allah made him a prophet, and cast upon him the awe of prophethood, so his awe occupied everyone who saw him from his beauty. The scholars differed concerning his resolve. There is no dispute that her resolve was toward disobedience, but as for Yusuf, he resolved toward her (﴿had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾). But when he saw the proof, he did not resolve; this is due to the obligation of infallibility for the prophets. Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Thus, that We might turn away from him evil and immorality; indeed, he was of Our chosen servants﴾). So in the speech there is an inversion of order: that is, had he not seen the proof of [[In ʿ: "raʾā al-burhān burhān."]] his Lord, he would have resolved toward her. Abu Hatim said: I was reading the strange words of the Qur'an to Abu 'Ubaydah, and when I came to his saying "And she certainly resolved toward him, and he resolved toward her," the verse, Abu 'Ubaydah said: this is by inversion of order, as if he meant: "And she certainly resolved toward him, and had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have resolved toward her." Ahmad ibn Yahya said: that is, Zulaykha resolved toward disobedience and persisted in it, and Yusuf resolved but did not commit what he resolved upon; so there is a difference between the two resolves. Al-Harawi mentioned these two views in his book. Jamil said:

I resolved upon a resolve of Buthaynah; had it appeared
it would have healed the burning of desires from my heart.

Another said:

I resolved and did not do it, and I almost did, and I wish
I had left Uthman's wives weeping over him.

All of this is an inner talk without intent. It was also said: his resolve toward her was a wish to be her husband. It was also said: his resolve toward her was to strike her and push her away from himself, and the proof was his restraint from striking, for had he struck her, it would have implied he intended her in the forbidden, so she resisted and he struck her. [[This is the one fitting to the infallible, not the other meanings.]] It was also said: Yusuf's resolve was a disobedience, and that he sat with her the way a man sits with his wife; and to this view went the majority of the exegetes and most of them, as al-Qushayri Abu Nasr mentioned, and Ibn al-Anbari, al-Nahhas, al-Mawardi and others. Ibn 'Abbas said: he untied the hamyan [[al-hamyan: the drawstring of the trousers.]] and sat between her thighs like one circumcising. He also said: she lay on her back and he sat between her legs, removing his garments. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he loosened the cord of his trousers. Mujahid said: he untied the trousers until they reached the buttocks, and he sat with her the way a man sits with his wife. Ibn 'Abbas said: when he said, ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in secret﴾ [Yusuf: 52], Gabriel said to him: "Nor when you resolved toward her, O Yusuf?!" At that he said: ﴿Nor do I absolve myself﴾ [Yusuf: 53]. They said: restraint in such a situation indicates sincerity and is greater in reward.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verses 23–24 (part 2 of 2):

I say: This was the reason Allah the Exalted praised Dhu al-Kifl, as will be explained in Surah Sad, God willing. [See vol. 15, p. 218, and vol. 11, p. 327.] According to this view, the answer to *lawla* (if not) is omitted, meaning: "Had it not been that he saw the proof of his Lord, he would have carried out what he intended." A similar example is ﴿Nay, if you knew with certainty of certainty﴾ [At-Takathur: 5]. Its answer is "you would not have competed [for worldly things]." [See vol. 20, p. 173.]

Ibn Atiyya said: This view has been narrated from Ibn Abbas and a group of the early scholars (al-salaf). They said: The wisdom in this is that it serves as an example for sinners, so that they may see that their repentance returns to the pardon of Allah the Exalted, just as the repentance of one better than them returned, and that nearness to sin did not destroy him. All of this is based on the claim of this group that Yusuf's intention reached the point where he sat between the legs of Zulaykha and began to undo his garments and his belt and similar things, while she had lain back for him. This was related by al-Tabari.

Abu Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam said: Ibn Abbas and those after him do not disagree that he intended (hamma) with her. They know Allah and the interpretation of His Book better, and they are more reverent toward the prophets than to speak about them without knowledge.

Al-Hasan said: Allah the Mighty and Majestic did not mention the disobedience of the prophets in order to reproach them for it, but He mentioned it so that you would not despair of repentance.

Al-Ghaznawi said: Although the slips of the prophets have wisdoms: increased fear, intense shame through embarrassment, freedom from self-admiration over one's deeds, enjoying the blessing of pardon after hope, and their being leaders in giving hope to those who slip.

Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: Some people said that an intention (hamm) did occur from Yusuf, but that intention was a movement of natural inclination without resolve to commit the act. Whoever is of this kind is not held accountable for it. A person who is fasting may have the thought of cold water or delicious food come to his heart, but if he does not eat or drink, and his determination to eat or drink does not become firm, he is not held accountable for what passed through his soul. The proof (burhan) turned him away from this intention so that it did not become a firm resolve.

I say: This is a good view, and al-Hasan was among those who held it.

Ibn Atiyya said: What I hold concerning this verse is that Yusuf being a prophet at the time of this incident is not sound, and no reliable narration supports it. If that is so, then he was a believer who had been given judgment and knowledge (hukm and ilm), and it is permissible for him to have the intention (hamm), which is the wish to do a thing without actually doing it, and to entertain a bad thought, even though there is sin in that. But if we suppose him to be a prophet at that time, then in my opinion it is only permissible for him to have the intention that is a passing thought, and nothing mentioned, such as untying his belt and similar things, can be attributed to him, because infallibility ('ismah) accompanies prophethood.

As for what is reported, that it was said to him: "You are written among the prophets, yet you act like fools," its meaning is the promise of prophethood to come later.

I say: What he mentioned of this detailed distinction is correct. But the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We revealed to him﴾ [Yusuf: 15] indicate that he was a prophet, as we have mentioned. This is the view of a group of scholars. If he was a prophet, then only this remains: that the intention he had was a thought that passes through the soul but does not settle in the chest. This is what Allah lifted from His creatures as a matter of blame, since the accountable person has no power to repel it. And His words: ﴿Nor do I absolve myself﴾ [Yusuf: 53], if they are the words of Yusuf, would mean: from this intention. Or it may be that he said this out of humility and acknowledgment, as the soul opposes what it was purified and absolved of before.

Allah the Exalted has told us about the condition of Yusuf from the time he reached maturity, saying: ﴿And when he reached his maturity, We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾ [Yusuf: 22], as its explanation has already been given. The report of Allah is true, His description is accurate, and His speech is the truth. Yusuf acted upon what Allah had taught him regarding the prohibition of adultery and its preliminaries, and betraying the master, the neighbor, and the stranger in regard to their family. He did not approach the wife of al-Aziz, nor did he respond to her solicitation. Rather, he turned his back on her and fled from her, as wisdom specific to him and as action in accordance with what Allah had taught him.

In the Sahih of Muslim, from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The angels said: 'My Lord, that is Your servant who intends to commit a sin, and he is more aware of it.' He said: 'Watch him. If he does it, then record it against him as one like it; but if he leaves it, record it for him as a good deed, for he left it only for My sake.'"

He (peace be upon him) also said, relating from his Lord: "When My servant intends a sin but does not do it, a good deed is recorded for him." If what the servant intends of sin is recorded for him as a good deed when he abandons it, then there is no sin. In the Sahih also: "Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper to them, so long as they do not act upon it or speak it." This has already been mentioned.

Ibn al-Arabi said: In the city of Peace (Baghdad) there was a leader among the leaders of the Sufis (al-Sufiyya), and what a leader he was, known as Ibn Ata! One day he spoke about Yusuf and his reports, until he mentioned Yusuf's innocence of what was attributed to him of something disliked. A man stood up from the back of the assembly, which was filled with people of every kind, and said: "O Shaykh! O our master! Then did Yusuf have an intention but not complete it?" He said: "Yes! For the care (of Allah) was from that point." Observe the sweetness of the scholar and the student, observe the sharpness of the layman in his question, and the scholar's answer in its brevity and completeness. For this reason the scholars of the Sufis said: The benefit of His words: ﴿And when he reached his maturity, We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾ [Yusuf: 22] is that He gave him that at the peak of desire, so that it would be a means of protection (ʿiṣmah).

I say: When his infallibility and innocence have been established by the praise of Allah the Exalted for him, then what Musab ibn Uthman said cannot be sound: that Sulayman ibn Yasar was one of the most handsome of people, and a woman desired him, offering herself to him, but he refused her and admonished her. She said: "If you do not do it, I will expose you!" So he left and abandoned her. Then he saw in his dream Yusuf the Truthful (peace be upon him) sitting, and he said: "Are you Yusuf?" He said: "I am Yusuf who intended, and you are Sulayman who did not intend?!" This implies that the rank of wilaya (sainthood) is higher than the rank of prophethood, which is impossible. And if we suppose that Yusuf was not a prophet, his rank would still be wilaya, and he would be protected just as he was. Even if the doors had been locked on Sulayman, and he had been engaged in speech and reply and conversation, with long companionship, he would have been at risk of temptation and great trial. And Allah knows best.

The words of the Exalted: (﴿Had it not been that he saw the proof of his Lord﴾). [The word "an" here is in the nominative position, meaning: had it not been the seeing of the proof of his Lord.] The answer is omitted because the listener knows it, meaning: what happened would have happened. This proof is not mentioned in the Qur'an. It is narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) that Zulaykha went to an idol adorned with pearls and rubies in a corner of the house, and she covered it with a cloth. He said: "What are you doing?" She said: "I am ashamed before this god of mine that it should see me in this condition." Yusuf said: "I have more right to be ashamed before Allah." This is the best of what has been said about it, because it contains the establishment of evidence.

It is also said that he saw written on the ceiling of the house: ﴿And do not approach adultery; indeed, it is an abomination and an evil way﴾ [Al-Isra: 32]. [See vol. 10, p. 253.]

Ibn Abbas said: A palm appeared, on which was written: ﴿But indeed, over you are guardians﴾ [Al-Infitar: 10]. [See vol. 19, p. 245.]

Some people said: He remembered the covenant of Allah and His pledge.

It is also said: He was called: "O Yusuf! You are written among the prophets, and you act like the foolish?!"

It is said: He saw the image of Yaqub on the walls, biting on his finger and threatening him, so he calmed down, and his desire came out through his fingertips. This was said by Qatada, Mujahid, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Abu Salih, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Al-A'mash narrated from Mujahid, who said: He loosened his trousers, and Yaqub appeared to him and said: "O Yusuf!" So he turned and fled.

Sufyan narrated from Abu Husayn, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Yaqub was pictured to him, and he struck his chest, and his desire came out through his fingertips. Mujahid said: Each of the sons of Yaqub had twelve male children, except Yusuf, who had only two sons, and his offspring diminished because of that desire. Other things have also been said.

In summary: that proof was one of the signs of Allah that Allah showed to Yusuf, so that his faith became strong and he refrained from disobedience.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Thus, that We might turn away from him evil and immorality﴾. The kaf in "kadhalika" (thus) may be in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject, with the meaning: "The proofs are thus." It may also be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: "We showed him the proofs in such a manner."

Al-su' (evil) means desire, and al-fahsha' (immorality) means physical intimacy. It is also said: al-su' means bad reputation, and al-fahsha' means adultery. It is also said: al-su' means betrayal of his companion, and al-fahsha' means committing the abomination. It is also said: al-su' means the punishment of the ruler al-Aziz.

Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, and Ibn Amir read "al-mukhlisin" with a kasra on the lam, and its meaning is: those who sincerely devoted their obedience to Allah. The rest read it with a fatha on the lam, and its meaning is: those whom Allah purified for His message. Yusuf (ﷺ) possessed both of these qualities, because he was sincere in obedience to Allah the Exalted and was chosen for the message of Allah the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 23–24 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him⁠—⁠from himself⁠—⁠﴾. She was the wife of al-'Aziz, and she asked him to lie with her. The root of al-muraawadah (seeking to seduce) is the desire and request made gently and softly. Al-rawd and al-riyad mean seeking pasture, and it has been said: it derives from ruwayd, as one says, "So-and-so walks ruwaydan," meaning gently. So al-muraawadah is gentleness in pursuit. It is said of a man, "He sought her from herself," and of a woman, "She sought him from himself." Al-rawd also means deliberation; one says, "arwadani," meaning "give me time."

(﴿And they closed the doors﴾) Ghallaqa is used for the many (doors), and one does not say ghalaqa al-bab; aghlaqa is used for both the many and the few, as al-Farazdaq said about Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala':

I kept closing doors and opening them
until I came to Abu 'Amr ibn 'Ammar.

It is said that there were seven doors; she closed them and then invited him to herself.

(﴿And she said, "Hayta laka"﴾) That is, come, approach, and come hither. It has no verbal noun (masdar) and no inflection. Al-Nahhas said: there are seven readings of it. Among the most excellent of them and the most sound in its chain is what al-A'mash related from Abu Wa'il, who said: I heard 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud reading "Hayta laka." I said: "Some people read it 'Hiyta laka.'" He said: "I read as I was taught." Abu Ja'far said: Some narrate it from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud from the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is not far-fetched, because his saying "I read as I was taught" indicates that it is marfu' (traced to the Prophet). This reading with a fathah on the ta' and the ha' is the sound reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Mujahid and 'Ikrimah, and with it read Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', 'Asim, al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: Do not stop in the Qur'an, for it is only like the saying of one of you: "Halumma" and "Ta'al." Ibn Abi Ishaq al-Nahwi read "Qalat hayti laka," with a fathah on the ha' and a kasrah on the ta'. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Ibn Kathir read "Hayta laka," with a fathah on the ha' and a dammah on the ta'. Tarafah said:

It is not that my people are the most distant when
a caller from the clan says "Hayta"

These are three readings in which the ha' is fathah. Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and Nafi' read "Wa qalat Hiyta laka," with a kasrah on the ha' and a fathah on the ta'. Yahya ibn Wathhab read "Wa qalat Hiyta laka," with a kasrah on the ha', after it a silent ya', and the ta' with a dammah. It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ikrimah: "Wa qalat Hiyta, laka," with a kasrah on the ha', after it a silent hamzah, and the ta' with a dammah. From Ibn 'Amir and the people of Syria: "Wa qalat Hiyta," with a kasrah on the ha', with the hamzah, and a fathah on the ta'. Abu Ja'far said: "Hayta laka," with a fathah on the ta', is because of the meeting of two silent letters, since it is a sound like mah and sah, which ought not to be inflected; and the fathah is light, because before the ta' there is a ya' like "ayna" and "kayfa." As for one who reads the ta' with a kasrah, he reads it so because the original is the kasrah, since a silent letter when moved is moved to the kasrah. As for one who reads with a dammah, it is because it carries the sense of an end-point, meaning: she said, "My call is for you." When the annexation is removed, it is built on the dammah, like "haythu" and "ba'du." As for the reading of the people of Madinah, there are two views: one is that the fathah is due to the meeting of two silent letters, as has passed. The other is that it is a verb from hay'a, yahay'u, like ja'a yaj'u, so that the meaning in "hi'ta" is: your state has become good. And "laka" is from a different statement, as you say: "laka a'ni" (for you, I mean). Whoever reads with a hamzah and a dammah on the ta' it is a verb meaning "I have prepared myself for you," and likewise whoever reads "Hiyta laka." Abu 'Amr rejected this reading. Abu 'Ubaydah Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna said: Abu 'Amr was asked about the reading of one who reads with a kasrah on the ha' and a dammah on the ta', hamzated, and he said: "Baatil! He made it from tahayya'tu! Go and survey the Arabs until you reach Yemen; do you know anyone who says this?!" Al-Kisa'i also said: "Hi'ta" was not related from the Arabs. 'Ikrimah said: "Hayta laka" means: I have prepared myself for you, and adorned myself, and beautified myself; and it is a reading not approved, because it was not heard in Arabic. Al-Nahhas said: it is good according to the Basrans, because it is said: "ha'a al-rajulu yuha'u wa yahay'u hay'atan," so "ha'a yahay'u" is like "ja'a yaj'u," and "hiyta" is like "ji'ta." The kasrah on the ha' in "Hayta" is a dialect of a people who prefer the kasrah on the ha' to its fathah. Al-Zajjaj said: The best of the readings is "Hayta" with a fathah on the ha' and the ta'. Tarafah said:

It is not that my people are the most distant when
a caller from the clan says "Hayta"

with a fathah on the ha' and the ta'. And a poet said about 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him:

Convey to the Commander of the Faithful, the brother of Iraq, when you come to him,
that Iraq and its people are at peace with you, so "Hayta, Hayta!"

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: "Hayta" is a word in Syriac, calling him to herself. Al-Suddi said: its meaning in Coptic [in the Nabataean ('ayn) dialect] is "Come, for you." Abu 'Ubayd said: al-Kisa'i used to say: it is a dialect of the people of Hawran that reached the people of the Hijaz, and its meaning is "Come hither." Abu 'Ubayd said: I asked a learned elder from Hawran, who mentioned that it is their language, and 'Ikrimah also said so. Mujahid and others said: it is an Arabic dialect by which she invites him to herself, and it is a word of urging and inviting toward things. Al-Jawhari said: it is said "hawwata bihi" and "hayyata bihi" when one shouts at him and calls him. He said:

Indeed the cooing dove has silenced me, so I doubted;
