had it been addressed by it, it would have called out.

That is, it shouted. Another said:

Every youth drives them with "hayyat" calls.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Ma'adha Allah"﴾ That is, I seek refuge in Allah and I ask Him for protection from what you call me to. It is a verbal noun, meaning: I seek refuge in Allah with refuge; the object is omitted and the verbal noun is put in the accusative by the omitted verb, and the verbal noun is annexed to the name of Allah, as the verbal noun is annexed to the object, as you say: "I passed by Zayd, the passing of 'Amr," that is, like my passing by 'Amr.

(﴿Indeed, he is my lord﴾) meaning her husband: he is my master who has honored me, so I will not betray him. This was said by Mujahid, Ibn Ishaq and al-Suddi. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, indeed Allah is my Lord, who has taken care of me with His kindness, so I will not commit what He has forbidden.

(﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers do not succeed﴾) In the report: she said to him, "O Yusuf! How beautiful is the form of your face!" He said, "My Lord fashioned me in the womb." She said, "O Yusuf! How beautiful is your hair!" He said, "It is the first thing that will decay of me in my grave." She said, "O Yusuf! How beautiful are your eyes!" He said, "With them I look to my Lord." She said, "O Yusuf! Raise your gaze and look at my face." He said, "I fear blindness in my Hereafter." She said, "O Yusuf! Shall I draw near to you while you distance yourself from me?!" He said, "I want by that nearness to my Lord." She said, "O Yusuf! I have spread out for you the qaytun [[al-qaytun: the small private chamber; a non-Arabic word, and it was said to be in the language of the people of Egypt and the Berbers.]] so enter with me." He said, "The qaytun will not shield me from my Lord." She said, "O Yusuf! I have spread out for you a silk bed; get up and fulfil my need." He said, "Then my share of Paradise would be lost," and other such words of hers, while he kept answering her, until she resolved to him. Some have mentioned that women kept inclining toward Yusuf with a desire of lust until Allah made him a prophet, and cast upon him the awe of prophethood, so his awe occupied everyone who saw him from his beauty. The scholars differed concerning his resolve. There is no dispute that her resolve was toward disobedience, but as for Yusuf, he resolved toward her (﴿had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾). But when he saw the proof, he did not resolve; this is due to the obligation of infallibility for the prophets. Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Thus, that We might turn away from him evil and immorality; indeed, he was of Our chosen servants﴾). So in the speech there is an inversion of order: that is, had he not seen the proof of [[In ʿ: "raʾā al-burhān burhān."]] his Lord, he would have resolved toward her. Abu Hatim said: I was reading the strange words of the Qur'an to Abu 'Ubaydah, and when I came to his saying "And she certainly resolved toward him, and he resolved toward her," the verse, Abu 'Ubaydah said: this is by inversion of order, as if he meant: "And she certainly resolved toward him, and had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have resolved toward her." Ahmad ibn Yahya said: that is, Zulaykha resolved toward disobedience and persisted in it, and Yusuf resolved but did not commit what he resolved upon; so there is a difference between the two resolves. Al-Harawi mentioned these two views in his book. Jamil said:

I resolved upon a resolve of Buthaynah; had it appeared
it would have healed the burning of desires from my heart.

Another said:

I resolved and did not do it, and I almost did, and I wish
I had left Uthman's wives weeping over him.

All of this is an inner talk without intent. It was also said: his resolve toward her was a wish to be her husband. It was also said: his resolve toward her was to strike her and push her away from himself, and the proof was his restraint from striking, for had he struck her, it would have implied he intended her in the forbidden, so she resisted and he struck her. [[This is the one fitting to the infallible, not the other meanings.]] It was also said: Yusuf's resolve was a disobedience, and that he sat with her the way a man sits with his wife; and to this view went the majority of the exegetes and most of them, as al-Qushayri Abu Nasr mentioned, and Ibn al-Anbari, al-Nahhas, al-Mawardi and others. Ibn 'Abbas said: he untied the hamyan [[al-hamyan: the drawstring of the trousers.]] and sat between her thighs like one circumcising. He also said: she lay on her back and he sat between her legs, removing his garments. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he loosened the cord of his trousers. Mujahid said: he untied the trousers until they reached the buttocks, and he sat with her the way a man sits with his wife. Ibn 'Abbas said: when he said, ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in secret﴾ [Yusuf: 52], Gabriel said to him: "Nor when you resolved toward her, O Yusuf?!" At that he said: ﴿Nor do I absolve myself﴾ [Yusuf: 53]. They said: restraint in such a situation indicates sincerity and is greater in reward.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verses 23–24 (part 2 of 2):

I say: This was the reason Allah the Exalted praised Dhu al-Kifl, as will be explained in Surah Sad, God willing. [See vol. 15, p. 218, and vol. 11, p. 327.] According to this view, the answer to *lawla* (if not) is omitted, meaning: "Had it not been that he saw the proof of his Lord, he would have carried out what he intended." A similar example is ﴿Nay, if you knew with certainty of certainty﴾ [At-Takathur: 5]. Its answer is "you would not have competed [for worldly things]." [See vol. 20, p. 173.]

Ibn Atiyya said: This view has been narrated from Ibn Abbas and a group of the early scholars (al-salaf). They said: The wisdom in this is that it serves as an example for sinners, so that they may see that their repentance returns to the pardon of Allah the Exalted, just as the repentance of one better than them returned, and that nearness to sin did not destroy him. All of this is based on the claim of this group that Yusuf's intention reached the point where he sat between the legs of Zulaykha and began to undo his garments and his belt and similar things, while she had lain back for him. This was related by al-Tabari.

Abu Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam said: Ibn Abbas and those after him do not disagree that he intended (hamma) with her. They know Allah and the interpretation of His Book better, and they are more reverent toward the prophets than to speak about them without knowledge.

Al-Hasan said: Allah the Mighty and Majestic did not mention the disobedience of the prophets in order to reproach them for it, but He mentioned it so that you would not despair of repentance.

Al-Ghaznawi said: Although the slips of the prophets have wisdoms: increased fear, intense shame through embarrassment, freedom from self-admiration over one's deeds, enjoying the blessing of pardon after hope, and their being leaders in giving hope to those who slip.

Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: Some people said that an intention (hamm) did occur from Yusuf, but that intention was a movement of natural inclination without resolve to commit the act. Whoever is of this kind is not held accountable for it. A person who is fasting may have the thought of cold water or delicious food come to his heart, but if he does not eat or drink, and his determination to eat or drink does not become firm, he is not held accountable for what passed through his soul. The proof (burhan) turned him away from this intention so that it did not become a firm resolve.

I say: This is a good view, and al-Hasan was among those who held it.

Ibn Atiyya said: What I hold concerning this verse is that Yusuf being a prophet at the time of this incident is not sound, and no reliable narration supports it. If that is so, then he was a believer who had been given judgment and knowledge (hukm and ilm), and it is permissible for him to have the intention (hamm), which is the wish to do a thing without actually doing it, and to entertain a bad thought, even though there is sin in that. But if we suppose him to be a prophet at that time, then in my opinion it is only permissible for him to have the intention that is a passing thought, and nothing mentioned, such as untying his belt and similar things, can be attributed to him, because infallibility ('ismah) accompanies prophethood.

As for what is reported, that it was said to him: "You are written among the prophets, yet you act like fools," its meaning is the promise of prophethood to come later.

I say: What he mentioned of this detailed distinction is correct. But the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We revealed to him﴾ [Yusuf: 15] indicate that he was a prophet, as we have mentioned. This is the view of a group of scholars. If he was a prophet, then only this remains: that the intention he had was a thought that passes through the soul but does not settle in the chest. This is what Allah lifted from His creatures as a matter of blame, since the accountable person has no power to repel it. And His words: ﴿Nor do I absolve myself﴾ [Yusuf: 53], if they are the words of Yusuf, would mean: from this intention. Or it may be that he said this out of humility and acknowledgment, as the soul opposes what it was purified and absolved of before.

Allah the Exalted has told us about the condition of Yusuf from the time he reached maturity, saying: ﴿And when he reached his maturity, We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾ [Yusuf: 22], as its explanation has already been given. The report of Allah is true, His description is accurate, and His speech is the truth. Yusuf acted upon what Allah had taught him regarding the prohibition of adultery and its preliminaries, and betraying the master, the neighbor, and the stranger in regard to their family. He did not approach the wife of al-Aziz, nor did he respond to her solicitation. Rather, he turned his back on her and fled from her, as wisdom specific to him and as action in accordance with what Allah had taught him.

In the Sahih of Muslim, from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The angels said: 'My Lord, that is Your servant who intends to commit a sin, and he is more aware of it.' He said: 'Watch him. If he does it, then record it against him as one like it; but if he leaves it, record it for him as a good deed, for he left it only for My sake.'"

He (peace be upon him) also said, relating from his Lord: "When My servant intends a sin but does not do it, a good deed is recorded for him." If what the servant intends of sin is recorded for him as a good deed when he abandons it, then there is no sin. In the Sahih also: "Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper to them, so long as they do not act upon it or speak it." This has already been mentioned.

Ibn al-Arabi said: In the city of Peace (Baghdad) there was a leader among the leaders of the Sufis (al-Sufiyya), and what a leader he was, known as Ibn Ata! One day he spoke about Yusuf and his reports, until he mentioned Yusuf's innocence of what was attributed to him of something disliked. A man stood up from the back of the assembly, which was filled with people of every kind, and said: "O Shaykh! O our master! Then did Yusuf have an intention but not complete it?" He said: "Yes! For the care (of Allah) was from that point." Observe the sweetness of the scholar and the student, observe the sharpness of the layman in his question, and the scholar's answer in its brevity and completeness. For this reason the scholars of the Sufis said: The benefit of His words: ﴿And when he reached his maturity, We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾ [Yusuf: 22] is that He gave him that at the peak of desire, so that it would be a means of protection (ʿiṣmah).

I say: When his infallibility and innocence have been established by the praise of Allah the Exalted for him, then what Musab ibn Uthman said cannot be sound: that Sulayman ibn Yasar was one of the most handsome of people, and a woman desired him, offering herself to him, but he refused her and admonished her. She said: "If you do not do it, I will expose you!" So he left and abandoned her. Then he saw in his dream Yusuf the Truthful (peace be upon him) sitting, and he said: "Are you Yusuf?" He said: "I am Yusuf who intended, and you are Sulayman who did not intend?!" This implies that the rank of wilaya (sainthood) is higher than the rank of prophethood, which is impossible. And if we suppose that Yusuf was not a prophet, his rank would still be wilaya, and he would be protected just as he was. Even if the doors had been locked on Sulayman, and he had been engaged in speech and reply and conversation, with long companionship, he would have been at risk of temptation and great trial. And Allah knows best.

The words of the Exalted: (﴿Had it not been that he saw the proof of his Lord﴾). [The word "an" here is in the nominative position, meaning: had it not been the seeing of the proof of his Lord.] The answer is omitted because the listener knows it, meaning: what happened would have happened. This proof is not mentioned in the Qur'an. It is narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) that Zulaykha went to an idol adorned with pearls and rubies in a corner of the house, and she covered it with a cloth. He said: "What are you doing?" She said: "I am ashamed before this god of mine that it should see me in this condition." Yusuf said: "I have more right to be ashamed before Allah." This is the best of what has been said about it, because it contains the establishment of evidence.

It is also said that he saw written on the ceiling of the house: ﴿And do not approach adultery; indeed, it is an abomination and an evil way﴾ [Al-Isra: 32]. [See vol. 10, p. 253.]

Ibn Abbas said: A palm appeared, on which was written: ﴿But indeed, over you are guardians﴾ [Al-Infitar: 10]. [See vol. 19, p. 245.]

Some people said: He remembered the covenant of Allah and His pledge.

It is also said: He was called: "O Yusuf! You are written among the prophets, and you act like the foolish?!"

It is said: He saw the image of Yaqub on the walls, biting on his finger and threatening him, so he calmed down, and his desire came out through his fingertips. This was said by Qatada, Mujahid, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Abu Salih, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Al-A'mash narrated from Mujahid, who said: He loosened his trousers, and Yaqub appeared to him and said: "O Yusuf!" So he turned and fled.

Sufyan narrated from Abu Husayn, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Yaqub was pictured to him, and he struck his chest, and his desire came out through his fingertips. Mujahid said: Each of the sons of Yaqub had twelve male children, except Yusuf, who had only two sons, and his offspring diminished because of that desire. Other things have also been said.

In summary: that proof was one of the signs of Allah that Allah showed to Yusuf, so that his faith became strong and he refrained from disobedience.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Thus, that We might turn away from him evil and immorality﴾. The kaf in "kadhalika" (thus) may be in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject, with the meaning: "The proofs are thus." It may also be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: "We showed him the proofs in such a manner."

Al-su' (evil) means desire, and al-fahsha' (immorality) means physical intimacy. It is also said: al-su' means bad reputation, and al-fahsha' means adultery. It is also said: al-su' means betrayal of his companion, and al-fahsha' means committing the abomination. It is also said: al-su' means the punishment of the ruler al-Aziz.

Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, and Ibn Amir read "al-mukhlisin" with a kasra on the lam, and its meaning is: those who sincerely devoted their obedience to Allah. The rest read it with a fatha on the lam, and its meaning is: those whom Allah purified for His message. Yusuf (ﷺ) possessed both of these qualities, because he was sincere in obedience to Allah the Exalted and was chosen for the message of Allah the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they raced each other to the door, and she tore his shirt from behind﴾. In this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, may He be exalted, "And they raced each other to the door." The scholars said: This is from the concise expression of the inimitable Qur'an, in which many meanings are gathered together. When he saw the proof of his Lord, he fled from her, and so they pursued each other: she wanted to bring him back to herself, and he wanted to flee from her. She caught up with him before he could get out. ﴿And she tore his shirt from behind﴾, that is, from his back. She seized the top of his shirt, so the shirt was torn at its collar, and the tearing descended to the bottom of the shirt.

Al-istibaq (racing) is seeking to be first to something, and from it comes al-sibaq (the race). Al-qadd is cutting, and it is used most often for what is lengthwise. Al-Nabigha said [a verse describing swords; the explanation of the verse has been given in the margin of p. 103 of this part]:

They cut the Salawqi (sword) whose weave is doubled,
and they kindle with the blades the fire of al-Hubahib.

Al-qatt, with a ṭa', is used for what is crosswise. Al-Mufaḍḍal ibn Harb said: I read in a codex, "When he saw his shirt torn (ʿuṭṭa) from behind," meaning it was split. Yaqub said: al-ʿatt is a split in healthy skin and in healthy cloth. The alif was dropped from "istabaqa" in pronunciation because it is unstressed and the lam after it is also unstressed, as one says: "jaʾani ʿAbd Allah" in the dual. Some Arabs say "jaʾani ʿAbd Allah" with the alif retained without a hamza, bringing together two unstressed letters, because the second is assimilated and the first is a vowel-extending soft letter. Some say "ʿAbd Allah" with the alif and the hamza, as you say when pausing.

This is a matter in which the Malikis alone have written in their books: when a shirt is pulled from behind, it tears from that side, and when it is pulled from the front, it tears from that side. **The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 12, verses 26–29:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said, "It was she who sought to seduce me from myself, and a witness from her own family testified."﴾ On this there are three issues.

**The first issue:** The scholars said: [[In (manuscript) ʿ: al-Hasan.]] When she declared herself innocent, and she was not truthful in her love for him (because it is the nature of the lover to prefer the beloved), he said, "It was she who sought to seduce me from myself." Yusuf spoke the truth in response to her slander and lying against him. Nawf al-Shami and others said: It seems that Yusuf, peace be upon him, had not yet explained the matter in full, but when she accused him, he became angry and spoke the truth.

**The second issue:** ﴿and a witness from her own family testified﴾. Because the two of them contradicted each other in their statements, the king needed a witness to know the truthful from the liar, so a witness from her family testified, that is, a judge from her family ruled, because it was a judgment from him and not a testimony. Four opinions have been stated about this witness:

The first: he was an infant in the cradle who spoke. Al-Suhayli said: this is the correct view, because of the hadith related from the Prophet ﷺ, which is his saying: "Only three have spoken in the cradle," and he mentioned among them the witness of Yusuf. Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: it has been said [[from ʿ]] that he was a child in the cradle in the house, and he was her maternal cousin. Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Four spoke while they were small," and he mentioned among them the witness of Yusuf. This is one view.

The second: the witness was the torn shirt. This was related by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid. It is a sound figurative usage from the standpoint of language, for the tongue of circumstance is more eloquent than the tongue of speech, and the Arabs attribute speech to inanimate objects and report about them what characterises them. This is abundant in their poetry and speech, and among the most charming of it is the saying of one of them: "The wall said to the peg, 'Why do you pierce me?' He said to it, 'Ask the one who hammers me.'" However, Allah's later words "from her own family" invalidate that the witness was the shirt.

The third: he was a creature among the creations of Allah, neither human nor jinn. Mujahid also said this, but the saying of Allah "from her own family" refutes it.

The fourth: he was a wise man of sound intellect who was among the counsellors of the minister, and he was from among the household of the woman and was with her husband. He said: "I have heard the rushing and the commotion from behind the door, and the shirt was torn. It is not known which of you was in front of the other. If the tearing of the shirt is from the front, then you are truthful, and if it is from behind, then he is truthful." They looked at the shirt, and behold, it was torn from behind. This is the view of al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Mujahid also, and al-Suddi. Al-Suddi said: he was her cousin. It was also related from Ibn ʿAbbas, and this is the sound view on the matter, and Allah knows best.

It was related from Ibn ʿAbbas (Israʾil related it from Simak from ʿIkrimah) that he said: he was a man with a beard. Sufyan related from Jabir from Ibn Abi Mulaykah from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: he was one of the king's special attendants. ʿIkrimah said: he was not a child, but a wise man. Sufyan related from Mansur from Mujahid that he said: he was a man. Abu Jaʿfar al-Nahhas said: the more fitting in meaning, and Allah knows best, is that he was a sensible, wise man whom the king consulted, and he brought this indication. Had he been a child, his testimony to Yusuf ﷺ would have made it unnecessary to resort to a customary proof, because a child's speech is a miraculous sign, and it would have been clearer than reasoning from custom. This does not contradict the hadith "Four spoke while they were small," among them the companion of Yusuf, meaning: small, not an elder. In this there is another proof: that Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, related the hadith from the Prophet ﷺ, and it is widely transmitted from him that the companion of Yusuf was not a child.

I say: It has been related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Hurayrah, Ibn Jubayr, Hilal ibn Yasaf [[it is with a kasra, and may be pronounced with a fatha]], and al-Dahhak that he was a child in the cradle. However, if he was a child who spoke, then the proof would be his very speech, without needing to reason from the shirt, and that would be a breach of custom and a kind of miracle. Allah knows best. The discussion of those who spoke in the cradle among the children will come in Surah al-Buruj, God willing. [[See vol. 19, p. 287.]]

**The third issue:** If we accept that the witness was a small child, then there is no evidence in it for acting upon indications (amarat), as we have mentioned. If he was a man, then it is valid to take it as a proof in judging by a sign in the matter of lost property and in many other cases. Malik said concerning thieves: if goods are found with them, and people come and claim them without having evidence, the ruler should wait for them in that matter, and if no one else comes, he gives them to those people. Muhammad said concerning household goods when a wife and husband dispute over them: what belongs to men belongs to the man, what belongs to women belongs to the woman, and what belongs to both belongs to the man. Shurayh and Iyas ibn Muʿawiyah used to act upon signs in legal rulings, and the root of this is this verse, and Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿If his shirt is torn from the front﴾. It is in the place of a conditional clause in the jussive. Within it there is a grammatical point that is difficult, because conditional particles turn the past into the future, and this does not apply to *kāna* (was). Al-Mubarrad Muhammad ibn Yazid said: this is due to the strength of *kāna*, and that it is used to express all verbs. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is *in yakun*, that is, *in yuʿlam* (if it is known), and knowledge has not yet occurred, and likewise the being (*kawn*), because it conveys the sense of knowledge. "Torn from the front" is the predicate of *kāna*, in the past verb form, as Zuhayr said:

*And he had folded his side over a hidden grudge,*
*So he neither revealed it nor advanced.* [[*Kashh* means the side; one says "he folded his side over such-and-such" when he conceals it. *Mustakinnah* means the rancour. Another reading is: "and did not hesitate."]]

Yahya ibn Yaʿmar and Ibn Abi Ishaq read *min qubul* with a *ḍamma* on the qaf, ba and lam, and likewise *duburu*. Al-Zajjaj said: they treat them as terminal adverbs like *qabla* and *baʿda*, as if he said: "from its front and from its back," and when the genitive complement is omitted, while it is still intended, the noun it modified becomes a terminal adverb itself, after it had been that the complement was terminal for it. It is also permissible to read *min qabla* and *min dabra* with a fatha on the ra and lam, likening them to diptotes, because they are definite and have been removed from their usual form. Mahbub related from Abu ʿAmr *min qabl* and *min dabr*, with the forms lightened and in the genitive.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So when he saw that his shirt was torn from behind, he said, "Indeed it is from your guile. Indeed, your guile is great."﴾ It has been said that the Aziz said this to her when she said: ﴿What is the recompense for one who intended evil for your wife?﴾ [Yusuf: 25]. It has also been said that the witness said it to her. *Kayd* means cunning and stratagem, and it has been discussed earlier in [[Surah al-Anfal, see vol. 7, p. 386.]].

*Indeed, your guile is great.* He said "great" because of the greatness of their temptation and their scheming to escape from their predicament. Muqatil related from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed the guile of women is greater than the guile of Satan, because Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, the plot of Satan is ever weak﴾ [al-Nisa: 76], and He said: ﴿Indeed, your guile is great﴾."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Yusuf, turn away from this.﴾ The one who said this was the witness. "Yusuf" is a singular vocative, meaning "O Yusuf," so the particle was omitted. "Turn away from this" means: do not mention it to anyone, and keep it secret. Then he turned to her and said: "And you, ask forgiveness for your sin," meaning: ask your husband's forgiveness for your sin, so that he does not punish you.

﴿Indeed, you were among those who erred.﴾ He did not say "among the female sinners" (*khāṭiʾāt*) because he intended to speak of the masculine and feminine together, so he gave precedence to the masculine. The meaning is: among the sinful people, or among the sinful folk, like the verses: ﴿Indeed, she was of a disbelieving people﴾ [al-Naml: 43] and ﴿and she was among the obedient﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12]. It has also been said that the one who said to Yusuf "turn away" and to her "ask forgiveness" was her husband, the king. On this there are two views. The first: he was not jealous, and for this reason he was calm. The lack of jealousy is found among many of the people of Egypt. The second: Allah the Exalted removed jealousy from him, and this was a kindness to Yusuf, so that he was spared her onslaught and he pardoned her. [[In manuscripts ʿ, W and Y: forbearance.]]

Mahbub related from Abu ʿAmr *min qabl* and *min dabr*, with the forms lightened and in the genitive.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So when he saw that his shirt was torn from behind, he said, "Indeed it is from your guile. Indeed, your guile is great."﴾ It has been said that the Aziz said this to her when she said: ﴿What is the recompense for one who intended evil for your wife?﴾ [Yusuf: 25]. It has also been said that the witness said it to her. *Kayd* means cunning and stratagem, and it has been discussed earlier in [[Surah al-Anfal, see vol. 7, p. 386.]].

*Indeed, your guile is great.* He said "great" because of the greatness of their temptation and their scheming to escape from their predicament. Muqatil related from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed the guile of women is greater than the guile of Satan, because Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, the plot of Satan is ever weak﴾ [al-Nisa: 76], and He said: ﴿Indeed, your guile is great﴾."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Yusuf, turn away from this.﴾ The one who said this was the witness. "Yusuf" is a singular vocative, meaning "O Yusuf," so the particle was omitted. "Turn away from this" means: do not mention it to anyone, and keep it secret. Then he turned to her and said: "And you, ask forgiveness for your sin," meaning: ask your husband's forgiveness for your sin, so that he does not punish you.

﴿Indeed, you were among those who erred.﴾ He did not say "among the female sinners" (*khāṭiʾāt*) because he intended to speak of the masculine and feminine together, so he gave precedence to the masculine. The meaning is: among the sinful people, or among the sinful folk, like the verses: ﴿Indeed, she was of a disbelieving people﴾ [al-Naml: 43] and ﴿and she was among the obedient﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12]. It has also been said that the one who said to Yusuf "turn away" and to her "ask forgiveness" was her husband, the king. On this there are two views. The first: he was not jealous, and for this reason he was calm. The lack of jealousy is found among many of the people of Egypt. The second: Allah the Exalted removed jealousy from him, and this was a kindness to Yusuf, so that he was spared her onslaught and he pardoned her. [[In manuscripts ʿ, W and Y: forbearance.]]

**The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 12, verses 26–29:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said, "It was she who sought to seduce me from myself, and a witness from her own family testified."﴾ On this there are three issues.

**The first issue:** The scholars said: [[In (manuscript) ʿ: al-Hasan.]] When she declared herself innocent, and she was not truthful in her love for him (because it is the nature of the lover to prefer the beloved), he said, "It was she who sought to seduce me from myself." Yusuf spoke the truth in response to her slander and lying against him. Nawf al-Shami and others said: It seems that Yusuf, peace be upon him, had not yet explained the matter in full, but when she accused him, he became angry and spoke the truth.

**The second issue:** ﴿and a witness from her own family testified﴾. Because the two of them contradicted each other in their statements, the king needed a witness to know the truthful from the liar, so a witness from her family testified, that is, a judge from her family ruled, because it was a judgment from him and not a testimony. Four opinions have been stated about this witness:

The first: he was an infant in the cradle who spoke. Al-Suhayli said: this is the correct view, because of the hadith related from the Prophet ﷺ, which is his saying: "Only three have spoken in the cradle," and he mentioned among them the witness of Yusuf. Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: it has been said [[from ʿ]] that he was a child in the cradle in the house, and he was her maternal cousin. Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Four spoke while they were small," and he mentioned among them the witness of Yusuf. This is one view.

The second: the witness was the torn shirt. This was related by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid. It is a sound figurative usage from the standpoint of language, for the tongue of circumstance is more eloquent than the tongue of speech, and the Arabs attribute speech to inanimate objects and report about them what characterises them. This is abundant in their poetry and speech, and among the most charming of it is the saying of one of them: "The wall said to the peg, 'Why do you pierce me?' He said to it, 'Ask the one who hammers me.'" However, Allah's later words "from her own family" invalidate that the witness was the shirt.

The third: he was a creature among the creations of Allah, neither human nor jinn. Mujahid also said this, but the saying of Allah "from her own family" refutes it.

The fourth: he was a wise man of sound intellect who was among the counsellors of the minister, and he was from among the household of the woman and was with her husband. He said: "I have heard the rushing and the commotion from behind the door, and the shirt was torn. It is not known which of you was in front of the other. If the tearing of the shirt is from the front, then you are truthful, and if it is from behind, then he is truthful." They looked at the shirt, and behold, it was torn from behind. This is the view of al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Mujahid also, and al-Suddi. Al-Suddi said: he was her cousin. It was also related from Ibn ʿAbbas, and this is the sound view on the matter, and Allah knows best.

It was related from Ibn ʿAbbas (Israʾil related it from Simak from ʿIkrimah) that he said: he was a man with a beard. Sufyan related from Jabir from Ibn Abi Mulaykah from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: he was one of the king's special attendants. ʿIkrimah said: he was not a child, but a wise man. Sufyan related from Mansur from Mujahid that he said: he was a man. Abu Jaʿfar al-Nahhas said: the more fitting in meaning, and Allah knows best, is that he was a sensible, wise man whom the king consulted, and he brought this indication. Had he been a child, his testimony to Yusuf ﷺ would have made it unnecessary to resort to a customary proof, because a child's speech is a miraculous sign, and it would have been clearer than reasoning from custom. This does not contradict the hadith "Four spoke while they were small," among them the companion of Yusuf, meaning: small, not an elder. In this there is another proof: that Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, related the hadith from the Prophet ﷺ, and it is widely transmitted from him that the companion of Yusuf was not a child.

I say: It has been related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Hurayrah, Ibn Jubayr, Hilal ibn Yasaf [[it is with a kasra, and may be pronounced with a fatha]], and al-Dahhak that he was a child in the cradle. However, if he was a child who spoke, then the proof would be his very speech, without needing to reason from the shirt, and that would be a breach of custom and a kind of miracle. Allah knows best. The discussion of those who spoke in the cradle among the children will come in Surah al-Buruj, God willing. [[See vol. 19, p. 287.]]

**The third issue:** If we accept that the witness was a small child, then there is no evidence in it for acting upon indications (amarat), as we have mentioned. If he was a man, then it is valid to take it as a proof in judging by a sign in the matter of lost property and in many other cases. Malik said concerning thieves: if goods are found with them, and people come and claim them without having evidence, the ruler should wait for them in that matter, and if no one else comes, he gives them to those people. Muhammad said concerning household goods when a wife and husband dispute over them: what belongs to men belongs to the man, what belongs to women belongs to the woman, and what belongs to both belongs to the man. Shurayh and Iyas ibn Muʿawiyah used to act upon signs in legal rulings, and the root of this is this verse, and Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿If his shirt is torn from the front﴾. It is in the place of a conditional clause in the jussive. Within it there is a grammatical point that is difficult, because conditional particles turn the past into the future, and this does not apply to *kāna* (was). Al-Mubarrad Muhammad ibn Yazid said: this is due to the strength of *kāna*, and that it is used to express all verbs. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is *in yakun*, that is, *in yuʿlam* (if it is known), and knowledge has not yet occurred, and likewise the being (*kawn*), because it conveys the sense of knowledge. "Torn from the front" is the predicate of *kāna*, in the past verb form, as Zuhayr said:

*And he had folded his side over a hidden grudge,*
*So he neither revealed it nor advanced.* [[*Kashh* means the side; one says "he folded his side over such-and-such" when he conceals it. *Mustakinnah* means the rancour. Another reading is: "and did not hesitate."]]

Yahya ibn Yaʿmar and Ibn Abi Ishaq read *min qubul* with a *ḍamma* on the qaf, ba and lam, and likewise *duburu*. Al-Zajjaj said: they treat them as terminal adverbs like *qabla* and *baʿda*, as if he said: "from its front and from its back," and when the genitive complement is omitted, while it is still intended, the noun it modified becomes a terminal adverb itself, after it had been that the complement was terminal for it. It is also permissible to read *min qabla* and *min dabra* with a fatha on the ra and lam, likening them to diptotes, because they are definite and have been removed from their usual form. Mahbub related from Abu ʿAmr *min qabl* and *min dabr*, with the forms lightened and in the genitive.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So when he saw that his shirt was torn from behind, he said, "Indeed it is from your guile. Indeed, your guile is great."﴾ It has been said that the Aziz said this to her when she said: ﴿What is the recompense for one who intended evil for your wife?﴾ [Yusuf: 25]. It has also been said that the witness said it to her. *Kayd* means cunning and stratagem, and it has been discussed earlier in [[Surah al-Anfal, see vol. 7, p. 386.]].

*Indeed, your guile is great.* He said "great" because of the greatness of their temptation and their scheming to escape from their predicament. Muqatil related from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed the guile of women is greater than the guile of Satan, because Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, the plot of Satan is ever weak﴾ [al-Nisa: 76], and He said: ﴿Indeed, your guile is great﴾."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Yusuf, turn away from this.﴾ The one who said this was the witness. "Yusuf" is a singular vocative, meaning "O Yusuf," so the particle was omitted. "Turn away from this" means: do not mention it to anyone, and keep it secret. Then he turned to her and said: "And you, ask forgiveness for your sin," meaning: ask your husband's forgiveness for your sin, so that he does not punish you.

﴿Indeed, you were among those who erred.﴾ He did not say "among the female sinners" (*khāṭiʾāt*) because he intended to speak of the masculine and feminine together, so he gave precedence to the masculine. The meaning is: among the sinful people, or among the sinful folk, like the verses: ﴿Indeed, she was of a disbelieving people﴾ [al-Naml: 43] and ﴿and she was among the obedient﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12]. It has also been said that the one who said to Yusuf "turn away" and to her "ask forgiveness" was her husband, the king. On this there are two views. The first: he was not jealous, and for this reason he was calm. The lack of jealousy is found among many of the people of Egypt. The second: Allah the Exalted removed jealousy from him, and this was a kindness to Yusuf, so that he was spared her onslaught and he pardoned her. [[In manuscripts ʿ, W and Y: forbearance.]]

God Almighty said: ﴿And women in the city said﴾. It is also said "nuswah" with a *damma* on the *nun*, which is the recitation of al-A'mash, al-Mufaddal and al-Sulami. The large plural is *nisa'*. It is permissible to say "waqalat niswatun" (and women said) and "qala niswatun" (and women said), like "qalat al-a'rabu" and "qala al-a'rabu" (the Bedouins said). This is because the story spread among the people of Egypt, so the women talked about it. It has been said that they were the wife of the cupbearer of al-Aziz, the wife of his baker, the wife of the keeper of his animals, and the wife of the keeper of his prison. It has also been said that they were the wife of the chamberlain, related from Ibn 'Abbas and others.

﴿She is seeking to seduce her young man (fata) from himself﴾. *Al-fata* in the speech of the Arabs means the young man, and the woman is *fatah*.

﴿She has been seized by love for him﴾. It has been said: *shaghafaha* means it overpowered her. It has also been said: his love entered beneath her *shighaf* (the membrane around the heart), related from Mujahid and others. 'Amr ibn Dinar narrated from 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: it entered beneath her *shighaf*. al-Hasan said: *al-shaghaf* is the innermost part of the heart. al-Suddi and Abu 'Ubayd [[In (ʿ), (w) and (y): Abu 'Ubayda.]] said: *shighaf al-qalb* is its covering, which is a skin over it. It has also been said: it is the middle of the heart. The meanings of these sayings are close, and the meaning is: his love reached her *shighaf* and overcame her. al-Nabigha said:

"Worry has come between that and a dweller within, entering as the *shighaf* that the fingers seek."
[[That is, the fingers of the physicians. He says: worry has prevented him from weeping over the abodes, for it entered the heart until it afflicted him with a disease.]]

It has also been said that *al-shighaf* is a disease. al-Asma'i recited for a rajiz (rajaz poet):

"He follows her, while she is for him a *shighaf*."

Abu Ja'far ibn Muhammad, Ibn Muhayşin and al-Hasan read *sha'afaha* with an unpointed 'ayn. Ibn al-A'rabi said: its meaning is that his love burned her heart. He said: the first reading is the one practised. al-Jawhari said: *sha'afahu al-hubb* means love burned his heart. Abu Zayd said: it made him ill. One says *shu'ifa bi-kadha* and he is *mash'uf*. al-Hasan read "qad sha'afaha", and said: it made her insides full of love. al-Nahhas said: its meaning according to most lexicographers is "it has taken her in every direction," because *shi'af al-jibal* are their heights, and one says *shughifa bi-dhalika shaghfan* (with the 'ayn sukun) when one is infatuated with it. However, Abu 'Ubayda recited the line of Imru' al-Qays:

"You would kill me, though you have *sha'af* her heart, as the man with tar-smeared camel (mahnu'a) is consumed by burning."
[[al-Mahnu'a: the one smeared with tar. When a camel is smeared with tar it finds pleasure with burning, like the burning of love with its pleasure.]]

He said: the anguish of love and its burning were compared to that. It is narrated from al-Sha'bi that he said: *al-shaghaf* with the dotted letter is love, and *al-sha'af* with the undotted letter is madness. al-Nahhas said: it has been reported "qad shaghifahā" with a kasra on the *ghayn*, but it is not known in the speech of the Arabs except "shaghafaha" with a fatha on the *ghayn*, and likewise "sha'afaha", meaning he left her infatuated. Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah narrated from al-Hasan: *al-shaghaf* is the veil of the heart, and *al-sha'af* is the core of the heart. So if love reached the *sha'af*, she would die. al-Hasan also said: it is said that *al-shaghaf* is the skin adhering to the heart which is not seen, which is the white skin, so her love adhered to her heart like the adherence of the skin to the heart. [[In (ʿ) and (w): the liver. This is not correct.]]

God Almighty said: ﴿Indeed, we see her in clear error﴾, that is, in this action. Qatadah said: "*fatahā*" is the young man of her husband, because Yusuf was among them in the status of slaves, and her command over him was executed. Muqatil narrated from Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi from Salman al-Farisi, who said: the wife of al-Aziz asked her husband to give her Yusuf as a gift, and he gave him to her, saying: "What will you do with him?" She said: "I will take him as a son." He said: "He is yours." So she raised him until he reached maturity, while she had within herself what she had. She would uncover herself to him, adorn herself, and invite him gently, but Allah protected him.

God Almighty said: ﴿So when she heard of their deceit﴾, that is, of their backbiting about her and their scheming to blame her. It has been said: she had informed them and entrusted them with her secret, but they disclosed her secret, and this was called deceit. And His saying: "she sent for them" contains an omission, meaning she sent for them, inviting them to a banquet so that she might draw them into what she had fallen into. Mujahid narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: the wife of al-Aziz said to her husband, "I want to prepare food and invite these women," and he said to her, "Do it." So she prepared food, then she *najjadat* the houses for them. *Najjadat* means she adorned them; *al-najd* is what the house is adorned with of furnishings, that is, it is decorated, and its plural is *nujud*, narrated from Abu 'Ubayd [[As it stands in the originals: probably Abu 'Ubayda, as is evident from al-Lisan.]]. *Al-tanjid* is decoration. She sent to them, asking them to attend her food, and that none of you who have been named should stay away. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: they were forty women, and they came unwillingly. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said about them:

"Until, when they came to her by force, and she prepared for them cushions and carpets (kababan)."
[[The line is as in the originals. Another version: anmatan (rugs).]]

Wahb ibn [Munabbih] said: so they came and took their seats.

﴿And she prepared for them a couch (muttaka')﴾, that is, she arranged for them seats on which they might recline. Ibn Jubayr said: in each seat there was a goblet containing honey, a citron, and a sharp knife. Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr read *mutkan*, lightly pronounced and without hamza, and *al-mutk* is the citron in the language of the Copts, and Mujahid explained it this way. Sufyan narrated from Mansur from Mujahid, who said: *al-muttaka'* with a heavy pronunciation is the food, and *al-mutk* with a light pronunciation is the citron. The poet said:

"We drink sin openly from the cups, and see the citron (mutk) lent among us."

The Azd Shanu'a tribe say: the citron is *al-mutkah*. al-Jawhari said: *al-mutk* is what the circumciser leaves behind. The origin of *al-mutk* is *al-zamawrad* [[Al-zamawrad: thin bread wrapped around meat or other things, or something resembling the citron.]]. *Al-matka'* among women is one who has not been circumcised [[Khafd al-jariyah: circumcising the girl. Likewise for boys. The custom is that khafd is specific to girls and khitan to boys.]]. al-Farra' said: a shaykh from the trustworthy people of Basra told me that *al-mutk* lightly pronounced is *al-zamawrad*. Some said it is the citron, related by al-Akhfash. Ibn Zayd: citron and honey with which one eats. The poet said [[He is Jamil ibn Ma'mar. Qulal is the plural of qullah, and the qullah is a large jar. It was said: a large pitcher. It was said: a small cup. Other things were also said.]]:

"We remained in blessing and reclined, and drank the lawful from its jars."

That is, we ate. al-Nahhas said: God's saying ﴿and she prepared (a'tadat)﴾ is from *al-'atad*, which is everything you make ready for something. The most accurate of what has been said about "*muttaka'*" is what 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: a seat. As for the saying of a group of exegetes that it means food, it is permissible with the implied meaning "food reclined," like "and ask the town" [Yusuf 12:82]. This omission is indicated by "and she gave each one of them a knife," because the presence of women with knives is only for food that is cut with knives. He said this in his book *I'rab al-Quran* [[Grammatical analysis of the Qur'an.]]. In his book *Ma'ani al-Quran*, he said: Ma'mar narrated from Qatadah, who said: "*al-muttaka'*" is food. It has also been said: "*al-muttaka'*" is whatever one leans on during food, drink or conversation, and this is what is known among the lexicographers, although the reports have been confirmed for this. al-Qutabi related that it is said: "*ittaka'na* at so-and-so's" meaning we ate. The origin of "*muttaka'*" is *mawtaka'*, and similar to it are *muttazin* and *muttaʿid*, since it derives from *wazanat*, *wa'adat* and *wakat*. It is said: *ittaka'a* yattaki'u *ittika'an*.

(﴿each one of them a knife﴾) is two objects. al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' related that *al-sikkin* (knife) can be masculine or feminine. al-Farra' recited:

"He made marks on the hump on a cold morning, with a knife whose handle is firmly fixed."
[[*'Ayyatha*: he made a mark on the camel's hump.]]

al-Jawhari said: the more common usage is masculine. He said:

"He seems a sincere adviser in what appears, but when he is alone, that is a knife, skilled at the throat."

al-Asma'i said: in *al-sikkin* only the masculine is known.

God Almighty said: ﴿And she said, "Come out before them"﴾, pronounced with a *damma* on the *ta'* to avoid meeting two sakins, because a kasra is heavy when a damma follows it, and the *ta'* was pronounced with a kasra according to the original. It was said: she said to them, "Do not cut and do not eat until I inform you." Then she said to her servant, "When I say to you, call for me *Ilan*, call Yusuf." *Ila* was an idol they worshipped. Yusuf, peace be upon him, was working in clay, having tied his loincloth and rolled up his arms, so she said to the servant, "Call *Ilan* for me," meaning call the Lord for me; *Ila* in Hebrew is the Lord. He said: the women were astonished and said, "How can he come?!" The servant went up and called Yusuf, and when he came down she said to them, "Cut what you have."

﴿So when they saw him, they were amazed by him and cut their hands﴾ with the knives until the blades reached the bone. This is what Wahb ibn Munabbih said. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he did not come out to them until she had adorned him. He came out to them suddenly, and they were stunned by him and bewildered at the beauty of his face and his adornment, and what was upon him, so they began to cut their hands, thinking they were cutting citrons. There is disagreement about the meaning of "*akbarnahu*". Juwaybir narrated from al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas: they magnified him [[In the margin of (ʿ): the meaning of "*akbarnahu*" is "they magnified him," and were stunned by his beauty]] and feared him. And from him also: they were overcome with astonishment and emitted fluid. The poet said:

"When they see the stallion from atop a small rock, they neigh and magnify the spilled semen."
[[*Al-qarrah*: a small mountain separated from the mountains; it was also said: a great rock. Other things were also said.]]

Ibn Sam'an narrated from a number of his companions: they said they emitted fluid from passion. Wahb ibn Munabbih: they fell in love with him until ten of them died in that gathering from astonishment, bewilderment and longing for Yusuf. It was also said: its meaning is that they menstruated from astonishment, as said by Qatadah, Muqatil and al-Suddi [[Ibn 'Atiyya said: "*akbarnahu*" meaning they magnified him and were amazed at his beauty; this is the well-known view. 'Abd al-Samad ibn 'Ali al-Hashimi narrated from his father from his grandfather: it means they menstruated, and he recited:

"We approach women during their purity, and do not approach women when they menstruate with great menstruation."

The judge Abu Muhammad said: this is a weak view, its meaning is objectionable, and the line is fabricated, so al-Tabari and other scholars said: 'Abd al-Samad is not among the transmitters of knowledge, may Allah have mercy on him. From the margin of (ʿ).]], the poet said:

"We approach women during their purity, and do not approach women when they have menstruated [great] menstruation."

Abu 'Ubayda and others denied this and said: it is not in the speech of the Arabs. But it is possible that they menstruated from the intensity of their magnification of him, and a woman may be frightened and miscarry her child or menstruate. al-Zajjaj said: one says *akbarnahu*, and one does not say *hadnahu*, so *al-ikbar* does not mean menstruation. al-Azhari replied: *akbarat* may mean she menstruated, because when a woman first menstruates she leaves the realm of childhood for adulthood. He said: the *ha'* in "*akbarnahu*" may be the *ha'* of pause, not the *ha'* of pronoun, but this is refuted, because the *ha'* of pause drops in connected speech. More preferable than this is the saying of Ibn al-Anbari: the *ha'* is a pronoun referring to the verbal noun of the verb, meaning they magnified a magnification, that is, they menstruated a menstruation. According to the first saying of Ibn 'Abbas, the *ha'* returns to Yusuf, meaning they magnified Yusuf and exalted him.

Qur'anic verse: ﴿And they cut their hands﴾. Mujahid said: they cut them until they threw them down. It was also said: they scratched them. Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid [from the manuscripts g and k]: he said: they slashed them with the knife. Al-Nahhas said: Mujahid means that it was not a cut by which the hand separates; rather it was a scratch and a slash, and this is known in the language, where one says when a person scratches the hand of his companion that he "cut his hand." Ikrimah said: "their hands" means their sleeves, but this is far-fetched. It was also said: their fingertips, meaning that they found no pain in the cutting and the wounding, because their hearts were occupied with Yusuf. The word "cutting" (taqti') indicates multiplicity, so the multiplicity may refer to one woman who wounded her hand in several places, or it may refer to their number.

Qur'anic verse: ﴿And they said: Ḥāsha lillāh﴾, that is, "Far be it from Allah" (ma'aadha Allah). Al-Asma'i narrated from Nafi' that he recited as Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' recited: "wa-qulna ḥāsha lillāh," with the alif affirmed, which is the original form; whoever omits it makes the lam in "lillāh" a substitute for it. There are four dialectal forms: one says ḥāshāka, ḥāshā laka, ḥāsha laka, and ḥasha laka. One also says ḥāshā Zaydin and ḥāshā Zaydan. Al-Nahhas said: I heard 'Ali ibn Sulayman say that I heard Muhammad ibn Yazid say: the accusative is preferable, because it is established that it is a verb, as in their saying "ḥāsha li-Zaydin," and a particle is not subject to deletion. The poet al-Nabigha said:
"And I do not except from the people any one"
Some said: ḥāsha is a particle, and uḥāshā is a verb. What indicates that ḥāshā is a verb is the occurrence of a prepositional particle after it. Abu Zayd narrated from a Bedouin: "O Allah, forgive me and whoever hears, except Satan and Abu al-Asbagh," and he put it in the accusative. Al-Hasan recited "wa-qulna ḥāsh lillāh" with the shin sukun, and also from him "ḥāsha al-ilāh." Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy recited "ḥāsha Allāh" without the lam, and from this is the poet's saying:
"Ḥāsha Abi Thawban, indeed in him is ... restraint from blame and insult"
Al-Zajjaj said: the origin of the word is from al-ḥāshiya, and al-ḥashā means the side; one says: I was in the ḥashā of so-and-so, meaning on his side. So your saying "ḥāsha li-Zaydin" means Zayd withdrew from this and kept away from it, and the exception is an expulsion and removal from the whole of those mentioned. Abu 'Ali said: it is a verb derived from al-muḥāshāh, meaning Yusuf kept aside and was in a side and region from what was attributed to him, or from being a human. So ḥāsha and ḥāsh in the sense of exception are, according to Sibawayh, prepositions, while according to al-Mubarrad and Abu 'Ali they are verbs.

Qur'anic verse: ﴿This is not a human (bashar)﴾. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: "mā" here is in the position of "laysa," as you say: laysa Zaydun qā'iman, and "mā hādhā basharan," and ﴿mā hunna ummahātihim﴾ [al-Mujadila: 2]. [See vol. 17, p. 272.] The Kufans said: when the bā' was deleted, it became accusative, and the explanation of this, according to what Ahmad ibn Yahya said, is that when you say "mā Zaydun bi-munṭaliqin," the position of the bā' is accusative, and likewise all the prepositional particles; when the bā' is deleted it becomes accusative to indicate its place. He said: this is the view of al-Farra'. He said: "mā" did not govern anything. The Basrans obliged them to say: "Zayd al-qamar," because the meaning is "like the moon." Ahmad ibn Yahya replied that the bā' is more inherent among the prepositions than the kāf, because the kāf can be a noun. Al-Nahhas said: only the view of the Basrans is correct, and this view is self-contradictory, because al-Farra' permitted explicitly "mā bi-munṭaliqin Zaydun," and recited:
"By Allah, if I were free, and you are not a free man nor a freed slave"
And he forbade the explicit accusative, and we know of no disagreement among the grammarians that it is permissible: "mā fīka bi-rāghibin Zaydun," and "mā ilayka bi-qāṣidin 'Amrun," and then they delete the bā' and put it in the nominative. The Basrans and Kufans narrated "mā Zaydun munṭaliqun" with the nominative; the Basrans narrated that it is the dialect of Tamim, and they recited:
"Do you make for me a rival, Taym, while Taym is not a match for one of noble lineage"
Al-nidd, al-nadīd and al-nadīda mean the like and the equal. Al-Kisa'i narrated that it is the dialect of Tihama and Najd. Al-Farra' claimed that the nominative is the stronger of the two; Abu Ishaq said: this is an error; the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the language of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) are stronger and more fitting. I say: in the codex of Hafsa (may Allah be pleased with her) it is "mā hādhā bi-bashar," as mentioned by al-Ghaznawi. Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: the women mentioned that the [form] of Yusuf is more beautiful than the form of a human; rather he is in the form of an angel. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin: 4] [see vol. 20, p. 113]. The reconciliation of the two verses is that their saying "ḥāsha lillāh" is an absolution of Yusuf from what the wife of al-'Aziz accused him of, namely solicitation; that is, Yusuf is far from this. Their saying "lillāh" means for the sake of His fear, that is, it is an absolution for Allah from this, that is, Yusuf has been saved from that. So this is not about form at all. The meaning is that in being free from sins he is like the angels, so there is no contradiction. It was also said: the intent is to exalt him above resemblance to humans in form, because of the extreme of his beauty; and his saying "lillāh" is an emphasis on this meaning. According to this meaning, the women said that out of their supposition that the form of an angel is more beautiful, and his saying the Exalted, ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin: 4] had not reached them, for it is from our Book. Some weak-minded people thought that if this statement were a false supposition on their part, it would be obligatory upon Allah to refute them and show their lie; this is false, since there is no obligation upon Allah the Exalted, and not everything that Allah, glory be to Him, reports of the disbelief of the disbelievers and the lies of liars must be accompanied by a refutation. Also, people of custom may say of the ugly that it is like a devil, and of the beautiful that it is like an angel, meaning that its like has not been seen, since people do not see angels; so this is based on a supposition that the form of an angel is more beautiful, or on reporting the purity of his character and his distance from accusations.

(In hādhā illā malakun) meaning: "This is not but an angel." The poet said:
"You are not a human, but an angel who descended from the air of heaven, pouring down"
It was narrated from al-Hasan: "mā hādhā bi-shiran" with kasra on the bā' and shīn, meaning: this is not a purchased slave; that is, such a one should not be sold. He placed the verbal noun in the place of the passive participle, as He said: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 96], meaning its game. Examples of this are many. It may also be that the meaning is: this is not a price, that is, its like is not priced or valued; so "purchase" here refers to the price paid for it, as when you say "mā hādhā bi-alf" to negate the speaker's statement "this is for a thousand." The bā' in this case is related to a deleted element, which is the predicate, as if he said: "this is not valued at a purchase." The reading of the majority is more fitting, because after it "in hādhā illā malakun karīm" is an exaggeration in praising him within the category of angels, to magnify his station; and because words like "bi-shirān" are written in the codex with a yā'.

Qur'anic verse: ﴿She said: That is the one you blamed me for﴾. When she saw their infatuation with Yusuf, she showed the excuse for herself by her saying "you blamed me for it," that is, for loving him. "Dhālika" means "hādhā," and this is al-Tabari's choice. It was said: the pronoun refers to the love, and "dhālika" is in its proper sense, and the meaning is: that is the love for which you blamed me, that is, the love of this is that. Blame is the attribution of ugliness. Then she confessed and said: ﴿And I did solicit him to himself, but he refused﴾ (fa-staʿṣama), that is, he abstained [in ḥ and ʿ: Know that when she displayed her excuse before the women in the intensity of her love for him, she uncovered the reality and said: "And I did solicit him to himself, but he refused."]. The term ʿiṣma (protection) is called so because it prevents committing sin. It was also said: "istaʿṣama" means "istaʿṣā" (refused), and the meaning is one.

(And if he does not do what I command him, he will certainly be imprisoned) She renewed the solicitation in the presence of the women and tore away the veil of modesty, and threatened imprisonment if he did not comply; she did this only when she no longer feared blame or speech, contrary to her first position, since that had been between her and him.

(And he will surely be among the humiliated) that is, the wretched. In the codex it is written "wa-layakūnan" with an alif, and it is read with a light nūn for emphasis; the nūn of emphasis is read heavy or light. Pausing on "layusjanan" with the nūn is because it is heavy, and pausing on "layakūnan" with the alif is because it is light; it resembles the nūn of declension in your saying: "I saw a man, and Zayd, and ʿAmr." Similar to this is His saying: "lanasfaʿan bi-l-nāṣiya" [see vol. 20, p. 125], and similar cases where one pauses with the alif, as in al-A'sha's saying:
"And do not worship Satan, and worship Allah, and go on in worship"
That is, he intended "fa-ʿbudā," and when he paused on it, the pause was with the alif.

God Almighty said: ﴿And women in the city said﴾. It is also said "nuswah" with a *damma* on the *nun*, which is the recitation of al-A'mash, al-Mufaddal and al-Sulami. The large plural is *nisa'*. It is permissible to say "waqalat niswatun" (and women said) and "qala niswatun" (and women said), like "qalat al-a'rabu" and "qala al-a'rabu" (the Bedouins said). This is because the story spread among the people of Egypt, so the women talked about it. It has been said that they were the wife of the cupbearer of al-Aziz, the wife of his baker, the wife of the keeper of his animals, and the wife of the keeper of his prison. It has also been said that they were the wife of the chamberlain, related from Ibn 'Abbas and others.

﴿She is seeking to seduce her young man (fata) from himself﴾. *Al-fata* in the speech of the Arabs means the young man, and the woman is *fatah*.

﴿She has been seized by love for him﴾. It has been said: *shaghafaha* means it overpowered her. It has also been said: his love entered beneath her *shighaf* (the membrane around the heart), related from Mujahid and others. 'Amr ibn Dinar narrated from 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: it entered beneath her *shighaf*. al-Hasan said: *al-shaghaf* is the innermost part of the heart. al-Suddi and Abu 'Ubayd [[In (ʿ), (w) and (y): Abu 'Ubayda.]] said: *shighaf al-qalb* is its covering, which is a skin over it. It has also been said: it is the middle of the heart. The meanings of these sayings are close, and the meaning is: his love reached her *shighaf* and overcame her. al-Nabigha said:

"Worry has come between that and a dweller within, entering as the *shighaf* that the fingers seek."
[[That is, the fingers of the physicians. He says: worry has prevented him from weeping over the abodes, for it entered the heart until it afflicted him with a disease.]]

It has also been said that *al-shighaf* is a disease. al-Asma'i recited for a rajiz (rajaz poet):

"He follows her, while she is for him a *shighaf*."

Abu Ja'far ibn Muhammad, Ibn Muhayşin and al-Hasan read *sha'afaha* with an unpointed 'ayn. Ibn al-A'rabi said: its meaning is that his love burned her heart. He said: the first reading is the one practised. al-Jawhari said: *sha'afahu al-hubb* means love burned his heart. Abu Zayd said: it made him ill. One says *shu'ifa bi-kadha* and he is *mash'uf*. al-Hasan read "qad sha'afaha", and said: it made her insides full of love. al-Nahhas said: its meaning according to most lexicographers is "it has taken her in every direction," because *shi'af al-jibal* are their heights, and one says *shughifa bi-dhalika shaghfan* (with the 'ayn sukun) when one is infatuated with it. However, Abu 'Ubayda recited the line of Imru' al-Qays:

"You would kill me, though you have *sha'af* her heart, as the man with tar-smeared camel (mahnu'a) is consumed by burning."
[[al-Mahnu'a: the one smeared with tar. When a camel is smeared with tar it finds pleasure with burning, like the burning of love with its pleasure.]]

He said: the anguish of love and its burning were compared to that. It is narrated from al-Sha'bi that he said: *al-shaghaf* with the dotted letter is love, and *al-sha'af* with the undotted letter is madness. al-Nahhas said: it has been reported "qad shaghifahā" with a kasra on the *ghayn*, but it is not known in the speech of the Arabs except "shaghafaha" with a fatha on the *ghayn*, and likewise "sha'afaha", meaning he left her infatuated. Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah narrated from al-Hasan: *al-shaghaf* is the veil of the heart, and *al-sha'af* is the core of the heart. So if love reached the *sha'af*, she would die. al-Hasan also said: it is said that *al-shaghaf* is the skin adhering to the heart which is not seen, which is the white skin, so her love adhered to her heart like the adherence of the skin to the heart. [[In (ʿ) and (w): the liver. This is not correct.]]

God Almighty said: ﴿Indeed, we see her in clear error﴾, that is, in this action. Qatadah said: "*fatahā*" is the young man of her husband, because Yusuf was among them in the status of slaves, and her command over him was executed. Muqatil narrated from Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi from Salman al-Farisi, who said: the wife of al-Aziz asked her husband to give her Yusuf as a gift, and he gave him to her, saying: "What will you do with him?" She said: "I will take him as a son." He said: "He is yours." So she raised him until he reached maturity, while she had within herself what she had. She would uncover herself to him, adorn herself, and invite him gently, but Allah protected him.

God Almighty said: ﴿So when she heard of their deceit﴾, that is, of their backbiting about her and their scheming to blame her. It has been said: she had informed them and entrusted them with her secret, but they disclosed her secret, and this was called deceit. And His saying: "she sent for them" contains an omission, meaning she sent for them, inviting them to a banquet so that she might draw them into what she had fallen into. Mujahid narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: the wife of al-Aziz said to her husband, "I want to prepare food and invite these women," and he said to her, "Do it." So she prepared food, then she *najjadat* the houses for them. *Najjadat* means she adorned them; *al-najd* is what the house is adorned with of furnishings, that is, it is decorated, and its plural is *nujud*, narrated from Abu 'Ubayd [[As it stands in the originals: probably Abu 'Ubayda, as is evident from al-Lisan.]]. *Al-tanjid* is decoration. She sent to them, asking them to attend her food, and that none of you who have been named should stay away. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: they were forty women, and they came unwillingly. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said about them:

"Until, when they came to her by force, and she prepared for them cushions and carpets (kababan)."
[[The line is as in the originals. Another version: anmatan (rugs).]]

Wahb ibn [Munabbih] said: so they came and took their seats.

﴿And she prepared for them a couch (muttaka')﴾, that is, she arranged for them seats on which they might recline. Ibn Jubayr said: in each seat there was a goblet containing honey, a citron, and a sharp knife. Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr read *mutkan*, lightly pronounced and without hamza, and *al-mutk* is the citron in the language of the Copts, and Mujahid explained it this way. Sufyan narrated from Mansur from Mujahid, who said: *al-muttaka'* with a heavy pronunciation is the food, and *al-mutk* with a light pronunciation is the citron. The poet said:

"We drink sin openly from the cups, and see the citron (mutk) lent among us."

The Azd Shanu'a tribe say: the citron is *al-mutkah*. al-Jawhari said: *al-mutk* is what the circumciser leaves behind. The origin of *al-mutk* is *al-zamawrad* [[Al-zamawrad: thin bread wrapped around meat or other things, or something resembling the citron.]]. *Al-matka'* among women is one who has not been circumcised [[Khafd al-jariyah: circumcising the girl. Likewise for boys. The custom is that khafd is specific to girls and khitan to boys.]]. al-Farra' said: a shaykh from the trustworthy people of Basra told me that *al-mutk* lightly pronounced is *al-zamawrad*. Some said it is the citron, related by al-Akhfash. Ibn Zayd: citron and honey with which one eats. The poet said [[He is Jamil ibn Ma'mar. Qulal is the plural of qullah, and the qullah is a large jar. It was said: a large pitcher. It was said: a small cup. Other things were also said.]]:

"We remained in blessing and reclined, and drank the lawful from its jars."

That is, we ate. al-Nahhas said: God's saying ﴿and she prepared (a'tadat)﴾ is from *al-'atad*, which is everything you make ready for something. The most accurate of what has been said about "*muttaka'*" is what 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: a seat. As for the saying of a group of exegetes that it means food, it is permissible with the implied meaning "food reclined," like "and ask the town" [Yusuf 12:82]. This omission is indicated by "and she gave each one of them a knife," because the presence of women with knives is only for food that is cut with knives. He said this in his book *I'rab al-Quran* [[Grammatical analysis of the Qur'an.]]. In his book *Ma'ani al-Quran*, he said: Ma'mar narrated from Qatadah, who said: "*al-muttaka'*" is food. It has also been said: "*al-muttaka'*" is whatever one leans on during food, drink or conversation, and this is what is known among the lexicographers, although the reports have been confirmed for this. al-Qutabi related that it is said: "*ittaka'na* at so-and-so's" meaning we ate. The origin of "*muttaka'*" is *mawtaka'*, and similar to it are *muttazin* and *muttaʿid*, since it derives from *wazanat*, *wa'adat* and *wakat*. It is said: *ittaka'a* yattaki'u *ittika'an*.

(﴿each one of them a knife﴾) is two objects. al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' related that *al-sikkin* (knife) can be masculine or feminine. al-Farra' recited:

"He made marks on the hump on a cold morning, with a knife whose handle is firmly fixed."
[[*'Ayyatha*: he made a mark on the camel's hump.]]

al-Jawhari said: the more common usage is masculine. He said:

"He seems a sincere adviser in what appears, but when he is alone, that is a knife, skilled at the throat."

al-Asma'i said: in *al-sikkin* only the masculine is known.

God Almighty said: ﴿And she said, "Come out before them"﴾, pronounced with a *damma* on the *ta'* to avoid meeting two sakins, because a kasra is heavy when a damma follows it, and the *ta'* was pronounced with a kasra according to the original. It was said: she said to them, "Do not cut and do not eat until I inform you." Then she said to her servant, "When I say to you, call for me *Ilan*, call Yusuf." *Ila* was an idol they worshipped. Yusuf, peace be upon him, was working in clay, having tied his loincloth and rolled up his arms, so she said to the servant, "Call *Ilan* for me," meaning call the Lord for me; *Ila* in Hebrew is the Lord. He said: the women were astonished and said, "How can he come?!" The servant went up and called Yusuf, and when he came down she said to them, "Cut what you have."

﴿So when they saw him, they were amazed by him and cut their hands﴾ with the knives until the blades reached the bone. This is what Wahb ibn Munabbih said. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he did not come out to them until she had adorned him. He came out to them suddenly, and they were stunned by him and bewildered at the beauty of his face and his adornment, and what was upon him, so they began to cut their hands, thinking they were cutting citrons. There is disagreement about the meaning of "*akbarnahu*". Juwaybir narrated from al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas: they magnified him [[In the margin of (ʿ): the meaning of "*akbarnahu*" is "they magnified him," and were stunned by his beauty]] and feared him. And from him also: they were overcome with astonishment and emitted fluid. The poet said:

"When they see the stallion from atop a small rock, they neigh and magnify the spilled semen."
[[*Al-qarrah*: a small mountain separated from the mountains; it was also said: a great rock. Other things were also said.]]

Ibn Sam'an narrated from a number of his companions: they said they emitted fluid from passion. Wahb ibn Munabbih: they fell in love with him until ten of them died in that gathering from astonishment, bewilderment and longing for Yusuf. It was also said: its meaning is that they menstruated from astonishment, as said by Qatadah, Muqatil and al-Suddi [[Ibn 'Atiyya said: "*akbarnahu*" meaning they magnified him and were amazed at his beauty; this is the well-known view. 'Abd al-Samad ibn 'Ali al-Hashimi narrated from his father from his grandfather: it means they menstruated, and he recited:

"We approach women during their purity, and do not approach women when they menstruate with great menstruation."

The judge Abu Muhammad said: this is a weak view, its meaning is objectionable, and the line is fabricated, so al-Tabari and other scholars said: 'Abd al-Samad is not among the transmitters of knowledge, may Allah have mercy on him. From the margin of (ʿ).]], the poet said:

"We approach women during their purity, and do not approach women when they have menstruated [great] menstruation."

Abu 'Ubayda and others denied this and said: it is not in the speech of the Arabs. But it is possible that they menstruated from the intensity of their magnification of him, and a woman may be frightened and miscarry her child or menstruate. al-Zajjaj said: one says *akbarnahu*, and one does not say *hadnahu*, so *al-ikbar* does not mean menstruation. al-Azhari replied: *akbarat* may mean she menstruated, because when a woman first menstruates she leaves the realm of childhood for adulthood. He said: the *ha'* in "*akbarnahu*" may be the *ha'* of pause, not the *ha'* of pronoun, but this is refuted, because the *ha'* of pause drops in connected speech. More preferable than this is the saying of Ibn al-Anbari: the *ha'* is a pronoun referring to the verbal noun of the verb, meaning they magnified a magnification, that is, they menstruated a menstruation. According to the first saying of Ibn 'Abbas, the *ha'* returns to Yusuf, meaning they magnified Yusuf and exalted him.

Qur'anic verse: ﴿And they cut their hands﴾. Mujahid said: they cut them until they threw them down. It was also said: they scratched them. Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid [from the manuscripts g and k]: he said: they slashed them with the knife. Al-Nahhas said: Mujahid means that it was not a cut by which the hand separates; rather it was a scratch and a slash, and this is known in the language, where one says when a person scratches the hand of his companion that he "cut his hand." Ikrimah said: "their hands" means their sleeves, but this is far-fetched. It was also said: their fingertips, meaning that they found no pain in the cutting and the wounding, because their hearts were occupied with Yusuf. The word "cutting" (taqti') indicates multiplicity, so the multiplicity may refer to one woman who wounded her hand in several places, or it may refer to their number.

Qur'anic verse: ﴿And they said: Ḥāsha lillāh﴾, that is, "Far be it from Allah" (ma'aadha Allah). Al-Asma'i narrated from Nafi' that he recited as Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' recited: "wa-qulna ḥāsha lillāh," with the alif affirmed, which is the original form; whoever omits it makes the lam in "lillāh" a substitute for it. There are four dialectal forms: one says ḥāshāka, ḥāshā laka, ḥāsha laka, and ḥasha laka. One also says ḥāshā Zaydin and ḥāshā Zaydan. Al-Nahhas said: I heard 'Ali ibn Sulayman say that I heard Muhammad ibn Yazid say: the accusative is preferable, because it is established that it is a verb, as in their saying "ḥāsha li-Zaydin," and a particle is not subject to deletion. The poet al-Nabigha said:
"And I do not except from the people any one"
Some said: ḥāsha is a particle, and uḥāshā is a verb. What indicates that ḥāshā is a verb is the occurrence of a prepositional particle after it. Abu Zayd narrated from a Bedouin: "O Allah, forgive me and whoever hears, except Satan and Abu al-Asbagh," and he put it in the accusative. Al-Hasan recited "wa-qulna ḥāsh lillāh" with the shin sukun, and also from him "ḥāsha al-ilāh." Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy recited "ḥāsha Allāh" without the lam, and from this is the poet's saying:
"Ḥāsha Abi Thawban, indeed in him is ... restraint from blame and insult"
Al-Zajjaj said: the origin of the word is from al-ḥāshiya, and al-ḥashā means the side; one says: I was in the ḥashā of so-and-so, meaning on his side. So your saying "ḥāsha li-Zaydin" means Zayd withdrew from this and kept away from it, and the exception is an expulsion and removal from the whole of those mentioned. Abu 'Ali said: it is a verb derived from al-muḥāshāh, meaning Yusuf kept aside and was in a side and region from what was attributed to him, or from being a human. So ḥāsha and ḥāsh in the sense of exception are, according to Sibawayh, prepositions, while according to al-Mubarrad and Abu 'Ali they are verbs.

Qur'anic verse: ﴿This is not a human (bashar)﴾. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: "mā" here is in the position of "laysa," as you say: laysa Zaydun qā'iman, and "mā hādhā basharan," and ﴿mā hunna ummahātihim﴾ [al-Mujadila: 2]. [See vol. 17, p. 272.] The Kufans said: when the bā' was deleted, it became accusative, and the explanation of this, according to what Ahmad ibn Yahya said, is that when you say "mā Zaydun bi-munṭaliqin," the position of the bā' is accusative, and likewise all the prepositional particles; when the bā' is deleted it becomes accusative to indicate its place. He said: this is the view of al-Farra'. He said: "mā" did not govern anything. The Basrans obliged them to say: "Zayd al-qamar," because the meaning is "like the moon."
