Ahmad ibn Yahya replied that the bā' is more inherent among the prepositions than the kāf, because the kāf can be a noun. Al-Nahhas said: only the view of the Basrans is correct, and this view is self-contradictory, because al-Farra' permitted explicitly "mā bi-munṭaliqin Zaydun," and recited:
"By Allah, if I were free, and you are not a free man nor a freed slave"
And he forbade the explicit accusative, and we know of no disagreement among the grammarians that it is permissible: "mā fīka bi-rāghibin Zaydun," and "mā ilayka bi-qāṣidin 'Amrun," and then they delete the bā' and put it in the nominative. The Basrans and Kufans narrated "mā Zaydun munṭaliqun" with the nominative; the Basrans narrated that it is the dialect of Tamim, and they recited:
"Do you make for me a rival, Taym, while Taym is not a match for one of noble lineage"
Al-nidd, al-nadīd and al-nadīda mean the like and the equal. Al-Kisa'i narrated that it is the dialect of Tihama and Najd. Al-Farra' claimed that the nominative is the stronger of the two; Abu Ishaq said: this is an error; the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the language of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) are stronger and more fitting. I say: in the codex of Hafsa (may Allah be pleased with her) it is "mā hādhā bi-bashar," as mentioned by al-Ghaznawi. Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: the women mentioned that the [form] of Yusuf is more beautiful than the form of a human; rather he is in the form of an angel. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin: 4] [see vol. 20, p. 113]. The reconciliation of the two verses is that their saying "ḥāsha lillāh" is an absolution of Yusuf from what the wife of al-'Aziz accused him of, namely solicitation; that is, Yusuf is far from this. Their saying "lillāh" means for the sake of His fear, that is, it is an absolution for Allah from this, that is, Yusuf has been saved from that. So this is not about form at all. The meaning is that in being free from sins he is like the angels, so there is no contradiction. It was also said: the intent is to exalt him above resemblance to humans in form, because of the extreme of his beauty; and his saying "lillāh" is an emphasis on this meaning. According to this meaning, the women said that out of their supposition that the form of an angel is more beautiful, and his saying the Exalted, ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin: 4] had not reached them, for it is from our Book. Some weak-minded people thought that if this statement were a false supposition on their part, it would be obligatory upon Allah to refute them and show their lie; this is false, since there is no obligation upon Allah the Exalted, and not everything that Allah, glory be to Him, reports of the disbelief of the disbelievers and the lies of liars must be accompanied by a refutation. Also, people of custom may say of the ugly that it is like a devil, and of the beautiful that it is like an angel, meaning that its like has not been seen, since people do not see angels; so this is based on a supposition that the form of an angel is more beautiful, or on reporting the purity of his character and his distance from accusations.

(In hādhā illā malakun) meaning: "This is not but an angel." The poet said:
"You are not a human, but an angel who descended from the air of heaven, pouring down"
It was narrated from al-Hasan: "mā hādhā bi-shiran" with kasra on the bā' and shīn, meaning: this is not a purchased slave; that is, such a one should not be sold. He placed the verbal noun in the place of the passive participle, as He said: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 96], meaning its game. Examples of this are many. It may also be that the meaning is: this is not a price, that is, its like is not priced or valued; so "purchase" here refers to the price paid for it, as when you say "mā hādhā bi-alf" to negate the speaker's statement "this is for a thousand." The bā' in this case is related to a deleted element, which is the predicate, as if he said: "this is not valued at a purchase." The reading of the majority is more fitting, because after it "in hādhā illā malakun karīm" is an exaggeration in praising him within the category of angels, to magnify his station; and because words like "bi-shirān" are written in the codex with a yā'.

Qur'anic verse: ﴿She said: That is the one you blamed me for﴾. When she saw their infatuation with Yusuf, she showed the excuse for herself by her saying "you blamed me for it," that is, for loving him. "Dhālika" means "hādhā," and this is al-Tabari's choice. It was said: the pronoun refers to the love, and "dhālika" is in its proper sense, and the meaning is: that is the love for which you blamed me, that is, the love of this is that. Blame is the attribution of ugliness. Then she confessed and said: ﴿And I did solicit him to himself, but he refused﴾ (fa-staʿṣama), that is, he abstained [in ḥ and ʿ: Know that when she displayed her excuse before the women in the intensity of her love for him, she uncovered the reality and said: "And I did solicit him to himself, but he refused."]. The term ʿiṣma (protection) is called so because it prevents committing sin. It was also said: "istaʿṣama" means "istaʿṣā" (refused), and the meaning is one.

(And if he does not do what I command him, he will certainly be imprisoned) She renewed the solicitation in the presence of the women and tore away the veil of modesty, and threatened imprisonment if he did not comply; she did this only when she no longer feared blame or speech, contrary to her first position, since that had been between her and him.

(And he will surely be among the humiliated) that is, the wretched. In the codex it is written "wa-layakūnan" with an alif, and it is read with a light nūn for emphasis; the nūn of emphasis is read heavy or light. Pausing on "layusjanan" with the nūn is because it is heavy, and pausing on "layakūnan" with the alif is because it is light; it resembles the nūn of declension in your saying: "I saw a man, and Zayd, and ʿAmr." Similar to this is His saying: "lanasfaʿan bi-l-nāṣiya" [see vol. 20, p. 125], and similar cases where one pauses with the alif, as in al-A'sha's saying:
"And do not worship Satan, and worship Allah, and go on in worship"
That is, he intended "fa-ʿbudā," and when he paused on it, the pause was with the alif.

God Almighty said: ﴿And women in the city said﴾. It is also said "nuswah" with a *damma* on the *nun*, which is the recitation of al-A'mash, al-Mufaddal and al-Sulami. The large plural is *nisa'*. It is permissible to say "waqalat niswatun" (and women said) and "qala niswatun" (and women said), like "qalat al-a'rabu" and "qala al-a'rabu" (the Bedouins said). This is because the story spread among the people of Egypt, so the women talked about it. It has been said that they were the wife of the cupbearer of al-Aziz, the wife of his baker, the wife of the keeper of his animals, and the wife of the keeper of his prison. It has also been said that they were the wife of the chamberlain, related from Ibn 'Abbas and others.

﴿She is seeking to seduce her young man (fata) from himself﴾. *Al-fata* in the speech of the Arabs means the young man, and the woman is *fatah*.

﴿She has been seized by love for him﴾. It has been said: *shaghafaha* means it overpowered her. It has also been said: his love entered beneath her *shighaf* (the membrane around the heart), related from Mujahid and others. 'Amr ibn Dinar narrated from 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: it entered beneath her *shighaf*. al-Hasan said: *al-shaghaf* is the innermost part of the heart. al-Suddi and Abu 'Ubayd [[In (ʿ), (w) and (y): Abu 'Ubayda.]] said: *shighaf al-qalb* is its covering, which is a skin over it. It has also been said: it is the middle of the heart. The meanings of these sayings are close, and the meaning is: his love reached her *shighaf* and overcame her. al-Nabigha said:

"Worry has come between that and a dweller within, entering as the *shighaf* that the fingers seek."
[[That is, the fingers of the physicians. He says: worry has prevented him from weeping over the abodes, for it entered the heart until it afflicted him with a disease.]]

It has also been said that *al-shighaf* is a disease. al-Asma'i recited for a rajiz (rajaz poet):

"He follows her, while she is for him a *shighaf*."

Abu Ja'far ibn Muhammad, Ibn Muhayşin and al-Hasan read *sha'afaha* with an unpointed 'ayn. Ibn al-A'rabi said: its meaning is that his love burned her heart. He said: the first reading is the one practised. al-Jawhari said: *sha'afahu al-hubb* means love burned his heart. Abu Zayd said: it made him ill. One says *shu'ifa bi-kadha* and he is *mash'uf*. al-Hasan read "qad sha'afaha", and said: it made her insides full of love. al-Nahhas said: its meaning according to most lexicographers is "it has taken her in every direction," because *shi'af al-jibal* are their heights, and one says *shughifa bi-dhalika shaghfan* (with the 'ayn sukun) when one is infatuated with it. However, Abu 'Ubayda recited the line of Imru' al-Qays:

"You would kill me, though you have *sha'af* her heart, as the man with tar-smeared camel (mahnu'a) is consumed by burning."
[[al-Mahnu'a: the one smeared with tar. When a camel is smeared with tar it finds pleasure with burning, like the burning of love with its pleasure.]]

He said: the anguish of love and its burning were compared to that. It is narrated from al-Sha'bi that he said: *al-shaghaf* with the dotted letter is love, and *al-sha'af* with the undotted letter is madness. al-Nahhas said: it has been reported "qad shaghifahā" with a kasra on the *ghayn*, but it is not known in the speech of the Arabs except "shaghafaha" with a fatha on the *ghayn*, and likewise "sha'afaha", meaning he left her infatuated. Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah narrated from al-Hasan: *al-shaghaf* is the veil of the heart, and *al-sha'af* is the core of the heart. So if love reached the *sha'af*, she would die. al-Hasan also said: it is said that *al-shaghaf* is the skin adhering to the heart which is not seen, which is the white skin, so her love adhered to her heart like the adherence of the skin to the heart. [[In (ʿ) and (w): the liver. This is not correct.]]

God Almighty said: ﴿Indeed, we see her in clear error﴾, that is, in this action. Qatadah said: "*fatahā*" is the young man of her husband, because Yusuf was among them in the status of slaves, and her command over him was executed. Muqatil narrated from Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi from Salman al-Farisi, who said: the wife of al-Aziz asked her husband to give her Yusuf as a gift, and he gave him to her, saying: "What will you do with him?" She said: "I will take him as a son." He said: "He is yours." So she raised him until he reached maturity, while she had within herself what she had. She would uncover herself to him, adorn herself, and invite him gently, but Allah protected him.

God Almighty said: ﴿So when she heard of their deceit﴾, that is, of their backbiting about her and their scheming to blame her. It has been said: she had informed them and entrusted them with her secret, but they disclosed her secret, and this was called deceit. And His saying: "she sent for them" contains an omission, meaning she sent for them, inviting them to a banquet so that she might draw them into what she had fallen into. Mujahid narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: the wife of al-Aziz said to her husband, "I want to prepare food and invite these women," and he said to her, "Do it." So she prepared food, then she *najjadat* the houses for them. *Najjadat* means she adorned them; *al-najd* is what the house is adorned with of furnishings, that is, it is decorated, and its plural is *nujud*, narrated from Abu 'Ubayd [[As it stands in the originals: probably Abu 'Ubayda, as is evident from al-Lisan.]]. *Al-tanjid* is decoration. She sent to them, asking them to attend her food, and that none of you who have been named should stay away. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: they were forty women, and they came unwillingly. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said about them:

"Until, when they came to her by force, and she prepared for them cushions and carpets (kababan)."
[[The line is as in the originals. Another version: anmatan (rugs).]]

Wahb ibn [Munabbih] said: so they came and took their seats.

﴿And she prepared for them a couch (muttaka')﴾, that is, she arranged for them seats on which they might recline. Ibn Jubayr said: in each seat there was a goblet containing honey, a citron, and a sharp knife. Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr read *mutkan*, lightly pronounced and without hamza, and *al-mutk* is the citron in the language of the Copts, and Mujahid explained it this way. Sufyan narrated from Mansur from Mujahid, who said: *al-muttaka'* with a heavy pronunciation is the food, and *al-mutk* with a light pronunciation is the citron. The poet said:

"We drink sin openly from the cups, and see the citron (mutk) lent among us."

The Azd Shanu'a tribe say: the citron is *al-mutkah*. al-Jawhari said: *al-mutk* is what the circumciser leaves behind. The origin of *al-mutk* is *al-zamawrad* [[Al-zamawrad: thin bread wrapped around meat or other things, or something resembling the citron.]]. *Al-matka'* among women is one who has not been circumcised [[Khafd al-jariyah: circumcising the girl. Likewise for boys. The custom is that khafd is specific to girls and khitan to boys.]]. al-Farra' said: a shaykh from the trustworthy people of Basra told me that *al-mutk* lightly pronounced is *al-zamawrad*. Some said it is the citron, related by al-Akhfash. Ibn Zayd: citron and honey with which one eats. The poet said [[He is Jamil ibn Ma'mar. Qulal is the plural of qullah, and the qullah is a large jar. It was said: a large pitcher. It was said: a small cup. Other things were also said.]]:

"We remained in blessing and reclined, and drank the lawful from its jars."

That is, we ate. al-Nahhas said: God's saying ﴿and she prepared (a'tadat)﴾ is from *al-'atad*, which is everything you make ready for something. The most accurate of what has been said about "*muttaka'*" is what 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: a seat. As for the saying of a group of exegetes that it means food, it is permissible with the implied meaning "food reclined," like "and ask the town" [Yusuf 12:82]. This omission is indicated by "and she gave each one of them a knife," because the presence of women with knives is only for food that is cut with knives. He said this in his book *I'rab al-Quran* [[Grammatical analysis of the Qur'an.]]. In his book *Ma'ani al-Quran*, he said: Ma'mar narrated from Qatadah, who said: "*al-muttaka'*" is food. It has also been said: "*al-muttaka'*" is whatever one leans on during food, drink or conversation, and this is what is known among the lexicographers, although the reports have been confirmed for this. al-Qutabi related that it is said: "*ittaka'na* at so-and-so's" meaning we ate. The origin of "*muttaka'*" is *mawtaka'*, and similar to it are *muttazin* and *muttaʿid*, since it derives from *wazanat*, *wa'adat* and *wakat*. It is said: *ittaka'a* yattaki'u *ittika'an*.

(﴿each one of them a knife﴾) is two objects. al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' related that *al-sikkin* (knife) can be masculine or feminine. al-Farra' recited:

"He made marks on the hump on a cold morning, with a knife whose handle is firmly fixed."
[[*'Ayyatha*: he made a mark on the camel's hump.]]

al-Jawhari said: the more common usage is masculine. He said:

"He seems a sincere adviser in what appears, but when he is alone, that is a knife, skilled at the throat."

al-Asma'i said: in *al-sikkin* only the masculine is known.

God Almighty said: ﴿And she said, "Come out before them"﴾, pronounced with a *damma* on the *ta'* to avoid meeting two sakins, because a kasra is heavy when a damma follows it, and the *ta'* was pronounced with a kasra according to the original. It was said: she said to them, "Do not cut and do not eat until I inform you." Then she said to her servant, "When I say to you, call for me *Ilan*, call Yusuf." *Ila* was an idol they worshipped. Yusuf, peace be upon him, was working in clay, having tied his loincloth and rolled up his arms, so she said to the servant, "Call *Ilan* for me," meaning call the Lord for me; *Ila* in Hebrew is the Lord. He said: the women were astonished and said, "How can he come?!" The servant went up and called Yusuf, and when he came down she said to them, "Cut what you have."

﴿So when they saw him, they were amazed by him and cut their hands﴾ with the knives until the blades reached the bone. This is what Wahb ibn Munabbih said. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he did not come out to them until she had adorned him. He came out to them suddenly, and they were stunned by him and bewildered at the beauty of his face and his adornment, and what was upon him, so they began to cut their hands, thinking they were cutting citrons. There is disagreement about the meaning of "*akbarnahu*". Juwaybir narrated from al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas: they magnified him [[In the margin of (ʿ): the meaning of "*akbarnahu*" is "they magnified him," and were stunned by his beauty]] and feared him. And from him also: they were overcome with astonishment and emitted fluid. The poet said:

"When they see the stallion from atop a small rock, they neigh and magnify the spilled semen."
[[*Al-qarrah*: a small mountain separated from the mountains; it was also said: a great rock. Other things were also said.]]

Ibn Sam'an narrated from a number of his companions: they said they emitted fluid from passion. Wahb ibn Munabbih: they fell in love with him until ten of them died in that gathering from astonishment, bewilderment and longing for Yusuf. It was also said: its meaning is that they menstruated from astonishment, as said by Qatadah, Muqatil and al-Suddi [[Ibn 'Atiyya said: "*akbarnahu*" meaning they magnified him and were amazed at his beauty; this is the well-known view. 'Abd al-Samad ibn 'Ali al-Hashimi narrated from his father from his grandfather: it means they menstruated, and he recited:

"We approach women during their purity, and do not approach women when they menstruate with great menstruation."

The judge Abu Muhammad said: this is a weak view, its meaning is objectionable, and the line is fabricated, so al-Tabari and other scholars said: 'Abd al-Samad is not among the transmitters of knowledge, may Allah have mercy on him. From the margin of (ʿ).]], the poet said:

"We approach women during their purity, and do not approach women when they have menstruated [great] menstruation."

Abu 'Ubayda and others denied this and said: it is not in the speech of the Arabs. But it is possible that they menstruated from the intensity of their magnification of him, and a woman may be frightened and miscarry her child or menstruate. al-Zajjaj said: one says *akbarnahu*, and one does not say *hadnahu*, so *al-ikbar* does not mean menstruation. al-Azhari replied: *akbarat* may mean she menstruated, because when a woman first menstruates she leaves the realm of childhood for adulthood. He said: the *ha'* in "*akbarnahu*" may be the *ha'* of pause, not the *ha'* of pronoun, but this is refuted, because the *ha'* of pause drops in connected speech. More preferable than this is the saying of Ibn al-Anbari: the *ha'* is a pronoun referring to the verbal noun of the verb, meaning they magnified a magnification, that is, they menstruated a menstruation. According to the first saying of Ibn 'Abbas, the *ha'* returns to Yusuf, meaning they magnified Yusuf and exalted him.

Qur'anic verse: ﴿And they cut their hands﴾. Mujahid said: they cut them until they threw them down. It was also said: they scratched them. Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid [from the manuscripts g and k]: he said: they slashed them with the knife. Al-Nahhas said: Mujahid means that it was not a cut by which the hand separates; rather it was a scratch and a slash, and this is known in the language, where one says when a person scratches the hand of his companion that he "cut his hand." Ikrimah said: "their hands" means their sleeves, but this is far-fetched. It was also said: their fingertips, meaning that they found no pain in the cutting and the wounding, because their hearts were occupied with Yusuf. The word "cutting" (taqti') indicates multiplicity, so the multiplicity may refer to one woman who wounded her hand in several places, or it may refer to their number.

Qur'anic verse: ﴿And they said: Ḥāsha lillāh﴾, that is, "Far be it from Allah" (ma'aadha Allah). Al-Asma'i narrated from Nafi' that he recited as Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' recited: "wa-qulna ḥāsha lillāh," with the alif affirmed, which is the original form; whoever omits it makes the lam in "lillāh" a substitute for it. There are four dialectal forms: one says ḥāshāka, ḥāshā laka, ḥāsha laka, and ḥasha laka. One also says ḥāshā Zaydin and ḥāshā Zaydan. Al-Nahhas said: I heard 'Ali ibn Sulayman say that I heard Muhammad ibn Yazid say: the accusative is preferable, because it is established that it is a verb, as in their saying "ḥāsha li-Zaydin," and a particle is not subject to deletion. The poet al-Nabigha said:
"And I do not except from the people any one"
Some said: ḥāsha is a particle, and uḥāshā is a verb. What indicates that ḥāshā is a verb is the occurrence of a prepositional particle after it. Abu Zayd narrated from a Bedouin: "O Allah, forgive me and whoever hears, except Satan and Abu al-Asbagh," and he put it in the accusative. Al-Hasan recited "wa-qulna ḥāsh lillāh" with the shin sukun, and also from him "ḥāsha al-ilāh." Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy recited "ḥāsha Allāh" without the lam, and from this is the poet's saying:
"Ḥāsha Abi Thawban, indeed in him is ... restraint from blame and insult"
Al-Zajjaj said: the origin of the word is from al-ḥāshiya, and al-ḥashā means the side; one says: I was in the ḥashā of so-and-so, meaning on his side. So your saying "ḥāsha li-Zaydin" means Zayd withdrew from this and kept away from it, and the exception is an expulsion and removal from the whole of those mentioned. Abu 'Ali said: it is a verb derived from al-muḥāshāh, meaning Yusuf kept aside and was in a side and region from what was attributed to him, or from being a human. So ḥāsha and ḥāsh in the sense of exception are, according to Sibawayh, prepositions, while according to al-Mubarrad and Abu 'Ali they are verbs.

Qur'anic verse: ﴿This is not a human (bashar)﴾. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: "mā" here is in the position of "laysa," as you say: laysa Zaydun qā'iman, and "mā hādhā basharan," and ﴿mā hunna ummahātihim﴾ [al-Mujadila: 2]. [See vol. 17, p. 272.] The Kufans said: when the bā' was deleted, it became accusative, and the explanation of this, according to what Ahmad ibn Yahya said, is that when you say "mā Zaydun bi-munṭaliqin," the position of the bā' is accusative, and likewise all the prepositional particles; when the bā' is deleted it becomes accusative to indicate its place. He said: this is the view of al-Farra'. He said: "mā" did not govern anything. The Basrans obliged them to say: "Zayd al-qamar," because the meaning is "like the moon." Ahmad ibn Yahya replied that the bā' is more inherent among the prepositions than the kāf, because the kāf can be a noun. Al-Nahhas said: only the view of the Basrans is correct, and this view is self-contradictory, because al-Farra' permitted explicitly "mā bi-munṭaliqin Zaydun," and recited:
"By Allah, if I were free, and you are not a free man nor a freed slave"
And he forbade the explicit accusative, and we know of no disagreement among the grammarians that it is permissible: "mā fīka bi-rāghibin Zaydun," and "mā ilayka bi-qāṣidin 'Amrun," and then they delete the bā' and put it in the nominative. The Basrans and Kufans narrated "mā Zaydun munṭaliqun" with the nominative; the Basrans narrated that it is the dialect of Tamim, and they recited:
"Do you make for me a rival, Taym, while Taym is not a match for one of noble lineage"
Al-nidd, al-nadīd and al-nadīda mean the like and the equal. Al-Kisa'i narrated that it is the dialect of Tihama and Najd. Al-Farra' claimed that the nominative is the stronger of the two; Abu Ishaq said: this is an error; the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the language of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) are stronger and more fitting. I say: in the codex of Hafsa (may Allah be pleased with her) it is "mā hādhā bi-bashar," as mentioned by al-Ghaznawi. Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: the women mentioned that the [form] of Yusuf is more beautiful than the form of a human; rather he is in the form of an angel. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin: 4] [see vol. 20, p. 113]. The reconciliation of the two verses is that their saying "ḥāsha lillāh" is an absolution of Yusuf from what the wife of al-'Aziz accused him of, namely solicitation; that is, Yusuf is far from this. Their saying "lillāh" means for the sake of His fear, that is, it is an absolution for Allah from this, that is, Yusuf has been saved from that. So this is not about form at all. The meaning is that in being free from sins he is like the angels, so there is no contradiction. It was also said: the intent is to exalt him above resemblance to humans in form, because of the extreme of his beauty; and his saying "lillāh" is an emphasis on this meaning. According to this meaning, the women said that out of their supposition that the form of an angel is more beautiful, and his saying the Exalted, ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin: 4] had not reached them, for it is from our Book. Some weak-minded people thought that if this statement were a false supposition on their part, it would be obligatory upon Allah to refute them and show their lie; this is false, since there is no obligation upon Allah the Exalted, and not everything that Allah, glory be to Him, reports of the disbelief of the disbelievers and the lies of liars must be accompanied by a refutation. Also, people of custom may say of the ugly that it is like a devil, and of the beautiful that it is like an angel, meaning that its like has not been seen, since people do not see angels; so this is based on a supposition that the form of an angel is more beautiful, or on reporting the purity of his character and his distance from accusations.

(In hādhā illā malakun) meaning: "This is not but an angel." The poet said:
"You are not a human, but an angel who descended from the air of heaven, pouring down"
It was narrated from al-Hasan: "mā hādhā bi-shiran" with kasra on the bā' and shīn, meaning: this is not a purchased slave; that is, such a one should not be sold. He placed the verbal noun in the place of the passive participle, as He said: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 96], meaning its game. Examples of this are many. It may also be that the meaning is: this is not a price, that is, its like is not priced or valued; so "purchase" here refers to the price paid for it, as when you say "mā hādhā bi-alf" to negate the speaker's statement "this is for a thousand." The bā' in this case is related to a deleted element, which is the predicate, as if he said: "this is not valued at a purchase." The reading of the majority is more fitting, because after it "in hādhā illā malakun karīm" is an exaggeration in praising him within the category of angels, to magnify his station; and because words like "bi-shirān" are written in the codex with a yā'.

Qur'anic verse: ﴿She said: That is the one you blamed me for﴾. When she saw their infatuation with Yusuf, she showed the excuse for herself by her saying "you blamed me for it," that is, for loving him. "Dhālika" means "hādhā," and this is al-Tabari's choice. It was said: the pronoun refers to the love, and "dhālika" is in its proper sense, and the meaning is: that is the love for which you blamed me, that is, the love of this is that. Blame is the attribution of ugliness. Then she confessed and said: ﴿And I did solicit him to himself, but he refused﴾ (fa-staʿṣama), that is, he abstained [in ḥ and ʿ: Know that when she displayed her excuse before the women in the intensity of her love for him, she uncovered the reality and said: "And I did solicit him to himself, but he refused."]. The term ʿiṣma (protection) is called so because it prevents committing sin. It was also said: "istaʿṣama" means "istaʿṣā" (refused), and the meaning is one.

(And if he does not do what I command him, he will certainly be imprisoned) She renewed the solicitation in the presence of the women and tore away the veil of modesty, and threatened imprisonment if he did not comply; she did this only when she no longer feared blame or speech, contrary to her first position, since that had been between her and him.

(And he will surely be among the humiliated) that is, the wretched. In the codex it is written "wa-layakūnan" with an alif, and it is read with a light nūn for emphasis; the nūn of emphasis is read heavy or light. Pausing on "layusjanan" with the nūn is because it is heavy, and pausing on "layakūnan" with the alif is because it is light; it resembles the nūn of declension in your saying: "I saw a man, and Zayd, and ʿAmr." Similar to this is His saying: "lanasfaʿan bi-l-nāṣiya" [see vol. 20, p. 125], and similar cases where one pauses with the alif, as in al-A'sha's saying:
"And do not worship Satan, and worship Allah, and go on in worship"
That is, he intended "fa-ʿbudā," and when he paused on it, the pause was with the alif.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 33–34:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "My Lord, prison is more beloved to me than what they invite me to.”﴾ That is, entering prison, so the mudaf (the omitted noun, "entering") has been elided. This was said by al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas. "More beloved to me" means easier for me and less burdensome than falling into disobedience, not that entering prison is in reality something loved. It is related that when Yusuf, peace be upon him, said, "Prison is more beloved to me," Allah revealed to him, "O Yusuf! You imprisoned yourself when you said, 'Prison is more beloved to me.' Had you said, 'Well-being is more beloved to me,' you would have been granted well-being." Abu Hatim related that ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, may Allah be pleased with him, recited "al-sajnu" with a fatha on the sin. It is also related that this was the reading of Ibn Abi Ishaq, ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Aʿraj and Yaʿqub, and it is a masdar of sajanahu sajnan.

(﴿And if You do not avert from me their plot﴾) That is, the plot of women. It has been said: the plot of the women who saw him, for they commanded him to obey the wife of al-Aziz, and said to him, "She is wronged, and you have wronged her." It has also been said: each one of them requested to be alone with him to advise him concerning the wife of al-Aziz, the aim being that she would rebuke him regarding her right and command him to assist her, so that perhaps he would respond. Thus each one of them began to be alone with him separately, saying to him, "O Yusuf! Fulfill my need, for I am better for you than your mistress," each one inviting him for herself and soliciting him. He said, "My Lord, she was one, and they have become a group."

It has also been said: the plot of the wife of al-Aziz in what she invited him to of indecency, and it was referred to with the plural form either to magnify her status in address, or to turn from explicit statement to allusion. Al-kayd means cunning and striving, and for this reason war is called kayd, because of people's cunning in it. ʿUmar ibn Lajaʾ said:

"Umm Bishr appeared to scheme against you, / and a scheme by display of adornment is what she schemes."

(﴿I will incline toward them﴾) is the answer to the condition, meaning: I would lean toward them, from ṣabā yaṣbū, when one inclines and yearns, ṣabwan and ṣabwatan. The poet said (he is Zayd ibn Dabbah):

"To Hind my heart inclined, / and Hind is one who causes such inclination."

That is, if You do not gently guard me from avoiding disobedience, I will fall into it.

(﴿And I would be among the ignorant﴾) That is, among those who commit sin and deserve blame, or among those who act in the manner of the ignorant. This indicates that no one refrains from disobedience to Allah except by Allah's help, and it also indicates the ugliness of ignorance and the blame upon its possessor.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So his Lord responded to him﴾ to what he said, "And if You do not avert from me their plot," he approached supplication, as if he said, "O Allah, avert from me their plot." So He answered his supplication, showed him kindness, and protected him from falling into fornication. "Their plot": it has been said, because they were a group who had solicited him for himself. It has been said: it means the plot of women. It has been said: it means the plot of the wife of al-Aziz, as mentioned in the verse before. The generality is more preferable.

So He answered his supplication, showed him kindness, and protected him from falling into fornication. "Their plot": it has been said, because they were a group who had solicited him for himself. It has been said: it means the plot of women. It has been said: it means the plot of the wife of al-Aziz, as mentioned in the verse before. The generality is more preferable.

Concerning this, there are four issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then it occurred to them﴾, meaning it became apparent to the Aziz and his counsellors, "after they had seen the signs", meaning the indications of Yusuf's innocence: the shirt torn from behind, the testimony of the witness, the cutting of the hands, and the women's lack of patience in meeting Yusuf. [It occurred to them] to imprison him, to conceal the story so that it would not spread among the common people, and to keep him away from her. It was also said: the signs are the blessings that used to be bestowed upon them as long as Yusuf was among them. The first view is more sound. Muqatil related from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying, "Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs," that he said: "The shirt is one of the signs, the testimony of the witness is one of the signs, the cutting of the hands is one of the signs, and the women's glorifying of him is one of the signs." It was also said: shame before people and fear of despair drove her to accept the veil in place of the fear of losing him, so that she might be satisfied when she was prevented from seeing him. She said:

"The longing of one who yearns while hoping for the meeting
is not like the longing of one who has no hope."

Or she was nearly [driven] by hope that he would tire of his imprisonment and surrender himself. His saying, exalted is He: (﴿they would imprison him﴾) "They would imprison him" is in the position of the subject (fa'il), meaning it became apparent to them that they should imprison him. This is the view of Sibawayh. Al-Mubarrad said: this is an error; the subject cannot be a clause. Rather, the subject is what is indicated by "occurred" (bada), which is a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "it occurred to them an occurrence," and it was omitted because the verb indicates it, as the poet said:

"It is right for him whose father is Abu Musa
that He who set the mountains firm should grant him success."

That is, "and the right was right," and it was omitted. It was also said: the meaning is "then there occurred to them an opinion they had not known," and this was omitted because the context indicates it. The verb "say" was also omitted, meaning they said: "They would imprison him." The lam is the answer to an implied oath; this was said by al-Farra'. The verb is masculine, not feminine; had it been feminine it would have been "yasjununahu" (they [feminine dual] would imprison him). This is supported by His saying "to them" (lahum) and not "to them" (feminine, lahunna). It is as though He reported about the women and their helpers, and the masculine was given precedence; this was said by Abu Ali. Al-Suddi said: the cause of Yusuf's imprisonment was that the wife of the Aziz complained to him that he had exposed her and spread her news; in this view, the pronoun in "lahum" refers to the king.

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for a while﴾, meaning for an unspecified period; this was said by many of the exegetes. Ibn Abbas said: until the rumour spreading in the city ceased. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: for six months. Al-Kiya related that it meant thirteen months. Ikrimah: nine years. Al-Kalbi: five years. Muqatil: [seven [[from manuscript ʿ. In Ruh al-Ma'ani and al-Razi, from Muqatil, twelve years.]]]. The discussion of "hin" (a while) and the rulings connected with it has already passed in "al-Baqarah".[[See vol. 1, p. 321 onward.]] Wahb said: he remained in prison for twelve years. "Hatta" here means "ila" (until), as in His saying: ﴿until the rising of dawn﴾ [al-Qadr: 5].[[See vol. 20, p. 134.]] God made the imprisonment a purification for Yusuf, peace be upon him, from his intention toward the woman. It seems that the Aziz, although he knew Yusuf's innocence, obeyed the woman regarding Yusuf's imprisonment. Ibn Abbas said: Yusuf stumbled three stumbles: when he intended her and was imprisoned; when he said to the cupbearer: ﴿Mention me to your lord﴾ [Yusuf: 42], and so he remained in prison several years; and when he said to his brothers: ﴿You are surely thieves﴾ [Yusuf: 70], and they said: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his stole before﴾ [Yusuf: 77].

The fourth: Yusuf, peace be upon him, was compelled by imprisonment to commit indecency, and he remained for five years, yet he did not consent to that, because of his great rank and noble standing. Had a man been compelled by imprisonment to commit adultery, it would not have been permissible for him, by consensus. If he was compelled by beating, the scholars have differed on it; the sound view is that if the coercion was severe, the sin of adultery and its prescribed punishment fall from him. Some of our scholars said that the prescribed punishment does not fall from him, but this is weak, for God, exalted is He, does not combine two punishments upon His servant, nor does He turn him between two trials, for this is among the greatest hardships in religion: ﴿and He has not placed upon you any hardship in religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78].[[See vol. 12, p. 99.]] The explanation of this will come in "al-Nahl", God willing.[[See vol. 10, p. 182 onward.]] Yusuf was patient and sought refuge in Him from the plotting, and He answered him, as has already been mentioned.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 36–38:

God Most High says: ﴿And there entered the prison with him two young men.﴾ "Fatayan" is the dual of "fata" (young man), and it is from the defective roots with yā'. As for their saying "al-futuww" (chivalry), it is anomalous. [[In manuscripts ʿayn, kāf and yā': "al-futuw is anomalous."]] Wahb and others said: Yusuf was taken to the prison bound, upon a donkey, and he was paraded about, [it was said:] "This is the recompense of one who disobeys his mistress," while he said: "This is easier than the garments of fire cut for them, the robes of pitch, the drink of boiling water, and the eating of the zaqqum tree." [[Muqattaʿat al-niran: this is like His saying, Exalted is He: "Garments of fire have been cut for them" (Qur'an 22:19), meaning they were sewn, fashioned and made into clothing for them.]]

When Yusuf reached the prison, he found in it people whose hope had been cut off and whose trials had grown severe. He began to say to them: "Be patient and be of good cheer, you will be rewarded." They said to him: "O young man! How good is your speech! Blessing has been bestowed upon us through your neighbourhood. Who are you, young man?" He said: "I am Yusuf, son of Safiyy Allah (the chosen of God), Yaʿqub, son of Dhabih Allah (the sacrificed one of God), Ishaq, son of Khalil Allah (the friend of God), Ibrahim." [[This is evidence of the (false) claim, since the one sacrificed is certainly Isma'il, peace be upon him.]]

Ibn ʿAbbas said: When the woman said to her husband, "This Hebrew slave has disgraced me, and I want you to imprison him," he imprisoned him. He would console the sorrowful in it, visit the sick in it, treat the wounded in it, pray the whole night, and weep until the walls of the houses, their roofs and the doors wept with him. The prison was purified through him, and the people of the prison became familiar with him. Whenever a man was released from the prison, he would return to sit in the prison with Yusuf. The keeper of the prison loved him and widened his circumstances within it. Then he said [to him]: "O Yusuf! I have loved you with a love I have never loved anything as I love you." He said: "I seek refuge in God from your love." He asked: "And why is that?" He said: "My father loved me and my brothers did to me what they did, and my mistress loved me and what you see befell me." 

He remained in his confinement until the king became angry with his baker and his cupbearer. That was because the king had been lenient with them, and they had become bored with him. So they secretly sent word to the baker and the cupbearer that they should both poison him. The baker agreed, but the cupbearer refused. The cupbearer went and informed the king of this, so the king ordered that both of them be imprisoned. They became familiar with Yusuf, and this is His saying: ﴿And there entered the prison with him two young men.﴾

It has also been said that the baker put poison in the food. When the food was brought, the cupbearer said: "O king! Do not eat, for the food is poisoned." The baker said: "O king! Do not drink, for the drink is poisoned." The king said to the cupbearer: "Drink!" He drank and it did him no harm. He said to the baker: "Eat!" He refused. The food was tested on an animal and it died on the spot. So he imprisoned them for a year, and they remained in the prison during that period with Yusuf.

The name of the cupbearer was Manja, and the other was Mujlith. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi from Ka'b. Al-Naqqash said: the name of one of them was Shuhram and the other Surham, the first with an unpointed/ shin (sh) and the other with an unpointed sin (s). Al-Tabari said: the one who saw that he was pressing wine was Nabu. Al-Suhayli said: he mentioned the name of the other but I did not specify it.

He said "fatayan" because they were both slaves, and a slave is called "fata," whether young or old. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Al-Qushayri said: Perhaps "fata" was a term for a slave in their custom, and for this reason He said: ﴿Your young man (fatah) is soliciting his self from himself﴾ (Qur'an 12:30). It is also possible that "fata" is a term for a servant even if he was not a slave. It is possible that they were imprisoned together with Yusuf, or after him, or before him, except that they entered the prison with him, into the place where he was.

﴿One of them said: "Indeed, I see myself pressing wine."﴾ That is, grapes. Yusuf had said to the people of the prison: "I interpret dreams." One of the two young men said to his companion: "Come, let us test this Hebrew slave," and they asked him without either of them having seen anything. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud. Al-Tabari related that they asked him about his knowledge, and he said: "I interpret visions," so they asked him about their dreams. Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said: they had seen a true vision and asked him about it, and therefore its interpretation was true. In the Sahih, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ: "The truest of you in vision is the truest of you in speech." It has also been said: it was a false vision which they asked him about as a test, and this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and al-Suddi. It has been said: of the two, the one who was crucified was the liar and the other the truthful one; this was said by Abu Mijlaz.

al-Tirmidhi related from Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Whoever feigns a dream falsely will be charged on the Day of Resurrection with tying a knot between two barley grains, and he will never be able to tie it between them." [[The addition is from the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi. Its commentator said: When I reflected upon it, it became clear that one who reports what he has not seen is tying an invalid knot in speech, of which he is unaware, i.e., he does not know it. So it is said to him: "Tie a knot between two barley grains," and he will never be able to do that, as a punishment for tying knots between words that had no reality, so that the punishment is of the same kind as the sin.]] Abu ʿIsa said: this is a good and sound hadith. And from ʿAli, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Whoever lies in his dream will be charged on the Day of Resurrection with tying a knot in a barley grain." He said: a good hadith.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: When they saw their dreams they woke up distressed, and Yusuf said to them: "Why do I see you distressed?" They said: "O our master! We have seen what we dislike." He said: "Then recount it to me." They recounted it to him. They said: "Inform us of the interpretation of what we have seen." This indicates that it was a dream seen in sleep.

﴿Indeed, we see you as one of the doers of good.﴾ His good conduct was that he would visit the sick, treat them, and console the grieving. Al-Dahhak said: when a man of the prison fell ill, he would attend to him; when he was in straits, he would widen things for him; when he was in need, he would gather for him and ask on his behalf. It has also been said: "min al-muhsinin" means "among the learned who excel in knowledge," as said by al-Farra'. Ibn Ishaq said: "min al-muhsinin" means "for us, if you interpret it," as one says: "Do such-and-such, and you are a doer of good." 

He said: "What did you see?" The baker said: "I saw as if I was baking bread in three baskets, and I placed it on my head, and a bird came and ate from it." The other said: "I saw as if I was taking clusters of white grapes and pressing them into three vessels, then I strained it and gave the king to drink, as was my custom before." That is His saying: ﴿Indeed, I see myself pressing wine﴾, that is, grapes, in the dialect of Oman; this was said by al-Dahhak. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Indeed, I see myself pressing grapes." Al-Asma'i said: al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman informed me that he met a Bedouin who had grapes with him, and said to him: "What do you have with you?" He said: "Wine." It has also been said that the meaning of "pressing wine" is "pressing grapes," where the qualifier has been omitted. One says khamrah, khamr and khumur, like tamrah, tamr and tumur.

﴿He said: "No food will come to you that you are given to eat except that I will inform you of its interpretation."﴾ That is, no food will come to you tomorrow from your household, except that I will inform you of its interpretation, so that you may know that I know the interpretation of your dreams. They said: "Do it!" He told them: "There will come to you such-and-such," and it was as he said. This was of the knowledge of the unseen, which was specific to Yusuf. He made clear that God singled him out with this knowledge because he had abandoned the religion of a people who do not believe in God, meaning the religion of the king. In my view, the meaning of the statement is: knowledge of the interpretation of your dream, knowledge of what food will come to you, and knowledge of the religion of God. So listen first to what concerns religion, that you may be guided. For this reason he did not interpret for them until he had invited them to Islam, and said: ﴿O my two companions of the prison, are many lords dispersed better, or God, the One, the Subduer? What you worship besides Him are but names﴾ (Qur'an 12:39–40), the whole verse, as will come.

It has also been said: He knew that one of them would be killed, so he invited them to Islam so that they might be prepared through it. It has also been said: Yusuf disliked interpreting for them what they had asked, because of what he knew of the harm that would befall one of them, so he turned away from their question and took up something else, and said: ﴿No food will come to you that you are given to eat﴾ in sleep, ﴿except that I will inform you﴾ of its explanation while awake. This was said by al-Suddi. They said to him: "This is the act of soothsayers and diviners." Yusuf, peace be upon him, said to them: "I am not a soothsayer, but this is among what my Lord has taught me. I do not inform you of it by way of divination and astrology, but it is by revelation from God, Mighty and Majestic."

Ibn Jurayj said: When the king wanted to kill a person, he would prepare for him a known food and send it to him. So the meaning is: no food will come to you that you are given to eat while awake. According to this, "turzaqanihi" means it is supplied to you from the king or from someone else. It may also mean God provides it for you. Al-Hasan said: he would inform them of what was hidden, like Jesus, peace be upon him. It has also been said: he invited them to Islam by this, and made the miracle by which they would be guided the informing of them of unseen things.

God Most High says: ﴿And I follow the religion of my fathers, Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub.﴾ Because they were prophets upon the truth.

(Ma kana) means: it is not fitting for us.

(Lana an nushrika billahi min shay') "min" is for emphasis, like your saying: "No one came to me." And His saying, Exalted is He: (Dhalika min fadli Allahi 'alayna) refers to His protecting him from fornication.

(Wa 'ala al-nas) means: upon the believers whom God has protected from polytheism. It has also been said: "This is of God's grace upon us" in that He made us prophets, and "and upon the people" in that He sent us as messengers to them.

(Wa lakinna akthara al-nas la yashkurun) for the blessing of tawhid and faith.

They became familiar with Yusuf, and this is His saying: ﴿And there entered the prison with him two young men.﴾

It has also been said that the baker put poison in the food. When the food was brought, the cupbearer said: "O king! Do not eat, for the food is poisoned." The baker said: "O king! The food was tested on an animal and it died on the spot. So he imprisoned them for a year, and they remained in the prison during that period with Yusuf.

The name of the cupbearer was Manja, and the other was Mujlith. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi from Ka'b. Al-Naqqash said: the name of one of them was Shuhram and the other Surham, the first with an unpointed/ shin (sh) and the other with an unpointed sin (s). Al-Tabari said: the one who saw that he was pressing wine was Nabu. Al-Suhayli said: he mentioned the name of the other but I did not specify it.

Al-Qushayri said: Perhaps "fata" was a term for a slave in their custom, and for this reason He said: ﴿Your young man (fatah) is soliciting his self from himself﴾ (Qur'an 12:30). It is also possible that "fata" is a term for a servant even if he was not a slave. It is possible that they were imprisoned together with Yusuf, or after him, or before him, except that they entered the prison with him, into the place where he was.

﴿One of them said: "Indeed, I see myself pressing wine."﴾ That is, grapes. Yusuf had said to the people of the prison: "I interpret dreams." One of the two young men said to his companion: "Come, let us test this Hebrew slave," and they asked him without either of them having seen anything. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud. Al-Tabari related that they asked him about his knowledge, and he said: "I interpret visions," so they asked him about their dreams. Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said: they had seen a true vision and asked him about it, and therefore its interpretation was true. In the Sahih, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ: "The truest of you in vision is the truest of you in speech." It has also been said: it was a false vision which they asked him about as a test, and this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and al-Suddi. It has been said: of the two, the one who was crucified was the liar and the other the truthful one; this was said by Abu Mijlaz.

[[The addition is from the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi. And from ʿAli, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Whoever lies in his dream will be charged on the Day of Resurrection with tying a knot in a barley grain." He said: a good hadith.

He said: "Then recount it to me." They recounted it to him. They said: "Inform us of the interpretation of what we have seen." This indicates that it was a dream seen in sleep.

﴿Indeed, we see you as one of the doers of good.﴾ His good conduct was that he would visit the sick, treat them, and console the grieving. Al-Dahhak said: when a man of the prison fell ill, he would attend to him; when he was in straits, he would widen things for him; when he was in need, he would gather for him and ask on his behalf. It has also been said: "min al-muhsinin" means "among the learned who excel in knowledge," as said by al-Farra'. Ibn Ishaq said: "min al-muhsinin" means "for us, if you interpret it," as one says: "Do such-and-such, and you are a doer of good." 

He said: "What did you see?" The baker said: "I saw as if I was baking bread in three baskets, and I placed it on my head, and a bird came and ate from it." Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 39–40:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿O two companions of the prison﴾ means: O two inhabitants of the prison. He mentioned "companions" because of how long they had remained in it, as when you say: "companions of Paradise" and "companions of the Fire."

(Are separate lords better) means: different in their smallness, greatness and moderation, or scattered in number.

(Or Allah, the One, the Irresistible?) It was also said: the address is to the two of them and to the people of the prison. Before them were idols that they worshipped besides Allah the Exalted, so he said this to establish the proof against them, meaning: gods of various kinds that neither harm nor benefit. "Or Allah, the One, the Irresistible," who has subdued everything. Its parallel is: ﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate?﴾ [An-Naml: 59]. It was also said: by "scattered" he pointed out that if the god were multiple, they would differ in will and would overpower one another, and he made clear that when they are scattered they are not gods.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿You worship besides Him only names﴾ He explained the impotence and weakness of the idols, saying: "You worship besides Him" meaning besides Allah, "only entities with names that have no meanings."

(Which you have named) from your own selves. It was also said: by "names" he meant the named things, meaning you worship only idols that have nothing of divinity except the name, because they are inanimate. He said "you worship" although he had begun by addressing the two, because he intended all who are in the same state of polytheism as they were.

(Only names you have named, you and your fathers) He omitted the second object for indication, and the meaning is: you named them "gods" from your own selves.

(For which Allah has sent down no authority) meaning no proof. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: (no authority) means no proof.

(Judgment belongs only to Allah) who is the Creator of all.

(He has commanded that you worship none but Him).

(That is the upright religion), meaning the straight.

(But most of mankind do not know.)
