**First issue:** Concerning this verse there are two matters. The first is His saying, ﴿As for one of you, he will give his lord wine to drink﴾. That is, he said to the cupbearer: "You will be restored to your post of giving the king drink after three days." And he said to the other: "As for you, you will be called up in three days, then you will be crucified, and birds will eat from your head." He said: "By God, I did not see anything." He said: "You saw, or you did not see; the matter about which you two inquire has been decided." The lexicographers (ahl al-lugha) report that *saqā* and *asqā* are two forms with one meaning, as the poet said [[This is Labid. Majd is the daughter of Taym ibn Ghalib ibn Fihr, and she is the mother of Kullab and Kulayb of Banu Rabi'a. The subject of *saqā* here is the rain.]]:

"Rain watered my people, Banu Majd, and gave drink to Numayr and the tribes of Hilal."

Al-Nahhas said: "Most lexicographers hold that the meaning of *saqāhu* is that he handed him (the drink) and he drank it, or he poured water into his throat, while the meaning of *asqāhu* is that he made for him a portion of drink." God the Exalted said: ﴿And We gave you to drink sweet water﴾ [al-Mursalat: 27] [[See vol. 29, p. 158.]].

**The second issue:** Our scholars said: If it is asked, whoever lies about his dream and the interpreter interprets it for him, is its ruling binding on him? We say: It is not binding on him. That was only the case with Yusuf, because he was a prophet, and a prophet's interpretation is a ruling, and he had said, "It will be such-and-such," and God the Exalted brought about what he reported, as He said, confirming his prophethood. If it is said: 'Abd al-Razzaq related from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, who said: A man came to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and said: "I saw in a dream as if I had grown green and then become barren, then green again and then barren." 'Umar said to him: "You are a man who believes, then disbelieves, then believes, then disbelieves, then dies a disbeliever." The man said: "I did not see anything." 'Umar said to him: "What was decreed for the companion of Yusuf has been decreed for you." We say: This is not for anyone after 'Umar, because 'Umar was a *muhaddath* [[*Muhaddath*: one who is inspired, or into whose heart something is cast, or upon whose tongue the right matter flows without intention (al-Qastallani). *Muhaddath* also means one whom the king speaks to, i.e., something is cast into his self.]], and whenever he suspected something it came to be, and whenever he spoke it occurred, as is related in his reports, which are many. Among them: a man entered upon him and he said to him: "I suspect you are a soothsayer," and it was as he suspected; al-Bukhari transmitted it. Among them: he asked a man about his name, and he said to him that it contained all the names of fire; so he said to him: "Go to your family, for they have been burned," and it was as he said; al-Muwatta' transmitted it. More elaboration on this will come in *Surat al-Hijr* [[See vol. 10, p. 42.]], God willing.

**Fifth-century Qur'an commentary of al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*, on Surah 12, verse 42:**

There are five issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** God's words: ﴿And he said to the one he thought would be saved﴾. Here "*thanna*" (thought, supposed) means "*ayqana*" (was certain), according to the view of most exegetes (*mufassirun*). Qatadah interpreted it as the ordinary sense of *thann*, which is the opposite of certainty. He said: "Joseph only supposed his deliverance, because the interpreter (*'abir*, dream-interpreter) makes a guess, and your Lord creates what He wills." The first view is more sound and better suited to the state of the prophets. What he said to the two young men about interpreting the dream was based on revelation (*wahy*). It is a supposition only in the judgment of people, whereas for the prophets their judgment is true in whatever way it occurs.

**The second issue:** God's words: "(Mention me in the presence of your lord)", that is, your master (*sayyid*). It is known in the language that a master may be called *rabb*. Al-A'sha said:

*My Lord is generous; He never spoils a favour,*
*And when one appeals to Him over the scrolls, He responds.*

[Another version reads: "(yunashid bi-l-mahariq)". He says: when one appeals to Him by what is in the books, He answers, that is, when asked, He gives. *Al-mahraq* is the page.]

That is, mention what you saw and my situation in interpreting the dream for the king, and inform him that I am wronged and imprisoned without fault.

In the Sahih of Muslim and others, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "None of you should say: 'Give your lord drink, feed your lord, help your lord.' Nor should any of you say: 'my lord (*rabbi*)'; let him say: 'my master (*sayyidi*), my guardian (*mawlaya*).' And none of you should say: 'my slave (*abdi*), my female slave (*amati*)'; let him say: 'my young man (*fatay*), my young woman (*fatati*), my boy (*ghulami*).'"

In the Qur'an: "Mention me in the presence of your lord" and "to your lord" and ﴿He is my lord; he has made my dwelling good﴾ [Yusuf: 23], meaning my companion, referring to the Aziz. It is said of anyone who sets right a thing and completes it: "He has *rabbahu* (reared/managed) it," so he is its *rabb* (lord, manager).

The scholars said: The Prophet's words "None of you should say" and "let him say" are guidance towards using the better term, not that using that term is forbidden. It is also reported from him (ﷺ): "that a female slave may bear her *rabb*," that is, her owner and master. This agrees with the Qur'an in using that word. So the prohibition in this matter means that we should not make these names a habit, thereby neglecting what is better and more appropriate.

It has been said that a man's saying "my slave" and "my female slave" carries two meanings. First, servanthood in truth belongs only to God Almighty, so when a person says to his owned slave "my slave" or "my female slave", he is exalting himself and attributing to himself what God attributed to Himself, which is not permissible. Second, the slave may take some harm from this, in belittling him by that designation, which leads him to disobedience.

Ibn Sha'ban said in *al-Zahi*: "The master should not say 'my slave' or 'my female slave', and the slave should not say 'my lord' or 'my lady'." This is to be understood in the sense we have mentioned.

It has also been said: The Prophet (ﷺ) only said "the slave should not say 'my lord'; let him say 'my master'" because *Rabb* is one of the names of God Almighty that is used by general agreement, whereas it is disputed whether *Sayyid* is one of God's names. If we say it is not one of God's names, the distinction is clear, as there is no confusion or difficulty. If we say it is one of His names, it is still not as famous or as commonly used as the word *Rabb*, so the distinction arises.

Ibn al-Arabi said: It is possible that this was permissible in the law (*shar'*) of Joseph (peace be upon him).

**The third issue:** God's words: ﴿But Satan caused him to forget the mention of his lord﴾. The pronoun in "*fa-ansahu*" (caused him to forget) has two views.

The first is that it refers to Joseph (peace be upon him): Satan caused him to forget the remembrance of God Almighty. This is because when Joseph said to the king's cupbearer, having known that he would be saved and return to his former position with the king, "(Mention me in the presence of your lord)", he forgot at that time to complain to God and seek His help, and inclined to rely on a created being. Therefore he was punished with a long stay.

Abd al-Aziz ibn Umayr al-Kindi said: Gabriel came to the Prophet Joseph (peace be upon him) in prison, and Joseph recognised him, and said: "O brother of those who warn! Why do I see you among the sinners?!" Gabriel (peace be upon him) said: "O pure son of the pure! The Lord of the Worlds sends you greetings, and says: 'Were you not ashamed, when you sought help from the children of Adam?! By My might! I will keep you in prison for several years.'" He said: "O Gabriel! Is He pleased with me?" He said: "Yes." He said: "I do not care now."

It is also reported that Gabriel came to him and rebuked him on behalf of God Almighty for that and for the length of his imprisonment, and said to him: "O Joseph! Who delivered you from being killed at the hands of your brothers?!" He said: "God Almighty." He said: "Who brought you out of the well?" He said: "God Almighty." He said: "Who protected you from indecency?" He said: "God Almighty." He said: "Who turned away from you the plots of women?" He said: "God Almighty." He said: "Then how did you trust a created being and leave your Lord, not asking Him?!" He said: "O Lord, a word slipped from me! I ask You, O God of Abraham, Isaac and the elder Jacob (peace be upon them), to have mercy on me." [In *ʿ* and *w*: "unless you show mercy to me."] Gabriel said to him: "Your punishment is that you will remain in prison for several years."

Abu Salamah reported from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "May God have mercy on Joseph! Had it not been for the word he said, '(Mention me in the presence of your lord)', he would not have stayed in prison for several years."

Ibn Abbas said: Joseph was punished with a long detention of several years when he said to the one of the two who was saved, "(Mention me in the presence of your lord)". Had Joseph remembered his Lord, He would have delivered him.

Isma'il ibn Ibrahim reported from Yunus, from al-Hasan, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Had it not been for the word of Joseph, that is, his saying '(Mention me in the presence of your lord)', he would not have remained in prison as long as he did." Then al-Hasan would weep and say: "We are struck by calamity, and so we complain to people."

It has also been said: The pronoun refers to the one who was saved, so he is the one who forgot. That is, Satan caused the cupbearer to forget to mention Joseph to his lord, that is, to his master. There is an ellipsis here, meaning: Satan caused him to forget the mention of Joseph to his lord. Some scholars preferred this view, saying: Had Satan not caused Joseph to forget the remembrance of God, he would not have deserved punishment by remaining in prison, since one who forgets is not held to account.

The advocates of the first view responded that forgetting may mean abandoning. When he abandoned the remembrance of God, and Satan called him to that, he was punished. The advocates of the second view answered them with God's words: ﴿And the one who was saved of the two said, and he remembered after a period﴾ [Yusuf: 45], which shows that the one who forgot was the cupbearer, not Joseph. Along with God's words: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ [al-Hijr: 42] [see vol. 10, p. 28], how can his forgetting be attributed to Satan, since Satan has no power over the prophets?

It is answered: As for forgetting, the prophets are not immune to it, except in one matter, namely reporting from God what they convey. In that they are protected. When forgetting occurs from them where it is possible, it is attributed absolutely to Satan. That applies only to what God has reported about them, and it is not permissible for us to say that about them. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Adam forgot, and his descendants forgot." And he said: "I am only a human; I forget as you forget." This has already been discussed.

**The fourth issue:** God's words: ﴿So he remained in prison for several years﴾. *Al-bid'* (several) is a portion of time, and its use is disputed. Ya'qub reported from Abu Zayd [thus in *ʿ* and *k*, and this is the reading in *al-Lisan*; in *ā* and *w*: "Ibn Zayd"]: It is said *bid'* and *bad'*, with the *ba* vowelled with fatha or kasra. Most of them said: One does not say *bid'* with "hundred" (i.e. 'bid' hundred'); it only goes up to ninety.

Al-Harawi said: The Arabs use *al-bid'* for what is between three and nine. *Al-bid'* and *al-bid'ah* are the same, and both mean a portion of a number.

Abu Ubaydah related that he said: *Al-bid'* is what is less than half of a decade (*al-'aqd*), meaning between one and four. But this is nothing.

In a hadith, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may God be pleased with him): "How many is *al-bid'*?" He said: "Between three and seven." He said: "Go, and increase the stake (*al-khatar*)." [*Al-khatar*, with a vowel on the first letter, means the wager or stake. The hadith concerns Abu Bakr al-Siddiq's wager with Quraysh on the Romans' victory over Persia. The Muslims loved the Romans to win over the Persians because they and the Romans were People of the Book, whereas Quraysh did not love that, since they and the Persians were neither People of the Book nor believers in a resurrection. Abu Bakr set the term between himself and them at six years according to one report, and three years according to another. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Go, increase the stake and extend the term." That was before gambling was forbidden. See the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi, in the commentary on the beginning of Surah al-Rum.]

This is also the view of most exegetes: that *al-bid'* is seven. Al-Tha'labi related this. Al-Mawardi said: This is the view of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may God be pleased with him) and Qutrub. Mujahid said: from three to nine. Al-Asma'i said: Ibn Abbas said: from three to ten. Al-Zajjaj related that it is between three and five. Al-Farra' said: *Al-bid'* is not used with ten and twenty up to ninety, and it is not used after a hundred.

Regarding the period during which Joseph was imprisoned, there are three views. The first is seven years, said by Ibn Jurayj, Qatadah and Wahb ibn Munabbih. Wahb said: Job remained in affliction for seven years, and Joseph remained in prison for seven years. The second is twelve years, said by Ibn Abbas. The third is fourteen years, said by al-Dahhak.

Muqatil reported from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Joseph remained in prison five and some years.

The derivation of the word is from *bada'tu al-shay'* (I cut the thing), meaning I cut it, so it is a portion of a number. God punished Joseph by imprisoning him for seven or nine years after the five years that had passed. Thus *al-bid'* is the duration of the punishment, not the whole period of imprisonment.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Joseph was imprisoned for seven years, Job remained in affliction for seven years, and Bukhtnassar was punished by transformation for seven years.

Abd Allah ibn Rashid al-Basri said, from Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah: *Al-bid'* is what is between five and twelve years.

**The fifth issue:** In this verse there is evidence for permissibility of relying on means (*asbab*), even when certainty is attained, because affairs are in the hand of their Causer. But He made them a chain, one linked to another, so moving them is a sunnah, and relying on the final outcome is certainty.

What indicates the permissibility of this is attributing what happened of forgetting to Satan, as happened to Moses in his meeting with al-Khidr. This is clear, so consider it.

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿And the king said, "Indeed I see seven fat cows..."﴾ [Yusuf 43]

When the relief for Yusuf (peace be upon him) drew near, the king saw his dream. Jibril (Gabriel) descended, greeted Yusuf, gave him the good news of relief, and said: "Indeed Allah will bring you out of your prison and establish you in the land. Its kings will submit to you, its tyrants will obey you, and He will give you the highest word over your brothers." This was because of a dream the king saw, which was such-and-such, and its interpretation was such-and-such. Yusuf did not remain in prison longer than the time in which the king saw the dream before he was released. Allah made the dream first a trial and hardship for Yusuf, and last a glad tiding and a mercy. This is because the great king, al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, saw in his sleep as if seven fat cows came out of a dry river, followed by seven lean ones, that is, emaciated ones. The lean ones approached the fat ones, seized them by their ears, and devoured them, except for two horns. He also saw seven green ears of grain, and seven dry ones came upon them and devoured them, until they reached them and nothing remained of them while they were still dry. Likewise the cows were lean, and they did not increase in flesh from eating the fat ones. The dream terrified him, so he sent for the people and the learned men among them, those skilled in soothsaying, astrology, fortune-telling, and magic, and the nobles of his people. He said: "O chiefs, give me your opinion concerning my dream," and he related it to them. The people said: ﴿confused dreams﴾ [Yusuf 44]. Ibn Juraij said: Ata' told me that "confused dreams" are false, mistaken dreams. Juwaybir related from al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas, who said: Some dreams are true, and some are confused dreams, meaning false ones. Al-Harawi said: The words of the Most High ﴿confused dreams﴾ mean mixtures of dreams. In the language, a ḍigh (bundle) is a bundle of something such as herbs, pasture, and the like. That is, they said: your dream is not clear, and "dreams" (aḥlām) means mixed visions. Mujahid said: "confused dreams" are their frightening aspects. Abu Ubayda said: "confused dreams" are those dreams that have no interpretation.

The Most High's words ﴿seven fat cows﴾: the feminine marker (the "ha") was dropped from "seven" (sab') to distinguish the masculine from the feminine. "Fat" (simān) is an adjective of "cows" (baqarāt). Outside the Qur'an it is permissible to say sab' baqarāt simānan, with "simānan" as an adjective of "seven"; likewise khuḍran (green). Al-Farra' said: the same applies to it, as in ﴿seven heavens in layers﴾ [Nuh 15]. Its derivation and meaning have already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah. Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: When goats and cows enter the city, if they are fat, they indicate years of plenty; if they are lean, they indicate years of hardship. If the city is a seaport and it is the season of travel, ships arrive according to their number and condition; otherwise they indicate successive trials, appearing like the faces of cows, as in the report: "some of them resemble others." In another report about trials: "like the horns of cows" (ṣayāṣī al-baqar, meaning their horns), meaning because of their resemblance. Unless they are all yellow, in which case they are diseases that afflict people; even if they are of varied colors, with dreadful horns, people will flee from them. Or if fire and smoke come out of their mouths, it indicates an army, a raid, or an enemy that will strike against them and descend upon their courtyard. The cow may also indicate a wife, a servant, provision, or a year, because of the offspring, provision, and vegetation in it.

﴿Seven lean ones devour them﴾: from ʿajufa, yaʿjufu, on the pattern of ʿaẓuma, yaʿẓumu; it is also transmitted as ʿajifa, yaʿjafu, on the pattern of ḥamida, yaḥmadu.

The Most High's words ﴿O chiefs, give me your opinion concerning my dream﴾: the plural of ru'yā is ru'an; that is, inform me of the judgment of this dream.

﴿If you are able to interpret dreams﴾: the word "ʿibāra" (interpretation) is derived from the crossing (ʿubūr) of a river. Whoever crosses a river reaches its shore, so the interpreter ("ʿābir") of a dream explains what its matter will come to. The lam in "li-l-ru'yā" is for specification, meaning: if you interpret, then specify it by saying "for the dream." This is what al-Zajjaj said.

There are two issues in this verse.

The first concerns His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Confused dreams﴾. Al-Farra' said: "It is also permissible to read it as 'adghath ahlam' (in the accusative)." Al-Nahhas said: "The accusative reading is weak, because the meaning is: you have not seen anything that has an interpretation; they are only confused dreams (adghath ahlam), i.e., mixtures." The singular of adghath is dighth (ضِغْث), which is said of anything mixed together from herbs, grass, or other things. The poet said:

*Like a bundle of a dream, from which its dreamer was deceived*

And: ﴿We are not versed in the interpretation of dreams﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "The meaning is: the interpretation of mixed-up dreams. They denied of themselves knowledge of what has no interpretation, not that they denied of themselves the knowledge of interpretation (ta'wil) in general." It was also said: "They denied of themselves the knowledge of ta'bir (interpretation of dreams)." On this view, adghath are bundles of dreams, some of which are true and some false. For this reason the cupbearer said: "I will inform you of its interpretation" (ta'wil), which shows that the people were unable to interpret it, not that they claimed it had no interpretation. It was also said: they did not intend an explanation, but wanted to erase it from the king's mind so that it would not preoccupy him; and on this view too they have knowledge.

"Ahlam" is the plural of hulm. Hulm (with a damma) is what the sleeper sees. One says from it: halama (with a fatha) and ihtalama, and one says: halamtu bi-kadha and halamtuhu. The poet said:

*So I carried her, while the Banu Rufayda [[Rufayda: a tribe of the Arabs, called the Rufaydat, just as the family of Hubayra are called the Hubayrat. Lisan.]] were beyond her... May her phantom, which is seen in dreams, not be far away.*

Its root is patience (al-ana), and from it comes hilm (forbearance), the opposite of frivolity. Thus what is seen in sleep is called hulm, because sleep is a state of patience, calm and rest.

The second issue: the verse is evidence against the view of those who say that a dream is interpreted according to its first (appearance) — because the people said "confused dreams" and it did not happen that way, since Yusuf interpreted it according to the years of drought and plenty, and it came to pass as he interpreted. The verse is also evidence against the corrupt belief that a dream is "on the foot of a bird": when it is interpreted, it comes true.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verses 45–46:

His saying, Exalted is He: (And the one of the two who was saved from them said) — meaning the king's cupbearer. "And he remembered after a period" (ba'da ummah): that is, after a time, according to Ibn Abbas and others. From this is His saying: ﴿until a specified term﴾ [[See p. 9 of this volume.]] [Hud: 8]. Its origin is the meaning of "a time" (al-hin). Ibn Durustawayh [[He is Abdullah ibn Ja'far ibn Durustawayh (with the dal and ra' vowelled with a damma), though Ibn Makula vowelled them with a fatha.]] said: "Ummah" cannot mean "time" except by omitting a noun (mudaf) and putting the noun that follows it (mudaf ilayhi) in its place, as if he said, Allah knows best: "and he remembered after the period of a time," or "after the span of a time," and similar expressions. Ummah means a large group of people. Al-Akhfash said: it is singular in form but plural in meaning, and every kind of animal is an ummah. In a hadith: "Were it not that dogs are an ummah among the ummahs, I would have ordered them killed."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and he remembered﴾, meaning he recalled Yusuf's need, which is the statement: "Mention me to your lord." Ibn Abbas recited, as transmitted by Affan from Hammam from Qatadah from Ikrimah from him: "wa-dhakara ba'da ummah." Al-Nahhas said: the well-known reading of Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah and al-Dahhak is "wa-dhakara ba'da amah" with a fatha on the hamza and the mim lightened, meaning "after forgetfulness." The poet said:

"I forgot, though I was never one to forget a tale,
As such is time, which destroys the minds."

On the authority of Shubayl ibn Azrah al-Dubai'i: "ba'da amh," with a fatha on the alif, sukun on the mim, and a pure ha', which is like "al-amah"; both are dialect forms, and both mean forgetting. It is said: amiha, ya'mahu, amhan, if he forgot. On this reading it is "wa-dhakara ba'da amah," as al-Nahhas mentioned. A man who is amih is one whose mind has gone. Al-Jawhari said: as for what occurs in the hadith of al-Zuhri, "amiha" meaning he acknowledged and confessed, this is a non-well-known dialect. Al-Ash'hab al-Uqayli recited "ba'da immah," meaning after a blessing, that is, after Allah had blessed him with deliverance. Then it is said: the youth forgot Yusuf by Allah's decree concerning his remaining in prison for a period. It is also said: he did not forget, but he feared that the king would mention the offence for which he and the baker had been imprisoned. So his saying "wa-dhakara" means he recalled and informed.

Al-Nahhas said: the original form of "idhdakara" is "idhtakara." The dhal is close in articulation to the ta', but they could not assimilate it into the ta' because the dhal is voiced (majhur) and the ta' is voiceless (mahmus). If they had assimilated, the voicing would have been lost. So they replaced the position of the ta' with a voiced letter, the dal, which was preferable to the ta' because the ta' is emphatic (mutbaqah). This became "idhdakara," and they assimilated the dhal into the dal because the dal is soft and lenient. Then he said: (I will inform you of its interpretation), meaning I will tell you. Al-Hasan recited "ana atikum bi-ta'wilihi" (I will bring you its interpretation) and said: how can the foreigner (al-ilj, meaning a non-Arab unbeliever) inform them? Al-Nahhas said: the meaning of "unabbi'ukum" (I will inform you) is sound and good, that is, I will inform you if you ask.

(So send me) — he addressed the king, but in the plural of respect; or he addressed the king and the people of his assembly.

(Yusuf) is a vocative of a singular noun, and likewise (the truthful one, al-siddiq), meaning one who is very truthful.

(Give us an interpretation) — that is, they sent him, so he came to Yusuf and said: "O truthful one!" and asked him about the king's dream.

(That I may return to the people) — that is, to the king and his companions.

(That they may know) the interpretation; or, "that they may know" your station in virtue and knowledge, so that you may be released. It is also possible that by "the people" he means the king alone, out of respect for him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 47:

There are two issues in this.

The first concerns His words, exalted is He: ﴿He said: You shall sow for seven years in succession﴾. When he informed him of the dream, he began to interpret it for him, saying: The seven fat cows and the green ears of grain are seven years of abundance (mukhsibat), and as for the lean cows and the dry ears, they are seven years of drought (mujdibat). This is His saying: (You shall sow for seven years in succession, da'aban), meaning continuous and consecutive. It is a verbal noun (masdar) of an unusual form, since the meaning of "tazra'una" (you sow) is "tad'abuna" (you persist) in your habit of cultivation for seven years. It is also said that it is a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning persisting. It is also said that it is an attribute of "seven years", meaning persistent. Abu Hatim reported from Ya'qub that it is read "da'aban" with a moved hamza, and Hafs related the same from 'Asim. Both are dialectal forms (lughatan) [[The two forms are "da'aban" with a moved hamza and "da'aban" with a sukun, the latter being the reading of the majority of the seven, as in the Tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyyah.]]. There are two opinions regarding it: the opinion of Abu Hatim, that it is derived from d-'-b (da'iba). Al-Nahhas said: the people of lexicography know only "da'aba". The other opinion is that it was vowelled because it contains one of the throat letters, as stated by al-Farra'. He said: Likewise, every word whose first letter is fathah and whose second letter is sakin, its emphasis (tathqil) is permissible if the second letter is a hamza, or ha', or 'ayn, or ghayn, or ha', or kha', and its root is "al-'adah" (habit). He said [[It is Imru' al-Qays, and the full verse is:

"And its neighbour Umm al-Rabab in Mai'sal"]]:

"Like your habit (da'bika) toward Umm al-Huwayrith before her."

The discussion of this has already passed in "Al 'Imran" [[See vol. 4, p. 22 and following.]].

(Then what you reap, leave it in its ear) It is said: so that it does not become infested with weevils, and so that it remains preserved longer. And thus is the matter in the lands of Egypt.

(Except a little of what you eat) meaning: extract what you need in proportion to the need. This statement is an imperative, while the first is a declarative. It is possible that the first is also an imperative, although the more apparent reading of it is declarative, so the meaning of "tazra'una" would be " izra'u" (sow!).

The second issue: this verse is a foundation for the doctrine of the legal benefits (al-masalih al-shar'iyyah), which are the preservation of religion, lives, intellect, lineage and property. Thus everything that includes the attainment of any of these matters is a benefit (maslahah), and everything that forfeits any of them is a corruption (mafsadah), and warding it off is a benefit. There is no disagreement that the aim of the Shari'ahs is to guide people to their worldly benefits, so that they may be enabled to know Allah, exalted is He, and to worship Him, both of which lead to the otherworldly happiness. Observing this is a grace from Allah, mighty and majestic is He, and a mercy by which He showed mercy to His servants, not as an obligation upon Him, nor as a due. This is the position of all the verifying scholars of the Ahl al-Sunnah, all of them, and its elaboration is in the books of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

There are two issues here.

The first concerns God's words ﴿seven hard [years]﴾, meaning the lean years of drought.

(﴿They will consume﴾) is a figurative usage (majaz), and the meaning is "their people will consume."

(﴿what you have stored up for them﴾) means what you have saved up for their sake. A similar expression is the poet's line:

"Your day, O deceived one, is heedlessness and negligence,
and your night is sleep, while death is bound to you."

The day does not become heedless and the night does not sleep. Rather, heedlessness occurs during the day and sleep during the night. Zayd ibn Aslam related on the authority of his father that Yusuf would set out the food for two people and bring it to one man, who would eat part of it. Then one day he brought it to him and he ate all of it. Yusuf said, "This is the first day of the seven hard years."

(﴿except a little﴾) is in the accusative because it is an exception (istithna').

(﴿of what you preserve﴾) means of what you hold back in order to sow, because preserving the seed is a way of safeguarding the food supply. Abu Ubaydah said, "tuhsinun" means "you secure." Qatadah said, "tuhsinun" means "you hoard" (tadakhkharun). The meaning is one and the same. This verse indicates the permissibility of hoarding (ihtikar) food until the time of need. [[This is open to question if the intention is high prices, because of what has been transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), "Whoever hoards a commodity intending to raise its price against the Muslims is a sinner, and God and His Messenger are free of him," narrated by Ahmad and al-Hakim on the authority of Abu Hurayrah in reports concerning the prohibition of hoarding.]]

The second issue is that this verse is a basis for the validity of the dream of a disbeliever, and that it comes to pass according to what he saw. This is especially so when it concerns a believer, and even more so when it is a sign for a prophet, a miracle for a messenger, a confirmation of one chosen for conveying the message, and a proof for the intermediary between God, majestic is His majesty, [and [[min ʿ.]]] His servants.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 49:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then after that there will come a year﴾. This is a report from Yusuf, peace be upon him, of what was not in the king's dream, but it is from the knowledge of the unseen (ʿilm al-ghayb) which Allah had bestowed upon him. Qatadah said: Allah increased him in knowledge of one year, though they had not asked him about it, to show his virtue and to make known his station in knowledge and his understanding.

﴿In which the people will be given rain (yughathu al-nas)﴾. It is from al-ighathah or al-ghawth. One says "ghawatha al-rajul," meaning he cried "Wa ghawthah!" (O help!). The noun is al-ghawth, al-ghuwath and al-ghawath. "Istaghathani fulan fa-aghathtuhu" means someone asked me for help and I helped him, and the noun is al-ghiyath; the waw changed to ya' because of the kasrah before it. Al-ghayth is rain, and "ghaatha al-ghayth al-ard" means the rain reached the land; "ghaatha Allahu al-bilad yaghithuha ghaythan" means Allah sent rain upon the lands, and "ghitati al-ardu tughathu ghaythan" means the land was rained upon, so it is a land that is *maghithah* and *maghyuthah*. Thus the meaning of "yughathu al-nas" is that the people will be rained upon.

﴿And in which they will press (wa-fihi yaʿsirun)﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they will press grapes and oil; this was reported by al-Bukhari. Hajjaj narrated from Ibn Jurayj who said: they will press grapes into wine, sesame into oil, and olives into oil. It was also said: he meant milking the milk in abundance, and this indicates abundance of vegetation. It was said: "yaʿsirun" means "yanjun" (they will be saved), and it derives from al-ʿusrah, which is the refuge (al-manjah). Abu ʿUbaydah said: al-ʿasar with a vowel on the first letter means refuge and deliverance, and likewise al-ʿusrah. Abu Zubayd said (he said it in lamenting his nephew who had died of thirst on the road to Makkah):

*Thirsty, he sought help, but was not helped... and indeed he had been a refuge for the one who was rescued.*

Al-manjud means the frightened one. "I‘tasartu bi-fulan" and "ta‘assartu" mean I sought refuge in him. Abu al-Ghawth said: "yaʿsirun" means they will be made to yield profit (yastaghillun), and it derives from pressing grapes. "I‘tasartu malahu" means I extracted it from his hand. ʿIsa recited "tuʿsarun" with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the sad, and its meaning is "they will be rained upon," from the saying of Allah: ﴿And We sent down from the rain-laden clouds abundant water﴾ [al-Naba' 78:14]. Likewise the meaning of "tuʿsirun" with a damma on the ta' and a kasrah on the sad, for those who read it so, is the same.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 12, verses 50–51:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me."﴾ That is, the messenger went and informed the king, and he said, "Bring him to me."

(When the messenger came to him), that is, commanding him to leave [the prison]. He said: (Return to your lord and ask him what is the matter with the women), that is, what is the state of the women (who cut their hands). He refused to leave until his innocence was established before the king (ʿind [[min ʿ. Wa-fi awk wa-wa: lil-malik.]]) regarding what he had been accused of, and that he had been imprisoned without any crime.

Al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, the noble, son of the noble, son of the noble, [son of the noble [[The addition is from Sahih al-Tirmidhi.]]] is Yusuf ibn Yaʿqub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim." He said: "If I had remained in prison as long as he remained, and then the messenger came to me, I would have answered." Then he recited: "So when the messenger came to him, he said, 'Return to your lord and ask him what is the matter with the women who cut their hands.'" He said: "And may Allah have mercy on Lut, for he used to take refuge in a mighty pillar [when he said, 'If only I had power against you, or could take refuge in a mighty pillar']. Allah did not send any prophet after him except in the highest place of his people."

Al-Bukhari related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on Lut; he used to take refuge in a mighty pillar. And if I had remained in prison as long as Yusuf remained, I would have answered the caller. And we have more right to doubt than Ibrahim, when he said to him: ﴿Have you not believed?' He said, 'Yes, but that my heart may be assured.﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:260]." It is also related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "May Allah have mercy on my brother Yusuf; he was indeed patient and forbearing. And if I had remained in prison as long as he remained, I would have answered the caller, and I would not have sought an excuse."

A similar hadith has been related through the chain of ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim, the companion of Malik, in the Book of Tafsir of Sahih al-Bukhari, and Ibn al-Qasim has no other narration in the Diwan (collection) except this. In the narration of al-Tabari: "May Allah have mercy on Yusuf. If I had been the one imprisoned, and then he had sent for me, I would have left quickly, if he was indeed forbearing and deliberate." And he (ﷺ) said: "I have marvelled at Yusuf, at his patience and his generosity, and Allah forgives him when he was asked about the cows. If I had been in his place, I would not have told them until I had stipulated that they should release me. And I have marvelled at him when the messenger came to him. If I had been in his place, I would have rushed them to the door." [[The hadith in Tafsir al-Tabari differs in wording from what is given here.]]

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: This action by Yusuf, peace be upon him, was deliberateness and patience, and a seeking of the clearing of his name. For he feared, as has been related, that if he left and gained a rank from the king, and remained silent about the matter of his sin, people would always regard him with that eye and say, "This is the one who seduced his master's wife." So Yusuf, peace be upon him, wished to demonstrate his innocence and to confirm his standing in chastity and goodness. Then he would leave for honour and rank. For this reason he said to the messenger: "Return to your lord and say to him, 'What is the matter with the women?'" The intention of Yusuf, peace be upon him, was only: "Say to him, let him investigate my sin and examine my case, whether I was imprisoned justly or unjustly." And he avoided the wife of the ʿAziz (the minister) out of good conduct, and in observance of the protection the mighty king had given him.

If it is asked: How did the Prophet (ﷺ) praise Yusuf for patience, deliberateness, and not rushing to leave, and yet he himself departs from a state for which he praised another? The answer is that the Prophet (ﷺ) only adopted for himself another view of opinion, which also has its own merit. He says: "If I had been the one, I would have rushed to leave, and then tried to demonstrate my excuse afterwards." This is because these stories and events are open to being followed by people until the Day of Resurrection. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished to lead people toward the more prudent of affairs. For one who abandons prudence in such an incident, who abandons the opportunity to leave such a prison, may end up remaining in his prison, and the one who would free him may lose interest in him. Although Yusuf, peace be upon him, was secure from that by his knowledge from Allah, others among people are not secure from that. Therefore the state to which the Prophet (ﷺ) went himself is a state of prudence, while what Yusuf, peace be upon him, did is a great patience and fortitude.

His saying, Exalted is He: "(So ask him what is the matter with the women)." He mentioned "the women" in general so that the wife of the ʿAziz would enter among them in the manner of generality, by allusion, so that she would not be directly named. That is good conduct and courtesy. In the speech there is an ellipsis, that is: "So ask him to find out what is the matter with the women."

Ibn ʿAbbas said: The king sent for the women and for the wife of the ʿAziz (and the ʿAziz had died), and he summoned them. ﴿He said, "What was your business when you sought to seduce Yusuf from himself?"﴾ That is, what was your affair? This is because each of them had spoken to Yusuf concerning her own desire, as mentioned earlier, or he meant the saying of each one, "You have wronged the wife of the ʿAziz," so that was a solicitation from them. ﴿They said, "Hashā lillāh (far be Allah from it)!"﴾ That is, "Maʿādh Allāh (God forbid)!" ﴿"We know of him no evil."﴾ That is, adultery. ﴿The wife of the ʿAziz said, "Now the truth has become manifest."﴾ When she saw their acknowledgement of Yusuf's innocence, and feared that they would testify against her if she denied it, she too confessed, and that was a kindness from Allah toward Yusuf.

"Haṣḥaṣa al-ḥaqq" means: it became clear and appeared. Its root is ḥaṣaṣa, and it was said ḥaṣḥaṣa, just as they said kubkibū for kabbabū, and kafkafa for kaffa, as al-Zajjaj and others said. The root meaning of al-ḥaṣṣ is the uprooting of a thing; it is said: ḥaṣṣa shaʿrahu when he uprooted it entirely by cutting. Abu al-Qays ibn al-Aslat said:

*"The helmet has shaved my head, so I do not taste sleep except a light doze."* [[al-bayḍa: the helmet; al-tahajjāʿ: a light nap.]]

And *sana ḥaṣṣāʾ* means a barren year with no good in it. Jarir said:

*"He comes to you without reproach or denial, one whom the barren year has driven, and the wolf."*

It is as if he meant to say "and the hyena," which is the year of drought, but he placed the wolf in its place for the sake of the rhyme. So the meaning of "haṣḥaṣa al-ḥaqq" is that it was cut off from falsehood, by its manifestation and its firmness. He said:

*"Unless someone conveys from me to Khidash, for he is a great liar, that when the truth becomes manifest, the wrongdoer is..."*

It was also said that it is derived from al-ḥiṣṣa (portion), so the meaning is: the portion of truth became distinct from the portion of falsehood. Mujahid and Qatadah said: its origin is taken from their saying, "ḥaṣṣa shaʿrahu" when he uprooted and cut it off, and from it comes "al-ḥiṣṣa" [[fi ʿ: fi.]] of land when a portion is cut from it. Al-ḥiṣḥiṣ with a kasra means dirt and stones, as al-Jawhari mentioned.

﴿"It was I who sought to seduce him from himself, and he is indeed among the truthful."﴾ This statement from her, even though he had not asked about it, is a manifestation of her repentance and a confirmation of Yusuf's truthfulness and his nobility, because the confession of one who confesses against himself is stronger than testimony against him. So Allah, Exalted is He, gathered for Yusuf both testimony and confession to manifest his truthfulness, so that no thought would enter his soul and no doubt would mix with it.

The nun is doubled in "khaṭbukunna" and "rāwadtunna," because it stands in the position of the mim and the waw in the masculine (form).

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verses 52–53:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾. Scholars differ over who said this. It has been said that it is the speech of the wife of al-'Aziz, and that it is connected to her saying: "Now the truth has come to light" (ḥaṣḥaṣa al-ḥaqq), meaning: I have acknowledged the truth, so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence [[from ʿ.]], that is, by lying about him, and I did not speak ill of him while he was absent. Rather, I was truthful and I refrained (ḥidtu [[in ʿ: kharajtu]]) from betrayal. Then she said: "Nor do I absolve myself," rather, I was the one who solicited him. On this view, she was affirming the Creator, and for this reason she said: "Indeed my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful."

It has also been said that it is the speech of Yusuf, meaning Yusuf said: "That is the matter which I did, in sending back the messenger, so that" al-'Aziz "may know that I did not betray him in his absence." This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah and others. The meaning of "in his absence" is that he (al-'Aziz) was absent. Yusuf said this in the presence of the king, but he said "so that he may know" in the third person, out of reverence for the king.

It has also been said that he said it when the messenger returned to him while he was still in prison. Ibn 'Abbas said: The messenger came to Yusuf, peace be upon him, with the news, and Jibril was with him speaking to him. Yusuf said: "That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that Allah does not guide the scheming of the betrayers," meaning: I did not betray my master in his absence. Then Jibril, peace be upon him, said to him: "O Yusuf! Not even when you untied the waistcloth and sat in the place of a man with a woman?!" Then Yusuf said: "Nor do I absolve myself," and the verse continues.

Al-Suddi said: The wife of al-'Aziz only said to him: "And not even when you untied your trousers, O Yusuf?!" Then Yusuf said: "Nor do I absolve myself."

It has also been said that "That is so that he may know" is the speech of al-'Aziz, meaning: that is so that Yusuf may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that I did not neglect to reward him for his trustworthiness.

(And that Allah does not guide the scheming of the betrayers): its meaning is that Allah does not guide the betrayers in their scheming.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Nor do I absolve myself﴾. It has been said that this is the speech of the woman. Al-Qushayri said: The apparent meaning is that His saying "That is so that he may know" and His saying "Nor do I absolve myself" are the speech of Yusuf. I say: If it is possible that it is the speech of the woman, then saying so is more appropriate, so that we may absolve Yusuf of untying the waistcloth and the trousers. And if we assume it is the speech of Yusuf, then it would be something that occurred to his heart, in accordance with the preferred view we previously mentioned regarding His saying: "And she resolved upon him."

Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: Some people say that "That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence," up to His saying "Indeed my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful," is the speech of the wife of al-'Aziz, because it is connected to her saying: ﴿It was I who solicited him, and indeed he is among the truthful﴾ [Yusuf: 51]. This is the view of those who deny that Yusuf, peace be upon him, had any inclination (hamm). Whoever builds upon their view says that from His saying: ﴿The wife of al-'Aziz said﴾ [Yusuf: 51] up to His saying "Indeed my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful" is a speech connected part to part, and there is no complete pause in it with respect to its reality. We do not choose this view nor do we adopt it.

Al-Hasan said: When Yusuf said "That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence," the prophet of Allah disliked that he might have praised himself, so he said: "Nor do I absolve myself," because the praise of the self (tazkiyat al-nafs) is blameworthy. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So do not claim purity for yourselves﴾ [al-Najm: 32]. We have explained this in (the commentary on) "al-Nisa'" [[see vol. 5, p. 246 onward and p. 12.]]. It has also been said that it is the speech of al-'Aziz, meaning: nor do I absolve myself from having an evil opinion of Yusuf.

(Indeed the self is a commander to evil): meaning, it inclines towards it.

(Except what my Lord has mercy upon): this is in the accusative position as an exception, and "mā" here has the meaning of "man" (whoever), meaning: except those whom my Lord has mercy upon, so He protects them. "Mā" may also mean "a great number of," as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Marry what is good for you of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 3] [[see vol. 5, p. 246 onward and p. 12.]]. This is a disjunctive exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), because it is the exception of one who is shielded by protection from the self that commands to evil.

It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "What do you say about a companion of yours: if you honour him, feed him and clothe him, it leads him to the worst end; and if you humiliate him, leave him naked and make him hungry, it leads him to the best end?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah! This is the worst companion on earth." He said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, it is indeed your own souls that lie between your sides."

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verses 52–53:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾. Scholars differ over who said this. It has been said that it is the speech of the wife of al-'Aziz, and that it is connected to her saying: "Now the truth has come to light" (ḥaṣḥaṣa al-ḥaqq), meaning: I have acknowledged the truth, so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence [[from ʿ.]], that is, by lying about him, and I did not speak ill of him while he was absent. Rather, I was truthful and I refrained (ḥidtu [[in ʿ: kharajtu]]) from betrayal. Then she said: "Nor do I absolve myself," rather, I was the one who solicited him. On this view, she was affirming the Creator, and for this reason she said: "Indeed my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful."

It has also been said that it is the speech of Yusuf, meaning Yusuf said: "That is the matter which I did, in sending back the messenger, so that" al-'Aziz "may know that I did not betray him in his absence." This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah and others. The meaning of "in his absence" is that he (al-'Aziz) was absent. Yusuf said this in the presence of the king, but he said "so that he may know" in the third person, out of reverence for the king.

It has also been said that he said it when the messenger returned to him while he was still in prison. Ibn 'Abbas said: The messenger came to Yusuf, peace be upon him, with the news, and Jibril was with him speaking to him. Yusuf said: "That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that Allah does not guide the scheming of the betrayers," meaning: I did not betray my master in his absence. Then Jibril, peace be upon him, said to him: "O Yusuf! Not even when you untied the waistcloth and sat in the place of a man with a woman?!" Then Yusuf said: "Nor do I absolve myself," and the verse continues.

Al-Suddi said: The wife of al-'Aziz only said to him: "And not even when you untied your trousers, O Yusuf?!" Then Yusuf said: "Nor do I absolve myself."

It has also been said that "That is so that he may know" is the speech of al-'Aziz, meaning: that is so that Yusuf may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that I did not neglect to reward him for his trustworthiness.

(And that Allah does not guide the scheming of the betrayers): its meaning is that Allah does not guide the betrayers in their scheming.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Nor do I absolve myself﴾. It has been said that this is the speech of the woman. Al-Qushayri said: The apparent meaning is that His saying "That is so that he may know" and His saying "Nor do I absolve myself" are the speech of Yusuf. I say: If it is possible that it is the speech of the woman, then saying so is more appropriate, so that we may absolve Yusuf of untying the waistcloth and the trousers. And if we assume it is the speech of Yusuf, then it would be something that occurred to his heart, in accordance with the preferred view we previously mentioned regarding His saying: "And she resolved upon him."

Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: Some people say that "That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence," up to His saying "Indeed my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful," is the speech of the wife of al-'Aziz, because it is connected to her saying: ﴿It was I who solicited him, and indeed he is among the truthful﴾ [Yusuf: 51]. This is the view of those who deny that Yusuf, peace be upon him, had any inclination (hamm). Whoever builds upon their view says that from His saying: ﴿The wife of al-'Aziz said﴾ [Yusuf: 51] up to His saying "Indeed my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful" is a speech connected part to part, and there is no complete pause in it with respect to its reality. We do not choose this view nor do we adopt it.

Al-Hasan said: When Yusuf said "That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence," the prophet of Allah disliked that he might have praised himself, so he said: "Nor do I absolve myself," because the praise of the self (tazkiyat al-nafs) is blameworthy. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So do not claim purity for yourselves﴾ [al-Najm: 32]. We have explained this in (the commentary on) "al-Nisa'" [[see vol. 5, p. 246 onward and p. 12.]]. It has also been said that it is the speech of al-'Aziz, meaning: nor do I absolve myself from having an evil opinion of Yusuf.

(Indeed the self is a commander to evil): meaning, it inclines towards it.

(Except what my Lord has mercy upon): this is in the accusative position as an exception, and "mā" here has the meaning of "man" (whoever), meaning: except those whom my Lord has mercy upon, so He protects them. "Mā" may also mean "a great number of," as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Marry what is good for you of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 3] [[see vol. 5, p. 246 onward and p. 12.]]. This is a disjunctive exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), because it is the exception of one who is shielded by protection from the self that commands to evil.

It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "What do you say about a companion of yours: if you honour him, feed him and clothe him, it leads him to the worst end; and if you humiliate him, leave him naked and make him hungry, it leads him to the best end?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah! This is the worst companion on earth." He said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, it is indeed your own souls that lie between your sides."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 54:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself."﴾ When the king's acquittal of the charge made against Yusuf was established, and his trustworthiness was confirmed in the story, and the king also understood his patience and steadfastness, his standing with the king became great, and he became certain of Yusuf's good qualities. So he said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself." Observe the king's words first, when his knowledge was confirmed, "Bring him to me" alone. Then, when Yusuf did what he did the second time [[In manuscripts ع and و and ى: he said the second time.]], he said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself."

It is narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih that he said: When Yusuf was summoned, he stopped at the door and said: "My Lord is sufficient for me against His creation; mighty is His protection, exalted is His praise, and there is no god but Him." Then he entered. When the king saw him, he got down from his throne and prostrated before him. Then the king seated him beside him on his throne and said: ﴿Indeed, today you are with us established and trusted.﴾ Yusuf said to him: ﴿Set me over the treasuries of the land; indeed, I am a knowing guardian.﴾ [Yusuf 55] "Guardian" of the treasuries, "knowing" of the ways of managing them. It was also said: "guardian" of the accounts, "knowing" of languages.

In a report: "May Allah have mercy on my brother Yusuf. Had he not said, 'Set me over the treasuries of the land,' he would have employed him immediately, but he deferred that for a year." It was also said: his being granted authority was deferred for a year only because he did not say, "If Allah wills." It has also been said about this story that when Yusuf, peace be upon him, entered upon the king, he said: "O Allah, I ask You by Your goodness over his goodness, and I seek refuge in You from his evil and the evil of others." Then he greeted the king in Arabic. The king said: "What is this tongue?" He said: "This is the tongue of my paternal uncle Isma'il." Then the king called for something [[From ع and و]] in Hebrew, and said: "What is this tongue?" He said: "The tongue of my fathers, Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub." The king spoke seventy languages, and whenever the king spoke in one language, Yusuf answered him in that same language. The king was impressed by his matter. At that time Yusuf was thirty years old. Then the king seated him on his throne and said: "I would like to hear my dream from you." Yusuf said: "Yes, O king! You saw seven fat cows, sleek and fair and handsome. The Nile uncovered them for you, and they came up to you from its bank, their udders flowing with milk [[Tashkhab: flowing.]]. While you were looking at them and marvelling at their beauty, the Nile receded, its water sank and its bed [[In ع and و: its dryness]] appeared. Out of its mire and mud came seven lean, dishevelled, dusty cows with shrunken bellies, having no udders or teats, with fangs and molars, and paws like the paws of dogs and snouts like the snouts of beasts. They mixed in among the fat ones and tore them apart like beasts of prey, eating their flesh, ripping their skins, breaking their bones and sucking their marrow. While you were watching and wondering how they overcame them though they were emaciated, no fatness or increase appeared on them after they had eaten them! Then suddenly there were seven green, fresh, soft, lush ears of grain, full of grain and water, and beside them seven dry ones with no water or greenness, in the same place of growth, their roots in the earth and water. While you were saying to yourself, 'What is this?! These are green and fruitful, and these are black and dry, though the place of growth is one and their roots are in the water,' a wind blew and scattered the leaves of the dry black ones over the green fruitful ones, and set fire to them, and they burned and became black and dusty. Then you woke up alarmed, O king." The king said: "By Allah, what is the matter with this dream? Even if it is a wonder greater than what I heard from you! So what do you think of my dream, O truthful one [[al-Siddiq: the truthful]]?"

Yusuf said: "I think you should gather provisions and sow a great deal of crops in these years of abundance. For if you sowed on a stone or on clay, it would grow, and Allah would bring forth growth and blessing in it. Then you should lift the crop in its stalks and ears, and build for it great storehouses. So the stalks and ears will be fodder for the animals, and the grain for the people. And you should command the people to bring up a fifth of their food to your granaries [[Ahra'ak: this is a large house in which the sultan's food is gathered; today these are grain stores. In او and ح: amra'ak, your princes]]. Then the food you have gathered will suffice you for the people of Egypt and those around it. People from all regions will come to you seeking food from you, and treasures will gather with you such as have never gathered for anyone before you."

The king said: "Who will manage these matters for me? Even if I gathered all the people of Egypt, they would not be able to cope, and they would not be trustworthy in it." Yusuf, peace be upon him, [at that point [[From ع and و]]] said: ﴿Set me over the treasuries of the land﴾ [Yusuf 55], meaning: over the treasuries of your land. "Treasuries" is the plural of khizana, and the alif and lam (al-) replaced the possessive [the idafa, i.e., the construction "treasuries of your land"], as in the saying of al-Nabigha:

They have a disposition that Allah has not given to any but them,
of generosity and forbearance, which is not false.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I will take him for myself﴾ is in the jussive (majzum) because it is the answer (jawab) to the imperative. This indicates that his saying, "That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence" [Yusuf 52], took place in the prison. It is possible that it took place before the king, and then he said in another assembly: ﴿Bring him to me﴾ [Yusuf 50] as an emphasis. "I will take him for myself" means: I will make him exclusively mine; I will entrust to him the affairs of my kingdom. So they went and brought him. This is indicated by: ﴿when he spoke to him﴾, that is, when the king spoke with Yusuf and asked him about the dream, and Yusuf answered, then the king said: ﴿Indeed, today you are with us established and trusted﴾, that is, firmly established, with a word that is carried out, "trusted," fearing no treachery.

**The first issue: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Set me over the treasuries of the land﴾.** Sa'id ibn Mansur said: I heard Malik ibn Anas say: "Egypt is the treasury of the land. Did you not hear his saying, 'Set me over the treasuries of the land'? That means over its safekeeping, so the noun was omitted." ﴿Indeed, I am a knowing guardian﴾ means: I am a guardian of what I have been entrusted with, and knowing of its affairs. In the *tafsir* (classical exegesis) it is said: "Indeed I am a reckoner and a scribe, and he was the first to write on papers." It was also said: "A guardian" means for the estimating of the provisions, and "knowing" means of the years of famine. Juwaybir related from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on my brother Yusuf. Had he not said, 'Set me over the treasuries of the land,' he would have employed him at once, but he deferred that for a year." Ibn 'Abbas said: When the year had passed from the day he asked for the leadership, the king summoned him. He went, and the king girded him with his sword [[radāhu bi-saifihi: invested him with it.]], placed for him a throne of gold, studded with pearls and rubies, and draped over it a silk brocade (*istabraq*). The throne was thirty cubits long and ten cubits wide, and on it were thirty mattresses and sixty cushions [[al-mirfaqah (with a kasra): the reclining cushion or pillow.]]. Then the king ordered him to go out, and he went out crowned, his complexion like snow and his face like the moon; the beholder could see his face through the purity of its colour. He sat upon the throne, and the kings submitted to him. The king entered his house with his women, and he entrusted to him the affairs of Egypt, dismissed Qitfir from what he had held, and put Yusuf in his place.

Ibn Zayd said: Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, had many treasuries apart from the food, and he handed over all his authority to him. Qitfir died during those nights, so the king married Yusuf to Ra'il, the wife of the *'Aziz*. When he went in to her, he said: "Is this not better than what you were seeking?" She said: "O truthful one (*al-siddiq*), do not blame me, for I was a beautiful, pampered woman, as you see, and my husband did not approach women; and you were, as Allah made you, of such beauty that my self overcame me." Yusuf found her a virgin and had intercourse with her, and she bore him two sons: Ifrathim ibn Yusuf and Manshā ibn Yusuf.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Indeed, his marriage to Zulaykha, the wife of the *'Aziz*, took place between the two visits of the brothers. That was because her husband had died while Yusuf was in prison; her wealth had gone, and her sight had become blind from weeping over Yusuf. She began to beg from people; some of them had mercy on her and some did not. Yusuf used to ride out once every week in a procession of about one hundred thousand of the nobles of his people. It was said to her: "If you were to present yourself to him, perhaps he would give you something." Then it was said to her: "Do not do it, for he may recall some of what you did, the seduction and the prison, and harm you." She said: "I know my beloved's character better than you do." Then she left him until he rode out in his procession, and she stood up and called out at the top of her voice: "Glory be to Him who made kings slaves through their disobedience, and made slaves kings through their obedience!" Yusuf said: "What is this?" So they brought her, and she said: "I am the one who served you [[fī 'a: uqaddimuka 'alā ṣudūr qawmī: "I used to place you before the chests of my people."]] on the soles of my feet, combed your hair with my hand, you were raised in my house, and I honoured your lodging. But what I neglected of my ignorance and my defiance has come, and I have tasted the evil of my affair. My wealth has gone, my pillar has collapsed, my humiliation has lengthened, my sight has been blinded, and after I was the envied one of the people of Egypt, I have become the pitied one. I beg from people; some of them have mercy on me and some have none. This is the recompense of the corrupters." Yusuf wept intensely. Then he said to her: "Do you still find anything of what was in your heart of your love for me?" She said: "By Allah, a single look at your face is dearer to me than the whole world, but give me the end of your whip." He gave it to her, and she placed it on her chest. He found the whip trembling and quivering in his hand from the palpitation of her heart. He wept, then went to his house and sent her a messenger: "If you are a widow, we will marry you; and if you are a married woman, we will make you wealthy." She said to the messenger: "I seek refuge in Allah that the king should mock me! He did not want me in the days of my youth, my wealth, my might and my honour; will he want me today, when I am an old, blind, poor woman?!" The messenger informed him of her words. When he rode out in the second week, she presented herself to him. He said to her: "Did the messenger not reach you?" She said: "I told you that a single look at your face is dearer to me than the world and all that is in it." So he ordered that she be attended to, her condition be set right, and she be prepared; then she was escorted to him. Yusuf stood to pray and supplicate Allah, and she stood behind him. He asked Allah, exalted is He, to restore to her her youth, her beauty and her sight, and Allah returned to her her youth, her beauty and her sight, until she became more beautiful than she had been on the day she sought to seduce him, as an honour to Yusuf (peace be upon him) because he had refrained from what Allah had forbidden. He had intercourse with her, and she was a virgin. He asked her, and she said: "O Prophet of Allah, my husband was impotent and did not approach women, and you were beyond description in beauty and loveliness." He said: They lived in a comfortable life, every day Allah renewing good for them both, and she bore him two sons, Ifrathim and Manshā.

It is also related that Allah cast into Yusuf's heart a love for her many times greater than what was in her heart. He said to her: "What is your state that you do not love me as you did the first time?" She said [to him]: "When I tasted the love of Allah, exalted is He, it occupied me from everything."

**The second issue:** Some scholars said: In this verse there is evidence that permits a virtuous man to work for a dissolute man or an unbelieving ruler, on condition that he knows he will be entrusted with an action in which he is not opposed, so that he can set right whatever he wishes. But if his work is subject to the choice of the dissolute man, his desires and his depravity, then that is not permitted. Others said: This was specific to Yusuf, and today it is not permitted; but the first view is preferable when it is upon the condition we have mentioned. And Allah knows best.

Al-Mawardi said: If the appointing authority is an oppressor, people have differed about the permissibility of accepting office from him, on two views. The first: it is permitted if one acts justly in what one is entrusted with, because Yusuf was appointed by Pharaoh, and because in his case what is considered is his own action, not the action of another. The second: it is not permitted, because it involves supporting the oppressors by assisting them and lending legitimacy to them by accepting their posts. Those who held this view answered regarding Yusuf's appointment by Pharaoh with two answers. The first: that the Pharaoh of Yusuf was a righteous man, and the tyrant was only the Pharaoh of Moses. The second: that he only managed his own possessions and not their affairs, so the responsibility for them was removed from him.

Al-Mawardi said: The most accurate way of applying these two views is to divide what one undertakes from the side of the oppressor into three categories. The first: what is permissible for its people to do without exercising independent judgment in carrying it out, such as the alms-tax (*sadaqat*) and the obligatory zakat; accepting such a task from the oppressor is permitted, because the text specifying its rightful recipients has already dispensed with the need for independent judgment regarding it, and the permissibility of its owners acting independently regarding it has dispensed with the need for imitation. The second category: what they may not handle alone and which requires independent judgment in its disbursement, such as the funds of *fay'* (booty obtained without fighting); accepting such a post from the oppressor is not permitted, because one would be disposing of it without right, and exercising judgment regarding what one has no right to. The third category: what may be undertaken by those qualified for it, and where independent judgment has a role, such as judgeships and rulings; the contract of appointment in this case is permissible. If the task is the enforcement of a ruling between two consenting parties, or mediation between two compelled parties, it is permitted; but if it is the imposition of compulsion, it is not permitted.

**The third issue:** This verse also indicates the permissibility of a person requesting a position for which he is qualified. If it is said: Muslim has related from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Samura, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "O 'Abd al-Rahman, do not ask for leadership, for if you are given it upon your request, you will be left to it, and if you are given it without asking, you will be helped in it." And from Abu Burda, who said: Abu Musa said: I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with two men from the Ash'aris, one on my right and the other on my left, and both of them asked for work, while the Prophet (ﷺ) was using the siwak. He said: "What do you say, O Abu Musa, or O 'Abd Allah ibn Qays?" I said: "By the One who sent you with the truth, they did not inform me of what was in their souls, and I did not perceive that they were seeking work." He said: "And it is as if I can see his siwak beneath his lip, contracted and drawn in." Then he said: "We will not appoint to our work whoever desires it," and he mentioned the hadith. Muslim and others also transmitted it. The answer is: Firstly, Yusuf (peace be upon him) only sought the authority because he knew that no one else could take his place in justice, in reform, and in delivering the poor to their rights; he saw that this was an obligation specifically incumbent upon him, since there was no one else. Likewise today: if a person knows of himself that he will uphold the truth in judgeship or *hisbah* (public accountability for good order), and there is no one else qualified to take his place, then it becomes incumbent upon him, and he must seek it and describe the qualities that entitle him to it, such as knowledge, competence and other things, as Yusuf (peace be upon him) did. But if there is someone else who is capable of it and qualified for it, and this is known, then it is better not to seek it, due to his (peace be upon him) saying to 'Abd al-Rahman: "Do not ask for leadership." Moreover, in asking for it and being eager for it, while knowing the abundance of its afflictions and the difficulty of escaping them, there is evidence that he seeks it for himself and for his own purposes; and whoever is like this is likely to be overcome by his self and perish. This is the meaning of his (peace be upon him) saying: "He will be left to it." Whoever refuses it, knowing its afflictions and fearing that he will fall short in its rights, flees from it; then if he is tested with it, it is hoped that he will be delivered from it. This is the meaning of his saying: "He will be helped in it."

Secondly: He did not say, "I am noble and generous," although he was, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The noble one, son of the noble, son of the noble, son of the noble, Yusuf ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim." Nor did he say, "I am handsome and attractive." He only said, "I am a guardian, knowing," so he commended himself by his guarding and his knowledge, not by lineage and beauty.

Thirdly: He said that only before one who did not know him, so he wished to make himself known, and this became an exception to the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿So do not claim purity for yourselves﴾.

Fourthly: He saw that this was an obligation specifically incumbent upon him, since there was no one else there. This is the most evident view. And Allah knows best.

**The fourth issue:** This verse also indicates that a person may describe himself by the knowledge and merit he possesses. Al-Mawardi said: This is not an unrestricted permission covering all qualities; rather, it is restricted to what is connected with the matter at hand or is related to an apparent means of earning, and it is prohibited in other matters, because of what it contains of self-praise and ostentation. Yet if the virtuous man distinguishes himself from that, it would be more becoming to his virtue. Yusuf was compelled to it by the necessity arising from his previous situation, and because he hoped to attain his family through it.

The Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 12, verses 56–57:

God the Exalted said: ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land, to settle therein wherever he willed﴾. That is: and like this favour which We bestowed upon him, in bringing him close to the king's heart and delivering him from prison, We established him in the land, that is, [[from ʿa, k, y.]] We empowered him to do what he wished. Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: God's words, "And thus We established Joseph in the land," are evidence for permitting *hiyal* (legal stratagems) to reach what is permissible, what brings benefit and righteousness, and to recover rights. A similar verse is God's words: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle [of grass] and strike with it, and do not break your oath﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 212.]] [p. 44], and the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri concerning the governor of Khaybar, who brought the Prophet ﷺ dates from it, and what the Prophet ﷺ said to him. [[The hadith: The Messenger of God ﷺ appointed a man over Khaybar, and he came to him with *Janib* dates, which is a good kind of date. The Messenger of God ﷺ said to him: "Are all the dates of Khaybar like this?" He said: "No, by God, O Messenger of God, we take a *sa'* of this for two *sa'*s, or three." He said: "Do not do that. Sell the mixed dates for dirhams, then buy *Janib* with the dirhams." (al-Bukhari).]]

I say: this is rejected in what follows. It is said: "We empowered him" and "We empowered for him," as God the Exalted said: ﴿We had established them in the land as We had not established you﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 391.]] [al-An'am: 6]. Al-Tabari said: The great king al-Walid ibn al-Rayyan appointed Joseph over the administration of Itfir (Potiphar) and dismissed him. Mujahid said: [Itfir] embraced Islam at his hands. Ibn Abbas said: [The king] made him king after a year and a half. Muqatil narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "If Joseph had said, 'I am a keeper, knowing, if God wills,' he would have been made king at that time." Then Itfir died, and al-Walid married him to Itfir's wife, Ra'il, and Joseph consummated the marriage with her and found her a virgin. She bore him two sons: Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph. Whoever claims she was Zulaikha says: Joseph did not marry her, and when she saw him in his procession she wept, then said: "Praise be to God who made kings slaves through disobedience, and praise be to God who made slaves kings through obedience." He took her in, and she was among his household until she died with him, and he did not marry her. This was reported by al-Mawardi, and it contradicts what was earlier narrated from Wahb. al-Tha'labi also mentioned it, but God knows best.

When the king entrusted the affairs of Egypt to Joseph, he treated the people gently and began calling them to Islam until they believed in him, and he established justice among them, so men and women loved him. Wahb, al-Suddi, Ibn Abbas and others said: Then came the years of plenty, and Joseph ordered the improvement of the fields and commanded them to expand cultivation. When the harvest ripened, he ordered it gathered, then built granaries for it. In that year a harvest was gathered in them so vast that the storehouses could not contain it. Then he gathered each year's harvest in the same way, until the seven years of plenty ended and the years of drought came. Gabriel descended and said: "O people of Egypt, be hungry, for God has imposed upon you hunger for seven years." Some of the wise said: Hunger and famine have two signs. The first: the soul loves food more than usual, hunger comes quickly to it, unlike what it was before, and it takes more food than it needs. The second: food disappears altogether, is not found at all, and becomes extremely scarce. Both signs came together in the time of Joseph. Men, women and children were crying out, "Hunger! Hunger!" They ate and were not satisfied, and the king awoke crying, "Hunger! Hunger!" He said: Joseph prayed for him, and God healed him of that. Then in the morning Joseph proclaimed throughout all the land of Egypt: "O people! Let no one sow a seed, lest it be wasted and nothing sprout." Those years came with a tremendous, indescribable terror. Ibn Abbas said: When the drought began, the king was in the middle of the night, and hunger struck him at midnight. The king cried out: "O Joseph! Hunger, hunger!" Joseph said: "This is the time of the drought." When the first year of the drought's years began, everything they had stored in the years of plenty was destroyed. The people of Egypt began buying food from Joseph. In the first year he sold it to them for money, until no dinar or dirham remained in Egypt that he had not collected. In the second year he sold it to them for jewellery and gems, until none of these remained in people's hands. In the third year he sold it to them for livestock and animals, until he possessed them all. In the fourth year he sold it to them for slaves and maidservants, until he gained control of all of them. In the fifth year he sold it to them for real estate and estates, until he owned all of them. In the sixth year he sold it to them for their children and wives, and enslaved them all. In the seventh year he sold it to them for their necks, until no free person or slave remained in Egypt who had not become his slave. The people said: "By God, we have never seen a king greater or more mighty than this." Joseph said to the king of Egypt: "How do you see the handiwork of my Lord in what He has entrusted to me? And now all of this is yours. What do you think of it?" He said: "I have entrusted the matter to you, so do what you wish. We are only followers of yours, and I am not one who disdains your worship and obedience. I am only one of your servants and one of your attendants." Joseph, peace be upon him, said: "I did not free them from hunger in order to enslave them, nor did I rescue them from affliction in order to become a affliction upon them.
