God the Exalted said: ﴿We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will﴾. That is, by Our kindness. *Rahmah* (mercy) means blessing and kindness.

(And We do not waste the reward of the good-doers). That is, their reward. Ibn Abbas and Wahb said: It means the patient, because of his patience in the well, in slavery, and in prison, and his patience in refraining from what God forbade, when the woman invited him to it. That is, what We give him in the Hereafter is better and greater than what We gave him in this world, because the reward of the Hereafter is everlasting, while the reward of this world comes to an end. Is there not in the Messenger of God, Joseph, an example
for one like you, imprisoned for injustice and falsehood?
He maintained beautiful patience in the prison for a while,
and beautiful patience brought him to kingship.

One of them wrote to a friend:

Beyond the narrow strait of fear lies the wide expanse of safety,
and the first thing to rejoice in is the end of sorrow.
So do not despair, for God gave Joseph dominion
over His treasuries after his release from prison.

Another recited:

When calamities reach their limit
and hearts nearly melt from them,
and affliction descends and consolation dwindles,
then at the utmost limit comes relief.

Poetry on this theme is abundant.

Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: God's words, "And thus We established Joseph in the land," are evidence for permitting *hiyal* (legal stratagems) to reach what is permissible, what brings benefit and righteousness, and to recover rights. [[The hadith: The Messenger of God ﷺ appointed a man over Khaybar, and he came to him with *Janib* dates, which is a good kind of date. The Messenger of God ﷺ said to him: "Are all the dates of Khaybar like this?" He said: "No, by God, O Messenger of God, we take a *sa'* of this for two *sa'*s, or three." He said: "Do not do that. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 58:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the brothers of Joseph came﴾, meaning they came to Egypt when the famine afflicted them, to buy grain. This is one of the instances of the brevity (ikhtisar) of the inimitable Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: When famine and hardship befell the people, and it reached the land of Canaan, Ya'qub (peace be upon him) sent his sons to obtain provisions (al-mira). The affair of Yusuf (peace be upon him) had spread throughout the regions, due to his gentleness, his nearness (to the people), his mercy, his compassion, his justice and his conduct. When hardship came upon the people, Yusuf (peace be upon him) would sit himself at the sale [[min ‘ayn wa-kaf wa-waw wa-yā’ (the variant readings noted in the manuscripts)]] to the people, giving them food according to the number of their heads, a wasq for each head [[The wasq is sixty sa', and the basic meaning of wasq is a load.]].

(And the brothers of Joseph came and entered upon him, and he recognized them) Yusuf, (but they did not recognize him) because they had left him as a child, and they did not imagine that after slavery he would reach that station of kingship, especially with the long passage of time, which was forty years. It was also said: they denied him because they believed he was an unbelieving king. It was also said: they saw him wearing silk, with a gold collar around his neck and a crown on his head, having adorned himself with the attire of the Pharaoh of Egypt, whereas Yusuf saw them in the same clothing and adornment he had known from them. It is also possible that they saw him from behind a screen and therefore did not recognize him. It was also said: they denied him because of an extraordinary matter, a test with which Allah tested Ya'qub.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 59–61:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾. It is said: "jahhaztu al-qawm tajhizan," meaning I made arrangements for the people, providing them with their provisions for the journey. The jihaz of the bride is what is needed when she is sent over to the husband. Some of the Kufans permitted the reading "al-jihaz" with a kasra on the jim. The jihaz in this verse is the food they had obtained from him. Al-Suddi said: Joseph's brothers had eleven camels with them, though they were ten men. They said to Joseph: "We have a brother who stayed behind with us, and his camel is with us." So he asked them why he had stayed behind. They said: "Because of his father's love for him." They mentioned to him that he had an older brother who went out into the wilderness and perished. He said to them: "I wished to see this brother of yours whom you mentioned, to know the nature of your father's love for him, and to know your truthfulness." It is also narrated that they left Simeon with him as a pledge until they brought his brother Benjamin. Ibn Abbas said: Joseph said to the interpreter: "Tell them: your language differs from our language, and your dress differs from our dress, so perhaps you are spies." They said: "By God! We are not spies, rather we are sons of one father, and he is a truthful old man." He said: "How many are you?" They said: "We were twelve, and one of our brothers went out into the wilderness and perished there." He said: "Where is the other?" They said: "With our father." He said: "Who will know your truthfulness?" They said: "No one here knows us, and we have made known to you our lineage, so with what will your soul be at ease regarding us?" Joseph said: (Bring me a brother of yours from your father) if you are truthful, and I am content with that. "Do you not see that I give full measure" that is, I complete it and do not diminish it, "and I will give you an extra camel-load for your brother." "But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me," a threat that he would not sell them food if they did not bring him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure﴾. This may have two meanings: the first is that he allowed them a lower price, which amounted to an increase in the measure. The second is that he measured out for them with a full measure.

(And I am the best of hosts) In this there are two meanings: the first is that he is the best of hosts, because he hosted them well, as said by Mujahid. The second, which is possible, means: the best of those among whom you have stayed, being trustworthy. On the first interpretation it is derived from "nuzul," which is food, and on the second from "manzil," which is a dwelling.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me﴾, meaning: I will not sell you anything from now on, because he had already given them their full measure on this occasion.

(And do not come near me) meaning: I will not give you a place near me as one close, and it does not mean that they would keep away from him and not return to him, for he urged them to return. Al-Suddi said: He demanded a pledge from them so that they would return, and Simeon was held as a pledge with him. Al-Kalbi said: Simeon was chosen from among them only because on the day of the well he was the most eloquent of them in speech and the best in opinion. "Taqrabun" is in a jussive position due to the prohibition, which is why the nun was dropped from it and the ya' was dropped, because it is the end of a verse; if it were a statement, it would be "taqrabunni" with a fatha on the nun.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: We will seek to get him from his father﴾, meaning: we will request him from him and ask him to send him with us.

(And indeed we will surely do it) meaning: we will guarantee bringing him and will devise means to achieve that. Question: How did Joseph permit himself to bring grief upon his father by demanding his brother? It is said in reply that there are four answers. The first: it is possible that God, mighty and majestic, commanded him to do so as a trial for Jacob, so that his reward would be greater, and he obeyed His command in it. The second: it is possible that he intended by this to alert Jacob to the condition of Joseph, peace be upon them both. The third: so that Jacob's joy would be doubled by the return of his two sons to him. The fourth: to give precedence to his brother's joy at being reunited with him before his other brothers, because of an inclination he had toward him. The first is the most apparent. And God knows best.

The Almighty's words: ﴿And he said to his young men﴾. This is the reading of the people of Madina, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim (recitation, *qira'a*). It is also the preference of Abu Hatim and al-Nahhas, among others.

All the other Kufans read *li-fityanihi* ("to his young men," with the longer plural form). Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading and said: "It is written this way in the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud)." Al-Tha'labi said: "Both are good dialectal forms, like *al-sibyan* and *al-sibyah*."

Al-Nahhas said: "*Li-fityanihi* contradicts the great majority of the codices (*al-sawad al-a'zam*), because in the consonantal text there is neither an alif nor a nun. The majority consensus should not be abandoned for this disconnected chain of transmission. Moreover, *fityah* is more fitting than *fityan*, because among the Arabs *fityah* denotes a small number, and a small group is more likely to put the goods in their saddlebags."

These young men were arranging their equipment, which is why they were able to place their merchandise in their baggage. It is also possible that they were free men, and they were his helpers. Their merchandise was the price of the food they had bought. It was said that it was dirhams and dinars. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was sandals, leather goods and the traveller's belongings, and this is called a *rahl* (saddlebag). Ibn al-Anbari said: "A container is called a *rahl*, and a house is also called a *rahl*."

He said: ﴿perhaps they will recognise it﴾, because it was possible that it would not be safe on the road. It was also said that he only did this so that they would return when they found it, since he knew that they would not accept food except at its price. It was said: so that they would use it to help them return to buy food. It was also said: he found it shameful to take the price of food from his father and his brothers. And it was said: so that they would see his generosity and be eager to return to him.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 12, verses 63–65:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When they returned to their father, they said, "O our father, measure has been withheld from us."﴾ Because he had said to them, "If you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure (kayl) for you with me." They informed him of what had happened with them and of his honour toward them, and that Shum'un (Simeon) was held as a pledge until he knew the truth of their words.

(﴿So send with us our brother, and we will measure﴾) That is, they said at that point, "So send with us our brother, and we will measure." The original form is *naktal* (نَكْتَالُ), but the damma on the lam was dropped for the jussive, and the alif was dropped because two unvocalized letters came together (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*). The reading of the people of the two sanctuaries (Ahl al-Haramayn), Abu 'Amr and 'Asim is *naktal* with the nun (نَكْتَلْ), while the rest of the Kufans read *yaktal* (يَكْتَلْ) with the ya. The first is the preference of Abu 'Ubayd, so that they would all be included among those who measure. He claimed that if it were with the ya, it would refer to the brother alone. Al-Nahhas said: This does not follow, because the statement must be one of two possibilities: either the meaning is "send our brother so that he measures with us," in which case it applies to all of them, or the sense is without inversion, in which case the statement itself contains evidence for all of them, through his saying, "If you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me."

(﴿And indeed we will be its guardians﴾) from any harm befalling him.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Shall I entrust him to you except as I entrusted his brother to you before?"﴾ That is, you have already been negligent with Yusuf, so how can I entrust you with his brother?

(﴿But Allah is the best of guardians﴾) It is in the accusative as a specification (*al-bayan*). This is the reading of the people of Madina, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim. The rest of the Kufans read *hafizan* (حافِظاً) as a circumstantial accusative (*al-hal*). Al-Zajjaj said: it is a specification. In this there is evidence that he agreed to send him with them. The meaning of the verse is: Allah's guarding of him is better than your guarding of him. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: When Ya'qub said, "But Allah is the best of guardians," Allah, may He be exalted, said: "By My might and My majesty, I will surely return both your sons to you after you have put your trust in Me."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when they opened their goods...﴾ (the verse) has no meaning in it that is problematic.

(*Ma nabghi*) The *ma* (مَا) here is an interrogative in the accusative position, and the meaning is: What more do we seek beyond this? He has fulfilled the measure for us and returned the price to us. They meant by this to set their father's heart at ease. It was also said that *ma* is a negation, meaning: We do not seek from you dirhams or merchandise; rather, this merchandise of ours, which has been returned to us, will suffice us. It was transmitted from 'Alqama that he read *ruddat ilayna* (رُدَّتْ إِلَيْنا) with a kasra on the ra', because the original was *ruddidat*, and when the two identical letters were assimilated, the vowel of the first dal was transferred to the ra'.

His saying: (*wa-namir ahlana*) means we bring food for them. The poet said:

*I sent you seeking provisions, but you stayed a full year,*
*When will your aid come to the one you help?*

Al-Sulami read *numir* with a damma on the nun, meaning we help them in obtaining provisions.

(*wa-nazdad kayla ba'irin dhalika kaylun yasir*) That is, the load of one camel for Benyamin.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 66:

There are two issues here. The first concerns His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You shall bring me﴾, meaning, you shall give me.

(a covenant from Allah) meaning a pledge by which one is bound (ʿahd yuwthaqu bihi). Al-Suddi said: They swore by Allah that they would return him to him and would not abandon him, and the lam in (you shall surely bring me) is the lam of oath.

(unless you are encompassed) Mujahid said: unless you perish or die. Qatadah said: unless you are overcome by it. Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative position (mawdiʿ nasb).

(When they had given him their covenant, he said: Allah is Witness over what we say) meaning, a guardian of the oath. It was also said: a keeper of the covenant, one who establishes it with management and justice.

The second issue: this verse is the basis for the permissibility of al-Hamalah (surety, guarantee) [[al-Hamalah: al-kafalah, i.e. suretyship]] regarding property (bi'l-ʿayn) and the guarantee of a person (al-wathiqah bi'l-nafs). The scholars have differed on this. Malik, all of his companions, and most scholars said: it is permissible when what is guaranteed is wealth. Al-Shafiʿi weakened suretyship for the face (al-hamalah bi'l-wajh) concerning wealth, though he also had a position like Malik's. ʿUthman al-Batti said: if one stands surety for a person in a case of retaliation (qisas) or wounding, then if he does not produce him, he is liable for the blood-money (diyah) and the arsh of the wound, and it is owed from the property of the offender, since there is no retaliation upon the surety. So these are three positions on suretyship for the face. The correct view is Malik's distinction in this matter: that it applies to wealth, and does not apply to a hadd or taʿzir punishment, as will be explained.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 67:**

There are seven issues in it.

The first issue: When they resolved to set out, he (Ya'qub) feared the evil eye (al-'ayn) for them. So he commanded them not to enter Egypt through one gate, and Egypt had four gates. He feared the evil eye for them because they were eleven men, all sons of one man, and they were people of beauty, perfection and physical presence. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Qatadah and others.

The second issue: If this is the meaning of the verse, then it contains evidence for taking precautions against the evil eye. The evil eye is real. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The evil eye can bring a man into the grave and a camel into the cooking pot." And his (ﷺ) seeking refuge (ta'awwudh): "I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah from every devil and venomous creature and from every envious, harmful eye" indicates this too. Malik narrated from Muhammad ibn Abi Umamah ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf that he heard his father say: "My father Sahl ibn Hunayf bathed at al-Kharrar [[al-Kharrar: a water source in Madinah.]], and he took off a robe he was wearing, while 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah was watching. He said: Sahl was a fair man with beautiful skin. 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah said to him: I have never seen anything like today, not even the skin of a virgin! Immediately Sahl was struck with fever, and his fever became severe. He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and was informed that Sahl had a fever and could not go out with you, O Messenger of Allah. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to him, and Sahl told him what had happened with 'Amir. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Why does one of you kill his brother? Why did you not say, "Blessings (barakta)" [[Barak: he said "May Allah bless him," and this statement nullifies the effect of the evil eye, whose meaning will come.]]? The evil eye is real. Perform ablution for him.' So 'Amir performed ablution, and Sahl went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with no harm on him." In another narration: "He bathed." 'Amir washed for him his face, his hands, his elbows, his knees, the edges of his feet, and the inside of his waist-wrap in a vessel, then poured it over him. So Sahl went out with the Messenger of Allah [[In 'A: with the people.]] (ﷺ) with no harm on him. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas rode one day, and a woman saw him and said: "Your amir knows that he has thin flanks." He returned to his house and fell down. It reached him what the woman had said, so he sent for her, and she washed for him. In these two hadiths is evidence that the evil eye is real, that it kills as the Prophet (ﷺ) said. This is the view of the scholars of the Ummah and the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah. Some groups of innovators (mubtadi'ah) denied it, but they are refuted by the Sunnah, by the consensus (ijma') of the scholars of this Ummah, and by what is observed in existence. How many a man has the evil eye brought to the grave, and how many a strong camel has it brought to the cooking pot! Yet this happens by the will of Allah, as He said: ﴿And they will not harm anyone by it except by the permission of Allah﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 102] [[See vol. 2, p. 55.]]. Al-Asma'i said: "I saw a man who was an evil-eye-causer. He heard a cow being milked, and its milk-stream pleased him, so he said: Which one of them is this? They said: It is so-and-so's, for another cow. They were deceiving about the other cow, so both of them died, the one deceived about and the one deceived for." Al-Asma'i said: "I also heard him say: When I see a thing that pleases me, I feel a heat coming out of my eye."

The third issue: It is obligatory for every Muslim who is impressed by something to bless it, for when he invokes blessing, the feared harm is averted without doubt. Do you not see his (ﷺ) saying to 'Amir: "Why did you not say, 'Blessings'?" This shows that the evil eye does not harm and does not spread when the one who looks says "Blessings," and that it spreads only when he does not bless. Blessing (al-tabrik) is to say: "Blessed is Allah, the best of creators! O Allah, bless him."

The fourth issue: If the one with the evil eye strikes with his eye and does not bless, he is commanded to bathe, and he is compelled to do so if he refuses, because the command implies obligation, especially in this case, since the affected person may face the danger of death. No one should prevent his brother from what benefits his brother and does not harm himself, especially when he is the cause of the harm and is the one who inflicted it.

The fifth issue: Whoever is known for striking with the evil eye is prevented from mixing with people, to remove his harm. Some scholars said: The ruler (imam) orders him to stay at home, and if he is poor, he provides him with what sustains him and restrains his harm from people. It has also been said that he is to be exiled. The hadith of Malik that we mentioned refutes these opinions, for the Prophet (ﷺ) did not order imprisonment or exile concerning 'Amir. Rather, a righteous man may be one who has the evil eye, and this does not discredit him or make him a sinner. Whoever says he should be imprisoned and ordered to stay at home is taking a precaution and averting harm. And Allah knows best.

The sixth issue: Malik narrated from Humayd ibn Qays al-Makki that he said: The two sons of Ja'far ibn Abi Talib were brought in to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said to their nurse: "Why do I see them emaciated?" [[Al-dari': the thin, wasted of body.]] Their nurse said: "O Messenger of Allah! The evil eye hastens to them, and what prevented us from seeking a charm (istirqa') for them is that we do not know what would suit you in that." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Seek a charm for them, for if anything could outrun destiny (qadar), the evil eye would have outrun it." This hadith is mursal (broken in its chain), but it is preserved through Asma' bint 'Umays al-Khath'amiyyah from the Prophet (ﷺ) by sound, connected, authentic routes. In it is evidence that charms (ruqa) are among the means by which calamity is averted, that the evil eye affects a person and makes him emaciated, i.e., weakens him and wears him down, and that this is by the decree and destiny of Allah the Exalted. It is said that the evil eye reaches children more quickly than adults. And Allah knows best.

The seventh issue: In the hadith of Abu Umamah the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered the one with the evil eye to bathe for the one affected, and here he ordered seeking a charm. Our scholars said: Seeking a charm against the evil eye is only when the one with the eye is not known. But when the person who struck with his eye is known, he is ordered to perform ablution, according to the hadith of Abu Umamah. And Allah knows best.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And I cannot avail you anything against Allah﴾ means: against anything I would fear for you. That is, caution does not benefit against what has been decreed.

(Verily the command) means: the decision and judgment belong to Allah.

(Upon Him I rely) means: I depend on Him and trust Him.

(And upon Him let those who rely, rely).

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 12, verses 68–70:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when they entered from where their father had commanded them﴾, meaning: from different gates.

(It did not avail them anything against Allah) if He intended to inflict harm upon them.

(Except a need) is an exception that is not from the first part.

(Within the soul of Ya'qub, he fulfilled it) meaning: a thought that occurred to his heart, which was his instruction that they should disperse. Mujahid said: "for fear of the evil eye," and the discussion of this has already preceded. It was also said: "so that the king would not see their number and their strength and then seize them out of envy or caution." This was said by some of the later scholars and was chosen by al-Nahhas, who said: "There is no meaning of the evil eye here." This verse indicates that a Muslim is obliged to warn his brother against what he fears for him, and to guide him to what contains the way of safety and salvation, for "religion is sincere advice" and "the Muslim is the brother of the Muslim."

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And indeed he﴾, meaning Ya'qub.

(He is full of knowledge because of what We taught him), meaning: concerning the matter of his religion.

(But most people do not know), meaning: they do not know what Ya'qub (peace be upon him) knew of the matter of his religion. It was also said: "Full of knowledge" means full of action, since knowledge is the first of the causes of action, so it was named by that which is its cause.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when they entered upon Yusuf, he took his brother to himself﴾. Qatadah said: "He embraced him and lodged him with himself." It was also said: he ordered that every two should lodge in one place, so his brother remained alone, and he took him to himself and said: "I pitied him for being alone." He said to him secretly, away from his brothers: (Indeed I am your brother, so do not grieve) meaning: do not be sad (over what they used to do).

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Then when he had furnished them with their provisions, he placed the drinking cup in his brother's saddlebag﴾. When Binyamin recognized that he was Yusuf, he said to him: "Do not send me back to them." He said: "I know Ya'qub's grief over me, so his grief will increase." Binyamin refused to leave. Yusuf said: "Your detention is not possible unless I attribute to you something that is not becoming of you." He said: "I do not care!" So he placed the cup in his saddlebag, either by himself, in a way that no one noticed, or by ordering some of his close attendants to do so. Al-tajhiz means dispatching and completing the matter, and from it comes "jahhaza 'ala al-jarih," meaning he killed him, and "najaza amrahu" (he completed his affair). The saqayah and the sawa' are one and the same thing: a vessel with two heads and a handle in its middle. The king would drink from it from one head, and grain would be measured with the other head. This was reported by al-Naqqash from Ibn Abbas. Everything from which one drinks is a sawa', and he recited:

"We drink wine from the sawa' openly."

[[The line appeared earlier on p. 178 of this part, with the variant reading: "We drink sin."]]

Its material has been disputed. Shu'bah reported from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The king's sawa' was a silver thing resembling a measure, of silver inlaid with jewels, placed on the head. Al-Abbas had one in the pre-Islamic period." Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked: "What is the sawa'?" He said: "The vessel." Al-A'sha said about it:

"For him there is a loaf at its head, and drinking vessels,
and a cooking pot, a cook, a sa' and a daysaq."

[[The daysaq is a table of silver. The line is from a poem praising al-Muhalliq, whose opening is:

"Sleeplessness kept me awake, this wakeful insomnia,
and there is no illness in me, nor am I lovesick."]]

Ikrimah said: it was of silver. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: it was of gold, and with it their food was measured, as an extreme of honouring them. It was also said: it was only used for measuring because grain was scarce. The word sa' is used as both masculine and feminine. Whoever makes it feminine says "a'wu'" like "adwur," and whoever makes it masculine says "a'way'" like "athwab." Mujahid and Abu Salih said: the sa' is the "tirjihalah" in the language of Himyar. Concerning it there are readings: "suwa'" is the reading of the common people; "sawgh" with a dotted ghayn is the reading of Yahya ibn Ya'mur, who said: "It was a vessel fashioned from gold." "Sawa'" with an undotted 'ayn is the reading of Abu Raja. "Sawu'" with a pointed sad, a silent waw and an undotted 'ayn is the reading of Ubayy. "Suyā'" with a ya between the sad and the alif is the reading of [[In 'a: Abu Ja'far. What is in Shawadhdh of Ibn Khalawayh is: Sawagh, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, with a dotted ghayn, and Ibn 'Atiyyah.]] Sa'id ibn Jubayr. "Sa'" with an alif between the sad and the 'ayn is the reading of Abu Hurayrah.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Then a caller called out: "O caravan, indeed you are thieves!"﴾, meaning: a caller called out and announced. The "adhdhana" here indicates repetition, as if he called out repeatedly: "O caravan." The 'ir (caravan) is that which is carried upon for grain, of donkeys, camels and mules. Mujahid said: "Their caravan was of donkeys." Abu Ubaydah said: "The 'ir is the loaded camels that are ridden." The meaning is: "O companions of the caravan," like His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], and like "O horse of Allah, ride!", meaning: O companions of the horse of Allah, and this will come. Here there are two objections. The first: If it is said: How did Binyamin consent to remain willingly, when in this there is disobedience to the father through increasing his grief, and Yusuf agreed to that? The second: How did Yusuf attribute theft to his brothers when they were innocent? As for the first, the answer is: grief had so overcome Ya'qub that the loss of Binyamin had little effect on him at all. Do you not see that when he lost him he said: ﴿Alas for Yusuf﴾ [Yusuf: 84] and did not turn to Binyamin? Perhaps Yusuf agreed with him to remain by revelation, so there is no objection. As for Yusuf's attributing theft to his brothers, the answer is: these people had indeed stolen him from his father, throwing him into the well, then selling him, so they deserved this name through that act, and so the application of that name to them was true. Another answer: he meant "O caravan, your situation is the situation of thieves," and the meaning is that something belonging to others came into your possession without the king's consent or knowledge. Another answer: that was a stratagem for the reuniting of his shared closeness with his brother, and separating him from them to himself. This is based on the view that Binyamin did not know about the placing of the sa' in his saddlebag, and he had not informed him of it himself. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verses 71–72:

There are seven issues here.

The first issue concerns the words of the Exalted: ﴿And for him who brings it is a camel's load, and I am its guarantor.﴾ "Al-ba'ir" (camel) here means the male camel, according to the view of most commentators (mufassirun). It was also said that it means the donkey, which is a dialect of some Arabs. This was reported from Mujahid, who also preferred it. Mujahid said: "Al-za'im" (guarantor) is the caller (mu'adhdhin) who said: "O caravan (ayyatuha al-'ir)." Al-za'im, al-kafil (surety), al-hamil (bearer of liability), al-darnin and al-qabil are all the same, and al-za'im means the leader. Imru' al-Qays said [[It is Imru' al-Qays. Al-faraniq: a beast of prey that cries out in front of the lion, as if warning people of it; it is a Persian loanword (mu'arrab). Al-azwar: the one who leans to one side; i.e., if Caesar (Qaysar) restores me to my kingdom, I will travel at such a fierce pace that the faraniq will lean aside from its intensity.]]:

*And I am a guarantor, if I return restored to my kingdom,*
*with a march from which you see the faraniq leaning aside.*

Layla al-Akhyaliyya said, mourning her brother [[As it stands in the original; perhaps it should be "mourning Tawbah." Regarding his being described as having a torn shirt, there are several opinions: first, that this alludes to beggars pulling at him. Second, that he gives his good garments preference, clothing others with them and making do with their worn ones. Third, that he had broad shoulders, and so the shirt would tear quickly at the collar. Fourth, that he fought many battles and was constantly on journeys, so his shirt was torn for that reason.]]:

*And his shirt is torn at the chest; you would think him,*
*on the day of the encounter, sick from shyness.*

*Until, when he raised the banner, you saw him*
*[under the banner] [[As in "Amali al-Qali," al-Shi'r wa-al-Shu'ara', and al-Hamasah. In some copies: "on the day of the tumult."]] over the army as a leader.*

The second issue: If it is asked, how could he guarantee the load of a camel when it is unknown, and the guarantee of an unknown thing is not valid? It is answered: the load of a camel was specified and known among them, like the wasq (a measure of weight), so the guarantee was valid. However, it [was] [[From manuscript ʿ.]] a substitute for property of the thief, and this is not lawful for the thief. Perhaps it was valid in their law, or this was a ju'l (reward for a specified service), and an offer of property to one who searches and seeks.

The third issue: Some scholars said: in this verse there are two proofs. The first: the permissibility of the ju'l (reward), which was permitted out of necessity, since uncertainty is allowed in it that is not allowed in other contracts. So if a man says, "Whoever does such and such, for him is such and such," it is valid. The nature of the ju'l is that one of its two parties is known and the other unknown, because of the necessity for it, unlike hire (ijarah), where the compensation and the thing compensated are determined on both sides. It is among the permissible contracts (al-'uqud al-ja'izah), in which either party may dissolve it. However, the one to whom the reward is promised may dissolve it before beginning and after beginning, if he agrees to waive his right; and the one who offers the reward may not dissolve it once the one to whom it is promised has begun the work. The presence of both contracting parties is not required in the contract of ju'l, like other contracts, because of His saying: "And for him who brings it is a camel's load." All of this was said by al-Shafi'i.

The fourth issue: Whenever a person says, "Whoever brings my runaway slave, for him is a dinar," he is bound by what he stipulated when the slave is brought. If someone brings it without a guarantee, he is bound to pay when he brings it, if he seeks the wage. This is because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever brings a runaway (slave), for him are forty dirhams," and he did not distinguish between one who brings it under a contract of guarantee or outside a contract. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: For this reason our companions (the Malikis) said: whoever does for a person what is obligatory for him to do for himself, he is bound to pay, and he is entitled to the equivalent wage if he is one who does such things for a wage. I say: al-Shafi'i disagreed with us on all of this.

The fifth issue: The second proof is the permissibility of kafalah (suretyship) for a man, because the guarantor who called out was other than Yusuf, peace be upon him. Our scholars said: If a man says, "I have taken responsibility," "I have undertaken," "I have guaranteed," "I am your hamil (bearer) or za'im or kafil or damin or qabil," or "it is due to you from me," "upon me," "to me," or "in my charge," all of that is binding suretyship (hamalah lazimah). The jurists differed concerning one who stands surety for the person or for the appearance (of a debtor): is he bound to guarantee the property or not? The Kufans said: whoever stands surety for a man's person is not liable for the right owed by the one sought if he dies. This is also one of al-Shafi'i's two opinions, the well-known one from him. Malik, al-Layth and al-Awza'i said: if he stands surety for his person, and the person owes property, then if he does not produce him he must pay the property, and he may recover it from the one sought. If he stipulates that he guarantees the person or the appearance and says, "I will not guarantee the property," then he is not liable for the property. The argument of those who require payment of the property is that the surety knew that the one whose appearance he guaranteed is not sought for blood but for property. So if he guarantees him to the creditor and does not bring him, it is as if he has made him lose it and removed him from him, and therefore the property is binding on him. Al-Tahawi argued for the Kufans, saying: As for guaranteeing the property upon the death of the one guaranteed [[From manuscripts ʿ and w.]], there is no meaning to it, for he only undertook the person and did not undertake the property, so it is absurd that he be bound to what he did not undertake.

The sixth issue: The scholars differed when one man stands surety for another for property: may the creditor take whichever of them he wishes? Al-Thawri, the Kufans, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq said: he may take whomever he wishes until he receives his right. This was Malik's view, then he retracted it and said: the surety is not taken except if the debtor becomes bankrupt or disappears, because beginning with the one who owes the right is preferable, unless he is destitute, in which case it is taken from the surety, because he is excused in taking it in this situation. This is a good view. The analogy (qiyas) is that a man may demand from whichever of the two he wishes. Ibn Abi Layla said: if a man guarantees property on behalf of his companion, the obligation transfers to the surety and the original debtor is discharged, unless the creditor stipulates against both of them that he may take whichever he wishes. He argued by analogy to the discharge of the dead from debt, by the guarantee of Abu Qatada [[The hadith: Salamah ibn al-Akwa' narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) was brought a funeral bier and said: "Does he owe any debt?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Has he left anything?" They said: "No." He said: "Pray over your companion." Abu Qatada said: "Pray over him, O Messenger of God, and I take on his debt." So he prayed over him.]]. Abu Thawr said something similar.

The seventh issue: za'amah (suretyship/guarantee) is valid only in rights that may be undertaken by proxy, of the kind that are attached to the liability (dhimmah) in property, and that are established and firm. Therefore the hamalah (guarantee) is not valid for kitabah (a contract of manumission by installments), because it is not a firm and established debt, since if the slave is unable to pay he is returned to slavery and the contract of kitabah is dissolved. As for every right that no one can undertake on behalf of another, such as the hudud (prescribed punishments), there is no kafalah in it, and the accused in a hadd case is imprisoned until his case is examined. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad deviated, permitting kafalah in hudud and in qisas (retaliation), and said: if the one slandered or the claimant in qisas says, "My evidence is present," he may take a surety for three days. al-Tahawi argued for them with what Hamzah ibn 'Amr narrated from Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah and al-Ash'ath, that they ruled by kafalah of the person in the presence of the Companions.

Malik, al-Layth and al-Awza'i said: if he stands surety for his person, and the person owes property, then if he does not produce him he must pay the property, and he may recover it from the one sought. If he stipulates that he guarantees the person or the appearance and says, "I will not guarantee the property," then he is not liable for the property. The argument of those who require payment of the property is that the surety knew that the one whose appearance he guaranteed is not sought for blood but for property. So if he guarantees him to the creditor and does not bring him, it is as if he has made him lose it and removed him from him, and therefore the property is binding on him. Al-Tahawi argued for the Kufans, saying: As for guaranteeing the property upon the death of the one guaranteed [[From manuscripts ʿ and w.]], there is no meaning to it, for he only undertook the person and did not undertake the property, so it is absurd that he be bound to what he did not undertake.

The sixth issue: The scholars differed when one man stands surety for another for property: may the creditor take whichever of them he wishes? Al-Thawri, the Kufans, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq said: he may take whomever he wishes until he receives his right. This was Malik's view, then he retracted it and said: the surety is not taken except if the debtor becomes bankrupt or disappears, because beginning with the one who owes the right is preferable, unless he is destitute, in which case it is taken from the surety, because he is excused in taking it in this situation. This is a good view. The analogy (qiyas) is that a man may demand from whichever of the two he wishes. Ibn Abi Layla said: if a man guarantees property on behalf of his companion, the obligation transfers to the surety and the original debtor is discharged, unless the creditor stipulates against both of them that he may take whichever he wishes. He argued by analogy to the discharge of the dead from debt, by the guarantee of Abu Qatada [[The hadith: Salamah ibn al-Akwa' narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) was brought a funeral bier and said: "Does he owe any debt?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Has he left anything?" They said: "No." He said: "Pray over your companion." Abu Qatada said: "Pray over him, O Messenger of God, and I take on his debt." So he prayed over him.]]. Abu Thawr said something similar.

The seventh issue: za'amah (suretyship/guarantee) is valid only in rights that may be undertaken by proxy, of the kind that are attached to the liability (dhimmah) in property, and that are established and firm. Therefore the hamalah (guarantee) is not valid for kitabah (a contract of manumission by installments), because it is not a firm and established debt, since if the slave is unable to pay he is returned to slavery and the contract of kitabah is dissolved. As for every right that no one can undertake on behalf of another, such as the hudud (prescribed punishments), there is no kafalah in it, and the accused in a hadd case is imprisoned until his case is examined. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad deviated, permitting kafalah in hudud and in qisas (retaliation), and said: if the one slandered or the claimant in qisas says, "My evidence is present," he may take a surety for three days. al-Tahawi argued for them with what Hamzah ibn 'Amr narrated from Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah and al-Ash'ath, that they ruled by kafalah of the person in the presence of the Companions.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verses 73–75:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "By Allah, you certainly know that we did not come to cause corruption in the land."﴾ It is related that they did not alight upon anyone with injustice, nor did they graze anyone's crops, and that they would place muzzles (al-akimmah) over the mouths of their camels so that they would not wreak havoc in people's crops. Then he said: (﴿And we were not thieves.﴾) It is related that they returned the merchandise (al-bidaah) that had been in their saddlebags. That is, whoever returns what he found, how could he be a thief?!

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "What then is its recompense, if you are liars?"﴾ The meaning: What is the recompense of the one who does it, if your lying becomes evident? So the brothers of Yusuf answered: (﴿Its recompense is: he in whose saddlebag it is found, he himself is its recompense.﴾) That is, he shall be enslaved and made a slave (yustaʿbad wa-yustaragg). "Fa-jaza'uhu" is the subject (mubtada'), and "man wujida fi rahlihi" is its predicate (khabar). The implied meaning: its recompense is the enslavement of the one in whose saddlebag it is found. Thus it is a metonymy (kinayah) for enslavement, and within the sentence there is a sense of emphasis, just as you say: "The recompense of the one who steals is amputation, so this is his recompense."

(﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.﴾) That is, thus do we act toward wrongdoers when they steal: that they be enslaved. This was from the religion and judgment of Ya'qub, peace be upon him. Their saying this is the saying of one who did not doubt himself, since they committed themselves to enslaving whoever was found in his saddlebag. The ruling for a thief among the people of Egypt was that he pay double the value of what he took; this was said by al-Hasan, al-Suddi and others.

Issue: It has already been mentioned in Surah al-Ma'idah [[See vol. 6, p. 162.]] that the amputation for theft abrogates (nasikh) what preceded it of the laws, or what was in the law of Ya'qub regarding the enslavement of the thief. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 76:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So he began with their bags before the bag of his brother﴾. Yusuf only began with their saddlebags to dispel accusation and suspicion from their hearts, lest he begin with his brother's bag. The word "wi'a'" (bag, container) is said with a damma or a kasra on the waw; both are dialectal forms. It is that in which goods are kept and protected.

(Then he extracted it from his brother's bag) meaning Binyamin. That is, he extracted the drinking-cup, or the sawa' (the royal measuring vessel), according to those who use the feminine form. And He said: ﴿And for him who brings it﴾ [Yusuf: 72], so He used the masculine. When his brothers saw that, they hung their heads, entertained every kind of suspicion, turned towards him and said: "Woe to you, O Binyamin! We have never seen the like of today. Your mother Rahil bore two thieving brothers!" Their brother said to them: "By God, I did not steal it, and I have no knowledge of who placed it in my belongings." It is related that they said to him: "O Binyamin! Did you steal?" He said: "No, by God." They said: "Then who put the cup in your saddlebag?" He said: "The one who put the merchandise in your saddlebags." It is said that whenever the searcher finished with a saddlebag, he asked God, mighty and majestic, for forgiveness, repenting of his action. The apparent sense of the words of Qatadah and others is that the one who asked forgiveness was Yusuf, because he was searching them and knew where the cup was, until he finished with them and reached Binyamin's saddlebag. He said: "I do not think this youth agreed to this, nor did he take anything." His brothers said to him: "By God, we will not leave until you search him, for that will be better for your soul and ours." So he searched, and brought out the drinking-cup. This searching by Yusuf implies that the crier had devised the theft by his own opinion. It is said that all of this was a command from God, most high, and what strengthens this is His saying: ﴿Thus did We contrive for Yusuf﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus did We contrive for Yusuf﴾. In this there are three issues.

The first: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿kidna﴾ means "We did," according to Ibn Abbas. Al-Qutabi said: "We devised." Ibn al-Anbari said: "We intended," as the poet said:

"Kadat wa kidtu wa tilka khayru irada... law 'ada min 'ahd al-sibba ma madda"

In this there is the permissibility of reaching objectives through stratagems, provided they do not contravene the Sharia and do not demolish a fundamental principle; this differs from Abu Hanifa, who permitted stratagems even when they contravene the fundamentals and nullify the legal purpose (tahlil).

The second: The scholars agree that before the year has elapsed a man may dispose of his property by sale or gift, provided he does not intend to flee from zakat. They agree that when the year has passed and the collector has come, it is not permissible for him to employ trickery, nor to reduce, nor to separate what is joined, nor to join what is separate. Malik said: if a man disposes of some of his property, intending thereby to flee from zakat a month or so before the year, zakat becomes binding on him when the year is complete, taking as evidence his saying, peace be upon him: "for fear of the zakat." Abu Hanifa said: if he intends by separating it to flee from zakat a day before the year, it does not harm him, because zakat is only obligatory on completion of the year, and the meaning of his saying "for fear of the zakat" only applies then. Ibn al-Arabi said: I heard Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Walid al-Fihri and others say: our shaykh, the chief judge Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Ali al-Damaghani, possessed tens of thousands [of dinars] of wealth. When the year's end came, he would summon his sons and say to them: "My age has grown great and my strength has weakened, and this is wealth I do not need, so it is yours." Then he would bring it out, and men would carry it on their necks to the houses of his sons. When the year's end came again and he summoned his sons for some matter, they would say: "O father! We only hoped for your life. As for the wealth, we have no desire for it while you are alive; you and your wealth are ours, so take it back to yourself." The men would walk with it until they placed it before him, and he would return it to its place. He intended by changing ownership to drop zakat, according to Abu Hanifa's opinion on separating what is joined and joining what is separate. This is a grave matter. Al-Bukhari, may Allah be pleased with him, composed in his Jami' a book on this subject and said: "Kitab al-Hiyal" (The Book of Stratagems).

I say: He included in it chapters, among them: "Chapter on zakat, and that what is joined is not separated nor what is separate joined, for fear of the zakat." He included the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, that Abu Bakr wrote to him the obligation of zakat, and the hadith of Talhah ibn Ubayd Allah that a Bedouin came to the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, with dishevelled hair, the hadith, and at its end: "He succeeds if he is truthful," or "He enters Paradise if he is truthful." Some people said: for every twenty and one hundred camels there are two hiqqas; if he destroys them intentionally, or gives them away, or resorts to a stratagem concerning them to flee from zakat, there is nothing upon him. Then he followed with the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, said: "The treasure of one of you on the Day of Resurrection will be a bald venomous snake with two black spots, and it will say: I am your treasure," the hadith. Al-Muhallab said: al-Bukhari only intended in this chapter to make you aware that every stratagem by which anyone tricks to drop zakat, the sin of that is upon him, because the Prophet, ﷺ, when he forbade joining and separating the flocks for fear of zakat, this meaning was understood from it. And it is understood from his saying "He succeeds if he is truthful" that whoever seeks to nullify any of God's obligations by a trick he devises, he will not succeed, and his excuse will not avail him before God. What the jurists permitted of the owner's disposal of his property near the end of the year is only what he does not intend thereby to flee from zakat. Whoever intends that, the sin for it is not removed, and God is his reckoner. This is like one who flees from fasting Ramadan a day before the sighting of the crescent and undertakes a journey he has no need of, out of aversion to God's obligation which He prescribed upon the believers; the threat is directed at him. Do you not see the punishment of one who withholds zakat on the Day of Resurrection, by whatever means he withholds it deliberately: how camels trample him, and his wealth is represented to him as a bald venomous snake? This shows that fleeing from zakat is not permissible, and he will be held to account for it in the Hereafter.

The third: Ibn al-Arabi said: some scholars of the Shafi'is said regarding His saying, may He be exalted: "Thus did We contrive for Yusuf; he could not take his brother," that it is evidence for the way of stratagem toward what is permissible and for extracting rights. This is a great error. And His saying, may He be exalted: "Thus We established Yusuf in the land," it has been said regarding it: just as We secured for Yusuf the sovereignty of his own self from the wife of al-Aziz, We secured for him sovereignty over the land from al-Aziz, or something similar that does not resemble what he mentioned. Al-Shafi'i said: similar to it is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle of grass and strike with it, and do not break your oath﴾ [Sad: 44]. This is not a stratagem; rather it is the carrying of the oath according to its wording or its intentions. Al-Shafi'i said: similar to it is the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri concerning the governor of Khaybar, that he came to the Prophet, ﷺ, with Janib dates, the hadith. The Shafi'is' aim from this hadith is that he, peace be upon him, instructed him to sell the mixed dates (jam') and buy Janib from the one to whom he sold the jam' or from another. The Malikis said: its meaning is "from another," lest it be Janib exchanged for jam', and silver dirhams are usury, as Ibn Abbas said: "Hariri for hariri, and the dirhams are usury."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿in the religion of the king﴾, that is, his sultan, according to Ibn Abbas. Ibn Isa: his customs, that is, he would be wronged without proof. Mujahid: in his judgment, which is the enslavement of thieves.

(Except that God wills) that is, except by God's willing that He make the drinking-cup in his saddlebag a pretext and an excuse for him. Qatadah said: rather, the king's judgment was beating and fining double, but God willed to make the judgment of the Children of Israel run on their tongues, as mentioned earlier.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We raise in degrees whom We will﴾, that is, through knowledge and faith. It is also read "narfa'u darajatin man nashau," meaning: We raise whom We will in degrees; this has passed in "al-An'am." And His saying: ﴿And over every possessor of knowledge is one who knows﴾. Israel related from Simak from Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas, who said: "There is one more knowing than this one, and one more knowing than that one, and God is above every knower." Sufyan related from Abd al-A'la from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: "We were with Ibn Abbas, may Allah have mercy on him, and he related a hadith, and a man marvelled at it and said: 'Glory be to God! And over every possessor of knowledge is one who knows!' Ibn Abbas said: 'Evil is what you said; God is the All-Knowing, and He is above every knower.'"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 77–79:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: "If he steals, a brother of his had stolen before."﴾ The meaning: that is, he followed his brother's example. Had he followed us, he would not have stolen. They only said this to disassociate themselves from his act, since he was not of their mother, and to say that if he stole, the lineage of his thieving brother had pulled him in, for sharing in ancestry resembles sharing in character. The scholars differed concerning the theft that they attributed to Yusuf. It is narrated from Mujahid and others that Yusuf's paternal aunt, the daughter of Ishaq, was older than Ya'qub, and the girdle (minṭaqah) of Ishaq had come into her possession because of her seniority, for they used to inherit by seniority. This ruling has been abrogated in our law, and whoever stole would be enslaved. Yusuf's aunt had nursed him and loved him intensely. When he grew up and reached youth, Ya'qub said to her: "Hand Yusuf over to me, for I cannot bear for him to be absent from me even for an hour." She was attached to him and feared separation from him, so she said to him: "Leave him with me for some days, that I may look at him." When Ya'qub had left her, she took the girdle of Ishaq and bound it on Yusuf under his garments. Then she said: "I have lost the girdle of Ishaq; search for whoever took it and whoever has it." They searched, then she said: "Examine the household," and they examined, and it was found with Yusuf. She said: "Indeed, by God, he is my bondsman; I may do with him as I wish." Then Ya'qub came to her and she informed him of the matter. He said to her: "It is up to you; if he did that, then he is your bondsman." So she kept him until she died. It was for this that his brothers reproached him in their saying: "If he steals, a brother of his had stolen before." From here Yusuf learned to place the drinking-cup in his brother's baggage, just as his aunt had done. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "She only ordered him to steal an idol that belonged to his maternal grandfather, so he stole it, broke it, and threw it on the road, and that was from them both a changing of the wrong. Therefore they accused him of theft and reproached him with it." Qatadah said likewise. In the Book of al-Zajjaj it is stated that it was a golden idol. 'Atiyyah al-'Awfi said: "He was with his brothers at a meal, and he looked at an 'irq [[al-'irq (with fatha) here means a piece of cooked meat.]] and hid it, and they reproached him for that." It was also said: "He used to steal food from the table for the needy," related by Ibn 'Isa. It was also said: "They lied about him in what they attributed to him," said by al-Hasan.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So Yusuf kept it secret within himself and did not reveal it to them.﴾ That is, he kept secret within himself their saying: "If he steals, a brother of his had stolen before." This was said by Ibn Shajarah and Ibn 'Isa. It was also said: he kept secret within himself their saying: "You are worse in position," then he spoke aloud: "And God knows best what you describe."

[Said by Ibn 'Abbas, meaning: you are worse in position than the one you attributed to this theft. The meaning of his saying "And God knows best what you describe" [[from ʿ.]] is: God knows that what you say is a lie, even if it pleases God.] It has been said that Yusuf's brothers at that time were not prophets.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: "O 'Aziz, indeed he has a father, an aged old man, so take one of us in his place."﴾ They addressed him with the title al-'Aziz, since at that moment he was in office, the former one [[that is Qitfir.]] having been dismissed or dead. Their saying "indeed he has a father, an aged old man," means great in standing, and they did not mean advanced in years, since that is known of an old man. "So take one of us in his place" means a slave in his stead. It has been said that this is figurative, for they knew it was not valid to take a free man to be enslaved in place of one whose enslavement the custom among them had firmly established. Rather, it is like when you say to one whose action you dislike: "Kill me and do not do such-and-such," while you do not want him to kill you, but you are exaggerating in seeking his concession. It is possible that their saying "so take one of us in his place" was literal, but it is unlikely of them, being prophets [[It has already passed that they are not prophets according to the sound view.]], that they would accept the enslavement of a free man. So nothing remains but that they meant by this the way of surety (ḥamālah), that is, take one of us in his place until your companion returns to you. Their aim in this was that Binyamin would reach his father and Ya'qub would know the clear truth of the matter. But Yusuf, peace be upon him, prevented this, since surety (ḥamālah) in the hudud and the like, in the sense of producing the guaranteed person only, is permissible by mutual consent, and is not binding if the claimant refuses. As for surety in such a matter, on condition that the surety bear what the guaranteed person would have borne of punishment, that is not permitted by consensus. In al-Wadihah it is stated that surety for the face only in all the hudud is permissible, except for life. The majority of jurists hold that suretyship for the person is permissible. It has been differed on from al-Shafi'i: at one time he weakened it, and at another time he permitted it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed we see you as among the doers of good.﴾ This may mean they described him by what they saw of his good conduct toward them in all his actions. It may also mean: indeed we see for you a favour upon us in this matter, if you bestow it upon us. This is the interpretation of Ibn Ishaq.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "God forbid."﴾ It is a verbal noun (maṣdar).

(an na'khudha) is in a position of accusative, that is, from taking.

(illa man wajadna) is in a position of accusative governed by "na'khudha."

(mata'ana 'indahu) means: God forbid that we take the innocent for the guilty and contravene what we have contracted upon.

(inna idhan la-zalimun) means: that we take another.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So Yusuf kept it secret within himself and did not reveal it to them.﴾ That is, he kept secret within himself their saying: "If he steals, a brother of his had stolen before." This was said by Ibn Shajarah and Ibn 'Isa. It was also said: he kept secret within himself their saying: "You are worse in position," then he spoke aloud: "And God knows best what you describe."

[Said by Ibn 'Abbas, meaning: you are worse in position than the one you attributed to this theft. The meaning of his saying "And God knows best what you describe" [[from ʿ.]] is: God knows that what you say is a lie, even if it pleases God.] It has been said that Yusuf's brothers at that time were not prophets.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: "O 'Aziz, indeed he has a father, an aged old man, so take one of us in his place."﴾ They addressed him with the title al-'Aziz, since at that moment he was in office, the former one [[that is Qitfir.]] having been dismissed or dead. Their saying "indeed he has a father, an aged old man," means great in standing, and they did not mean advanced in years, since that is known of an old man. "So take one of us in his place" means a slave in his stead. It has been said that this is figurative, for they knew it was not valid to take a free man to be enslaved in place of one whose enslavement the custom among them had firmly established. Rather, it is like when you say to one whose action you dislike: "Kill me and do not do such-and-such," while you do not want him to kill you, but you are exaggerating in seeking his concession. It is possible that their saying "so take one of us in his place" was literal, but it is unlikely of them, being prophets [[It has already passed that they are not prophets according to the sound view.]], that they would accept the enslavement of a free man. So nothing remains but that they meant by this the way of surety (ḥamālah), that is, take one of us in his place until your companion returns to you. Their aim in this was that Binyamin would reach his father and Ya'qub would know the clear truth of the matter. But Yusuf, peace be upon him, prevented this, since surety (ḥamālah) in the hudud and the like, in the sense of producing the guaranteed person only, is permissible by mutual consent, and is not binding if the claimant refuses. As for surety in such a matter, on condition that the surety bear what the guaranteed person would have borne of punishment, that is not permitted by consensus. In al-Wadihah it is stated that surety for the face only in all the hudud is permissible, except for life. The majority of jurists hold that suretyship for the person is permissible. It has been differed on from al-Shafi'i: at one time he weakened it, and at another time he permitted it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed we see you as among the doers of good.﴾ This may mean they described him by what they saw of his good conduct toward them in all his actions. It may also mean: indeed we see for you a favour upon us in this matter, if you bestow it upon us. This is the interpretation of Ibn Ishaq.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "God forbid."﴾ It is a verbal noun (maṣdar).

(an na'khudha) is in a position of accusative, that is, from taking.

(illa man wajadna) is in a position of accusative governed by "na'khudha."

(mata'ana 'indahu) means: God forbid that we take the innocent for the guilty and contravene what we have contracted upon.

(inna idhan la-zalimun) means: that we take another.

The scholars differed concerning the theft that they attributed to Yusuf. This ruling has been abrogated in our law, and whoever stole would be enslaved. Yusuf's aunt had nursed him and loved him intensely. When he grew up and reached youth, Ya'qub said to her: "Hand Yusuf over to me, for I cannot bear for him to be absent from me even for an hour." She was attached to him and feared separation from him, so she said to him: "Leave him with me for some days, that I may look at him." When Ya'qub had left her, she took the girdle of Ishaq and bound it on Yusuf under his garments. Then she said: "I have lost the girdle of Ishaq; search for whoever took it and whoever has it."
