**The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 80:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When they despaired of him﴾, meaning they despaired, like ʿajiba and istaʿjaba (both mean "he wondered"), and sakhira and istaskhara (both mean "he mocked").

(*Khalaṣū*) means they withdrew, being apart, and he was not with them.

(*Najiyyan*) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the pronoun in *khalaṣū*. It is singular but stands for a plural, as in this verse, and it may also refer to a single person, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and We brought him near in confidence﴾ [Maryam: 52]. [[See vol. 11, p. 113.]] Its plural is *anjiyah*. The poet said:

*Indeed, when the people became confidants (anjiyah),*
*and the people were shaken like the buckets' ropes (al-arshiyah),*
*then, there, advise me, and do not advise Biyah.*

[[This is Suhaym ibn Wathil al-Yarbuʿi, describing a people whom travel and journeying had exhausted. They lay down beside their mounts and tossed about on them, and some of them clung to their camels for fear of falling. It is said that he gave it as an example of a grave matter arising. *Al-arshiyah* are the ropes used for drawing water. The point is that he was steady of heart. *"Awṣīnī wa-lā tuwṣī"* is written with the *yāʾ* because he is addressing a feminine listener.]]

Ibn Kathir recited *"istā'asū"*, *"wa-lā tā'asū"*, *"innahu lā yā'as"* and *"afa-lam yā'as"* with an *alif* and without a hamzah, by way of metathesis (*qalb*): the hamzah was moved forward and the *yāʾ* was moved back, and then the hamzah was changed into an *alif* because it was quiescent and preceded by a *fatḥah*. The established reading is the reading of the majority, because the verbal noun (maṣdar) only comes with the *yāʾ* first, as in *yaʾsan*. *Al-īyās* is not the verbal noun of *ayisa*. Rather, it is the verbal noun of *asta-hu awsan wa-īyāsan*, meaning "I gave him." Some said that *ayisa* and *yaisa* are two dialects, meaning: when they despaired of the return of their brother to them, they consulted among themselves, without anyone else from the people mixing with them, conferring privately about what had befallen them. *Al-najiyy* is on the pattern *faʿīl* in the sense of *munājī* (one who confers privately).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The eldest of them said﴾. Qatadah said: he was Rubil, who was the oldest of them in age. Mujahid said: he was Shamʿun, who was the oldest of them in judgment. Al-Kalbi said: Yahudha (Judah), who was the most intelligent of them. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb and Ibn Ishaq said: he was Lawi, and he was the father of the prophets.

(*Did you not know that your father has taken from you a solemn covenant (mawthiqan) in the name of God*) means a pledge from God to guard his son and return him to him.

(*And before this, you neglected Yusuf*): *"fa-lammā"* is in the accusative position, coordinated with *"anna"* (that). The meaning is: Did you not know that your father has taken from you a solemn covenant from God, and know your neglect concerning Yusuf? This was mentioned by al-Nahhas and others. The *"min"* in His saying *"wa-min qablu"* is attached to *"taʿlamū"* (you know). It is also permissible that *"fa-lammā"* be superfluous, so that the two adverbial phrases, *"min qablu"* and *"fī Yūsuf"*, are attached to the verb *"farraṭtum"* (you neglected). It is also permissible that *"fa-lammā"* together with the verb form a verbal noun, with *"min qablu"* attached to a hidden verb, the sense being: your neglect concerning Yusuf took place before this. Thus *"mā"* and the verb are in the nominative position as the subject, and the predicate is the hidden verb to which *"min qablu"* is attached.

(*So I will never leave the land*) [[In ى: i.e., from the land.]] means I will remain in it and will not leave, staying there. It is said: *baraḥa barāḥan wa-burūḥan*, meaning he departed. When negation enters, it becomes affirmative.

(*Until my father gives me leave*) to return, for I am ashamed before him.

(*Or God decides for me*) regarding passage with my brother, so that I may go with him to my father. It was also said: the meaning is, *"or God decides for me by the sword,"* so that I fight and take my brother, or I am unable and withdraw with an excuse. This is because Jacob had said: ﴿You must bring him back to me, unless you are encompassed (by misfortune)﴾ [Yusuf: 66]. Whoever fights and is unable is indeed encompassed by it.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: when Yahudha became angry and took up the sword, no hundred thousand could turn his face away; the hair on his chest would stand up like needles, and it would pierce through his garments. It is reported in a narration that Yahudha said to his brothers, and he was the most fiercely angry of them: "Either you hold off the king and whoever is with him, and I will hold off the people of Egypt for you, or you hold off the people of Egypt for me, and I will hold off the king and whoever is with him for you." They said: "Rather, you hold off the king and whoever is with him, and we will hold off the people of Egypt for you." So he sent one of his brothers, and they counted the markets of Egypt and found nine markets in it. Each one of them took a market. Then Yahudha entered upon Yusuf and said: "O king! If you do not release our brother to us, I will certainly let out a cry that will leave no pregnant woman in your city without making her miscarry what is in her womb." This was specific to them when they were angry. Yusuf provoked him and said a word to him, so Yahudha became angry and his anger intensified, and his hair bristled out. Likewise, each one of the sons of Jacob, when he became angry, his skin would prickle and his body would swell, and the hairs of his back would appear from under his garment, until from every hair a drop of blood would drip. When he struck the earth with his foot, it would shake and the buildings would collapse. If he shouted a cry, no pregnant woman or animal or bird that heard it would fail to give birth to what was in its womb, complete or incomplete. His anger would not subside except by his shedding blood, or by a hand from the offspring of Jacob seizing him. When Yusuf knew that his brother Yahudha's anger had become complete and perfect, he spoke to a young son of his in Coptic and ordered him to place his hand between the shoulders of Yahudha from where he could not see him. He did so, and his anger subsided and he dropped the sword. He turned right and left, perhaps he would see one of his brothers, but he did not see him. He went out hastily to his brothers and said: "Has any of you been present with me?" They said: "No!" He said: "Then where has Shamʿun gone?" They said: "He went to the mountain." So he went out and met him, and he was carrying a huge rock. He said: "What are you doing with this?" He said: "I am going to the market which fell to my share, to smash the heads of everyone in it with it." He said: "Go back and return it, or throw it into the sea, and do not speak a word. By Him who took Abraham as a close friend! A hand from the offspring of Jacob has touched me."

Then they entered upon Yusuf, and Yusuf was the most forceful of them. He said: "O company of the Hebrews! Do you think that there is no one stronger than you?" Then he went to a huge stone from the millstones and kicked it with his foot, so that it was flung from behind the wall. (*Al-rakl* is striking with one foot, and he kicked it, *yarkuluhu*, as al-Jawhari said.) Then he seized Yahudha with one of his hands and threw him down on his side [[In ع وى: "on his side." In و: "on his jaw."]], and said: "Bring the blacksmiths; I will cut off their hands and feet and strike their necks." Then he climbed onto his throne and sat on his couch, and ordered his cup to be placed before him. Then he struck it with a tap, and its sound came out. He turned to them and said: "Do you know what it is saying?" They said: "No!" He said: "It says: there is no worry, nor grief, nor distress on the heart of my father about these men, except because of them." Then he struck it a second time and said: "It tells me that these men took a young brother of theirs, envied him, took him away from his father, and then destroyed him." They said: "O Governor! Cover for us, as God covered for you, and be gracious to us, as God was gracious to you." He struck it a third time and said: "It says: these men threw their young one into the well, then sold him as a slave for a paltry price, and they claimed to their father that the wolf had eaten him." Then he struck it a fourth time and said: "It tells me that you committed a sin eighty years ago, and you have not asked God's forgiveness for it, nor repented to Him." Then he struck it a fifth time and said: "It says: the brother whom they claimed was lost will not be gone for long before he returns and informs the people of what they did." Then he struck it a sixth time and said: "It says: If you were prophets, or sons of prophets, you would not have lied, nor disobeyed your father. I will make you an example for the worlds." Bring the blacksmiths; I will cut off their hands and feet. Then they humbled themselves, wept, and showed repentance, and said: "If only we had found our brother Yusuf while he was alive, we would surely be obedient to his hand, and dust that he would tread upon with his foot." When Yusuf saw this from his brothers, he wept and said to them: "Get out of my sight! I have let you go out of respect for your father. Were it not for him, I would have made you an example."

﴿Return to your father﴾. This was said by the one who said: "I will never leave this land."

(﴿O our father, indeed your son has stolen﴾). Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Abu Razin read: "indeed your son has been made to steal" (*suriqa*, with the *sin* vowelled with a *damma* and the *ra'* doubled and vowelled with a *kasra*, in the passive). Al-Nahhas said: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn 'Umar related to me, saying: Ibn Shadhan [[This is al-'Abbas ibn al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, as in *Ghayat al-Nihaya*.]] related to us, saying: Ahmad ibn Abi Surayj al-Baghdadi related to us, saying: I heard al-Kisa'i reading: "O our father, indeed your son has stolen" with the *sin* vowelled with a *damma* and the *ra'* doubled and vowelled with a *kasra*, in the passive form, meaning that he was attributed to theft and accused of it, like "I declared him a traitor" (*khawwantuhu*), "I declared him a sinner" (*fassaqtuhu*), and "I declared him guilty" (*jarartuhu*) when you attribute these qualities to him. Al-Zajjaj said: *saraqa* (he stole) may have two meanings: one, that he was known for theft; the other, that he was accused of theft. Al-Jawhari said: *al-sariq* and *al-sariqa* (with a *kasra* on the *ra'* in both) denote the stolen object itself, while the verbal noun is *sariq* (*saraqan*, with a *fatha*).

﴿And we did not testify except to what we knew﴾. In this there are four issues.

The first: His saying: ﴿And we did not testify except to what we knew﴾. They mean: we have never testified except to what we knew. As for now, we have testified based on outward appearance, and we do not know the unseen. It seems they had come under suspicion because of Benjamin's words: "Someone has placed this in my bag; whoever placed your merchandise in your bags..." This was said by Ibn Ishaq. It is also said that the meaning is: we did not testify before Joseph that the thief is enslaved except to what we knew of your religion. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

﴿And we were not guardians of the unseen﴾. That is, we did not know at the time we took him from you that he would steal, so we would not have taken him. Mujahid and Qatadah said: "We did not know that your son would be enslaved and that our affair would come to this. We only said that we would guard our brother as far as we are able." Ibn 'Abbas said: They mean that he stole at night while they were asleep, and *al-ghayb* (the unseen) means "night" in the dialect of Himyar. It is also reported from him: "We did not know what he did during his night and day, nor his going and coming." It is also said: As long as he was in our sight, no fault could occur; but when he went out of our sight, his circumstances were hidden from us. It is also said that the meaning is: the theft was taken from his baggage, and we brought it out and looked at it, but we have no knowledge of the unseen, so perhaps they stole it and he did not steal.

The second: This verse includes the permissibility of testimony by whatever means knowledge of the matter is obtained, for testimony is bound to knowledge both rationally and legally. Therefore it is not heard except from one who has knowledge, and it is not accepted except from such a person. This is the basic principle regarding testimonies. For this reason our companions [the Malikis] said: the testimony of a blind person is permissible; the testimony of one who overhears is permissible; the testimony of a mute person is permissible if his gesture is understood; and likewise testimony based on handwriting, when one is certain that it is his handwriting or the handwriting of so-and-so, is valid. So whoever acquires knowledge of something may testify to it, even if the one against whom it is testified did not call him as a witness. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Except those who bear witness to the truth while they know﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 86]. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of the best of witnesses? The best of witnesses is the one who brings his testimony before being asked for it." This has already been discussed in *al-Baqara* [[See vol. 3, p. 399.]].

The third: Malik's view differed concerning *shahadat al-murur* (testimony of passing by), which is when a person says: "I passed by so-and-so and heard him say such-and-such." If he has fully grasped the statement, he testifies according to one of his two opinions; according to the other opinion, he does not testify until the one who heard it has made him a witness to it. The correct view is that the testimony is delivered when the statement has been fully grasped. This is the view of the majority of scholars, and it is the truth, because the required objective has been achieved and it becomes obligatory on him to convey the knowledge. So he is the best of witnesses if he informs the one for whom testimony is given, and the worst of witnesses if he conceals it. [And Allah knows best.] [[From manuscripts K and Waw.]]

The fourth: If a man claims a testimony that his lifetime could not contain, it is rejected, because he has claimed something false, and the evident reality refutes him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 82:

There are two issues in this.

The first: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Ask the town in which we were, and the caravan in which we came﴾. By this they sought to establish their testimony before him and to remove suspicion from themselves, lest he suspect them. So their saying ﴿Ask the town﴾ means ask its people, and the word is elided. By "the town" they mean Egypt. It is also said: a town from its villages where they stayed and from which they obtained provisions. It is also said that the meaning is: ﴿Ask the town﴾ even though it is inanimate, for you are a prophet of Allah, and Allah makes the inanimate speak to you. On this view there is no need for any elision. Sibawayh said: it is not permissible to say "Speak to Hind," meaning "the servant of Hind," because this is ambiguous. The discussion of "the caravan" is the same as the discussion of "the town" in every respect.

﴿And indeed we are truthful﴾ in what we say.

The second: In this verse there is a point of jurisprudence, namely that everyone who is upon the truth, and knows that he may be suspected of being other than what he is, or fears that he may be thought so, should remove from himself the accusation and every doubt, and should openly state the truth he holds, so that no one has any ground for speech against him. Our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) did exactly this when two men passed by him while he was coming out with Safiyyah, returning her from the mosque, and he said to them: "Slow down, for she is Safiyyah bint Huyayy." They said: "Glory be to Allah!" and it weighed heavily upon them. The Prophet said: "Indeed, Satan reaches into a person as the blood flows, and I feared that he might cast something into your hearts." Related by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

**First issue:** Concerning this verse there are two matters. The first is God's saying: ﴿Nay, but your souls have embellished a matter for you﴾, meaning they adorned it (for you).

(For you, your own selves [claimed] that my son stole, though he did not steal, and that this happened only because of a matter God wills.)

(﴿So patience is beautiful﴾), meaning: my condition is one of beautiful patience, or beautiful patience is more fitting for me, as was mentioned at the beginning of the surah.

**Second issue:** It is obligatory for every Muslim, when he is afflicted with something disliked in himself, his child, or his property, to meet it with beautiful patience (al-sabr al-jamil), contentment, and submission to the One who brings it upon him, who is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise. He should take as his example the Prophet of God, Ya'qub (Jacob)[[In manuscript ʿayn: "Ya'qub". In manuscript Ya: "Ayyub" (Job) instead of "Ya'qub". This is a scribal error.]], and all the other prophets, may the blessings of God be upon them all.

Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah related from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, who said: "There are no two draughts that a servant swallows more beloved to God than the draught of a calamity that a servant swallows with good patience and good consolation, and the draught of anger that a servant swallows with forbearance and pardon."

Ibn Jurayj related from Mujahid regarding God's saying ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾, that it means: "I will not complain of this to anyone."

Qatil ibn Sulayman related from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever complains (batha) does not have patience."

It has already been mentioned in (the commentary on) al-Baqarah[[See vol. 2, pp. 174–175.]] that patience is at the first moment of the blow, and that the reward is for one who mentions his calamity and says "Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un" (Indeed we belong to God and to Him we return), even if a long time has passed since it.

Juwaybir related from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Ya'qub was given, in exchange for Yusuf, the reward of a hundred martyrs. Likewise, whoever from this Ummah seeks God's reward in his calamity, he will have a reward like the reward of Ya'qub, peace be upon him."

God's saying ﴿It may be that God will bring them all to me﴾. He (Ya'qub) thought that Yusuf (ﷺ) had not died, but that news of him had only been cut off, because Yusuf had been carried away as a slave who owned nothing for himself. Then the king bought him, and he was in the king's house, not appearing to the people. Then he was imprisoned. When he gained power, he devised a way for his father to learn of his news, but he did not send a messenger, because he disliked that his brothers should know of it, lest they prevent the messenger from reaching him. He said "them all" (bihim) because they were three: Yusuf, his brother, and the one who stayed behind for the sake of his brother, who is the one who said: ﴿So I will not leave this land﴾.

(﴿Indeed He is the All-Knowing﴾), of my condition.

(﴿the All-Wise﴾), in what He decrees.

**Issue 1:** Concerning His words, exalted is He: ﴿And he turned away from them﴾, meaning he turned away from them. This happened because when news of Benjamin reached Ya'qub, his grief was complete and his distress reached its height, and God renewed his calamity over Yusuf. So he said, "Alas for Yusuf!" and forgot his son Benjamin, so he did not mention him. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Ya'qub did not have what is in our book of *istirja'* (saying "Indeed we belong to God and to Him we return"). Had he had it, he would not have said, "Alas for Yusuf!" Qatada and al-Hasan said: the meaning is "Woe is my grief!" [In the margin: "Wa huzna!"] Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: "Woe is my lamentation!" Kuthayyir said:

"Alas for the heart, how it turned away,
and for the soul, when it was consoled, it consoled itself."

*Al-asaf* is intense grief over what has passed. The address is as if to say: "Come, O grief, for this is one of your times." Al-Zajjaj said: the original form is *ya asafi*, and the *ya* was replaced by an *alif* for the lightness of the *fatha*.

﴿and his eyes turned white from grief﴾. It is said: he did not see with them for six years, and that he became blind, as Muqatil said. It is also said: the eye may turn white while some vision remains. God knows best the condition of Ya'qub. His eyes turned white from weeping, but the cause of weeping is grief, which is why He said "from grief." It is also said that Ya'qub was praying while Yusuf was sleeping in front of him, and he snored in his sleep. Ya'qub turned toward him, then he snored a second time and Ya'qub turned toward him, then he snored a third time and Ya'qub turned toward him, out of joy at him and at his snoring. So God, exalted is He, revealed to His angels: "Look at My chosen one and the son of My friend, standing in My private conversation, turning toward other than Me. By My might and My majesty! I will surely pluck out the two eyeballs with which he turned, and I will surely separate him from the one he turned toward for eighty years, so that those who act may know that whoever stands before Me must watch My gaze." This shows that turning in prayer, even if it does not invalidate the prayer, still brings punishment for it and a deficiency in it. Al-Bukhari related from 'A'isha, who said: I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about turning in prayer, and he said: "It is a snatching that Satan snatches from the prayer of the servant." What the scholars say on this will come later, in full, at the beginning of Surat al-Mu'minun, God willing.

**Issue 3:** Al-Nahhas said: If people ask about the meaning of the intensity of Ya'qub's grief (peace be upon him, and upon our Prophet), the scholars have three answers. Among them: when Ya'qub (peace be upon him) knew that Yusuf (peace be upon him) was alive, he feared for his religion, so his grief intensified because of that. It is also said that he grieved only because he had entrusted him to them while he was young, and so he regretted that. The third answer, which is the clearest of them, is that grief is not forbidden. What is forbidden is wailing, tearing garments, and speaking what is not fitting. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The eye weeps and the heart grieves, and we do not say what displeases the Lord." God, mighty and majestic, has explained this by His words: ﴿so he was *kazim*﴾, meaning *makzum*, filled with grief, holding it in and not revealing it. From this comes *kazm al-ghayz* (suppressing anger), which is concealing it. So the *makzum* is one whose path of grief is blocked. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿when he called out while he was *makzum*﴾ [al-Qalam: 48], meaning full of distress. [See vol. 18, p. 253.] It is also permissible for *makzum* to mean *kazim*, that is, one who contains his grief. From Ibn 'Abbas: *kazim* means *maghmum* (distressed). The poet said:

"If I am one who holds back over a great calamity,
then today my tongue is loosened."

Ibn Jurayj related from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: his eyes went away from grief, "so he was *kazim*," and he said: that means *makrub* (anguished). Muqatil ibn Sulayman related from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words, "so he was *kazim*": he said: that means *kamad* (inwardly consumed). He says: he knew that Yusuf was alive and that he did not know where he was, so he was consumed by that. Al-Jawhari said: *al-kamad* is hidden grief. One says of him: *kamida al-rajul*, so he is *kamad* and *kamid*. (Al-Nahhas.) It is said: so-and-so is *kazim* and *kazim*, that is, grieved and not complaining of his grief. The poet said:

"I urged my people on, and I counted their fighting as a reward from God,
while the people, from fear of death, were holding back (their grief)."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 85–86:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They said, "By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph"﴾. That is, his sons said to him: "By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph." Al-Kisa'i said: fata'u and fati'tu (taf'al), meaning "I have not ceased doing that" (ma ziltu). Al-Farra' claimed that "la" (not) is implied, meaning "la tafta'" (you will not cease), and he recited [[The verse is by Imru' al-Qays, and "yamin" may be read in the nominative as a subject with an implied predicate, the sense being "the oath of Allah binds me," or in the accusative with an implied verb, as is common in Arabic speech, as in their saying: amanatu Allah (I entrust to Allah). He describes that he embraced his beloved, so the watchers frightened her and urged him to depart, and so he said to her this, meaning: "I will not leave," and "la" was omitted. Al-awsal (sing. wasl) are the joints.]]:

"So I said: 'By the oath of Allah, I will not cease sitting, even if they cut off my head and my joints before you.'"

That is, "I will not cease." Al-Nahhas said: What al-Kisa'i said is sound and correct. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh claimed that "la" is implied in the oath, because there is no ambiguity in it; and if it were affirmative (wajiban), it would be with the lam and the nun (la-, in the emphatic form). They said to him [the phrase] because they knew with certainty that he would persist in that. It is said: ma zala yaf'alu kadha, and ma fati'a and fata'a; these are two dialects, and they are not used except with negation. The poet said [[He is Aws ibn Hajar al-Tamimi, a pre-Islamic poet.]]:

"Then I did not cease, until as if its dust were a canopy of a windy day that is raised."

That is, "I did not cease," so "tafta'" means "tabrah" (you will not leave). Ibn Abbas said: "tazal" (you will not cease).

(Until you become ḥaraḍan) that is, destroyed (ta'if). Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said: wasted by sickness (danifan min al-maraḍ), which is short of death. The poet said:

"My worry travelled by night and made me ill, and indeed it had already increased me in sickness.
Likewise love, before today, is what brings about greed."

Qatadah said: "old and decrepit." Al-Dahhak: "worn out and decayed." Muhammad ibn Ishaq: "corrupt, without reason." Al-Farra': "al-ḥāriḍ is one whose body and mind are corrupted; and so is al-ḥaraḍ." Ibn Zayd: "ḥaraḍ is one who has been returned to the lowest age." Al-Rabi' ibn Anas: "one whose skin is dry over the bone." Al-Mu'arrij: "melting from grief." Al-Akhfash: "gone." Ibn al-Anbari: "perishing." All of these are close in meaning. The root of ḥaraḍ is corruption in the body or the mind from sorrow, or love, or old age, according to Abu 'Ubayda and others. Al-'Araji said:

"I am a man whom love has seized, and it has wasted me, until I am worn out, and until illness has wasted me."

Al-Nahhas said: it is said ḥaraḍa, yaḥraḍu, ḥaraḍan; and ḥaruḍa, ḥurūḍan and ḥurūḍatan, when one wears out and falls ill. A man is ḥāriḍ and ḥaraḍ, except that ḥaraḍan is not dualised nor pluralised, and similarly qamin and ḥariyy are not dualised nor pluralised. Al-Tha'labi: Among the Arabs there are those who say ḥāriḍ for the masculine and ḥāriḍa for the feminine; when described with this word, it is dualised, pluralised and feminised. It is also said: ḥariḍa, yaḥraḍu, ḥarāḍatan, so he is ḥarīḍ and ḥaraḍ. It is also said: rajul muḥraḍ, and it is recited:

"The horses pursued him for a whole day, and had they reached him he would have become wasted."

Imru' al-Qays said:

"I see the man with many herds becoming wasted, like a young camel in the lands, sick."

[[al-Adhwad: plural of dhawd, a herd of camels from three to nine. Al-bakr: a young camel. He says: I see the man of wealth overtaken by old age and sickness, and then death; so the abundance of his wealth does not avail him, just as the young camel is overtaken by that.]]

Al-Nahhas said: the scholars of language have related "aḥraḍahu al-hamm" when worry makes him ill. Anas recited "ḥuraḍan" with a dammah on the ḥa' and a sukun on the ra', that is, like a stick of ushnan (a cleansing plant). Al-Hasan recited with a dammah on both the ḥa' and the ra'. Al-Jawhari said: al-ḥaraḍ and al-ḥuraḍ are ushnan.

(Or that you become of those who perish) that is, the dead, and this is the saying of all. Their aim was to prevent Ya'qub from weeping and grieving out of compassion for him, though they were the cause of that.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said: "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah"﴾.

The true meaning of bathth in the language is what befalls a person of destroying things which he cannot manage to conceal; it is from "bathathtuhu", meaning I scattered it. So calamity is called bathth metaphorically. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"I stood at the abode of Maya, my she-camel; I did not cease weeping there and addressing it,
and I gave it drink (asqīhi, I invoke for it rain), until its stones and its meadows nearly spoke to me of what I was pouring out."

Ibn Abbas said: "baththi" is "hammi" (my worry). Al-Hasan: "my need." It was said: the greatest of sorrow; and the true meaning is what we have mentioned.

﴿and my grief to Allah﴾ is coordinated with it; he repeated it without its wording.

﴿and I know from Allah what you do not know﴾, that is, I know that the dream of Joseph is true and that I shall prostrate to him. Said by Ibn Abbas. Qatadah: "I know from Allah's goodness to me what makes me think well of Him." It was also said: Ya'qub said to the Angel of Death, "Have you taken the soul of Joseph?" He said, "No," and this confirmed his hope. Al-Suddi said: "I know that Joseph is alive; for when his son informed him of the conduct of the king, his justice, his character and his words, Ya'qub's soul sensed that it was his son, and he became hopeful and said, 'Perhaps it is Joseph.'" [He said: there is no truthful one on earth except that he is a prophet. It was also said: I know from the answering of the prayers of the distressed what you do not know.]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 87:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O my sons, go and seek out news of Yusuf and his brother﴾. This indicates that he was certain of his (Yusuf's) being alive, either through a dream, or through God, exalted is He, making the wolf speak as in the beginning of the story, or through the Angel of Death informing him that he had not taken his soul; and this last is the most apparent. Al-tahassus (seeking out, searching) means seeking a thing through the senses, and it is a tafa''ul form from al-hiss (sense perception). That is: go to this one who asked you for your brother and tricked you into taking him, and ask about him and about his way (religion). It is related that the Angel of Death said to him: "Seek him from here!" and he pointed toward the direction of Egypt. It is also said that Ya'qub was alerted to Yusuf by the return of the merchandise and the detention of his brother and the showing of honour, and therefore he directed them toward the direction of Egypt rather than any other.

(And do not despair of the mercy of God) meaning: do not lose hope in the relief of God. This was said by Ibn Zayd, meaning: the believer hopes for God's relief, while the disbeliever despairs in hardship. Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: "of the mercy of God."

(Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of God except the disbelieving people) This is evidence that despair (al-qunut, i.e. al-ya's) is among the major sins, and its explanation will come in "al-Zumar" [[See vol. 15, p. 267.]], God willing.

God Most High says: ﴿So when they entered upon him, they said, "O ruler (al-'Aziz)!"﴾, that is, the one who is mighty (al-mumtani').

(﴿Adversity has touched us and our family﴾) This is the third time they returned to Egypt. The sentence contains an ellipsis: they set out for Egypt, and when they entered upon Yusuf they said, "Adversity (masshana)" meaning "has struck us," "and our family, adversity (al-durr)," meaning hunger and need. This is evidence that it is permissible to complain when suffering, meaning hunger. Indeed, it is obligatory for a person who fears for himself harm from poverty or other things to make his condition known to one from whom he hopes for benefit, just as it is obligatory for him to complain of his pain to the physician so that he may be treated. This does not detract from trust in God (tawakkul), so long as the complaint is not made in a spirit of discontent (tasakhkhut). Patience (sabr) and steadfastness (tajallud) in calamities are better, and abstaining from asking (ta'affuf 'an al-mas'alah) is more excellent. The best way to complain is to ask the Master (al-Mawla) to remove the affliction, and that is the statement of Ya'qub: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God, and I know from God what you do not know﴾ [Yusuf: 86], that is, of His beautiful handling, His subtle kindness, and His beneficence toward His servants. As for complaining to one who cannot relieve, that is folly, unless it is done as a outpouring of grief and a means of consolation, as Ibn Duraid said:

Do not think, O time, that I am humbled
by a misfortune that drenches me like the sweat of the mida (a camel's sweat)...

I have experienced such that, if the spheres
had fallen upon him from all sides of the air, he would not have complained.

But it is the sigh of one whose chest is burdened,
when the foam [[the froth that the camel throws from its mouth; ghamā: it fell; it is said: ghamā al-ba'īr when it shakes its head and its lip]] surges up from its sides and spills over.

God Most High says: ﴿And we have brought merchandise﴾. The bidā'ah (merchandise) is a portion of wealth intended for the purchase of something. It is said: abda'tu al-shay' and istab'adtuhu, meaning I made it merchandise. And in the proverb: "Like one who sends dates to Hajar" [[Hajar: a city in Bahrain]].

God Most High says: ﴿poor (muzjāh)﴾. It is an attribute of bidā'ah. Al-izjā' is driving with a push, and from it is God's statement: ﴿Have you not seen that God drives clouds﴾ [al-Nur: 43] [[see vol. 12, p. 287]]. The meaning is that it is merchandise that is pushed along and that not everyone would accept. Tha'lab said: "al-bidā'ah al-muzjāh" is that which is deficient, not complete. Scholars differed about its identity here. It was said that it was dried meat and hays [[so in the originals; and in al-Bahr: dried meat and wild...]], reported by al-Waqidi from Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him. It was said: worn-out sacks and ropes, reported from Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: the goods of the Bedouins, wool and ghee, said by Abdullah ibn al-Harith. It was said: the green seed (al-habbah al-khadra') and the terebinth (al-sanawbar), which is al-batm, the seed of a tree in al-Sham, from which oil is pressed for making soap, said by Abu Salih. They sold these for dirhams that were not current for food but were current among people. They said: "Take these from us, reckoned as good coins that are current for food." It was said: they were inferior dirhams, said also by Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: they did not bear the image of Yusuf, whereas the dirhams of Egypt bore the image of Yusuf. Al-Dahhak said: sandals and leather. And from him: it was roasted flour sifted. And God knows best.

God Most High says: (﴿So give us full measure and be charitable to us﴾). In this are four issues.

The first: God's statement, ﴿So give us full measure﴾. They mean: as you sell for good dirhams, do not shortchange us for the value of our dirhams. This is the view of most exegetes. Ibn Jurayj said: "give us full measure" means the measure that he had measured for their brother. "And be charitable to us" means: show favor to us by [giving us] the difference between the price of good and inferior [coins]. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi and al-Hasan, because charity is forbidden to prophets. It was said the meaning is: "be charitable to us" by giving more than our due, said by Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna. Mujahid said: charity was forbidden only to our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn Jurayj said: the meaning is "be charitable to us" by returning our brother to us. Ibn Shajarah said: "be charitable to us" means overlook for us, and he cited the verse of the poet:

Be charitable to us, O son of 'Affan, and count it as a deed of merit,
and appoint al-Ash'ari over us for a number of nights.

(﴿Indeed God rewards the charitable﴾) meaning in the Hereafter. It is said: this is one of the ma'arid (indirect expressions), because they did not hold that he was upon their religion, so they did not say, "God will reward you for your charity," but they spoke words that suggested that they meant it, while they could justify it by interpretation. This was said by al-Naqqash. And in a hadith: "Indeed, in indirect speech (al-ma'arid) there is a sufficient alternative to lying." [[al-ma'arid: plural of mi'rad, from ta'rid, which is the opposite of explicit speech.]]

The second: Malik and other scholars used this as evidence that the wage of the measurer (al-kayyal) is upon the seller. Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn Nafi' said: Malik said: They said to Yusuf, "So give us full measure," and it was Yusuf who measured. Likewise the weigher, the counter and others, because when a man sells a known quantity of his food and the contract obliges him, it is obligatory upon him to deliver it and to separate the buyer's right from his own, unless he sells him something specific, a heap (ṣubrah) [[the heap: food gathered like a mound]] or something that does not require measuring, and he lets him take possession of it; then whatever befalls the sold item is the buyer's. This does not apply to what requires measuring by volume or weight. Do you not see that the seller does not deserve the price except after delivery, and if it is destroyed before delivery, it is his loss?

The third: As for the wage of the money-changer (naqd), it is also upon the seller, because the buyer who hands over his dirhams says, "They are good," so it is you who claim they are inferior; look to your own interest. Also, the benefit accrues to him, so the fee falls upon him. Likewise, it is not obligatory upon the one against whom retaliation (qisas) is due, because it is not obligatory upon him to cut off his own hand, unless he submits to it willingly. Do you not see that it is incumbent on him to ransom his hand and to settle for it if the one seeking retaliation requests this from him? So the wage of the cutter is upon the one seeking retaliation. Al-Shafi'i, in the well-known report from him, said: it is upon the one who is to have the retaliation carried out against him, like the seller.

The fourth: It is disliked for a man to say in his supplication: "O God, be charitable to me," because charity is only given by one who seeks reward, whereas God Most High bestows reward out of His grace for all blessings, there is no lord other than Him. Al-Hasan heard a man saying, "O God, be charitable to me," and al-Hasan said: "O sir! God does not give charity; only one who seeks reward gives charity. Ibn ʿAbbas said: when he said to them, "Do you know what you did with Joseph," and so on, Joseph smiled — and when he smiled, his front teeth were like strung pearls — so they likened him to Joseph and said to him by way of question, "Are you indeed Joseph?" It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas that his brothers did not recognize him until he removed the crown from his head, and there was a mark on his forehead, and Jacob had a similar mark, a birthmark. When he said to them, "Do you know what you did with Joseph," he lifted the crown from himself, and they recognized him, and said, "Are you indeed Joseph?" Ibn ʿAbbas also said: Jacob wrote to him asking for the return of his son, and in the letter was: "From Jacob, the chosen one of God, son of Isaac, the sacrificed one of God, son of Abraham, the friend of God, to the Chief of Egypt. To proceed: we are a family of trials and tribulations. God tested my grandfather Abraham with Nimrod and his fire; then He tested my father Isaac with the sacrifice; then He tested me with a son who was the dearest of my children to me, until my sight was lost from weeping. I did not steal, and I did not give birth to a thief. Peace." When Joseph read the letter, his joints trembled, his skin shivered, he let his eyes weep, and his patience failed, so he revealed the secret. (He said, "I am Joseph") That is, I am the one who was wronged, and the intended meaning is his being killed. He did not say "I am he," to magnify the story.

(God has indeed favoured us) That is, with deliverance and sovereignty.

(Indeed, whoever fears God and is patient) That is, fears God and endures patiently against afflictions and against sins.

(then indeed God does not waste the reward of the good-doers) That is, those who are patient in His trial and who devote themselves to His obedience. Ibn Kathir read "innahu man yattaqi" with the yaʾ affirmed, and reading with it is permissible if "man" is taken to mean "the one who," and "yattaqi" enters into the relative clause, so the yaʾ is retained and "wa-yasbir" is in the nominative. It is also possible that "wa-yasbir" is in the jussive, taking "yattaqi" to be in a jussive position and "man" as a conditional particle, with the yaʾ retained, and the sign of the jussive being the elision of the damma that was on the yaʾ originally, as the poet said:

"Then call, when you enter Damascus, / O Yazid ibn Khalid ibn Yazid"

Another said:

"Has it not reached you, while news spreads, / what the she-camels of the Banu Ziyad suffered?"

The reading of the majority is clear, and the hāʾ in "innahu" refers to the matter (al-hadith), and the clause that follows is the predicate.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "By God, God has certainly preferred you over us"﴾ The original form has two hamzas, the second of which is softened, and it is not permissible to pronounce it fully. The active participle is mu'thir, and the verbal noun is ʾīthār. It is said: "I stirred up the dust (athartu al-turāb ithāratan), so I am muthir," and it is also on the pattern af'ala, then it was made defective, and the original is athyar [[So in the original and in Iʿrab al-Quran of al-Nahhas. (and indeed we were sinners) That is, we were guilty, from the verb khati'a yakhta'u, when one commits a sin. Implicit in this is a request for pardon. From the same root is his peace be upon him saying: "If the slave-girl of one of you commits fornication, let him flog her with the prescribed punishment and not reproach her," that is, not blame her. Al-Asmaʿi said: "I reproached him" and "ʿarrabtu ʿalayhi" have the same meaning, when I found his action ugly. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: there is no corruption of the bond of kinship and the right of brotherhood between me and you, and for you is my pardon and forgiveness. The root meaning of tathrib is corruption, and this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. (May God forgive you) is a future form carrying the sense of supplication; he asked God to cover them and have mercy upon them. So he carried it. Related by al-Suddi.

(and bring me all your family) so that you may make Egypt your home. Masruq said: they were ninety-three, between men and women. **Verse 94–99**

Allah's words: ﴿When the caravan departed﴾, meaning it set out from Egypt towards Syria. It is said *fasala fusulan* and *fasaltuhu faslan*, so the verb is both intransitive and transitive.

(Their father said) meaning he said to those of his relatives who were present but had not gone to Egypt, who were his grandchildren: (Indeed I smell the scent of Joseph). It is also possible that some of his sons had left, and he said to those who remained: "Indeed I smell the scent of Joseph, were it not that you think me senile."

Ibn Abbas said: a wind blew and carried the scent of Joseph's shirt to him, and the distance between them was a journey of eight nights. al-Hasan said: a journey of ten nights. He also reported: a journey of a month. Malik ibn Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the one who brought his scent is the one who brought the throne of Bilqis before Sulayman, peace be upon him, could blink. Mujahid said: a wind blew and *fasafaqati* the shirt (*safaqat al-rih al-shay'* and *safaqtuhu* means when the wind turns a thing right and left and returns it), so the fragrances of Paradise spread in this world and reached Ya'qub. He found the scent of Paradise and knew that there is nothing in this world of the scent of Paradise except what was in that shirt. At that point he said: "Indeed I find" (*wajad*), that is, I smell, so it is a finding by the sense of smell.

(Were it not that you think me senile): Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said: "were it not that you think me foolish." From this is the verse of al-Nabigha:

*Except Sulayman, when the King said to him:*
*"Stand among the people and restrain them from folly (al-fand)."*

That is, from foolishness. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: "were it not that you call me a liar." *Al-fand* is lying, and *afnada* means he lied. From this is the verse of the poet:

*Is there in the boasting of the noble any crookedness (awad)?*
*Or in the word of the truthful any falsehood (fand)?*

That is, any lie. It is also said: "were it not that you disparage me," said by Abu Amr. *Al-tafnid* is disparagement. The poet said:

*O my two companions, leave off blaming me and disparaging me;*
*what has passed of my affair cannot be returned.*

Ibn al-A'rabi said: "were it not that you weaken my opinion (tufannidun)," meaning were it not that you weaken my judgement. This was also said by Ibn Ishaq. *Al-fand* is weakness of judgement due to old age. A fourth view: "you mislead me" (tudallilun), said by Abu Ubaydah. al-Akhfash said: "you blame me" (talumunni); *al-tafnid* is blame and weakening of opinion. al-Hasan, Qatadah and Mujahid also said: "you make me senile" (tuharrimun). All these meanings are close, and they all return to incapacitation and weakening of opinion. It is said *fannadahu tafnidan* when he made him incapable, as the poet said:

*He destroyed me with blame and disparagement.*

It is also said *afnada* when one speaks in error. *Al-fand* is error in speech and in opinion, as al-Nabigha said: "...restrain them from folly (al-fand)." That is, prevent them from corruption of the intellect. From this it is said: blame is *tafnid*. The poet said:

*O my two blamers, leave off reproach and desist,*
*long has passion been, and you have multiplied disparagement.*

It is also said: *afnada* a man, meaning time corrupted him. From this is the verse of Ibn Muqbil:

*Leave time to do what it wills, for it,*
*when charged with corrupting people, corrupts.*

Allah's words: ﴿They said: "By Allah, you are surely in your old error."﴾ That is, you are surely in a loss of the right path. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd said: in your past error of loving Joseph, which you do not forget. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: in your old madness. al-Hasan said: this is disobedience to parents (uquq). Qatadah and Sufyan said: in your old love. It is also said that they only said this because they thought Joseph had died. It is also said that the one who said this to him was whoever remained with him of his sons and did not have news. It is also said that it was said to him by those of his family and relatives who were with him. It is also said: his grandchildren, who were young. Allah knows best.

Allah's words: ﴿Then when the bearer of good news came, he cast it over his face﴾, that is, over his eyes.

(And he regained his sight): "an" here is superfluous (za'ida). The bearer of good news is said to have been Shim'un. It is also said Yahudha. He said: "I will take the shirt today as I took it earlier stained with blood," said by Ibn Abbas. Allah's words: ﴿Then when the bearer of good news came, he cast it over his face﴾, that is, over his eyes.

(And he regained his sight): "an" here is superfluous (za'ida). The bearer of good news is said to have been Shim'un. It is also said Yahudha. He said: "I will take the shirt today as I took it earlier stained with blood," said by Ibn Abbas. From al-Suddi: he said to his brothers: "You know that I brought him the shirt of grief, so let me take him the shirt of joy." Yahya ibn Yaman reported from Sufyan: when the bearer of good news came to Ya'qub, he said to him: "On what religion did you leave Joseph?" He said: "On Islam." He said: "Now the blessing is complete." al-Hasan said: when the bearer of good news reached Ya'qub, he found nothing with him to reward him, so he said: "By Allah, we have nothing to give you, and we have not baked bread for seven nights, but may Allah make the agonies of death easy for you." I say: this supplication is among the greatest of rewards and the finest of gifts and treasures. This verse indicates the permissibility of giving and gifts upon good news. On this subject is the long hadith of Ka'b ibn Malik, in which: "When the one whose voice I heard bringing me good news came, I took off my two garments and gave them to him for his good news," and the hadith is mentioned in full. It has already been given in full in the story of the three who were left behind (see vol. 8, p. 282 onwards). Ka'b's giving of his two garments to the bearer of good news, although he had no others, is evidence for the permissibility of such conduct when one hopes for the attainment of what gives joy. It is also evidence for the permissibility of showing joy after grief and distress has passed. From this category is the permissibility of celebrating a child's completion of memorising the Qur'an (*hidhaq al-sibyan*, from *hadhaqa al-ghulam al-Qur'an*, meaning he excelled in it; in one manuscript: the permissibility of rejoicing at the completion of children's memorisation) and of feeding people on that occasion. Umar slaughtered a camel after memorising Surat al-Baqarah. Allah knows best.

Allah's words: ﴿He said: "Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?"﴾ He reminded them of his saying: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and grief to Allah, and I know from Allah what you do not know﴾ [Yusuf: 86].

Allah's words: ﴿They said: "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins; indeed we were sinners."﴾ There is an ellipsis in the speech; the estimate is: when they returned from Egypt, they said: "O our father." This indicates that the one who said to him "By Allah, you are surely in your old error" was his grandchildren or others of his relatives and family, not his sons, since they were absent, and that would have been an increase in disobedience. Allah knows best. They only asked him for forgiveness because they had inflicted on him the pain of grief, the sin of which would not be removed except by his pardoning them. I say: this ruling applies to anyone who harms a Muslim in his person, his property, or otherwise, wronging him. He is obliged to seek his pardon, inform him of the wrong and its extent. Is general pardon beneficial or not? There is disagreement on this. The correct view is that it is not beneficial, since if he informs him of a wrong of great weight it may be that the wronged person's soul will not be content to pardon it. Allah knows best. In Sahih al-Bukhari and others, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever has a wrong against his brother, in his honour or anything else, let him seek his pardon today, before there is no dinar or dirham. If he has good deeds, they will be taken from him in proportion to his wrong; and if he has no good deeds, the sins of his companion will be taken and laid upon him." al-Muhallab said: the words of the Prophet ﷺ, "it is taken from him in proportion to his wrong," require that the wrong be of known extent, specified and identified. Allah knows best.

Allah's words: ﴿He said: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you."﴾ Ibn Abbas said: he delayed his supplication until the last part of the night (*sahar*). al-Muthanna ibn al-Sabbah reported from Tawus: it was the last part of Friday night, which coincided with the night of Ashura. In the chapter on supplication for memorisation, from the book of al-Tirmidhi, from Ibn Abbas, who said: while we were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, came to him and said, "May my father and mother be your ransom, this Qur'an has slipped from my breast, and I find I am unable to retain it." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "Shall I not teach you words by which Allah will benefit you and benefit whomever you teach, and which will fix what you have learned in your breast?" He said: "Yes indeed, O Messenger of Allah! Teach me." He said: "When it is Friday night, if you can stand in prayer during the last third of the night, for it is a witnessed hour in which supplication is answered. My brother Ya'qub said to his sons: 'I will ask my Lord to forgive you,' meaning until the Friday night comes." And he mentioned the hadith. Ayyub ibn Abi Tamimah al-Sakhtiyani reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you" refers to the bright nights, the thirteenth, fourteenth and fifteenth, for supplication is answered in them. From Amir al-Sha'bi: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you," that is: I will ask Joseph; if he pardons you, I will ask my Lord to forgive you. Sunayd ibn Dawud mentioned: Hushaym told us, Abd al-Rahman ibn Ishaq told us, from Muharib ibn Dithar, from his paternal uncle, who said: I used to go to the mosque in the last part of the night, and I passed the house of Ibn Mas'ud and heard him saying: "O Allah, You commanded me and I obeyed, You called me and I answered; this is the last part of the night, so forgive me." I met Ibn Mas'ud and said: "I hear you saying words in the last part of the night." He said: "Ya'qub delayed his sons until the last part of the night by his saying: 'I will ask my Lord to forgive you.'"

Allah's words: ﴿When they entered upon Joseph﴾, that is, into a palace he had there.

(He drew his parents to him): It is said that Joseph sent with the bearer of good news two hundred riding beasts and provisions, and asked Ya'qub to bring him his family and children all together. When they entered upon him, he drew his parents to him, that is, he embraced them. By "his parents" he meant his father and his maternal aunt, for his mother had died at the birth of his brother Binyamin. It is also said that Allah restored his mother to life to fulfil the dream, so that she prostrated to him. This was said by al-Hasan. It has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah that Allah restored to life for His Prophet, peace be upon him, his father and mother, and they believed in him.

Allah's words: ﴿Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, in safety﴾. Ibn Juraij said: that is, "I will ask my Lord to forgive you, if Allah wills." He said: this is an instance of the Qur'an placing words before or after their proper order. al-Nahhas said: Ibn Juraij holds that they had already entered Egypt, so how could he say "Enter Egypt, if Allah wills"? It is also said that he only said "if Allah wills" for blessing and to express certainty. "In safety" means safe from famine, or from Pharaoh, for they could not enter it except with his permission.

**Qur'an 12:100: "And he raised his parents upon the throne."** Qatadah said: "He means the couch." Its meanings have already been discussed. The word "throne" (ʿarsh) is sometimes used to mean kingship itself, or the king himself. From this is the verse of al-Nabighah al-Dhubyani:

*"Thrones, they perished after might and security."*

This has already been mentioned [see vol. 7, p. 220].

**Qur'an 12:100: "And they fell down before him in prostration."** There are three issues.

**First issue:** The pronoun in "fell down before him" (*lahu*) has been said to refer to God Most High, meaning: "They fell down in prostration in thanks to God, with Yusuf as a qiblah (direction of prayer) to fulfil his dream." This is reported from al-Hasan. Al-Naqqash said: "This is wrong. The pronoun refers to Yusuf, based on the Qur'an's words at the beginning of the surah: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf 12:4]." It was their custom for the lowly to prostrate to the noble, and the young to the old. Ya'qub, his maternal aunt and his brothers prostrated to Yusuf, peace be upon him. Then his skin shivered and he said: ﴿This is the interpretation of my dream from before﴾. There were twenty-two years between Yusuf's dream and its interpretation.

Salman al-Farisi and Abdullah ibn Shaddad said it was forty years. Abdullah ibn Shaddad added: "That is the longest a dream has ever been delayed." Qatadah said thirty-five years. Al-Suddi, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrimah said thirty-six years. Al-Hasan, Jisr ibn Farqad and Fudayl ibn ʿIyad said eighty years.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Yusuf was thrown into the well when he was seventeen years old, and he was away from his father for eighty years. He lived for twenty-three years after he met his father, and he died at the age of one hundred and twenty. In the Torah it is one hundred and twenty-six years. Yusuf had children by the wife of the Aziz: Ephraim, Manasseh, and Rahmah, who was the wife of Ayyub. Between Yusuf and Musa there were four hundred years.

It has been said that Ya'qub remained with Yusuf for twenty years, then he died, peace be upon him. It has also been said that he stayed with him for eighteen years. Some of the narrators said forty-some years. Between Ya'qub and Yusuf there were thirty-three years until God gathered them together. Ibn Ishaq said eighteen years. God knows best.

**Second issue:** Sa'id ibn Jubayr reported from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, concerning the words ﴿and they fell down before him in prostration﴾, that he said: "It was not prostration. It was a custom among them, and they would bow their heads in a gesture. That was their greeting."

Al-Thawri, al-Dahhak and others said: "It was prostration like the prostration we know. It was their greeting." It has also been said that it was a bowing like the ruku' (bowing in prayer), not falling to the ground. Their greeting was also by bowing and leaning. God has abrogated all of this (naskh, abrogation) in our law and made speech a replacement for bowing.

The exegetes agree that this prostration, in whatever form it was, was a greeting and not worship. Qatadah said: "This was the greeting of kings among them, and God gave this nation the greeting of the people of Paradise, which is peace (salam)."

I say: This bowing and leaning, which was abrogated for us, has become a custom in Egypt and among the non-Arabs (ʿajam). So too is the standing of some people for others. If one of them is not stood for, he feels in himself as if he is not esteemed and has no status. Likewise, when they meet, some bow to others. This is a continuous custom and an established inheritance, especially when rulers and leaders meet. They have turned away from the Sunnahs and have shunned the Sunnahs.

Anas ibn Malik reported: We said: "O Messenger of God, should some of us bow to others when we meet?" He said: "No." We said: "Should some of us embrace others?" He said: "No." We said: "Should some of us shake hands with others?" He said: "Yes." Abu ʿUmar recorded this in *al-Tamhid*.

If it is said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Stand up for your master and your best," meaning Sa'd ibn Mu'adh. We say: That is specific to Sa'd because of the particular situation. It has also been said that their standing was to help him down from the donkey. Furthermore, it is permissible for an elderly man if that does not affect his soul. But if it affects him, and he is pleased with it and sees a share of himself in it, then it is not permissible to help him in that, because of the Prophet's ﷺ words: "Whoever is pleased that people should stand for him, let him take his seat in the Fire."

It is reported from the Companions, may God be pleased with them all, that there was no face more honourable to them than the face of the Messenger of God ﷺ, yet they did not stand for him when they saw him, because they knew he disliked it.

**Third issue:** If it is asked: What do you say about gesturing with the finger? The answer: That is permissible if the person is far from you, so that you may indicate to him the time of greeting. If he is near, then it is not. It has also been said that it is forbidden both near and far, because of what came from the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Whoever imitates others who are not of us is not of us." He also said: "Do not greet like the Jews and the Christians. The Jews greet with the palms and the Christians with gestures."

When one greets, he should not bow, nor kiss the hand along with the greeting. Bowing expresses humility, which is only fitting for God. As for kissing the hand, it is an action of the non-Arabs, and they are not to be followed in the actions they have invented to glorify their great ones. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not stand at my head as the non-Arabs stand before the heads of their Chosroes (akasirah)." This is similar to it.

There is no harm in shaking hands. The Prophet ﷺ shook hands with Ja'far ibn Abi Talib when he came from Abyssinia, and he commanded it and encouraged it, saying: "Shake hands, and resentment will leave." Ghalib al-Tammar reported from al-Sha'bi that the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, when they met, shook hands, and when they returned from a journey, they embraced.

[[In some manuscripts: the fourth issue. It is noted that the issues are three.]]

If it is said: Malik disliked shaking hands? We say: Ibn Wahb reported from Malik that he disliked shaking hands and embracing. Sahnun and others among our companions adopted this view. But it has also been reported from Malik the opposite, namely the permissibility of shaking hands, and this is what the meaning of what is in the *Muwatta'* indicates. Groups of scholars from the early and later generations held that shaking hands is permissible.

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: Malik only disliked shaking hands because he did not see it as a general matter in religion, nor as a practice transmitted as widely as the greeting. Had it been a Sunnah from him, it would have been equal to it.

I say: There is a hadith about shaking hands which shows encouragement to it and persistence in it and keeping to it. It is what al-Bara' ibn ʿAzib reported: "I met the Messenger of God ﷺ and he took my hands. I said: 'O Messenger of God! I used to think shaking hands was for the non-Arabs.' He said: 'We have more right to shaking hands than they do. There are no two Muslims who meet and one of them takes the hand of his companion out of affection and sincere advice, except that their sins fall away between them.'"

**Qur'an 12:100: "He has been good to me, as he brought me out of the prison."** He did not say "out of the well," using courtesy, so that he would not remind his brothers of their deed after his pardon of them, by saying: ﴿There is no reproach upon you﴾.

I say: This is the principle among the shaykhs of the Sufis: "Mentioning the harshness at the time of purity is harshness." This is a sound saying, indicated by the Book.

It has also been said: Because his entry into prison was by his own choice, through his words: ﴿My Lord, the prison is dearer to me than what they call me to﴾ [Yusuf 12:33]. But his being in the well was by God's will for him.

It has also been said: Because in prison he was with thieves and sinners, but in the well he was with God Most High. Also, the favour of deliverance from prison was greater, because he entered it on account of their command, and he also entered it by his own choice when he said: "The prison is dearer to me." So the distress in it was greater. He also said in it: ﴿Mention me to your lord﴾ [Yusuf 12:42], and for that he was punished in it.

**"And he brought you from the desert."** It is reported that Ya'qub's dwelling was in the land of Canaan, and they were people of livestock and the open country. It has also been said that Ya'qub had moved to the desert (badiyah) and settled there, and that God did not send a prophet from among the people of the desert.

It has also been said that he had gone out to Bada, which is a place, and Jamil meant it in his words:

*"You are the one who made Shaghb dear to me, toward Bada... and my homelands are other lands than these two."*

[[Shaghb: a place between Medina and Syria. Bada is reported with and without tanwin.]]

Ya'qub had a mosque at this place, under a mountain. It is said: "The people went to Bada (badw), when they came to Bada, just as it is said: 'They raided al-Ghawr (ghawran),' meaning they came to al-Ghawr." The meaning is: "And he brought you from the place of Bada." Al-Qushayri mentioned this, and al-Mawardi related it from al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas.

**"After Satan had sown discord between me and my brothers."** By provoking envy, as Ibn ʿAbbas said. It was also said: He spoiled what was between me and my brothers. He attributed their wrongdoing to Satan out of his noble courtesy.

(Inna Rabbi latifun lima yasha') — that is, gentle toward His servants. Al-Khattabi said: al-Latif is the one who is kind to His servants, who treats them with subtle care from where they do not know, and who brings about their welfare from where they do not expect, as in His saying: ﴿Allah is Gentle (Latif) with His servants; He provides for whom He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 19] [[See vol. 16, p. 16.]]. It was also said: al-Latif is the One who knows the finest details of affairs, and what is meant here is honouring and gentleness. Qatadah said: "He was gentle to Yusuf by bringing him out of the prison, bringing him his family from the desert, and removing from his heart the incitement of Satan."

It is related that when Ya'qub came with his family and offspring and approached the land of Egypt, and news of this reached Yusuf, he asked Pharaoh—whose name was al-Rayyan—for permission to go out to meet his father Ya'qub, and informed him of his arrival. He granted him permission and ordered the chiefs of his court to ride with him. Yusuf went out with the king accompanying him, with four thousand commanders, each commander with a host whom only Allah knows the number of, and the people of Egypt rode with them to meet Ya'qub. Ya'qub was walking leaning on the hand of Yahudha. Ya'qub looked at the horses, the people and the troops and said: "O Yahudha! Is this the Pharaoh of Egypt?" He said: "No, this is your son Yusuf." When each of them drew near the other, Yusuf went to greet him first with the salam, but he was prevented from doing so [[That is, Ya'qub (peace be upon him) prevented him, because the one arriving gives the salam, as stated by al-Ayni in "Iqd al-Juman". And al-Alusi said: so that it would be known that Ya'qub was more honoured by Allah than he was.]], and Ya'qub was more deserving of this and superior to him. So Ya'qub began with the salam, saying: "Peace be upon you, O remover of sorrows!" He wept and Yusuf wept with him: Ya'qub wept for joy, and Yusuf wept because of the sorrow he saw in his father. Ibn Abbas said: "Weeping is of four kinds: weeping from fear, weeping from anguish, weeping from joy, and weeping for show."

Then Ya'qub said: "Praise be to Allah, who has brought comfort to my eyes after worries and sorrows." He entered Egypt with eighty-two members of his household, and they did not leave Egypt until they numbered six hundred thousand and more, and they crossed the sea with Musa (peace be upon him). This was narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Mas'ud related that they entered Egypt as ninety-three persons, men and women, and they left with Musa as six hundred [thousand] [[From "ع" (manuscript).]] and seventy thousand. Al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham said: they entered it as seventy-two thousand, and they left with Musa as six hundred thousand. Wahb [ibn Munabbih] [[From "ع".]] said: Ya'qub and his sons entered Egypt as ninety persons, men, women and children, and they left it with Musa fleeing from Pharaoh as six hundred thousand and five hundred and some seventy fighting men, apart from the offspring, the elderly and the disabled; the offspring were one million and two hundred thousand, apart from the fighters.

The historians said: Ya'qub remained in Egypt for twenty-four years in the most prosperous condition and blessing, and he died in Egypt. He bequeathed to his son Yusuf that he should carry his body and bury it beside his father Ishaq in al-Sham, and he did so, then returned to Egypt. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Ya'qub (ﷺ) was transported in a coffin of teak to Bayt al-Maqdis, and this coincided with the day Esau died, and both were buried in one grave. From this, some Jews transport their dead to Bayt al-Maqdis, those of them who do so. Ya'qub and Esau were born in one womb, were buried in one grave, and their lifespans together were one hundred and forty-seven years [[In manuscripts ع, ك and ى: "forty-nine." The well-known figure is what is mentioned.]].

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 101:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿My Lord, You have given me of the kingdom and taught me of the interpretation (ta'wil) of events﴾. Qatadah said: No one, neither a prophet nor anyone else, wished for death except Yusuf (peace be upon him), when his blessings were complete and his affairs were gathered together, and he longed to meet his Lord, Mighty and Majestic. It has also been said that Yusuf did not wish for death itself, but rather wished to die upon Islam, meaning: when my appointed time comes, cause me to die as a Muslim. This is the view of the majority (al-jumhur). Sahl ibn Abd Allah al-Tustari said: None wishes for death except three: a man ignorant of what comes after death, or a man who flees from the decrees of Allah the Exalted upon him, or one who longs for and loves the meeting with Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

It is established in the Sahih, from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "None of you should wish for death because of a harm that has befallen him. If he must wish for it, let him say: O Allah, keep me alive as long as life is good for me, and cause me to die when death is good for me." Related by Muslim.

Also in it, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "None of you should wish for death, nor pray for it before it comes to him, for when one of you dies his deeds are cut off, and a believer's lifespan increases only in good."[[It has been said: the reason its conjunction with the negative is valid is that it has the meaning of a prohibition. Ibn Hajar said: In it there is an indication that the first is a prohibition in its proper form, and that he combined the two dialects of dropping the weak letter and retaining it.]]

Given that this is established, how can it be said that Yusuf (peace be upon him) wished for death, for leaving the world and cutting off deeds? This is far-fetched! Unless it is said that this was permissible in his law (shar'). As for the permissibility of wishing for death and supplicating for it when trials appear and overwhelm, and when there is fear for the loss of religion, this is as we have explained in the book "al-Tadhkirah".

The "min" in His words "of the kingdom" is partitive (lil-tab'id), and likewise His words "and taught me of the interpretation of events", because the kingdom of Egypt was not the whole of kingship, and the science of interpreting dreams was not the whole of all sciences. It has also been said that "min" is for genus (lil-jins), as in His words: ﴿So avoid the abomination of idols﴾ (al-Hajj: 30).[[See vol. 12, p. 54.]] It has also been said that it is for emphasis (lil-ta'akkud), meaning: You gave me the kingdom and taught me the interpretation of events.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ is in the accusative as an adjective (na't) of the vocative, which is "Rabb", and this is a construct vocative. The implied meaning is: O my Lord! It is also permissible for it to be a second vocative.

Al-Fatir means the Creator. He, glory be to Him, is the Originator of all beings, that is, their Creator, their Initiator, their Producer, and their Innovator absolutely, without any material or prior model. This meaning has already been discussed fully in "al-Baqarah", at His words: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ (al-Baqarah: 117).[[See vol. 2, p. 86 onward.]] We have also explained it further in "al-Kitab al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna".

(You are my Guardian): that is, my Helper and the one who manages my affairs in this world and the Hereafter.

(Cause me to die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous): he means his three fathers, Ibrahim, Ishaq, and Ya'qub. Allah took him, pure and good (ﷺ), in Egypt. He was buried in the Nile in a chest of marble. That was because when he died, people competed over him, each wishing to bury him in their own quarter, hoping for his blessing. They came together over this until they nearly fought. So they decided to bury him in the Nile at the point where the water divides in Egypt, so that the water would pass over him and then spread throughout all of Egypt, and they would thus all share in it. They did so. When Musa departed with the Children of Israel, he brought him out of the Nile and, after four hundred years, transported his coffin to Bayt al-Maqdis, where they buried him with his fathers, in fulfillment of his supplication: "and join me with the righteous." His age was one hundred and seven years.

It is related from al-Hasan, who said: Yusuf was thrown into the well when he was seventeen years old. He spent eighty years in slavery, in prison, and in kingship. Then his affairs were gathered together for him, and he lived after that twenty-three years. His children included Ifraithim (Ephraim), Manshah (Manasseh), and Rahmah, the wife of Ayyub, according to the view of Ibn Lahi'ah. Al-Zuhri said: Nun ibn Ifraithim was born to Ifraithim ibn Yusuf, and Yusha' was born to Nun. He is Yusha' ibn Nun, the young man of Musa who was with him, the one entrusted with his affairs. Allah granted him prophethood during the time of Musa (peace be upon him), and he became a prophet after him. He is the one who conquered Jericho (Arihá) and killed the tyrants who were there, and the sun was made to stand still for him, as previously mentioned in "al-Ma'idah".[[See vol. 6, p. 130 onward.]] Musa ibn Manshah was born to Manshah ibn Yusuf, before Musa ibn Imran. The People of the Torah (Tawrat) claim that he is the one who sought out the scholar to learn from him until he reached him, and that the scholar is the one who tore the ship, killed the boy, and built the wall, and that Musa ibn Manshah was with him until he reached what he reached. Ibn Abbas used to deny this, and the truth is what Ibn Abbas said, and so it is in the Qur'an. Then there were nations and generations between Yusuf and Musa, and among them was Shu'ayb, may the blessings of Allah and His peace be upon them all.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 102–104:

Allah's statement: ﴿That is of the news of the unseen﴾ — "that" is the subject (ibtida'), and "of the news of the unseen" is the predicate (khabar).

"We reveal it to you" is a second predicate. Al-Zajjaj said: It is also permissible that "that" (dhalika) means "the one which" (alladhi), and "We reveal it to you" is its predicate, meaning: "The one which is of the news of the unseen, We reveal it to you." That is, it is what We have related to you, O Muhammad, of the matter of Yusuf, from the reports of the unseen. "We reveal it to you" means: We teach you by revealing this to you.

"And you were not with them" — that is, with the brothers of Yusuf — "when they agreed upon their plan" — concerning casting Yusuf into the well.

"While they were scheming" — that is, scheming against Yusuf in casting him into the well. It was also said: "they were scheming" against Ya'qub when they brought him the shirt stained with blood. That is, you did not witness those circumstances, but Allah informed you of them.

Allah's statement: ﴿And most people, even if you strive eagerly, will not be believers﴾ — It is thought that when the Arabs asked him about this story and he informed them, they would believe, but they did not believe, so the verse was revealed as consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ). That is: you are not able to guide whomever you wish to guide. You say: ḥaraṣa yaḥraṣu, like ḍaraba yaḍribu. In a weak dialect: ḥariṣa yaḥraṣu, like ḥamida yaḥmadu. Al-ḥirṣ (eagerness) is seeking a thing by choice. [[Al-Raghib said in Mufradat al-Qur'an: al-ḥirṣ is excessive greed and excessive desire.]]

Allah's statement: ﴿And you do not ask them for any payment for it﴾ — "min" here is extra (ṣila), meaning: you do not ask them for a reward.

"It is not" — that is, it (what is) is the Qur'an and the revelation.

"Except a reminder" — that is, an admonition and a reminder "to the worlds."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 102–104:

Allah's statement: ﴿That is of the news of the unseen﴾ — "that" is the subject (ibtida'), and "of the news of the unseen" is the predicate (khabar).

"We reveal it to you" is a second predicate. Al-Zajjaj said: It is also permissible that "that" (dhalika) means "the one which" (alladhi), and "We reveal it to you" is its predicate, meaning: "The one which is of the news of the unseen, We reveal it to you." That is, it is what We have related to you, O Muhammad, of the matter of Yusuf, from the reports of the unseen. "We reveal it to you" means: We teach you by revealing this to you.

"And you were not with them" — that is, with the brothers of Yusuf — "when they agreed upon their plan" — concerning casting Yusuf into the well.

"While they were scheming" — that is, scheming against Yusuf in casting him into the well. It was also said: "they were scheming" against Ya'qub when they brought him the shirt stained with blood. That is, you did not witness those circumstances, but Allah informed you of them.

Allah's statement: ﴿And most people, even if you strive eagerly, will not be believers﴾ — It is thought that when the Arabs asked him about this story and he informed them, they would believe, but they did not believe, so the verse was revealed as consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ). That is: you are not able to guide whomever you wish to guide. You say: ḥaraṣa yaḥraṣu, like ḍaraba yaḍribu. In a weak dialect: ḥariṣa yaḥraṣu, like ḥamida yaḥmadu.
