The Almighty's words: ﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth do they pass by, turning away from it?﴾ Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: "ay" (how many) is combined with the particle of comparison (the kaf of tashbih), and it became a compound with it, so that the meaning in the speech is "kam" (how many). The discussion of this has been fully covered in "Al 'Imran" (see vol. 4, p. 228 onward). The discussion of "the signs in the heavens and the earth" has been covered in "al-Baqarah" (see vol. 2, p. 192 onward). It has also been said that the signs are the traces of the punishments of the past nations, meaning: they are heedless and turn away from reflecting on them.

Ikrimah and Amr ibn Fa'id read "wal-ard" (and the earth) in the nominative as a mubtada' (subject), with its khabar (predicate) being ﴿they pass by it﴾. Al-Suddi read it in the accusative, by implying a verb, and the pause on both of these readings falls on "al-samawat" (the heavens). Ibn Mas'ud read: "yamshuna 'alayha" (they walk upon it).

The Almighty's words: ﴿And most of them do not believe in God except that they associate others with Him.﴾ It was revealed concerning a people who acknowledged God as their Creator and the Creator of all things, yet they worshipped idols. This was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, Amir al-Sha'bi, and most of the exegetes. Ikrimah said it refers to His words: ﴿And if you ask them who created them, they will surely say, "God"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 87], then they describe Him by other than His attributes and set up rivals to Him. Also from al-Hasan: they are People of the Book who have both shirk and faith; they believed in God and disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ), so their faith is not valid. This was related by Ibn al-Anbari. Ibn Abbas said: it was revealed concerning the talbiyah of the pagans of the Arabs: "Here I am, O God, no partner have You, except a partner who is Yours; You possess him and what he possesses." Also from him: they are the Christians. Also from him: they are the mushabbihah (anthropomorphists), who believed in a general way and associated partners in a detailed way. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and the meaning is: ﴿And most of them do not believe in God﴾, that is, with the tongue, ﴿except that they are disbelievers in their hearts.﴾ This was mentioned by al-Mawardi from al-Hasan as well. Ata' said: this is about supplication, because the disbelievers forget their Lord in ease, but when affliction befalls them they become sincere in supplication. Its illustration is His words: ﴿and they thought they were encompassed﴾ [Yunus: 22], to the end of the verse, and His words: ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side﴾ [Yunus: 12], to the end of the verse. In another verse: ﴿And when evil touches him, he has long supplication﴾ [Fussilat: 51]. It has also been said: the meaning is that they call upon God to save them from destruction, but when He saves them, one of them says: "Had it not been for so-and-so, we would not have been saved," and "Had it not been for the dog, a thief would have entered upon us," and similar things, thereby attributing God's blessing to so-and-so and attributing His protection to the dog. I say: many of the common folk of the Muslims fall into this statement and the one before it. There is no power nor strength except with God, the Most High, the Mighty.

It has also been said: this verse was revealed concerning the story of the smoke. When the people of Makkah were overcome by the smoke in the years of drought, they said: ﴿Our Lord, remove from us the punishment; indeed, we are believers﴾ [al-Dukhan: 12]. That was their faith, and their shirk was their return to disbelief after the punishment was removed. Its illustration is His words: ﴿Indeed, you will return [to disbelief]﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15]. Return can only occur after a beginning, so the meaning of "except that they are polytheists" is "except that they are returning [to shirk]." And God knows best.

The Almighty's words: ﴿Then do they feel secure that an overwhelming punishment from God will not overtake them?﴾

Ibn Abbas said: "mujallalah" (all-encompassing). Mujahid said: a punishment that covers them; its parallel is His words: ﴿On the Day when the punishment will cover them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 55]. Qatadah said: a calamity that befalls them. Al-Dahhak said: it means the thunderbolts and the catastrophes.

(Or that the Hour will not come upon them) meaning the Resurrection.

(Suddenly) is in the accusative as a hal (circumstantial state), and its origin is the verbal noun. Al-Mubarrad said: a hal after an indefinite noun has come from the Arabs, and that is their saying: "An affair occurred bagh'tatan and fajatan (suddenly)." Al-Nahhas said: the meaning of "baghtatan" is an affliction that strikes from where one did not expect.

(While they are unaware) is an emphasis (tawkid). Regarding His words "baghtatan," Ibn Abbas said: the cry will be shouted at the people while they are in their markets and places, as He said: ﴿It will seize them while they are disputing﴾ [Ya-Sin: 49], as will come later.

The Almighty's words: ﴿Say: This is my way.﴾ It is a mubtada' and khabar: that is, say, O Muhammad, "This is my path, my sunnah, and my method." This was said by Ibn Zayd. Al-Rabi' said: it is my call. Muqatil said: it is my religion. The meaning is one, that is, what I am upon and what I call to leads to Paradise.

(Upon insight) means upon certainty and truth, and from this one says: "So-and-so is mustabsir (clear-sighted) in this matter."

(I) is an emphasis.

(And whoever follows me) is a conjunction ('atf) upon the pronoun (the hidden pronoun in the verb, being connected).

(And glory be to God) meaning: say, O Muhammad, "Glory be to God."

(And I am not of the polytheists) who take rivals besides God.

(And whoever follows me) is a conjunction ('atf) upon the pronoun (the hidden pronoun in the verb, being connected).

(And glory be to God) meaning: say, O Muhammad, "Glory be to God."

(And I am not of the polytheists) who take rivals besides God.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 109–110:

His saying, exalted is He: (And We sent not before you [any messengers] except men to whom We revealed [[The recitation of Nafi' and the majority is: yuha, in the passive voice.]] from among the people of the cities). This is a refutation of those who said: ﴿Why was not an angel sent down to him?﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 393.]] [al-An'am: 8], meaning: We sent men among whom there was no woman, no jinn, and no angel. This also refutes what is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Among women there are four prophetesses: Hawwa', Asiya, the mother of Musa, and Maryam." Something of this has already been discussed in "Al 'Imran" [[See vol. 4, p. 82 onward, and vol. 6, p. 251.]]. "From the people of the cities" means the towns. God did not send a prophet from the people of the desert (badiyah), because harshness and coarseness prevail among the people of the desert, and because the people of the cities are more intelligent, more forbearing, more virtuous, and more knowledgeable. Al-Hasan said: God never sent a prophet from the people of the desert, nor from women, nor from the jinn. Qatadah said: "From the people of the cities" means from the people of the metropolitan centres (amsar), because they are more knowledgeable and more forbearing. The scholars said: it is a condition of the Messenger that he be a human male (rajulan adamiyyan madaniyyan), and they said "human" as a safeguard against His saying: ﴿Some men from the jinn used to seek refuge with men from the jinn﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 8 onward.]] [al-Jinn: 6]. And God knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have they not travelled in the land and seen﴾ the end of the peoples who denied their prophets, so that they might take heed.

(And the abode of the Hereafter is better) is a mubtada' (subject) and its khabar (predicate). Al-Farra' claimed that "the abode" is the Hereafter itself, and that the noun was idafa'd to itself because of the difference in wording, as in "yawm al-Khamis" and "barihat al-Ula". The poet said:

"Even if the dwellings of 'Abs had become desolate for you... you would recognise humiliation with the recognition of certainty"

meaning, certain recognition. Al-Kisa'i argued from their saying: "salat al-Ula", and al-Akhfash argued from "masjid al-Jami'". Al-Nahhas said: the idafa of a thing to itself is impossible, because a thing is only idafa'd to something other than itself in order to be defined by it; the better reading is "al-salat al-Ula", and whoever says "salat al-Ula" means: at the time of the first obligatory prayer; it was called "al-Ula" because it was the first prayer performed when prayer was made obligatory, and the first to be made manifest, and for this reason it is also called "al-Zuhr". The estimated meaning is: "wa-la-dar al-hal al-akhirah khayr" (the abode of the state of the Hereafter is better). This is the view of the Basrans. The "abode" here is intended to mean Paradise, i.e., it is better for the righteous. It has been recited as "wa-lal-dar al-akhirah". Nafi', 'Asim, Ya'qub and others read (afala ta'qilun) with the ta' as address; the rest read it with the ya' as a report.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when the messengers despaired﴾ — its recitation and meaning have already been mentioned [[See p. 241 of this part.]].

(And they thought that they had been denied): this verse contains the declaration of the prophets' purity and their infallibility from what is not fitting for them. This subject is great, and its danger is immense; it is necessary to pause over it, lest a person slip and end up in the depths of Hell. The meaning: We sent before you, O Muhammad, only men, then We did not punish their peoples with torment [[From manuscripts ‘ayn and ha' and the Jumal's citation from al-Qurtubi. In others: bil-'iqab.]]. "Until, when the messengers despaired," meaning they gave up hope of their people's faith. "And they thought that they had been denied," with the shaddah (kudhdhibu), meaning they became certain that their people had denied them. It has also been said the meaning is: they supposed that those among their people who believed in them had denied them, not that the people had denied; rather the prophets thought and supposed that they (the believers) would deny them, i.e., they feared that doubt would enter the hearts of their followers, so "wa-zannu" retains its ordinary sense on this interpretation. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa', al-Hasan, Qatadah, Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Yahya ibn Wuthab, al-A'mash and Khalaf read "kudhibu" with the light form (takhfif), meaning the people thought that the messengers had lied to them about the punishment they had announced, and that they had not been truthful. It has also been said: the meaning is that the nations thought the messengers had lied in what they promised them of victory. In a report from Ibn 'Abbas: the messengers thought that God had broken what He had promised them. It has been said that this report is not sound, because such a thought cannot be attributed to the messengers, and one who entertains such a thought does not deserve victory, so how could He say: (Our help came to them)?! Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: if the report is sound, it is not far-fetched that what is meant is that such a thought passed through the hearts of the messengers without their confirming it in their souls (from ‘ayn; this is the correct reading, while in others it is "al-bashar"). In a hadith: "God, exalted is He, has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper, so long as they do not speak it with the tongue or act upon it." It is also permissible to say they came close to that supposition, as in your saying: "I reached the dwelling," meaning I drew near to it. Al-Tha'labi and al-Nahhas mention from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: they were human, and they grew weak from the length of the trial, and forgot, and thought they had been let down. Then he recited: ﴿Until the Messenger and those who believed with him say: When will the help of God come?﴾ [[See vol. 3, p. 33 onward, and p. 273.]] [al-Baqarah: 214]. Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim said: its explanation for us is that the messengers feared, after God had promised victory, not out of any doubt in God's promise, but out of suspicion in their own souls that they may have produced some occurrence that breaks that condition and covenant which had been entrusted to them; so when the period grew long, despair and misgivings entered them from this direction. Al-Mahdawi related from Ibn 'Abbas: the messengers thought that they had been let down, in the manner that befalls human beings, and he cited the saying of Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾ [[See vol. 3, p. 33 onward, and p. 273.]] [al-Baqarah: 260], and so on. The first recitation is preferable. Mujahid and Humayd read "qad kadhabu" with a fatha on the kaf and dhal, lightened, meaning: the people of the messengers thought that the messengers had lied, because of what they saw of God's, exalted and majestic is He, grace in delaying the punishment. It is also possible that the meaning is: and when the messengers became certain that their people had lied against God by their disbelief, Our help came to the messengers. In al-Bukhari, from 'Urwah, from 'A'ishah: he asked her about the saying of God, mighty and majestic is He: "Until, when the messengers despaired," and said: I asked: Were they denied, or did they deny? She said: They were denied. I said: Then they were certain that their people had denied them, so is it not conjecture? She said: Indeed, by my life, they were certain of that. I said to her: "And they thought that they had been denied." She said: God forbid! The messengers did not think such a thing about their Lord. I said: Then what is this verse? She said: They are the followers of the messengers who believed in their Lord and affirmed them; the trial lengthened for them, and the help was delayed from them, until, when the messengers despaired of those among their people who denied them, and the messengers thought that their followers had denied them, Our help came to them at that time. [[The addition is from Sahih al-Bukhari.]] [[From ‘ayn.]]

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: "Our help came to them" there are two views: the first is that the help of God came to the messengers, said by Mujahid; the second is that the punishment of God came to their people, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

(So whom We will is delivered [[The recitation of Nafi' and likewise the rest of the seven is with two nuns, except 'Asim, as will come.]]). It has been said: the prophets and those who believed with them. It is narrated from 'Asim: "fa-nujjiya man nasha'" with a single nun and the yā' vowelled with fatha, and "man" in the nominative position, as the substitute for the unnamed agent; Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading because it is so written in the Uthmanic codex and in all the codices of the regions with a single nun [[Meaning in the orthography.]]. Ibn Muhaysin read "fa-naja," as a past verb, and "man" in the nominative position because it is the subject; according to the reading of the others, it is in the accusative as the object.

(And Our punishment is not turned back) meaning Our torment.

(From the guilty people) meaning the disbelieving polytheists.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 111:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly there was in their stories﴾, meaning in the story of Yusuf, his father, and his brothers, or in the stories of the earlier nations.

(a lesson) meaning a reflection, a reminder, and an admonition.

(for people of understanding) meaning, of intellects. Muhammad ibn Ishaq related from al-Zuhri, from Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Harith al-Taymi: Ya'qub lived one hundred and forty-seven years, and his brother Esau died with him on one day, and they were buried in one grave. That is His saying: "Certainly there was in their stories a lesson for people of understanding," to the end of the surah.

(It was not a narration that could be invented) meaning, the Qur'an was not a narration that could be invented, or this story was not a narration that could be invented.

(But it is a confirmation of what was before it) meaning [but there was [[from ʿ and k.]] confirmation; it is also permissible to read it in the nominative, meaning "but it is a confirmation of what was before it," i.e. what came before it of the Torah, the Gospel, and the rest of God's books. This is the interpretation of those who claim that "what was before it" refers to the Qur'an.

(and a detailed explanation of everything) of what the servants need, of the lawful and the unlawful, and of the laws and rulings.

(and a guidance and a mercy for a people who believe).
